articles.title: US Agencies Urge Organizations to Harden Refrigeration Controllers
articles.context: A second wave of attacks hit more than 100 supermarkets and a blood bank this week, but only supermarkets suffered losses
articles.full_text:
The US government is urging healthcare, chemical, food, and transportation organizations to harden their industrial refrigeration and cold chain monitoring systems.

Over the past weeks, threat actors have been hacking monitoring systems to tamper with fridges and freezers in supermarkets and blood banks across Europe, causing millions in losses.

Hundreds of supermarkets were hit on October 11, when the attackers turned the temperatures in fridges to 50 degrees Celsius (122 degrees Fahrenheit) and set freezers to defrost, spoiling food and, in some cases, causing fires.

A second wave of attacks hit more than 100 supermarkets and a blood bank this week, but only supermarkets suffered losses. Quick action from staff prevented the compromise of blood products and samples, the French Blood Establishment (EFS) said.

Russian hacktivist groups such as Noname057(16) and Z-Pentest Alliance reportedly claimed hacking Danfoss, leading to speculation that they mounted the supermarket attacks. However, nothing has been confirmed, and Iranian hacktivists or state-sponsored hackers may also be responsible, BBC notes.

CISA, the FBI, HHS, USDA, and DoT say they “are aware of malicious cyber actors targeting electronic temperature controllers and commercial refrigeration controllers in retail grocery and cold storage facilities.”

Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

“The actors may exploit vulnerabilities or weaknesses in unpatched or internet-accessible controllers to remotely alter settings and force units into continuous heating and defrost cycles, which can cause widespread inventory loss and equipment hazards,” the agencies note (PDF).

Hackers may exploit authentication bypasses, code injection, and weak configurations to access the management systems and tamper with refrigerator and cold storage systems’ temperature or cause denial-of-view conditions, the agencies say.

According to internet intelligence firm Censys, out of 6,695 internet-exposed refrigeration controllers identified on October 9, only 3,124 (or 47%) remain accessible from the web as of November 5.

The company’s analysis covers the widely used Copeland/Dixell XWEB and Danfoss StoreView controllers: XWEB exposure dropped 35% (3,708 to 2,420), while StoreView dropped 76% (3,004 to 708).

Per the US government’s recommendations, taking the control systems off the internet is the best action organizations can take to prevent attacks. If web access is necessary, these systems should be protected by a firewall or edge device.

Organizations should also isolate OT devices, restrict access to trusted identities, enforce strong password policies and phishing-resistant multifactor authentication, keep systems updated, maintain backups offsite, and enable logging and monitoring.

articles.title: ARTEX Offensive AI Tool Activity Far Exceeds Reported Campaigns, Censys Finds
articles.context: The use of a new AI-powered offensive security tool by cyber threat actors appears to be spreading well beyond the campaigns first identified
articles.full_text:
The use of a new AI-powered offensive security tool by cyber threat actors appears to be spreading well beyond the campaigns first identified.

This tool, called ARTEX, is an open-source, AI model-driven, autonomous penetration testing framework released on GitHub by a user known as ‘Autumn-27’ in July 2026.

While ARTEX has already been integrated in several known malicious campaigns since October, a new report by internet traffic scan provider Censys estimated its use could be much more widespread than previously thought.

ARTEX's Growing Use by Cyber Threat Actors

Written in Go with an embedded Next.js web console, ARTEX offers an offensive command-and-control (C2) platform that communicates with several AI agents and can be plugged in to large language models (LLMs).

In October, two threat intelligence companies attributed its use as part of threat actor operations.

First, in early October, CrowdStrike linked ARTEX to a campaign against South Korean financial institutions. The analysts found ARTEX was used alongside Anthropic’s Claude AI model during the campaign, which ran from late September to early October 2026. CrowdStrike assessed with moderate confidence that the attacker is a Chinese speaker and financially motivated.

Later in October, Microsoft linked ARTEX to a large-scale compromise of ConnectWise customer tenants which led to IT management software provider taking a number of its cloud services offline. Microsoft attributed the campaign to Storm-0940, a China-state-aligned cyber threat actor also known as CovertNetwork-1658 or ORB07.

More recently, on November 4, the Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) warned financial and cryptocurrency organizations that a threat group tracked as ‘Crafty Falcon’ had been targeting them in successive attacks using several AI-powered tools, including ARTEX.

The original GitHub repository for ARTEX was taken down by its creator in October 2026 due to widespread threat actor abuse. The author claimed they were not involved in the ARTEX-linked attacks and that the tool was only meant for authorized penetration testing.

Nevertheless, the framework continues to proliferate globally via community forks, including localized variations such as ScopeWeaver and a commercial version dubbed ARTEX PRO.

In a separate report, Check Point researchers showed AI agents in ARTEX control panels are running large-scale attacks with little human input for just a few hundred dollars, though they still fail and hallucinate successes.

Censys Uncovers ARTEX's Global Footprint

A report published on November 5 by Silas Cutler, principal security researcher at Censys Advanced Research Collective (ARC), has provided further insights into ARTEX's use and the infrastructure surrounding it.

The researcher found that 1465 hosts worldwide are exposing an ARTEX console to the public internet. About 650 of these hosts sit within two blocks of identically configured hosting, leaving roughly 815 distinct-looking deployments.

This suggests that ARTEX is not simply appearing on a handful of isolated systems, but across hundreds of seemingly distinct deployments worldwide, indicating a much broader footprint than initially reported.

Additionally, Censys telemetry showed that 155 internet-exposed ARTEX hosts (10.6%) also run at least one other artefact categorized by Censys as a threat.

These include other AI attack frameworks, reconnaissance platforms, tunneling tools and traditional malicious command-and-control (C2) servers such as Vshell, Cobalt Strike and Adaptix C2.

An asset-discovery and vulnerability-scanning platform dubbed ScopeSentry, which is maintained by the creator of ARTEX, is also listed by Censys as a threat artefact.

The researchers also found ARTEX sharing infrastructure with other popular AI-powered penetration-testing tools, including CyberStrikeAI, PentAGI, HexStrike AI and RedAmon. CyberStrikeAI, in particular, appeared alongside ARTEX on 70 hosts.

"Operators appear to be using multiple agent frameworks side by side," Cutler suggested.

articles.title: Grocery Giant Ahold Delhaize Estimates Financial Toll of October Cyberattack
articles.context: Dutch-Belgian grocery giant Ahold Delhaize estimates that last month’s cyberattack, which disrupted operations in the US and the Benelux, will wipe €200 million to €250 million...
articles.full_text:
Dutch-Belgian grocery giant Ahold Delhaize estimates that last month’s cyberattack, which disrupted operations in the US and the Benelux, will wipe €200 million to €250 million ($224 million to $280 million) off its fourth-quarter net sales.

The company, whose brands include Albert Heijn, Delhaize, Food Lion and Hannaford, published the estimate this week with its third-quarter results. The attack occurred after the quarter had closed.

The cybersecurity incident is also expected to cost Ahold Delhaize €75 million to €100 million ($84 million to $112 million) in fourth-quarter underlying and IFRS operating income. On top of that, the company faces incident response and remediation expenses, but believes these will have little effect on its IFRS operating income for 2026.

As a result, the retailer has revised its 2026 guidance downward. It now projects diluted underlying earnings per share, at constant exchange rates, to grow in the low single digits, rather than in the mid to high single digits it had previously forecast.

Free cash flow is now expected to reach around €2.1 billion ($2.36 billion), down from at least €2.3 billion ($2.58 billion). Ahold Delhaize attributes the reduction to the cyberattack and to newly introduced Serbian rules governing payments to suppliers.

The company first reported the incident in mid-October, announcing that it had disconnected some systems after detecting a security issue on its network. On October 19, it confirmed it had been hit by a cyberattack and said it had no evidence at the time that customer, associate or partner data had been stolen.

Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

“As part of our protocols to assess and mitigate cybersecurity incidents, we took some systems offline to help protect our IT environment. To differing degrees, this mainly affected our online capabilities in the Benelux and the U.S., as well as our Benelux supply-chain operations,” Frans Muller, Ahold Delhaize’s president and CEO, said in a statement accompanying the latest financial report.

“While most of the disruption was contained within two weeks, work continues to fully restore our normal operations,” he said.

Ahold Delhaize has yet to disclose what type of attack it experienced.

“While the cybersecurity incident has, understandably, demanded significant attention, it is important that we keep it in perspective. Our response demonstrates the resilience of our business; the incident does not define our business,” Muller said.

This is not the first time the company’s systems have been targeted. In November 2024, a ransomware attack disrupted several of its US brands, including Hannaford supermarkets and Giant Food pharmacies. The INC Ransom group claimed responsibility, and Ahold Delhaize later disclosed that the personal information of more than 2.2 million people had been compromised.

articles.title: D-Link warns of multiple zero-days in DGS-3130 Series switches
articles.context: Successful exploitation could allow attackers to obtain sensitive device data, make unauthorized credential/configuration changes, leak SNMP communities, or cause service...
articles.full_text:
D-Link shared mitigation measures for multiple unpatched security flaws affecting DGS-3130 series managed Gigabit stackable switches.

These switch models provide multi-gigabit uplinks, allowing enterprise network administrators to eliminate data bottlenecks, and are designed primarily for small-to-medium businesses (SMBs) and metro Ethernet deployments.

While D-Link didn't share details on these flaws and has yet to publicly disclose the CVE IDs for easier tracking, it said Spectrum Community Solutions network engineer Giresh Kumar Enugu found the bugs in the D-Link Discovery Protocol (DDP) authentication, access control, and information handling.

Successful exploitation could allow attackers to obtain sensitive device data, make unauthorized credential/configuration changes, leak SNMP communities, or cause service disruptions and device resets.

The zero-days affect multiple DGS-3130-30TS firmware versions, and the company is still investigating the impact on other D-Link switching platforms and firmware security mechanisms (including SSH service security configuration, safeguards underlying operating-system credentials, and handles firmware encryption/embedded cryptographic keys).

"The reported vulnerabilities involve the D-Link Discovery Protocol (DDP) and certain components of the device's firmware security architecture," D-Link said.

"According to the security researcher, successful exploitation of certain vulnerabilities may allow an attacker with access to the affected network to obtain sensitive device information, perform unauthorized administrative operations, modify device configuration, or disrupt network services."

Until it releases new firmware to address these flaws, D-Link asked admins to disable DDP to remove the primary known attack vector, remove unnecessary or default SNMP community strings, and restrict SSH, web UI, and SNMP accessibility solely to isolated management networks and designated admin hosts.

D-Link also advised admins to maintain offline switch configuration backups and track device logs for unexpected configuration changes, unprompted reboots, or factory resets.

In September, D-Link warned customers of a maximum-severity zero-day (tracked as CVE-2026-86296) with a public proof-of-concept (PoC) exploit and no patch, affecting legacy DIR-822A dual-band Wi-Fi routers.

articles.title: OpenSSH Rushes Patches for ‘SSHole’ Authentication Bypass
articles.context: Only some of those run Alpine, but each attempt is a single connection, so an attacker can afford to try all of them,” Detectify co-founder and principal security researcher...
articles.full_text:
OpenSSH has rolled out emergency patches for a high-severity authentication bypass that allows attackers to log in using very long passwords.

Dubbed SSHole and tracked as CVE-2026-123158 (CVSS score of 8.1), the security defect affects the OpenSSH server (sshd) on Linux distributions that use the musl libc implementation with the Pluggable Authentication Module (PAM) disabled.

A “misinterpretation of whether a string is intended to be a password hash” allows attackers to access certain accounts using any password that has between 257 and 1,024 characters.

Some accounts, such as root, should never accept a password, but in Linux distributions such as Alpine, OpenWrt, Buildroot, Yocto, and others, they do, Wakefield security researcher Özgün Kültekin says.

According to OpenSSH developer Damien Miller, the flaw is not in sshd itself, but can be exploited via sshd. Fixes were included in OpenSSH 10.6p2.

“We are making this release as fast as possible (we learned of the problem yesterday) because we have recently observed multiple cases of rapid bug rediscovery by AI agents, sometimes within hours, and so now consider long embargo periods to be a dangerous practice that primarily benefits attackers,” Miller said.

Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

On Thursday, Alpine Linux urged users to immediately apply the OpenSSH patches and restart sshd to replace the running daemon, or disable password logins and restart sshd.

“The attacker needs the name of an account whose password field is * (an account with no password set, which is normal for key-only accounts), and needs the machine to have at least one other account with a $5$ or $6$ password hash,” Alpine Linux warns.

Since version 3.16, Alpine Linux uses “*” to secure the root account, and $5$ or $6$ in password hashes show whether the SHA-256 or SHA-512 crypt was used.

“An attacker who can reach your SSH port can log in without knowing any password. It takes one connection, works every time, and needs no retries,” Alpine Linux notes.

Affected Alpine Linux deployments run OpenSSH without PAM, have password authentication enabled, have an account with the password field “*” (such as root, a key-only user created with adduser without a password, the alpine user in the official tiny-cloud images, or a user coming from a directory service through musl-nscd), and have at least one local account with a $5$ or $6$ password hash.

“Affected releases: every Alpine release we checked, 3.21 through 3.24 and edge, and the older releases that no longer receive regular updates (3.16 to 3.20),” Alpine Linux says.

“We haven’t seen any reports of exploitation yet, but the details are public, and the attack is simple, so I expect scanning to start within hours. Finding targets is very easy. Shodan lists around 22 million systems with SSH open on port 22, and the real number is higher because Shodan doesn’t see everything. Only some of those run Alpine, but each attempt is a single connection, so an attacker can afford to try all of them,” Detectify co-founder and principal security researcher Fredrik Almroth said.

“We’d be extremely surprised if we didn’t see SSH brute-forcers attempting this by the weekend. It’s virtually free to try and an easy win if it works. If your organization is affected, update to the latest version where possible, and disable password-based authentication as a temporary mitigation if you can’t,” WatchTowr head of threat intelligence Jake Knott said.

articles.title: Microsoft Paint RCE Fix Now Available, but Windows Update Won't Deliver It
articles.context: Attack Conditions and Exploitation Status An attacker could exploit the flaw by sending "a specially crafted packet to an affected service over the network," the advisory says,...
articles.full_text:
A fix for CVE-2026-83844, a remote code execution flaw in Windows Paint, is now in the Microsoft Store. Paint gets this fix only through a Store update, not through Windows updates.

The fixed build, 11.2609.401.0, was the newest Paint build in all ten countries The Hacker News checked today.

The flaw is an out-of-bounds read that could let an attacker run code over a network. Microsoft rates it as Important, with a CVSS score of 8.1, and says that a successful attack requires a deep understanding of the target system. The flaw was not known to be exploited or publicly disclosed when the company published it on October 13.

Brian Vitko of RFF, a device-management software maker, checked which Paint builds the Store offered in six countries earlier this week. He found that the newest in each was 11.2605.81.0, a build without the fix.

His test virtual machine has since moved to the fixed build on its own, through Store auto-update. That is one machine, and how quickly other PCs will get the build is not yet clear.

Which Build Counts as Fixed

Microsoft's security advisory names 11.2609.401.0 as the fixed build. The CVE record for the flaw, which the company also publishes, still lists Paint as affected only below 11.2605.91.0. Its NVD entry shows the same range.

So a scanner that reads the CVE record would treat any build from 11.2605.91.0 up as fixed. A copy at 11.2609.401.0 or later passes under both numbers.

As recently as last week, the advisory gave 11.2605.91.0 as the fixed build, according to a forum question on Microsoft Q&A. The advisory's revision history still shows only its October 13 entry, with no note about the change.

How to Check Every Copy of Paint

Paint, like other Store apps, is installed separately for each user account on a PC. Windows can also keep a provisioned copy that it installs for each new user. A check of only the signed-in account can miss older copies.

Vitko's test write-up gives two commands to run in a PowerShell window opened as administrator. The first lists every user's copy of Paint, and the second lists the provisioned copy.

Get-AppxPackage -AllUsers -Name Microsoft.Paint | Select-Object Version, @{ n = 'Users'; e = { $_.PackageUserInformation.UserSecurityId.Username -join ', ' } }

Get-AppxProvisionedPackage -Online | Where-Object DisplayName -eq 'Microsoft.Paint' | Select-Object Version

For any copy below 11.2609.401.0:

Update Paint through the Store, or let the Store auto-update install the fixed build. In Intune and other device-management tools, the Store app update scan does this across many PCs.

Run both commands again and check that every copy shows 11.2609.401.0 or later.

The advisory lists no workaround or mitigation. Before the fix reached the Store, Vitko suggested removing Paint where nobody needs it, for every user and from the provisioned copy. He did not test that step.

Attack Conditions and Exploitation Status

An attacker could exploit the flaw by sending "a specially crafted packet to an affected service over the network," the advisory says, but it does not name the service. The attack would require no sign-in and no user assistance.

The flaw was not in the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog run by the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency when The Hacker News checked today. The catalog was last updated earlier this week.

articles.title: Malicious Browser Extensions Could Use Claude Dispatch to Run Code on Users' Computers
articles.context: The attack needs Dispatch, a Claude feature that lets people send tasks from their phone to Claude Desktop
articles.full_text:
A browser extension that can run scripts on claude.ai could make Claude Desktop run code on a person's computer, researchers at Forever Security, an endpoint security company, showed in a test.

The attack needs Dispatch, a Claude feature that lets people send tasks from their phone to Claude Desktop. The flaw that makes this possible can still be exploited, the researchers said earlier this week.

Claude Desktop is an AI agent that can run commands on the computer where it is installed. The researchers found that Dispatch also accepted an ordinary signed-in session on claude.ai, the Claude website, even though the site showed no link to it. That let an extension running on the site send Claude Desktop instructions as if the user had sent them.

The researchers say Anthropic, the company that makes Claude, told them on October 13 that Dispatch would be retired, with the end of October as the target. The Dispatch help page, last updated late last week, does not mention a retirement.

It says Dispatch is closed to new users and that people who already use it on some Pro, Max, and Ultra plans "can keep using it for now."

How the Attack Worked

The attack needs two things, according to a technical write-up by Forever Security researcher Gal Weizman: an extension that can run scripts on claude.ai, and a person signed in to both claude.ai and Claude Desktop with Dispatch turned on.

The extension could be malicious, a legitimate one that received a compromised update, or a legitimate one with a security flaw. Dispatch itself only works while the computer is awake and the desktop app is open.

In the test, a script on the user's claude.ai page opened Dispatch and sent Claude four prompts as if it were the user. The prompts asked Claude to install an npm package.

Claude first hesitated over the unfamiliar package, but a follow-up message, delivered in the user's voice, got it to go ahead.

Claude asks before it acts, but those approval prompts appeared in the web page the extension controlled. The script clicked any "Allow" button every second, so no one had to be watching.

Claude then ran a global npm install, and the package's install script opened the Calculator app. No browser exploit was needed. The same step could have stolen files or installed a backdoor, given Claude's permissions on the computer, the researchers say.

The test was run with the browser and Claude Desktop on the same computer, and the researchers report no real attacks. Because Dispatch connects devices, the extension could also reach Claude Desktop on a different computer signed in to the same Claude account, they say. That case is described but not shown.

The same reach could link a home computer to a work laptop when someone uses a single personal Claude account on both devices, with Dispatch turned on. The researchers have seen personal Claude accounts with cross-device Dispatch turned on, on work computers at their customers.

The researchers reported the flaw to Anthropic on May 14. The company accepted it as valid on May 19 but closed the report as a duplicate of an issue it had already found internally, according to the researchers.

"Anthropic is retiring Dispatch, but not the design behind it," the researchers wrote, adding that two other Claude features, Claude Code Remote Control and Claude Cowork sessions, let extensions carry out the same attack. Their write-up does not include a test of those features, and they plan a follow-up post.

What Dispatch Users Can Do

In Claude Desktop, Dispatch is part of Cowork and appears in the left-side panel. The Dispatch help page says users should know how to quickly disconnect or revoke access before turning the feature on, but it does not explain how.

The researchers recommend these steps:

Turn off cross-device Dispatch if you do not need it. If you do need it, review how devices are paired, approved, and removed.

Treat browser extensions like other software on the computer: check their permissions, control what gets installed, and review updates that give them more access.

Monitor what AI agents do on the computer, including unexpected package installations, setting changes, access to credentials, and external connections.

articles.title: Attacks on supermarket and blood storage systems prompt US warning
articles.context: On October 13, after the first attacks in France, refrigeration supplier Danfoss advised its Dutch customers to disconnect their systems from the public internet and reconnect...
articles.full_text:
Attackers don’t have to steal information to cause serious harm. Sometimes, changing a temperature setting is enough.

On November 5, the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), and three other federal agencies issued a warning urging operators to secure industrial refrigeration and cold-chain monitoring systems.

The warning follows cyberattacks on supermarket refrigeration systems across Europe. Separately, France’s national blood service confirmed that the monitoring and control systems at three of its cold-storage sites had been affected. Staff intervened before any blood products or samples were compromised. The incident showed how a connected cooling system can put essential supplies at risk.

On October 13, after the first attacks in France, refrigeration supplier Danfoss advised its Dutch customers to disconnect their systems from the public internet and reconnect only through a secure network.

A Danfoss spokesperson told NOS that most stores followed the advice. When similar attacks reached the Netherlands on November 2, major supermarket chains were reportedly unaffected. At least 17 businesses, mainly butcher shops and small neighborhood stores, had their refrigeration systems compromised.

Danfoss said that the affected systems were still accessible through unsecured connections and used default passwords. The spokesperson said the attacks could have been prevented if the recommended precautions had been taken.

CISA and its partners warned that attackers may exploit authentication bypass flaws, code-injection vulnerabilities, or weak configurations in refrigeration controllers. Successful attacks could let them change temperatures or force equipment into continuous heating or defrost cycles.

The agencies recommend reducing that risk by keeping control panels off the public internet, isolating operational equipment from business networks, changing default passwords, using strong authentication, patching firmware, and replacing unsupported devices. They also recommend setting safe operating limits and alerts for temperature changes outside those limits.

What about home appliances?

You don’t need an industrial refrigeration unit to adopt some of these precautions.

Check whether you need remote access. If you never use a device while away from home, disable that feature. Check the manufacturer’s instructions first; disabling remote access may also affect alerts or smart-home integrations.

Check who can access the appliance, including suppliers, and how that access is protected.

Change default passwords and secure the associated account. Use a strong password and enable two-step verification wherever the appliance or app supports it. Protecting the app account matters as well as protecting the appliance itself.

Keep firmware and apps updated. Turn on automatic updates where available, and don’t ignore manual update prompts.

“One of the best cybersecurity suites on the planet.”

According to CNET. Read their review →

articles.title: CISA, FBI Urge Action to Protect Industrial Refrigeration Networks
articles.context: The US government has urged organizations to take action to protect refrigeration systems from attacks that seek to remotely alter settings, including temperatures
articles.full_text:
The US government has urged organizations to take action to protect refrigeration systems from attacks that seek to remotely alter settings, including temperatures.

The advisory, issued by the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), the FBI and other federal agencies, said that US authorities “are aware of malicious cyber activity targeting industrial refrigeration and cold chain monitoring systems globally.”

The warning follows a number of recent incidents in which hackers accessed internet-connected refrigeration systems and have attempted to tamper with temperatures.

Such attacks can have had huge real-world impacts, including ruining food and medical supplies.

On October 11, 2026, it was reported that several supermarket chains in France and other countries in Europe were forced to destroy food stock after hackers compromised systems administered by refrigeration systems provider Danfoss. The attackers reportedly programmed systems to reach temperatures as high as 50 °C (122°F).

A similar incident occurred on November 1, with supermarkets in at least nine European countries reportedly impacted.

Most recently, a cyber-attack targeting refrigeration equipment provider Coolworld saw cold storage rooms in France's National Blood Service (EFS) turned to a boiling temperature of 110°C (230°F).

The US advisory, published on November 5, warned operators and owners of refrigeration systems in the US to be vigilant for similar attacks.

This is particularly in sectors such as healthcare, chemical, food and agriculture, and transportation, which widely use these systems for automated and remote monitoring of temperatures, continuous temperature logging, defrost cycle management and energy optimization.

“The actors may exploit vulnerabilities or weaknesses in unpatched or internet-accessible controllers to remotely alter settings and force units into continuous heating and defrost cycles, which can cause widespread inventory loss and equipment hazards,” the authoring agencies wrote.

They noted that hackers can use techniques like authentication bypass, arbitrary code injection and weak configurations to gain remote access to these internet-exposed systems.

Urgent Action Required to Protect Refrigeration Systems

The authoring agencies set out a number of immediate actions security teams should take to mitigate risks to industrial refrigeration and cold chain monitoring systems, based on the recent threats observed. These include:

Ensure control system devices, particularly controller panels are not exposed to the internet

Should remote access be necessary, protect these systems using a firewall or edge device and update them to the latest version to reduce security vulnerabilities

Isolate operational technology devices from business networks

Change default passwords and implement strong authentication policies, including phishing-resistant multi-factor authentication (MFA)

Establish a structured lifecycle management process to identify, retire and replace legacy devices that are end of life

Limit access to only those devices and IP addresses authorized to make changes

Maintain backup systems offsite and offline and regularly test them

CISA’s acting executive assistant director for cybersecurity Chris Butera, commented: “Every organization that depends on refrigeration and monitoring systems should assume it could be a target. We urge you to review the joint fact sheet and take action now to close known security gaps.”

Refrigeration Systems Taken Offline Following Europe Incidents

Data published by Censys on November 5 revealed there has been a 53% reduction in internet-exposed refrigeration controllers across the Danfoss StoreView and Copeland/Dixell XWEB products that were compromised during the supermarket incidents on October 11 and November 2, respectively.

The big fall in exposure is consistent with provider action or owners disconnecting devices, Censys noted.

So far, the incidents have not been attributed to a particular threat actor.

articles.title: Railway’s AI agents go off the track on a rival’s network
articles.context: Amir Boldo, co-founder and chief product and technology officer of Above Security, cautioned against describing agents as attackers, as they can execute attacker-like sequences...
articles.full_text:
AI agents operated by cloud infrastructure and application hosting platform, Railway, have attempted to access a rival platform’s infrastructure, prompting the cloud provider’s leadership to acknowledge the incident on social media.

Railway senior product engineer Jake Runzer acknowledged running agents to perform signups and agentic testing on similar platforms after Primcloud founder Josh Manders publicly questioned why Railway employees were attempting to breach his infrastructure.

Runzer said he had halted the testing harness after it began reaching too far. Railway co-founder and CEO Jake Cooper apologized, saying the models were “getting a bit too good at this point,” and pledged to prohibit non-manual external testing.

According to Manders, the agents attempted to receive credentials from an application container, request platform secrets, access cloud-provider metadata, discover internal databases and caches, and scan all 65,536 addresses on Primcloud’s internal network twice.

The activity reportedly involved 24 scripted commands over 15 minutes.

“An agent can act without a person directing every step,” said Diana Kelley, chief information security officer at Noma Security. “It doesn’t remove the responsibility of the people and organizations that deploy it.”

Primcloud said its defenses blocked every attempt and that “nothing” was accessed. The incident follows Railway’s own security disclosure involving encrypted customer environment variables.

The engineer was acting on his own

Cooper said the employee had developed the testing tool independently, using personal accounts, a personal credit card, and his own time. He added that Runzer ran it against a single external provider and halted it proactively within 15 minutes, adding that Railway had addressed the incident internally.

“I can confirm they ran this tool once and only once,” Cooper said in an X post. “Railway does not condone these actions. We expect all our employees to uphold our standards of conduct, whether acting on behalf of Railway or in a personal capacity.”

Although that timeline checks out with Manders’ own account, some details remain murky. After publicly calling out Runzer on X, Manders posted a follow-up, saying he had observed another attempt to access the account after his initial warning.

“I see you tried to access the account after this tweet too, Jake,” he had written more than 30 minutes after his first post.

Primcloud does not have a bug bounty program, according to its Acceptable Use Policy (AUP). It forbids unauthorized probing, scanning, or vulnerability testing without prior written consent.

‘The AI did it’ is not an accountability strategy

Experts condemn Railway’s “rogue AI” explanation for the incident.

Amir Boldo, co-founder and chief product and technology officer of Above Security, cautioned against describing agents as attackers, as they can execute attacker-like sequences without any malicious intent.

Execution traces can establish what an agent did, but they cannot independently prove intent, he said, adding that investigators need evidence spanning instructions, identities, permissions, inputs and tool calls. “You can’t put an agent on trial. You can hold each party accountable for its part,” Boldo said.

Ronald Lewis, head of cybersecurity governance at Black Duck, argued that users may not fully appreciate that delegating work to an agent also delegates the authority associated with their identity.

“We now have to ask what happens when trusted identity is delegated to a non-deterministic system capable of independently deciding how to use it,” Lewis said. Cooper confirmed in his X post that Railway had addressed the incident internally and was reinforcing its expectations for employee conduct, including when employees act in a personal capacity.

articles.title: The Flood is Coming And The Pipes Were Already Full
articles.context: Who gets a vulnerability first, how fast a fix reaches the people running the code, whether the operators who can't move on an attacker's timeline get a head start
articles.full_text:
An update on Athena, and some unsolicited predictions on what's coming next

On Saturday, Dario Amodei published We Must Pace the Frontier. I agree with him. Go read it if you haven't. I've spent the summer looking at what these models find, and the gap he describes between what they can do and what the rest of us are ready for is the one I've been staring at since May.

The hardest piece of his plan is the one that asks governments to coordinate. They're in a difficult spot: regulate too little and a US company accidentally builds the weapon, regulate too much and it gets built somewhere else, and open source isn't governable either way. Where governments can act is on consumption: not what the models can do, but what happens to what they find. Who gets a vulnerability first, how fast a fix reaches the people running the code, whether the operators who can't move on an attacker's timeline get a head start. That's what Gold Eagle is.

It matters because of where the risk actually lands. The danger in Dario's essay isn't a model in a lab. It's a model pointed at the power grid, the water system, the hospital network, all of it running on decades of software with the same exploitable design. The frontier is where the capability comes from. Consumption is where it does damage, and that's the end you can still defend.

So pacing has two ends. The frontier end is Dario's and the government's problem, and it's hard. The consumption end is ours: the disclosure processes, the patch pipelines, and the software itself, everything that has to absorb what the models produce. Pacing buys time on the frontier end. This post is a status report on how we're spending it, in three parts:

We start disclosing Athena findings this month, beginning with 50.

We joined Anthropic's Project Glasswing and are finding our own vulnerabilities, and I'll show you what that looks like.

We built infrastructure to make both possible, and we're going to open it up.

The short version: I'm more worried than I was in May, and more sure about what to do about it.

The first 50

Athena has been taking in findings since June. The intake numbers are public: more than 40,000 findings, 42% of them critical or high, across more than 500 projects, with more than 2,000 patches produced. What hasn't been public is how much of that we've been sitting on. Generating fixes was never the bottleneck. Disclosing them responsibly, at a scale nobody has ever tried, is.

On September 28, we start. We're beginning with about fifty, and none of them are the scary ones. That's deliberate. The frightening findings, the live pre-auth RCEs, go through Akrites on embargo, which I'll come back to. The first 50 are low-stakes on purpose: a small batch to get the flywheel turning and find out what breaks before the thousands behind them hit it.

All 50 are silent fixes: vulnerabilities already fixed at head, sometimes years ago, where nobody ever filed a CVE. Your scanner has nothing to say about them, and the old versions are still running everywhere. This pattern showed up in Athena almost immediately. A big share of what the models find only affects old versions, because the models scan what's actually deployed, and what's deployed is old.

Two systems fail at once with silent fixes, and neither is anyone's fault. Upstreams typically won't merge fixes to old versions, and they're right not to: the code was rewritten years ago, there's no branch to merge into, and "upgrade" is the correct answer. And the advisory layer has nothing to work with, because CVEs don't get filed for things already fixed at head. It's the one class of finding where acting doesn't step on anyone else's process, because there isn't one.

For each one, where the project has no path for accepting fixes to old versions, we're doing three things.

We publish the patch. Plain .patch files, in a public Chainguard repo that says exactly what it is on the tin, under the project's original license. This is deliberately not a maintainer-of-last-resort move. We have plans for that, and I'll get to them below, but they're for projects nobody maintains anymore. These are active projects that already fixed the bug at head. We're not forking anything, not claiming stewardship, not creating a new namespace, and not inviting anyone to build from it. It's a place to put patches for the people who can't upgrade yet, and nothing more. The durable fix is still upgrading, but this step reflects today's reality, where most of what's deployed isn't upgraded.

We publish the advisory. A Chainguard OSV feed, with fully enumerated affected version ranges and the exact symbols affected. Not "some 2.x releases, probably." Athena partner scanners are integrating with it now, so these show up where your team already looks.

We ship the fix. Patched versions land in Chainguard Libraries for every Chainguard customer the moment the advisory goes live.

We're not planning to contact maintainers ahead of each of these. They already deal with more noise than anyone should, and we don't want to add to it, least of all for bugs they fixed years ago. If you maintain a project and you'd rather hear from us in advance going forward, or you have any other concerns about how this touches your project, let us know at cna@chainguard.dev and we'll happily work with you.

We're becoming a CNA

A silent fix used to be mostly harmless. Nobody had written the bug down, and finding it from a fix commit took real expertise and real time. That's over. A model can go from a public fix commit to a working exploit against every version that never got the fix in an afternoon. The finding exists whether we publish it or not. The only question is whether defenders get a copy, too.

Once people know about a bug, the world needs a signal to upgrade, and the signal the world already has is the CVE. Scanners, KEV, and every compliance regime key on it. Silent fixes had none. So, in support of the Gold Eagle initiative, and in partnership with CISA, Chainguard is in progress to become a CVE Numbering Authority, scoped to open source vulnerabilities processed through Athena where upstream already fixed the flaw without an identifier, or where no maintainer is left to assign one, and no more specific CNA covers the project.

The uncomfortable part: this will put new noise in your scanners. Old versions that scanned clean last week will light up. That's better than no noise and a breach. Silence in that channel was never safety, it was just nobody having looked yet.

We also go to great lengths to keep each advisory as narrow as it can be. Every entry is enriched with the exact introduced and fixed ranges across every release branch, not a single version floor, and carries module, class, and function level detail on what's actually affected. That's what reachability scanners need to filter out the false positives for your codebase, so the noise you do see should be the noise that matters.

The narrowness is the point. We assign only where there is no upstream to defer to. If a vulnerability exists at the latest version and the maintainer is reachable, the project's own CNA assigns it, and we are the reporter, never the assigner. Every assignment clears the same gates: a reproduced finding, never raw model output; a defensible commit range; affected versions in real use; the maintainer notified with a response window; and withdrawal if the maintainer shows us we're wrong. Projects that become their own CNA leave our scope. This is a transitional role, not a territorial one.

Where the rest goes

The map for everything else is simple. If a vulnerability exists at the latest version and the maintainer is reachable, that's Plan A, and it runs through Akrites, the shared disclosure body the Linux Foundation launched in June, and that we helped found. If it exists at latest and the project is unmaintained, that's maintainer-of-last-resort territory, and we're working with other Akrites members to stand that up inside Akrites, where it belongs. And Gold Eagle, the federal clearinghouse that came out of June's executive order, is the layer that gets prioritized findings in front of the critical infrastructure operators who can't move on an attacker's timeline.

We spent a good part of the summer waiting on both of those and helping build them. Akrites goes operational this month. I'll be straight about the tradeoff: one shared incident response team across dozens of organizations is slower at first than everyone acting alone. That's the cost of choosing "maintainers deal with one trusted counterpart" over "maintainers deal with thirty strangers," and we'd make it again. The disclosure and upstreaming numbers get published either way, pretty or not.

A model found all of it in an afternoon

The second reason I'm worried is less about process and more about what I've seen. We joined Anthropic's Project Glasswing. Lots of organizations have, at this point, roughly 200 across 15-plus countries, so our joining isn't news on its own. What matters is what it means for Athena: we now have Mythos, and we're running it against the software we build and ship.

Here's the shape of one run, and I've picked it because it's the least reassuring result we have.

One widely used open source project. One run, about six hours. The harness came back with more than a dozen validated vulnerabilities, most of them pre-authentication remote code execution, reachable with no credentials and no operator action. Every one was reproduced three times in a clean VM before it counted, under the rule I'll describe in a minute: the model doesn't get to claim a finding, the host has to reproduce it. This is not an abandoned package. It's one of the most heavily scanned, tested, and fuzzed projects in the ecosystem, code that has survived years of expert review and relentless fuzzing. A model found all of it in an afternoon. These go through Akrites like everyone else's findings, and I'm not going to say more about the specific project here than that.

Here's what I'll say instead. Watching what these models find, and how long it takes a fix to reach anyone once they find it, is what worries me. It isn't the models themselves. It's the race between two clocks. On one, the industry is trying to absorb a short-term rush of findings through disclosure processes that were already behind. On the other, attacker capability is advancing toward the point where compromising critical infrastructure at scale becomes cheap. Right now, the second clock is running faster than the first, and I don't see anything that closes that gap on its own.

Sandboxes and sandboxing

Which is the other reason the sandbox matters. Producing a finding like the one above means building and detonating a working exploit against real code, over and over, driven by an agent nobody is watching in real time. That is dangerous to run, and this summer has been a run of examples of people running it unsafely. The incident Dario built his essay around, OpenAI's agents breaking out of a cyber evaluation and ending up inside Hugging Face's production infrastructure, started with a zero-day in the package cache the agents had been given. Package infrastructure is what we build, so that one landed close to home. Pillar Security spent a week in July publishing sandbox escapes across Cursor, Codex, Gemini CLI, and Antigravity, and the finding that tied them together was that the agent almost never broke the sandbox head-on. It wrote a file it was allowed to write, and something trusted outside the box ran it later. None of these was a problem of insufficient sandboxes. They were a problem of insufficient sandboxing: the boundary existed, and everything interesting happened in the gaps around it. Denylists don't contain any better than containers do.

Everything Athena does, from developing an exploit to proving a patch closes the hole, runs inside a microVM, the same primitive our package builds, image builds, and CI have run on for years. Matt wrote up the architecture in July. The short version: every job gets a hardware-virtualized guest with its own kernel and a root filesystem built from scratch, egress is enforced at the hypervisor and allowlisted to package registries and nothing else, the first forbidden connection destroys the VM, and no credentials ever enter the guest. And because a shared primitive multiplies the blast radius of any weakness, we point AI agents at the sandbox itself with instructions to break it. Every finding lands as a failing test first, then the fix.

The harness starts with a person

The harness that runs inside those sandboxes is the part I find most interesting, and it starts with a person. Ian Beer spent about six months writing a zero-click iOS exploit chain, and if you read the write-up as a search, you can see the shape of it: poke at a target, go deep, hit a dead end, back up, eventually connect enough dots to reach a working exploit. No human holds six months of that in working memory. He kept it in notes and pulled back the slice he needed each session. His notebook was the environment.

That's what we built, sharded across many agents in parallel: a tree search where every agent starts fresh with a scoped surface and a distilled trail of what's already known, and continuity lives in durable findings rather than anyone's context window. The rule I care most about is that the host casts the vote, never the model. A finding only counts if the host can replay it against a clean instance: the check fails before, the replay runs, the check passes after. Nothing enters the record until reality agrees, and that one rule is most of why the false positive rate is as low as it is.

A few things we learned building this, if you're working on something similar:

Fresh context, bounded job. Every agent starts clean with a scoped surface. Continuity lives in findings written for a stranger, not a transcript.

Every write gated on evidence. Without a precondition, a postcondition, and a host-runnable replay, it doesn't enter the record.

Research steers, it doesn't prove. It decides where an agent looks next and never counts as a finding.

Record dead ends as findings, too. A false positive collides with reality and starves on its own. A false negative is silent, permanent, and the failure that actually costs you the deep bugs.

Taste beats fleet size. In a search like this, the model's per-step judgment about where to look is the base of an exponent, and parallelism only shows up inside a logarithm. You cannot buy your way out of worse taste with more agents. That's the concrete, non-marketing reason we wanted Mythos, and why Glasswing matters more than how many agents you can run.

Put the pieces together, and the loop closes. Find, contain, fix, ship. All of it on one primitive.

What we built to do this, and what we're opening up

None of this was possible on off-the-shelf infrastructure. Over the last year, we rebuilt our factory on three new primitives, and every one of them started as something we needed for ourselves before it was anything we could sell.

The sandbox is the microVM you just read about: the isolation boundary that lets us run untrusted code and hostile agents without the blast radius reaching anything that matters. The harness is the search that runs inside it, the thing that found those pre-auth RCEs. And the third is CI as a function: our own fleet stopped sending code out to a CI system a year ago. The checks run in the loop, and changes arrive already proven, at more than ten times the CVE volume we were handling before.

We built all three because we had to; we've been running our entire operation on them, and over the coming quarters, we're going to start opening them up directly. If you are running untrusted AI workloads, or trying to find real vulnerabilities in your own code, or drowning in CI that tells you less than you'd like, these are the tools we reached for. Soon you'll be able to reach for them too.

So what is the endgame here?

Here's the unsolicited prediction. Everyone is worried about Mythos zero-days right now, and almost nobody was keeping up with ordinary CVEs before any of this started. The median enterprise is months behind on patches that have had fixes, advisories, and scanner coverage for years. That's the system we're about to pour thousands of new findings into. Faster disclosure and faster patching only help the people who can move on them, and most of the world can't move at the speed a model sets. If you take one thing from this post, take this: the flood is coming, and the pipes were already full.

Which is why none of the above is the finish line. Everything in this post makes us faster, and all of it accepts a losing premise: that the goal is to keep pace with a discovery rate set by frontier models. The vulnerability classes those models exploit aren't defects in today's software. They're its design. Memory corruption, deserialization, injection, confused deputies: consequences of how the stacks under every enterprise application were built. You cannot patch your way out of an architecture.

So the endgame is new foundations: a stack built secure by construction, where the dominant vulnerability classes can't be written in the first place, filling the role Spring Boot fills today, across every enterprise language, underneath the frameworks and the registries they pull from. For forty years, migration costs protected every incumbent platform. Nobody rewrote the COBOL because nobody could afford to. Agents just collapsed that cost.

We're working on this, and I'll say more when there's more to say. Why us: we see the world's pre-disclosure findings before almost anyone, so we know which bug classes matter, and we have the one tool that can prove a foundation removed them. Point Mythos at it before you ship, and you know.

Dario is right that pacing buys time, and everything above is how we're spending it. But a paced frontier only matters if the software underneath survives the frontier we already have. If the dominant vulnerability classes can't be written, the critical infrastructure built on them can't be broken by them, and a frontier model in the wrong hands has far less to reach. Pacing limits the risk by slowing the capability. Foundations limit it by taking away the target, and that's the only version of this I can see that ends the treadmill instead of running faster on it.

The Programmer's Credo says we do these things not because they are easy, but because we thought they would be easy when we started. This is the first one where I didn't even think that. We're doing it anyway.

If you maintain a project any of this touches, or if you're finding vulnerabilities, join at chainguard.dev/athena. And if any of this sounds like something you want to build, we're hiring.

articles.title: CPython flaw exposes AI inference servers to sandbox escape attacks
articles.context: “By exploiting this vulnerability, attackers could gain a foothold inside servers responsible for processing millions of user requests,” Darius Houle, a security researcher at...
articles.full_text:
A memory-safety flaw in CPython can allow malicious AI model templates to escape code sandboxes and execute arbitrary code inside inference servers, according to security researchers at RunSybil.

“By exploiting this vulnerability, attackers could gain a foothold inside servers responsible for processing millions of user requests,” Darius Houle, a security researcher at RunSybil, wrote in a blog post. “They also could strike directly at the underlying cloud infrastructure hosting those workloads.”

The researchers demonstrated how a specially crafted model could exploit the flaw to bypass Jinja, a Python-based templating engine used to structure interactions between users and LLMs, sandbox protections, and execute code in the process of serving the model. The attack could expose AI hosting providers that allow customers to upload and run their own models, potentially giving attackers a foothold inside infrastructure processing requests for multiple customers, the post added.

However, the Python Security Response Team (PSRT), which handles security reports involving CPython, disputed the security implications of the demonstration in a response to CSO. “We acknowledge the underlying CPython bug reported by RunSybil and appreciate their contribution to fixing it. However, we do not consider the demonstrated sandbox escape to be a CPython security vulnerability,” the team said.

The disagreement centres on whether the interpreter should be responsible for preventing sandbox escapes. While RunSybil argues that the flaw creates risks for AI inference infrastructure, PSRT says executing untrusted Python code within a sandbox is outside CPython’s security threat model.

Exploiting Python’s type-handling mechanism

“The bug we discovered abuses CPython’s handling of generic types to accomplish a breakout,” Houle wrote. “We exploited it using objects that sandboxes make available in every template, even in empty sandbox contexts.”

The researchers found that CPython can use a cached list of parameters even after an object has been modified through a callback. When the interpreter subsequently looks for a newly introduced parameter in the original list, it can receive an invalid index. An assertion designed to catch the condition is disabled in normal release builds, allowing the interpreter to access memory outside the expected bounds.

RunSybil used this behavior to retrieve references to Python objects that the sandbox was supposed to keep inaccessible.

“While an invalid address will generally crash the interpreter, an address pointing to a useful live Python object gives our callback a reference to that object (even when the sandbox never intends to expose it),” Houle wrote.

The researchers then used the recovered object references to access Python classes and functions needed to construct executable code.

Malicious model templates enable code execution

To demonstrate the attack, RunSybil modified the Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct model by inserting a backdoored chat_template.jinja file. When the model was loaded and used through an inference-serving engine such as vLLM, the template enabled arbitrary code execution in the serving process.

“Breaking out of the chat template sandbox and executing code represents a supply chain risk that endangers inference providers, library developers, and model users,” Houle wrote.

The researchers said they shared proof-of-concept exploits with multiple inference providers supporting bring-your-own-model (BYOM) features, which allow customers to upload models from external sources.

Python disputes vulnerability classification

RunSybil disclosed the issue to CPython, the Pallets Project, which maintains Jinja, and Hugging Face. The researchers said they encountered conflicting views about which project should address the underlying problem.

CPython maintains that the interpreter does not support sandboxing untrusted Python code as a security boundary. In its response to CSO, the PSRT referred to the project’s security policy, which states that sandbox escapes should be addressed by the maintainers of the affected sandboxing software.

“Escapes from such sandboxes are therefore outside our security threat model and should be addressed by the maintainers of the affected sandboxing software,” the team said.

The team also disputed RunSybil’s suggestion that there was no coordinated remediation process. It said the researchers had submitted the report by email rather than through CPython’s designated private GitHub vulnerability reporting channel.

Fix backported to three Python branches

RunSybil submitted a patch to CPython, which was merged into the main development branch on Aug. 14. According to the PSRT, the fix was also backported to the 3.13, 3.14, and 3.15 branches as a regular bug fix rather than a security fix.

The distinction matters because RunSybil had raised concerns that the fix would not reach all supported Python versions.

The researchers said the absence of a backport to Python 3.12 could delay adoption of the fix across AI infrastructure deployments.

“With major portions of the AI ecosystem still solidly aligned on Python 3.12, we might not see organic adoption of our memory-safety fixes until late 2028, when it reaches its end-of-life date,” Houle wrote. The researchers recommend that AI hosting providers treat sandboxed code, template engines and expression evaluators as best-effort security controls rather than relying on them as standalone security boundaries.

articles.title: UK ministers seek powers to investigate when AI agents are let off the leash
articles.context: The episode, and the potential for more damage from poorly designed AI agent deployments, have prompted MPs to question whether UK law can deal with such threats
articles.full_text: The UK government is paving the way for rules requiring essential service operators and digital providers to guard against losing control of AI agents and report incidents when safeguards fail. An amendment to the Cyber Security and Resilience Bill, which is passing through Parliament, would give ministers powers to regulate the deployment and reporting of agentic AI in certain organizations. The new clause was introduced during the bill's third reading in the House of Lords this week. In an explanatory note, ministers outlined plans for safeguards, notification of affected organizations, preservation of evidence, and government-led incident reviews. The measures would require consultation and parliamentary approval through secondary legislation. The move follows a series of incidents. Last month, OpenAI revealed that its agents repeatedly strayed beyond their intended scope, prompting the company to notify more than 100 organizations about the issues. That came after July's incident, in which an OpenAI agent accessed the internet and breached machine learning platform Hugging Face. The episode, and the potential for more damage from poorly designed AI agent deployments, have prompted MPs to question whether UK law can deal with such threats. Speaking to The Register, Stuart Davey, a partner at law firm Pinsent Masons, described the clause as "quite novel." Rather than directly imposing new duties, it would allow ministers to introduce rules and investigatory powers covering regulated organizations. Davey said that could include powers "to look where there has been such an AI agentic compromise or issue, and do some things... appoint inspectors, enter and search premises, seize and retain documents." Under the proposals, the minister could confer certain powers on regulators, requiring action from targeted organizations. Potentially affected organizations include gas and electricity suppliers, managed service providers, and cloud providers deploying AI agents for customers. Foundation model developers would not automatically fall within scope simply because they build the underlying technology. "Where there's a security or operational compromise in relation to a relevant network or information system, that would seem to capture those managed service providers or cloud computing providers who are using AI, and there's that loss of control," said Davey. He advised cloud and managed service providers to track whether the proposed measures become law. Evin McMullen, CEO and co-founder of AI identity and control infrastructure company AmanTrue, said the amendment recognizes loss of oversight or control as a security risk but does not itself impose new duties. "The amendment allows future regulations to introduce investigatory and enforcement powers where an incident involves an AI agent, targeting organizations running essential digital services," he said. "The deployer of an AI agent chooses its permissions, connects it to systems, and gives it access to data. When something goes wrong, the deployer is the party that will be expected to explain what happened. "Accountability stays with the organization that put the agent into the system, and ultimately with executives and the board. Whether model builders are captured will depend on how the regulations are written and whether a builder sits in a regulated category or a regulated supply chain." ®

articles.title: Sarajevo Cyber Security Summit 2026 puts the Western Balkans’ cyber resilience in focus
articles.context: A vulnerability cannot be prioritized sensibly if the organization cannot determine whether the affected asset is exposed, business-critical or even still in use
articles.full_text:
Cyber Security Summit 2026 in Sarajevo will examine the practical security questions organizations face when a supplier, network device or critical digital service fails: what breaks, who decides, and how quickly can operations recover?

A serious cyber incident does not need to begin on an organization’s core network to interrupt its operations. A compromised supplier account, an exposed edge device or an outage at a cloud provider can be enough to cut off access to a critical application, delay a transaction or halt a production process.

That is the operational reality behind “supply chain risk”. The issue is not simply whether an organization has deployed a firewall, endpoint protection or multi-factor authentication. It is whether it understands the dependencies that keep essential services running, has rehearsed the failure of those dependencies, and can recover without improvising under pressure.

ENISA’s 2026 Threat Landscape offers a useful measure of the problem. Of the targeted organizations in its dataset, 73% were classified as essential or important entities under NIS2. Public administration was the most targeted sector, accounting for 32% of cases. ENISA also identifies cyber dependencies, including third-party and supply-chain attacks, as a source of potentially large-scale and high-impact incidents; ransomware remained the incident type with the greatest short-term impact.

The sixth Cyber Security Summit, organized by the e-Transformacija Association, will take place on November 18–19, 2026 at the Hills Congress Center Sarajevo. Its program places these questions alongside post-quantum cryptography, AI-enabled threats, network security, data-center resilience and incident recovery.

Post-quantum readiness is a migration problem, not a future problem

Quantum computing is often presented as a distant concern. That framing is no longer adequate for organizations that hold information with a long confidentiality life: financial records, intellectual property, health data, identity data and strategically sensitive communications.

In August 2024, NIST finalized its first three post-quantum cryptography standards: FIPS 203 for key establishment and FIPS 204 and FIPS 205 for digital signatures. NIST has urged organizations to start the transition because a full migration across products, protocols and suppliers will take time.

The immediate concern is not that today’s widely used public-key cryptography has already been broken by a quantum computer. It has not. The concern is harvest now, decrypt later: an adversary may collect encrypted data now, retain it, and attempt to decrypt it once a cryptographically relevant quantum computer becomes available. For long-lived secrets, the exposure can begin long before the machine that makes decryption practical exists.

That makes the first step an inventory exercise, not a wholesale replacement program. Security leaders need to establish where cryptography is used, identify data that must remain confidential for years, and ask suppliers whether their products and services can support cryptographic agility. They should also plan the operational consequences of replacing certificates, key-management workflows, VPNs, signing mechanisms and embedded-device firmware.

The program includes a session, Quantum Is Coming: Can You Afford To Wait?, led by Srebrenko Šehić of LevelBlue. The organizer says the session will examine the quantum threat, the “harvest now, decrypt later” scenario and practical post-quantum options for existing systems.

Asset visibility is the beginning of resilience

For many teams, the more immediate challenge is simpler and harder: they do not have a reliable view of the systems they depend on. Hybrid environments combine on-premises infrastructure, cloud services, remote access, network appliances, APIs, SaaS platforms and third-party administration. A vulnerability cannot be prioritized sensibly if the organization cannot determine whether the affected asset is exposed, business-critical or even still in use.

That is why an asset inventory should be treated as an operational capability, not a compliance spreadsheet. It needs to link systems to business services, owners, privileged identities, data flows and recovery dependencies. Only then can a security team assess the full path from an exposed router or compromised identity to a material business interruption.

The summit agenda includes Damir Avdić’s session, Walls Won’t Save You: Router or Weapon?, and a panel on data-center security and resilience, from network architecture to post-attack recovery. These are useful prompts for a broader question: can a security program show how a control failure would propagate through the business, rather than merely report that a control exists?

AI will accelerate the attack cycle, but it does not remove accountability

AI is changing the economics of cyber operations. The UK National Cyber Security Centre assesses that, by 2027, AI-enabled tools will almost certainly make elements of intrusion operations more efficient and increase the frequency and intensity of cyber threats. It expects AI to enhance reconnaissance, vulnerability research, exploit development, social engineering and the processing of stolen data.

The important distinction is that this does not make fully autonomous, end-to-end advanced attacks inevitable in the near term. The NCSC judges them unlikely by 2027, while expecting skilled attackers to use AI-assisted automation to increase scale and evade detection. Human operators will remain part of the attack chain.

Defenders face a comparable discipline. AI can support alert triage, code review, anomaly detection and threat analysis, but it cannot compensate for weak identity controls, poor data governance or unclear incident authority. Where organizations deploy more autonomous AI agents, the NCSC recommends limiting their access to the resources required for a task, using sandboxing, maintaining logging and monitoring, and retaining meaningful human oversight.

Cyber Security Summit 2026 will address that strategic challenge through Ilijana Vavan’s session, Redefining Resilience: Cybersecurity Strategy in an AI-Driven World. Dr Emir Vajzović is scheduled to examine the capability gap between formal credentials and the practical skills needed to work effectively in an AI-shaped environment.

The questions security leaders should be able to answer

The most useful outcome from a conference discussion is not another list of tools. It is a sharper set of decisions for boards, executives and security leaders: Which services, suppliers and identities could interrupt our most important business processes? How quickly would we detect a compromise, contain it and restore a priority service? Which encrypted data must remain confidential long enough to justify post-quantum migration planning now? Where does AI have authority to act, and where must a person approve or stop it? Have our recovery plans been tested against the failure of a third party, rather than only against an internal outage?

Those questions are as relevant to public institutions and critical-infrastructure operators as they are to banks, manufacturers and technology companies. The difficult work is not selecting the next security product. It is building an operating model that connects technology controls with accountable decisions, tested recovery and the dependencies that actually sustain a business.

For the Western Balkans, that is the practical resilience challenge: not preventing every intrusion, but ensuring that one compromise does not become a prolonged operational crisis.

More information and the current program are available from the Cyber Security Summit 2026 website.

articles.title: ENISA Warns of Cyberattacks Targeting Refrigeration Systems Across Europe
articles.context: However, authorities haven’t confirmed whether those specific flaws were exploited in the attacks
articles.full_text:
ENISA warns of cyberattacks on European refrigeration systems, exposing risks to supermarkets, food supplies and industrial controls.

The European Union has issued a coordinated cybersecurity warning after a series of attacks hit commercial refrigeration systems in several Member States. The incidents, which began in October and continued with a new wave on November 1 and 2, have raised concerns about the security of equipment that plays an essential role in food distribution and other critical operations.

In a joint statement published on November 4, ENISA, the European Commission, Europol and European cybersecurity coordination bodies urged organisations to take immediate steps to protect vulnerable systems.

“Following a new wave of incidents having occurred on 1-2 November, ENISA, the European Commission (DG CNECT), Europol’s European Cybercrime Centre (EC3), the Network of the EU national computer security incident response teams (EU CSIRTs Network) and the European cyber crisis liaison organisation Network (EU- CyCLONe), advise organisations to take immediate action to mitigate exposure in the affected systems.” reads the advisory.

The warning highlights the need for “immediate action to mitigate exposure”, as attackers continue to target systems that are often overlooked in traditional cybersecurity strategies.

The attacks have already had tangible consequences. In France, hackers targeted refrigeration management systems used by hundreds of supermarkets, remotely changing their settings and forcing freezers into continuous defrost mode. Some systems reportedly reached temperatures of up to 50 degrees Celsius, destroying large quantities of fresh and frozen food. According to reports, around 300 Intermarché and Netto stores and fewer than 100 Coopérative U outlets were affected. Other retailers also reported disruptions to their cooling equipment.

The French incidents also exposed a broader problem: the security of industrial control systems that manage physical processes. These systems are increasingly connected to corporate networks and remotely accessible, but they don’t always receive the same security attention as traditional IT infrastructure.

BFMTV revealed the attackers targeted equipment from the Danish maker Danfoss that many French stores use to regulate their cold. Fresh and frozen stock was destroyed, and the Paris prosecutor says there were also fires.

Targeted devices were older Danfoss refrigeration controllers that had reached the end of their support life and no longer received security updates. Other systems were running outdated firmware. Researchers had previously identified vulnerabilities in some Danfoss controllers, including weaknesses that could allow attackers to bypass authentication. However, authorities haven’t confirmed whether those specific flaws were exploited in the attacks.

The European response reflects the fact that these incidents aren’t isolated technical problems. ENISA says national cybersecurity teams and EU crisis management authorities are sharing information and coordinating their investigations. The agencies also stress the importance of “rapid information-sharing” and a coordinated response to understand the scale of the campaign and help affected organisations.

ENISA has also published a collection of technical advisories from national CSIRTs to help organisations identify the risks and apply appropriate protective measures. These recommendations are particularly relevant to companies operating refrigeration equipment, supermarkets, food distribution networks and other facilities that depend on industrial control systems.

The statement also draws attention to existing European cybersecurity legislation. Since September 11, 2026, manufacturers of hardware and software products have been required to report severe incidents and actively exploited vulnerabilities through the Cyber Resilience Act’s Single Reporting Platform. The main cybersecurity requirements of the CRA will apply from December 11, 2027, requiring manufacturers to adopt security-by-design principles and provide security support throughout the product lifecycle, including timely vulnerability fixes.

The NIS2 Directive also requires organisations within its scope to manage cybersecurity risks affecting their operations and report significant incidents to their national CSIRT or competent authority. ENISA is supporting these efforts through its Secure by Design and Default Playbook, technical advisories and initiatives aimed at improving product security across the European market.

The refrigeration attacks are a reminder that cybersecurity failures can have consequences well beyond data theft or temporary IT outages. Manipulating an industrial controller can destroy food stocks, disrupt business operations and potentially affect services that people depend on every day. Organisations must therefore treat the security of operational technology as a core part of their risk management strategy, rather than an issue to address only after an incident.

“The main cybersecurity requirements laid down in the Cyber Resilience Act (CRA) will apply as of 11 December 2027. Manufacturers of hardware and software products (‘products with digital elements’) will be required to implement security-by-design and ensure security support during the lifecycle of such products, including the remediation of vulnerabilities without delay.” concludes the Agency’s advisory. “In addition, entities to which the NIS2 Directive (Directive (EU) 2022/2555) applies must implement measures to manage the cybersecurity risks to their operations, and report significant incidents to their national CSIRT or authority. Furthermore, ENISA is actively contributing to strengthening cybersecurity across the EU by promoting secure-by-design and secure-by-default principles in the EU market.”

Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon

Pierluigi Paganini
