articles.title: France Blood Service Cyber-Attack Sends Blood Storage Temperatures to 110°C
articles.context: The company specified that only a limited number of Coolworld units were affected and added that "the vulnerability currently being reported in the media concerns a component...
articles.full_text:
Read more about the wave of cyber-attacks on refrigeration control systems in Europe:

Major French Supermarket Chains Hit by Cyber-Attack, Food Stock Impacted

French Supermarket Cyber-Attack Impacts More Refrigeration Controllers

Cyber-Attack on Refrigeration Systems Hits Supermarkets Across Europe

Cold storage rooms in France's National Blood Service (EFS) were turned to a boiling temperature of 110°C (230°F) in a cyber-attack targeting temperature-controlled storage and refrigeration equipment provider Coolworld.

On November 3, French investigative weekly newspaper Le Canard enchaîné reported a new wave of attacks targeting refrigeration systems in France.

The outlet said unauthorized actors took control of some refrigeration controllers in EFS’s cold storage rooms in the night between November 1 and 2, notably in facilities in the Burgundy and Franche-Comté region, in east-central France.

These cold storage units host blood samples used for health monitoring but also plasma intended for transfusions. While they are typically kept at -30°C (-22°F), the newspaper reported some rooms hit up to 110°C (230°F). This does not mean the equipment or any blood samples reached these temperatures.

The refrigeration control systems of the affected EFS cold rooms are maintained by Coolworld, a Dutch temperature control rental company operating in France, Germany, Ireland, the Netherlands and the UK.

Coolword confirmed on November 4 it was "aware of the cybersecurity incident involving remote monitoring software used in refrigeration systems" and said it "responded promptly by implementing the appropriate measures," without sharing any details on those measures.

The company specified that only a limited number of Coolworld units were affected and added that "the vulnerability currently being reported in the media concerns a component supplied by a third-party provider and not directly controlled by Coolworld."

No Operational Impact on Blood Samples

The French Ministry of Health sought to reassure the public and told Le Canard enchaîné that the incident had caused no operational disruption because it had been detected in time.

According to the EFS, an on-call technician noticed an abnormal rise in temperature in the cold storage rooms overnight, allowing the issue to be identified before it could affect operations.

Speaking to French national news channel BFMTV, EFS president Frédéric Pacoud said that while the EFS “could have lost samples or bags of plasma intended to treat patients,” the early warning meant “there was no compromise to the safety of blood products.”

The EFS also told French media it notified the country's national cybersecurity agency (ANSSI). At this stage, nothing indicates that any EFS IT systems are impacted by the attack.

The EFS was approached for comment but had not responded at the time of publication.

Image credit: Igor Paszkiewicz / Shutterstock.com

articles.title: Fake software installers are turning your PCs into profit centers for hackers
articles.context: The campaign was found distributing three monetization components, some of which may have legitimate uses when installed knowingly
articles.full_text:
Users looking for cracked commercial software, free games, plugins, and unofficial utilities could be signing up for more than a free download. Microsoft has observed an evolving campaign that uses trojanized installers to turn the downloading Windows devices into money-making machines, consuming their computing resources and internet bandwidth without informed consent.

The campaign uses fake download pages and Inno Setup-style installers to deliver multiple software packages during a single installation session, Microsoft said in a blog post.

The campaign was found distributing three monetization components, some of which may have legitimate uses when installed knowingly.

“Organizations can reduce their exposure to this activity by preventing the use of untrusted software sources, enabling potentially unwanted application protection, and monitoring for unexpected software installations and persistence mechanisms,” the company said, adding that its Defender XDR detects and blocks several payloads and behaviors related to the campaign.

Fake installers used for real money

The campaign begins with users downloading installers advertised as cracked software, games, activators, plugins, or unofficial utilities. Microsoft observed lures posing as products like Navicat Premium and FabFilter audio plugins, alongside gaming and utility downloads.

The installers use an Inno Setup-style wrapper to stage temporary executables under Windows’ temporary directories. Numbered payloads subsequently execute and coordinate the delivery of additional software.

Microsoft said the campaign features an offer-based delivery mechanism. The installer communicates with rotating infrastructure using HTTP callbacks containing parameters such as “d=inno” and “r=offer_execution”. These requests allow the campaign to track individual software offers, allowing multiple payloads to succeed or fail independently within the same installation session.

The first monetization branch is WorldProxyPool, which installs proxyware to route third-party internet traffic through the victim’s device. It also creates SYSTEM-level scheduled tasks for agent startup, watchdog execution, and updates.

Another branch installs CharityEngine and Berkeley Open Infrastructure for Network Computing (BOINC), alongside components such as VirtualBox, to facilitate distributed computing.

A third installs utility-style software associated with Advanced Windows Manager and Windows Manager. These applications may participate in advertising, software distribution, or affiliate-driven monetization.

Microsoft urges defenders to scrutinize unofficial software

Microsoft recommends preventing downloads from untrusted sources, particularly cracked software, key generators, unofficial game installers, and activation tools.

Organizations using Microsoft Defender Antivirus should enable cloud-delivered protection, maintain tamper protection, and configure reputation-based protection to block untrusted applications and downloads, the company said. It also recommends evaluating Attack Surface Reduction (ASR) rules that restrict executable files based on prevalence, age, or trusted-list criteria.

For detection and investigation, organizations were advised to check execution from Inno temporary directories, especially when files such as “eld*.exe, set_*.exe”, “FirstFast[1].exe”, or “SecondRunner[1].exe” appear.

Microsoft also recommends correlating outbound requests containing “d=inno” and “r=offer_execution” or “r=offer_execution_fail” with process activity, scheduled-task creation, and software installations.

Unexpected WorldProxyPool, CharityEngine, BOINC, or VirtualBox installations warrant investigation, it said.

Defender XDR customers can use Microsoft’s published advanced hunting queries to identify related activity, while a list of indicators of compromise (IOCs) was also shared to help defenders outside the Microsoft ecosystem.

articles.title: Chrome 157 fixes 213 security issues, including 7 critical flaws
articles.context: If one is available, click Relaunch to apply it
articles.full_text:
On November 3, Google issued Chrome 157 to the stable channel for Windows, Mac and Linux. The update is rolling out over the coming days and weeks.

Most users are on Chrome’s Stable channel. The desktop update brings Chrome to versions 157.0.8103.38/.39 for Windows and Mac and 157.0.8103.38 for Linux. It includes 213 security fixes, including seven vulnerabilities rated Critical by Google.

Chrome for Android was also updated to 157.0.8103.38. It will become available on Google Play over the coming days.

How to update Chrome

The easiest option is to allow Chrome to update automatically. But you can end up lagging behind on updates if you never close your browser or if something goes wrong, such as an extension preventing the update.

If you don’t want to wait for the rollout to reach you, you can update manually. Open About Google Chrome from Chrome’s settings or Help menu. Chrome will check for updates. If one is available, click Relaunch to apply it.

Chrome 157.0.8103.39 is up to date

You can find an explanation of the version numbering system and step-by-step instructions in our guide: How to update Chrome on every operating system.

Technical details

Some of the security fixes deserve a closer look.

Google rates seven vulnerabilities in the update as Critical. One, a memory corruption flaw in ANGLE, affects Chrome for Android. It could potentially allow a remote attacker to run code outside the sandbox through a specially crafted HTML page.

Mobile protection, anywhere, anytime.

CVE-2026-121229: Memory corruption in ANGLE, which could allow a remote attacker to potentially execute arbitrary code outside the sandbox via a crafted HTML page.

ANGLE is Chrome’s graphics translation layer. A buffer overflow occurs when a program puts more data into an area of memory than it can hold, overwriting data in adjoining memory. An attacker can exploit this to make the vulnerable process run malicious code.

Chrome vulnerabilities that enable remote code execution outside the browser sandbox are particularly valuable to attackers because they can turn a visit to a malicious or compromised website into direct code running on the underlying operating system, often without requiring additional exploitation steps.

CVE-2026-121035: Use-after-free in Prerender.

Chrome’s Prerender component helps pages open faster by loading and preparing a page in the background before you navigate to it. If you then visit that page, Chrome can display the prepared version almost instantly instead of loading it from scratch.

This goes beyond just downloading content: Chrome also starts rendering the page and running its JavaScript.

A use-after-free vulnerability occurs when a program attempts to access a memory location after it has been freed. That can cause crashes or, in some cases, allow an attacker to run their own code.

CVE-2026-121156: Buffer overflow in Dawn.

Dawn powers WebGPU in Chrome, allowing websites to use a device’s graphics processor for rendering and computational tasks. It checks and translates WebGPU instructions into commands that the device’s underlying graphics system can understand.

A buffer overflow occurs when a program writes more data to a block of memory than it can hold. This can cause a crash or, in some cases, allow an attacker to run code.

articles.title: 3AM Ransomware Used Human-AI Hybrid Tactics in UK School Estate Compromise
articles.context: Bitdefender described the attack as “the first case of this kind that we have documented in Europe
articles.full_text:
A UK school estate was compromised by the 3AM ransomware group via a unique hybrid human-AI operation, an investigation by Bitdefender has found.

The incident, which took place from September 10 to 19, 2026, resulted in the attackers’ encrypting 37 machines and building domain trust in the compromised estate to reach other schools.

Notably, the investigation revealed that parts of the post-compromise techniques were undertaken by a human operator at the keyboard, while other parts behaved like an AI agent.

Bitdefender described the attack as “the first case of this kind that we have documented in Europe.”

The researchers continued: “What this attack does show is that the hybrid approach works, and we assess that it makes economic sense for attackers, with a person setting the goals and an [AI] model handling the mechanical work. We can expect hybrid attacks like this one to become more common in 2027.”

How 3AM’s Hybrid Attack Unfolded

The research blog, published on November 3, attributed the attack to a 3AM ransomware affiliate. 3AM is a ransomware-as-a-service (RaaS) operation, whose Rust-based encryptor was first observed in February 2023.

The researchers were not able to determine how the attacker gained initial access to the school estate. The first recorded activity started on September 10, when the attackers’ accessed credentials stored the estate’s backup infrastructure, before decrypting them with the Windows Data Protection API.

From September 12-13, the threat actor tested connections to other hosts from a machine where SQL Server was the parent process. They sent a sequence of commands to the target’s Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI) service, authenticating with stolen administrator credentials. The commands’ outputs were then read by either a person or AI model, who would then choose the next command and repeat the cycle.

A PowerShell command was first used, and re-ran unchanged 41 seconds later, before a single call was changed 49 seconds after that. Next, 47 seconds later, PowerShell was replaced with wmic, the older built-in command-line interface to WMI.

The researchers noted that the fact the complete rewrite arrived as fast as the minor changes before it indicates the commands were written by an AI agent.

The next nine retries followed a similar pattern of the delay before the next command being issued taking between 40 to 101 seconds, whatever the size of the change, while moving on to a new task to minutes.

“That split, longer time between tasks and shorter between retries, is what it looks like if a person is choosing the next step and a model is handling the retries,” the Bitdefender researchers wrote.

In contrast, later commands before the retry sequence were simpler and were sent between two and 16 minutes apart indicative of the pace of someone reading the output and deciding what to do next.

On September 14, the attacker made efforts to gain persistence in the compromised environments. These include running credential dumping tool Mimikatz and creating two backdoor domain-administrator accounts by separate routes.

Next, the attackers copied and 40 financial-related files via the Windows robocopy tool, which were subsequently exfiltrated to their command-and-control (C2) endpoint using HTTP POST.

“The registry-as-transport channel is an unusual choice and a strong indicator to hunt for,” the researchers noted.

On September 19, the attacker joined three separate Active Directory domains with two-way trusts and pushed the backdoor account’s access across the estate within an approximately three-hour window. The researchers said this part of the attack was the clearest example of the hybrid human-AI approach being deployed.

The work involved in joining the estate’s separate domains is highly mechanical, requiring it to be set up correctly on both sides, with one wrong detail stopping everything.

The attackers built the trusts and then ran a series of diagnostic probes and restarted the service that maintains the secure channel between domains. Bitdefender said the hybrid human-AI model suits this work, involving repetitive configuration where the fix comes from a human reading the error.

This work resulted in the attackers reaching 50 machines from the unmanaged host.

Finally, the threat actor made attempts to remove endpoint detection and response (EDR) tools, before decrypting 37 out of the 50 machines accessed.

How to Defend Against Hybrid AI Ransomware Attacks

Bitdefender noted that the attack involved typical approaches observed in other ransomware incidents, including backup credential theft, rogue domain administrators, trusts between domains and use of built-in legitimate tooling.

However, the hands-on work was split between human and AI operators, making use of their respective abilities.

“The approach looks pragmatic: the model takes the mechanical, repetitive work, and nothing in it needed skill or spend that these attackers did not already have,” the researchers commented.

They also noted that the involved of an AI model changes what the traces look like during an incident.

Bitdefender offered the following recommendations for defenders to protect against future attacks that follow a similar playbook:

Keep the administrative accounts of separate domains separate, and never keep privileged credentials for several domains in one place

Treat backup infrastructure as a target, and review your backup strategy for malicious intent

Restrict remote execution and administrative shares

Block interpreters and shells on machines that never use them

Put an endpoint agent on every machine

articles.title: Cyberattack on French plasma stores is enough to make your blood boil
articles.context: News about cyberattacks targeting refrigeration devices across Europe emerged on Monday morning after retailers arrived to work, only to find puddles on the floor after cyber...
articles.full_text: Attackers tampered with cold-storage settings used by France's civilian blood service after compromising a refrigeration supplier, the organization said. The French Blood Establishment (EFS) confirmed the incident on Tuesday, saying its own systems had not been directly targeted. Safeguards prevented any loss of blood products. The affected equipment stored blood samples and frozen plasma, including plasma intended for transfusion. "The EFS' monitoring and alarm systems enabled the rapid identification of these anomalies and the implementation of necessary measures to ensure that no blood samples or products were compromised," it said. "Thus, depending on the circumstances, as soon as the incident occurred, the affected equipment was either brought under control without impacting the products and samples, or neutralized; the products stored in these cold rooms were preventively transferred to other facilities." The EFS did not name the supplier publicly. According to reports, attackers changed cold-room temperature settings from -30°C to 110°C. That does not mean the equipment or its contents reached the higher temperature. The organization added that it notified the country's cybersecurity agency, ANSSI, and the Ministry of Health. News about cyberattacks targeting refrigeration devices across Europe emerged on Monday morning after retailers arrived to work, only to find puddles on the floor after cyber criminals activated defrost modes. Reports of the supermarket attacks describe remotely activated defrost cycles and temperatures as high as 50°C, forcing retailers to discard spoiled food. The attackers have not been identified. More retailers have reported disruption since the initial disclosures on Monday. Stores across Belgium, Ireland, Luxembourg, and Sweden were the first to report issues, although cases from Estonia, Finland, Germany, Portugal, Romania, and the Netherlands have since been confirmed. Richard Horne, chief executive of the UK's National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), told BBC Radio 4's Today program on Wednesday that he was aware of "a couple of impacts" in the UK's own food supply chain. No affected UK businesses have publicly identified themselves, although the British Association of Independent Meat Suppliers (AIMS) told the BBC that some of its more than 300 members had become "collateral" in the attacks, with two reporting that their fridges had begun defrosting. The latest wave of cold-store attacks comes a month after the first, which affected French supermarket chains Carrefour, Coopérative U, Intermarché, Monoprix, and others. Both supermarket waves involved remote interference with refrigeration controls, causing stock losses. Whether the attack affecting EFS used the same access route remains unclear. Some affected chains identified Danfoss controllers in their systems; others said they did not use the company's equipment. CERT-FR published an advisory at the time of the attacks urging organizations to remediate vulnerabilities in Danfoss AK-SM and AK-SC controllers. The attacks in France followed reports of compromises at US military commissaries, which also led to food wastage in August. ®

articles.title: Xen Hypervisor Flaws Let One Malicious VM Read and Write Any Other VM's Memory
articles.context: " Xen's advisory does not mention any attacks that exploit the flaws or specify what access within the VM an attacker needs
articles.full_text:
Two flaws in the Xen hypervisor allow a malicious guest virtual machine (VM) to read and write the memory of other VMs on the same host, including dom0.

Dom0 is the VM that, by default, has full permissions and manages the others. Patches are out, and there is no known mitigation, the Xen Project said in an advisory on November 3.

All Xen versions from 4.6 onward are vulnerable, while 4.5 and earlier are not. The flaws are tracked as CVE-2026-102703 and CVE-2026-102704, under Xen advisory XSA-523.

The Xen Project credited AI company Anthropic with finding the flaws using its Claude model. Stephan Lipp of Ada Logics then validated the finding, and the CodeAnt AI Security Research Team later independently reported the same issue.

The flaws are in grant copy, the operation Xen uses to copy data between VMs. Each VM tells Xen which of its memory pages other VMs may use, and Xen checks those permissions.

To save time on a batch of copies within the same memory page, Xen reuses checks it has already made. In some cases, it did not check again when it should have. That mistake is what lets a malicious guest read and write memory it does not own.

XCP-ng, an open-source virtualization platform built around Xen, said in its update notes that "a single compromised guest can break out of its isolation and take over the whole host."

Xen's advisory does not mention any attacks that exploit the flaws or specify what access within the VM an attacker needs.

Qubes OS is a security-focused desktop operating system that keeps software in separate Xen-based compartments called qubes. A bulletin said that every supported release and configuration is affected. Its fix is for Qubes 4.3, the only release it still supports.

Because every Xen version from 4.6 on is vulnerable, other products built on those versions are affected until their makers add the XSA-523 patches. As of November 4, Debian's security tracker listed the xen package in its bookworm, trixie, and forky releases as vulnerable, and in sid as fixed.

Fixes and Restarts by Platform

These are the fixes published so far:

Xen source: the advisory has patches for xen-unstable to Xen 4.19.x, and for Xen 4.18.x to 4.17.x.

Xen 4.6 to 4.16: the advisory has no patch for these versions. Xen 4.16's security support ended on December 2, 2024.

XCP-ng 8.3: xen-4.17.7-4.2.xcpng8.3, released November 3. Hosts must be rebooted. Vates, which backs XCP-ng, rates the impact as Critical.

Qubes OS 4.3: Xen packages 4.19.6-3 in dom0. Dom0 must be restarted, and Anti Evil Maid users must reseal their secret passphrase because the new Xen binaries change PCR18 and PCR19.

Qubes told users on November 3 to keep installing updates as normal. The fixed packages were then in its security-testing repository, due to move to the stable one over the next two weeks after community testing.

XSA-523 is separate from XSA-500, an earlier grant copy flaw that Xen disclosed on July 28, and it has its own patches.

articles.title: Radio With No Radar: Why Agent Runtime Security Fails Without the Layers Beneath It
articles.context: With more than 280 app integrations, more than 1,000 detection controls and more than 1 million agents detected, Reco brings agent security, posture management and threat...
articles.full_text:
Nearly every agent security pitch now ends on the same promise: the product stops the bad action in real time. The promise holds for one kind of agent, the kind whose traffic passes through a gateway the enterprise owns. Most agents never touch one.

One recent case shows what that gap looks like in practice. An employee asked an AI assistant to trigger a mass-email automation. The automation hit a recipient-limit policy and failed, so the assistant, which was also connected to the employee's personal mailbox, offered to send the batch from there instead. The employee approved without registering that the assistant was about to route around the sanctioned system. An unknown number of external recipients received email from a personal account rather than the approved channel.

No jailbreak was involved. The assistant did exactly what it was built to do, and the fix was not retraining a model. It was a single runtime rule that blocks any attempt to reach more than fifty external domains and explains to the user what the tool is about to do. Knowing where to apply a rule like that depends on seeing which agents exist, what they are connected to and what normal looks like for each. That visibility is the part most runtime pitches skip.

The runtime is the application, not the pipe

The year's largest agent launches placed agents inside platforms the buyer does not own. Claudeforce runs Claude inside Salesforce's trust boundary, Claude Tag lives inside Slack and Copilot lives inside Microsoft 365. Workday, which says AI now drives more than a quarter of its new annual contract value, runs its agents inside Workday. In each case the agent's tools are the application's features, its knowledge is the application's data and its permissions are the application's permission model.

A gateway can only inspect what passes through it. An agent that runs inside Salesforce, fires from a Flow, reads CRM records and writes case comments sends nothing past an inspection point, and the same is true of a Copilot agent assembling a document from SharePoint or a Slack-native agent reading years of channel history. The OWASP Agentic Skills Top 10 describes this gap as the "unreachable skill" scenario under AST09, No Governance: a capability deployed inside a third-party platform where no external scanner can go.

Security has made a move like this before. Firewalls once inspected packets by source, destination and port, until applications stopped mapping cleanly to ports and malicious traffic began to look identical to legitimate traffic. The inspection point moved up the stack to the application, where the signal lives. Agent runtime needs the same move, with a complication the earlier one never faced: the application layer belongs to someone else. A gateway-only strategy protects the agents an enterprise hosts itself, which are the fewest and the slowest growing.

The inspection point is also a target

In March 2026, attackers compromised LiteLLM, the open-source gateway that routes agent traffic to model providers. The malicious packages were live for about forty minutes, and CloudSEK later put the exposure at more than 2,500 organizations. LiteLLM is the kind of component a security-conscious team adds on purpose to watch AI traffic, which made the inspection point itself the attack vector.

None of this argues against gateways. It argues against treating any single component as the whole strategy. A gateway is more software in the supply chain, with its own release pipeline and dependencies, and it concentrates exactly the traffic an attacker wants. When enforcement is a shared component, its failure is a shared failure.

A millisecond verdict needs a memory

Runtime decisions are made in milliseconds, and the hard cases are the gray ones. A support agent pulling customer data may be doing its job or exfiltrating it. A coding agent reading a repository may be gathering context or performing reconnaissance. A finance agent creating an OAuth connection may be doing integration work or making the first move of a compromise. The action alone does not carry the verdict. The agent's identity and owner, its permissions, its normal behavior, the sensitivity of the data, the destination and the delegation chain behind the request do.

Chains raise the bar. Enforcement that evaluates only the last hop sees an authorized agent performing an action it has permission for, and misses that the authority arrived through a chain nobody approved. Judging the whole chain at runtime means already knowing it, and that knowledge cannot be assembled in a millisecond. Enforcement without that map is an air-traffic controller with a radio but no radar: commands can be issued, but the picture of which plane is headed where does not exist.

What real agent runtime looks like

Three properties follow. Enforcement has to sit where the agents are, across several vantage points such as native platform hooks, API-level controls, the MCP layer, the browser and the endpoint, rather than at a single gateway. Every verdict has to be computed against a live map of identity, permissions, connectivity and activity (IPCA), plus data sensitivity and delegation, which is what turns the gray cases into judgments. And the response menu has to be wider than block.

Mature enforcement is graduated. It allows the known-good, warns where justification is plausible, redacts where the data is the problem and blocks where the chain is hostile. It routes the highest-stakes actions to a human and keeps a kill switch for the provably compromised agent that suspends it, revokes its grants and preserves the trail. Every verdict is logged with its full causal path, because an incident review and a regulator want the same five things: the agent, the chain, the data, the destination and the policy.

Do not buy the end state

Irregular's Dan Lahav calls the mistake the end-state fallacy: assuming the properties of the eventual equilibrium apply to the transition actually underway. In runtime purchasing, it is the belief that inline enforcement will eventually see everything, so the unglamorous layers can be skipped. That end state is not available this year from any vendor at any price. Runtime coverage is partial and platform hooks are arriving unevenly.

What can be bought now, everywhere, is the stack runtime depends on: discovery across every vantage point, posture on every platform, identity and ownership for every agent and context for every decision. Each enforcement point that opens later then snaps into a map that already knows what normal looks like. The full argument for where enforcement belongs is in From AI Runtime to Agent Runtime.

The first ninety days, in order

A sequence that follows the stack bottom-up looks like this.

Window

The work

How to know it is real

Weeks 1 to 2: get the number

Connect what is already running (the identity provider, major platforms, network tools, the email layer) and let discovery work across every vantage point at once. No gateway deployment, no endpoint rollout, no rerouted traffic.

Time to first insight is days, not quarters. The discovered population is several multiples of the list IT keeps.

Weeks 3 to 6: names and configurations

Every discovered agent gets a named human owner or is suspended. Configuration debt is triaged, starting with the platforms hosting the most reachable agents: guest-user exposures, intake features wired to agent triggers, sharing rules from three years ago. Guardrails go on customer-facing and privileged agents first.

A human raises a hand within a day when asked "whose is this?"

Weeks 7 to 12: the queue and the path

Context-aware risk tiering so review starts with the agent that can actually hurt the business, a least-privilege review cadence on the top tier and a sanctioned route for business teams to ship agents with secure defaults.

Any critical rating can be explained as a chain, and builders are offered a path instead of only a block.

The enablement path matters because the builders are coming either way. Blocking teaches evasion, while a good path teaches compliance.

Teams can place themselves with a four-level test. Blind means the board's three questions (how many agents exist, what they can reach and who is accountable) have no current answer. Inventoried means the population is discovered, counted and refreshed continuously. Governed means every agent has an owner, posture is managed against baselines and risk is tiered with context. Instrumented means enforcement operates where agents run, with graduated verdicts and a full causal path in every alert. Most enterprises are at the first level, whatever the policy document says, and a vendor selling instrumentation to a blind organization is selling enforcement that can act but cannot judge.

Seven questions that sort vendors

Every vendor deck now says agent security. These questions separate vendors that built for the problem from vendors that renamed a product, because each is easy to answer well only if the architecture underneath exists.

Ask

What a good answer looks like

Can you find agents that never authenticate through SSO?

Yes, across several independent vantage points, each seeing something the others cannot.

For an agent you rated critical, show me the chain.

A complete, reachable attack path (capability, reachability, asset) that an analyst can verify, not an aggregate score.

Does the same finding produce different severities on different agents?

Yes, demonstrated on a sandboxed agent and a customer-facing one.

When one agent invokes another, can you reconstruct the delegation chain?

Original requester, every hop and the final action. An audit trail that starts at the last agent is not one.

What context feeds an allow, block or redact verdict?

Identity, permissions, delegation and data sensitivity, not the prompt alone.

What happens to my protection if your enforcement component is compromised?

A specific answer that addresses the LiteLLM incident directly.

How long until I see my real agent inventory?

Days. A quarter is a different product.

Platforms built around the map rather than the individual agent can answer these directly. One leading example is Reco, whose Reco Graph connects every human and non-human identity, application, permission and agent action into a single live view, so that reach, not configuration, is the unit of analysis. One measured program that applied this approach moved its posture score from 47% to 91% across 21 platforms in 30 days.

Learn more about Reco's agent discovery at reco.ai/platform.

The full ninety-day sequence, the four-level self-assessment and all fifteen vendor questions are in The Agent Security Checklist: Your First 90 Days.

About Reco

Reco is the leader in Agent Security. The Reco Platform secures agents and their operating environments where applications, identities, permissions, and workflows intersect. It discovers an organization's entire third-party ecosystem, prioritizes real risk over alert volume and remediates with precision across every human identity, agent, app and permission in the environment. Built on the Reco Graph, with new integrations delivered in hours through the Reco Factory and pre-built agent and app intelligence from the Reco Library. Security leaders at Fortune 500 enterprises choose Reco to bring order to agent proliferation and the chain reactions that follow. With more than 280 app integrations, more than 1,000 detection controls and more than 1 million agents detected, Reco brings agent security, posture management and threat detection together in one place. Learn more at reco.ai.

articles.title: Police Seize 100+ Servers After Four-Year Investment Fraud Probe
articles.context: A long-running international operation to disrupt a multimillion-dollar investment fraud operation scored another impressive victory this week after police seized 100 servers...
articles.full_text:
A long-running international operation to disrupt a multimillion-dollar investment fraud operation scored another impressive victory this week after police seized 100 servers and shuttered several scam websites.

Led by the German Itzehoe Public Prosecutor's Office, the action day on November 3 targeted the company believed to be responsible for hosting the fraudulent investment websites.

Victims were lured to these sites by deceptive ads promising huge gains with no downside. After they recorded their interest, personal data would be shared by the company with criminal groups operating scam call centers, according to Europol.

Scammers impersonating brokers then used a variety of social engineering tactics to persuade the victims to invest their funds in the fictitious schemes. Online accounts set up to perpetrate the scheme apparently displayed illusory gains, persuading them to plough more money into the funds.

When victims asked to withdraw their money, brokers used delaying tactics to block payments before cutting contact and leaving them with no way to recover their funds, Europol claimed.

Investigators estimate losses to exceed €4m ($4.5m), with potential victims in as many as 50 countries.

Read more on investment fraud: Cops Arrest Suspected Multimillion-Dollar Fraud Mastermind.

Alongside the server seizures, the action day on Tuesday resulted in the arrest of seven suspects who will be extradited to Germany. Authorities also searched 17 locations and seized other evidence and assets.

The operation involved cooperation from Albania, Cyprus, Finland, Germany, Israel, Kosovo, and North Macedonia, highlighting the transnational nature of this fraud scheme. Scam call centers have been identified in Albania, Kosovo and North Macedonia, according to Europol.

Four Years in the Making

The case dates back to 2022, when a German couple complained to local authorities that they couldn’t withdraw their funds from an investment scheme they had enrolled in.

An action day on September 6, 2022, led to searches in Belgium and Latvia, and the arrest of two suspects. Evidence was seized which helped police identify seven other members of the network, including the managers of call centers which were used in the scams.

Another action day came on May 13, 2025, when police conducted eight searches simultaneously in Albania, Cyprus and Israel. That resulted in the arrest of one suspect in Cyprus and the seizure of more evidence including electronic devices, documents and cash, Europol said at the time.

Police are not claiming, as they have done in the past, to have dismantled the network.

According to the FBI, investment fraud was the highest-grossing cybercrime type in 2025, amassing nearly $8.7bn for cybercriminals. Other schemes that have come to light in Europe over recent years include an €89m ($100m) ring that was smashed in 2023 and a financial crime organization that made €15m ($17m) until it was disrupted in 2021.

articles.title: CVE-2026-58868: Critical Android Bug Could Let Attackers Run Remote Code
articles.context: Google has fixed CVE-2026-58868, a critical Android vulnerability affecting versions 14 through 17
articles.full_text:
Critical Android flaw CVE-2026-58868 could allow remote code execution without user interaction on devices running Android 14 through 17.

Google has fixed CVE-2026-58868, a critical Android vulnerability affecting versions 14 through 17. The flaw is a critical Android vulnerability caused by a heap buffer overflow in the onOutputReceived function of FrameDecoder.cpp. The flaw can trigger an out-of-bounds write, potentially allowing a remote attacker to execute arbitrary code on a vulnerable device. Exploitation requires neither user interaction nor additional execution privileges, making it a potential zero-click attack.

“cve-2026-58868 In onOutputReceived of FrameDecoder.cpp, there is a possible out-of-bounds write due to a heap buffer overflow.” reads the advisory. “This could lead to remote code execution with no additional execution privileges needed. User interaction is not needed for exploitation.”

Devices receive the fix through security patch level 2026-11-01 or later, depending on manufacturers and carriers. Google is now aware of active exploitation of the flaws in its November 2026 bulletin.

Google’s November 2026 Android security bulletin addresses 216 vulnerabilities, including 23 rated Critical. Two of these flaws, CVE-2026-58876 and CVE-2026-58936, affect the System component and could allow remote code execution without user interaction.

The bulletin also lists five other Critical flaws in the System component. Three could lead to privilege escalation, while two could cause denial-of-service conditions. Another Critical vulnerability affects the Framework component and could also allow remote code execution.

Six Critical vulnerabilities affect the Android kernel. Two involve Bluetooth code, three affect the protected Kernel-based Virtual Machine (pKVM), and one is in the Human Interface Device (HID) component. The most severe kernel flaw could allow a remote attacker to gain elevated privileges without user interaction.

The November 5 patch level also addresses Critical vulnerabilities in MediaTek modem code and a closed-source Qualcomm component. Google’s bulletin lists eight Critical MediaTek modem flaws, while MediaTek’s own November security bulletin details six of them: CVE-2026-20499 and CVE-2026-20545 through CVE-2026-20549.

MediaTek describes these six vulnerabilities as out-of-bounds write flaws caused by missing bounds checks, integer overflow or improper input validation. The company says it is not aware of any active exploitation in the wild.

The Qualcomm issue is tracked as CVE-2026-25285 and affects a closed-source component. Google does not provide further technical details in its bulletin.

One of the critical issues fixed by Google is CVE-2026-58882 (aka SMS of Death), which could allow attackers to remotely disable a phone by sending a specially crafted SMS message. The flaw affects decodeWapPdu, a function responsible for processing WAP Push messages, a type of content delivered through the SMS infrastructure.

The vulnerability is particularly concerning because exploitation reportedly requires no user interaction. An attacker only needs the victim’s phone number to send a malicious message. The message doesn’t appear in the SMS inbox, so the victim may have no indication of what caused the problem.

The issue also raises concerns about the reliability of mobile communications during an attack. According to a technical analysis published on October 29 by security researcher Mark B, a malformed WAP Push message can crash com.android.phone, the Android system component responsible for handling telephony functions. The crash can terminate ongoing calls, including emergency calls.

Tests on several Android phone models reportedly reproduced the crash consistently. The phone can also become stuck in a crash loop because Android retries processing the malicious message whenever the device starts. As a result, the device may continue crashing until the offending message is removed.

There is an important distinction, however. Google’s security bulletin and the CVE record identify the vulnerable decodeWapPdu function, but neither explicitly confirms that CVE-2026-58882 is the same issue described in the researcher’s SMS of Death report. The technical overlap is worth investigating, but the two reports shouldn’t be treated as definitively describing the same vulnerability without further confirmation.

Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon

Pierluigi Paganini

(SecurityAffairs – hacking, CVE-2026-58868)

articles.title: Fake Interview of Software Engineer Led to Binance Mega-Heist
articles.context: Threat actors targeted multiple software engineers at Binance with sophisticated social engineering and zero-day malware in a months-long campaign that led to a record-breaking...
articles.full_text:
Threat actors targeted multiple software engineers at Binance with sophisticated social engineering and zero-day malware in a months-long campaign that led to a record-breaking digital heist last week, the crypto exchange has revealed.

Binance revealed the news in a lengthy post on X (formerly Twitter) on November 3.

“It was not a single isolated breach or a simple phishing incident,” it explained.

“The attackers combined a range of techniques, including social engineering by fake recruitment interviews, malicious software downloads, compromised internal AI tooling, endpoint compromise, and an advanced transaction-authorisation method.”

Read more on crypto theft: Hackers Exploit BTCPay Server Flaw to Steal Cryptocurrency.

The main point of intrusion appears to have stemmed from an interview the threat group set up with an unnamed “Software Engineer B” in September.

An individual posing as a project director contacted the engineer via a legitimate job-hunting platform, having spotted from their profile that they worked at Binance.

The first-round interview was held with a fictitious HR representative, during which the interviewer shared a social media account with the engineer, including personal photos and videos posted, in order to build trust, Binance said.

“The second interview was conducted in a popular social chat app, near the end of the interview, Engineer B was instructed to download an ‘assignment’ containing a malicious code repository onto his work computer,” it continued. “The repository contained malicious code that executed during the setup process, initiating a series of unauthorized activities.”

According to Binance, the “zero-day malware” used obfuscation and evasion techniques to ensure it was not detected by the engineer’s endpoint security tools. These included replacing a legitimate development tool component with a malicious version to execute commands and connect with a C2 server.

The Pathway to Wallet-Signing Operations

On October 20, the attacker accessed an internal AI tool via Engineer B’s computer to compromise the machines of two other Binance employees: Wallet DevOps Engineer A and Wallet Software Engineer C.

The former had been scoped out back in June when they unwittingly downloaded a malicious version of Homebrew, a third-party package manager for macOS, after clicking on a malicious search ad.

Although the Binance team “detected the anomaly, replaced the device, and rotated all related credentials” at the time, the engineer’s role and those of his colleagues had already been exposed to the hackers.

After compromising Engineer A’s machine, they found out he had a container deployment permission token on his computer.

“On October 29 between 17:15 and 19:56, the attacker logged onto Software Engineer C’s computer, used the credentials stolen from Wallet DevOps Engineer A, deployed a container, and triggered a malicious script to launch the attack,” the report explained.

Between 20:05 UTC and 20:09 UTC, five Binance hot wallets then sent 233.46 million XRP to an attacker-controlled address, while Binance hot wallets on Solana and Optimism sent around 970,500 SOL and 44.2 million OP to attacker-controlled addresses.

Clean-Up Time

Binance said it has since rebuilt the affected wallet system and internal AI tool along with the latter’s access controls, and that it has replaced affected devices.

It also decommissioned engineer credentials and tokens, enhanced security scans across employee devices, improved AI-based behavioral anomaly detection and strengthened wallet service risk controls.

The firm admitted it had already detected and prevented 57 suspected North Korean attacks this year alone. It is currently conducting a review of the incident, setting up a security research fund with industry partners, and has already increased investment in AI-enabled detection, protection and monitoring tools.

Experts from Fortra questioned the controls that were originally in place to protect employee, and especially developer, machines.

“In a world where quiet quitting exists, it should come as no surprise that employees are interviewing on company time. Organizations need to counter this with adequate controls in place. Particularly, controls around what can be downloaded and executed on a corporate laptop, as well as the permissions granted to the user,” argued Tyler Reguly, associate director, security R&D at Fortra.

“At the end of the day, developer laptops are among the hardest devices in an organization to lock down safely without being detrimental. Organizations need to find the balance point."

articles.title: Russian Police Arrest 3 Suspected VasyGrek Hackers, Dismantle Criminal Infrastructure
articles.context: Utilizing diverse frameworks and their own custom malware allows the adversary to tailor tooling to specific attack conditions and reduce the likelihood of detection
articles.full_text:
Russian authorities have arrested three suspected members of a threat group known as VasyGrek and dismantled its criminal infrastructure.

Also known as Fluffy Wolf, the threat actor has a history of targeting Russian and international companies since 2016.

The Ministry of Internal Affairs of the Russian Federation (MVD) said members of the group are "suspected of embezzling funds from the accounts of organizations, as well as creating, distributing, and using malicious software."

In one September 2025 case highlighted by the ministry, the attackers are said to have sent a phishing email to an unnamed organization, masquerading it as business correspondence and instructing recipients to open a reconciliation report that triggered the execution of malware.

The incident resulted in losses of 660,000 rubles ($8,000) from the organization's bank account, with the attackers transferring the funds to accounts under their control.

"The attacks utilized a vast network of phishing domains imitating financial and accounting service websites, as well as virtual servers located in foreign countries," MVD said. "Tools for covert remote administration were acquired from the dark web."

The rare law enforcement action saw Russian authorities conducting searches at the suspects' residences and the office premises they used to conduct the operations. It also led to the seizure of computer equipment, communication devices, and other items of evidentiary value.

According to reports from Russian cybersecurity company BI.ZONE and F6, VasyGrek is assessed to be a financially motivated threat actor that gains initial access by sending phishing emails with attachments disguised as financial documents.

Some of the key tools in its arsenal include off-the-shelf stealers and trojans, like MetaStealer, PureCrypter, PureLogs Stealer, WarZone RAT, XMRig, BurnsRAT, PureHVNC, PureRAT, Pay2Key, and PowerLoader, as well as legitimate remote access software such as Remote Utilities.

In a report published this week, Kaspersky said it recorded over 100 attempted attacks orchestrated by VasyGrek against organizations in Russia, Belarus, and Kazakhstan between January and September 2026. These attacks have also been observed using decoy documents to drop a Golang backdoor capable of executing arbitrary commands on the infected device.

The attacks primarily singled out entities in the metallurgical sector, along with wholesale suppliers of raw materials and industrial supplies and government agencies. Other targets included organizations in the healthcare, oil and gas, energy, finance, and agriculture sectors.

"The group expanded its attack geography: while previously its primary target was Russian organizations, this year, potential victims also included companies from Belarus and Kazakhstan," Nikita Nazarov, head of advanced threat research at Kaspersky, said.

"The attackers used multi-stage infection schemes and legitimate online services to host malicious components, which helped conceal their activity and hinder attack analysis."

The development comes as BI.ZONE it detected multiple attacks targeting Russian organizations using malware families like LxBase RAT, CoreRAT, and NightStrike RAT.

While LxBase RAT, a commercial trojan that costs $119 per month, is distributed via mass phishing campaigns, CoreRAT infection chains make use of phishing emails containing 7zSFX and Rust droppers for delivery. The activity has been attributed to Core Werewolf, which is assessed to share some level of overlap with Vortex Werewolf.

Attacks deploying NightStrike RAT have been associated with a hacktivist-turned-cyber espionage cluster dubbed Insolent Werewolf. Initial access is achieved using ClickFix-style attacks to deploy NetSupport Manager to gain remote access.

"Insolent Werewolf also utilizes Octowave Loader to deploy AdaptixC2 and Havoc post‑exploitation framework implants in compromised systems," BI.ZONE said, adding the group's malware arsenal includes other remote access trojans like CapDoor and NightWire.

"A RAT written in C++, NightStrike has presumably been created by the developer of NightWire, based on similarities in coding style. Utilizing diverse frameworks and their own custom malware allows the adversary to tailor tooling to specific attack conditions and reduce the likelihood of detection."

articles.title: CISA Confirms Hackers Exploiting WordPress Core Flaw During Software Upgrades
articles.context: "WordPress Core contains a time-of-check time-of-use (TOCTOU) race condition vulnerability that could allow unauthenticated attackers to execute code on the server during the...
articles.full_text:
The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has added a security flaw in WordPress Core to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, citing evidence of active exploitation.

The high-severity vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-119977 (CVSS score: 8.1), is a case of Time-of-check Time-of-use (TOCTOU) race condition that could be exploited to achieve arbitrary code execution on affected servers. Patches for the flaw were released late last month.

"WordPress Core contains a time-of-check time-of-use (TOCTOU) race condition vulnerability that could allow unauthenticated attackers to execute code on the server during the upgrade window," CISA said. "This is due to predictable, web-accessible staging paths used during full-package core upgrades."

Details of the flaw emerged last week when Wordfence said exploiting the vulnerability does not require an account on the site. That said, it does require an attacker to exploit a brief window during a complete Core update that could allow unauthenticated code execution.

During the first 21 hours after public disclosure, the WordPress security company said it recorded more than 18,500 requests targeting staged "setup-config.php" installer paths. As of writing, 12,632 attacks attempting to exploit the flaw have been blocked in the last 24 hours.

Telemetry data from Previdian shows that three exploitation attempts have been recorded against its honeypot censors from an IP address geolocated in the U.K. The exploitation events were observed on October 30, 2026.

With exploitation now officially confirmed by CISA, Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies have time until November 6, 2026, to apply the fixes.

articles.title: Node-RED authentication hole being exploited in the wild
articles.context: “That creates a concerning possibility where industrial operations could be disrupted by attackers who never intended to target critical infrastructure in the first place
articles.full_text:
Months after Siemens released fixes for an authentication hole in flow-based programming tool Node-RED, it remains unpatched by many users and attackers are taking advantage of it in the wild.

The problem involves open source IoT/IIoT systems, including those embedded in critical infrastructure, deployed outside the control of CISOs and CIOs. Security firm VulnCheck discovered the exploits and disclosed details in a blog post on Monday.

“On October 30, 2026, one of our canaries caught an attacker exploiting CVE-2026-58115, an unauthenticated Node-RED admin API flaw, to deploy a flow that downloads and runs a Linux bot. The request came from an IP in Microsoft’s ASN (AS8075),” the post said. “We have since seen 16 events from the same IP against this CVE, covering several different payloads.”

The core problem is that Node-RED ships with the authentication option disabled; users are supposed to change the setting before it goes live.

Patrick Garrity, the VulnCheck security researcher who wrote the post, said the fact that Node-RED deployments are popular among those outside IT makes them susceptible to unsophisticated errors like this.

“They are put in place by relatively nontechnical people,” Garrity said in an interview.

Aman Mahapatra, chief strategy officer for New York City-based technology consulting firm Tribeca Softech, said the Node-RED hole is not new, but it is still being leveraged in the wild.

“The condition being exploited is one Node-RED has carried for years as a default: unless an administrator configures authentication, anyone who can reach the editor can deploy flows, and the project’s own documentation says as much,” he said. “Node-RED is popular precisely because engineers can wire it up without involving IT, which also means it rarely appears in an asset inventory. It is the same pattern behind this week’s supermarket refrigeration attacks: equipment installed outside the security team’s view, reachable from the internet, with authentication switched off.”

Mahapatra pointed out that the biggest danger is the nature of the way users tend to deploy Node-RED.

“It is integration middleware. A typical deployment speaks Modbus, OPC UA, MQTT or S7 to controllers on one side and to databases, brokers and cloud services on the other, and it stores credentials for all of them,” he said. “A compromised instance is a credential vault for every system it touches and a bridge across an IT/OT boundary that the network diagram says does not exist.”

Another problem is that industrial system patches tend to happen on pre-planned schedules, rather than responding to emergent issues or suggested setting changes.

“Siemens published its advisory on August 11, and VulnCheck caught exploitation on October 30, three days after shipping its own detections,” Mahapatra said. “Eleven weeks is a short runway in OT, where firmware updates wait for planned maintenance windows, so a meaningful share of affected gateways will remain unpatched well into next year.”

Frank Dickson, principal analyst at Dickson Research, added that the details of the exploits are a good news/bad news situation for CISOs. The good news is that the attacks did not appear to have targeted industrial systems. The bad news is the attackers found and accessed those systems anyway.

Noah Kenney, principal consultant at Digital 520, agreed.

“They don’t necessarily need to understand the equipment or operations connected to these gateways. They’re simply looking for systems capable of executing their commands,” he said. “That creates a concerning possibility where industrial operations could be disrupted by attackers who never intended to target critical infrastructure in the first place. Even generic malware consuming system resources or interfering with network communications could have operational consequences.”

Dickson added that closing this hole may not resolve the exposure. “The report also found that some attackers skipped the bot and left web shells, hidden back doors for running commands later,” Dickson said. “Patching closes the door. It does not evict anyone already inside.”

articles.title: Critical Langflow flaws enable authentication bypass and RCE
articles.context: Exploiting it could allow attackers to bypass security restrictions and gain access to features that would normally require authentication
articles.full_text:
IBM patched critical vulnerabilities in Langflow, an open-source framework for building AI agents, LLM-powered workflows, and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems. The flaws could allow attackers to bypass authentication, leak API credentials, and execute arbitrary code.

Langflow, now owned by IBM, is popular in enterprise environments because it offers a visual experience that doesn’t require coding knowledge to create AI workflows and agents. Vulnerabilities in the framework have been exploited in the wild to steal AI and developer credentials before, most recently in August.

This latest round of security patches fix four vulnerabilities, two of which are rated critical with 9.8 CVSS score. One flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-93680, stems from an incomplete remediation of a previous auto-login security issue. Exploiting it could allow attackers to bypass security restrictions and gain access to features that would normally require authentication.

Another flaw, CVE-2026-110186, allows unauthenticated remote attackers to execute arbitrary code through Model Context Protocol (MCP) tool enumeration. A third vulnerability, CVE-2026-110193, which is rated as high severity, also allows for code and command execution on the server due to an issue in a third-party library used by the Agentic Assistant. However, exploiting this flaw requires authentication with at least a low-privileged account.

The fourth vulnerability, CVE-2026-110192, is an information disclosure issue due to insufficiently protected API credentials. It is rated as 6.5 on the CVSS scale.

The flaws affect Langflow OSS versions 1.0.0 to 1.12.8 and were fixed in the newly released 1.13.0 version, which is available both from the PyPI repository and as a Docker image.

“Before upgrading, back up the database, secret key, and uploaded files,” IBM said in its advisory. “If the deployment uses automatic login, prepare the existing account for password sign-in as described in the installation and Docker upgrade instruction.”

The company also released patches for three medium-severity flaws in Hono, an API and web application development framework used inside Langflow for request routing and backend web server tasks. The company advises users to upgrade Hono to version 4.13.5.

articles.title: Germany Busts 'Crime-as-a-Service' Investment Fraud Outfit
Democracy without a safety net.
articles.context: Britain’s National Cyber Security Centre warns that AI-powered malware is highly likely to feature in financially motivated cyberattacks against critical infrastructure, including hospitals, airports, and power stations, by 2028. Ivanti has patched two additional Connect Secure vulnerabilities exploited in zero-day...
articles.full_text:
CISA scales back its Election Day role. Google takes down a massive Android TV botnet. The UK warns of AI-powered attacks on critical infrastructure. German lawmakers face potential spyware threats. An AI-enabled infostealer ranks its victims. Ivanti patches more exploited zero-days. NATO launches cyber war games in Estonia. A Harvard breach exposes data linked to 850,000 email addresses. Our guest is Alex Weinert, Chief Product Officer at Semperis, on protecting the identity fabric in the AI era. Democracy is calling. And texting.

Today is Tuesday November 3rd 2026. I’m Dave Bittner. And this is your CyberWire Intel Briefing.

CISA steps back from the midterms.

The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency is taking a dramatically reduced role in today’s midterm elections, abandoning the coordinated national election security operation it has maintained since 2018, the New York Times reports.

Under the Trump administration, CISA has lost roughly a third of its workforce, scaled back intelligence sharing, and discontinued election-specific cybersecurity assessments. There will be no national election security war room or scheduled press briefings, leaving state and local officials with less federal support for responding to cyber threats, technical disruptions, and disinformation.

CISA insists it's fully prepared, pointing to regional teams available to assist election officials and hundreds of security-related engagements.

Former officials disagree, warning that the retreat leaves dangerous gaps in nationwide threat awareness and coordination.

States have significantly strengthened their election defenses since 2016, including expanded use of paper ballots. But experts say the federal government's ability to identify and communicate threats that cross state lines has substantially weakened.

Google dismantles a set-top-box botnet.

Google says it has dismantled a massive botnet built from more than 1.3 million Android TV set-top boxes shipped with malware already installed.

The botnet, dubbed XCPE, allegedly originated with Chinese manufacturer Videostrong Technology, which Google says secretly turned customers' devices into residential proxies, renting their internet connections to third parties for activities including advertising fraud and other cybercrime.

Google severed ties with Videostrong and took legal action against the infrastructure controlling the botnet. Researchers say the disruption could also cut off access to more than 10 million additional compromised devices.

The malware wasn't limited to streaming boxes. Researchers also found it on Android-based healthcare equipment, karaoke machines, and digital signage.

Google says it has addressed the weakness that allowed the malware to activate during initial device setup. The case highlights a troubling supply-chain threat: devices compromised before customers even plug them in.

The UK’s NCSC warns of likely attacks on critical infrastructure.

Britain’s National Cyber Security Centre warns that AI-powered malware is highly likely to feature in financially motivated cyberattacks against critical infrastructure, including hospitals, airports, and power stations, by 2028.

In its annual State of the Cyber Nation report, the NCSC also predicts Russia and China will routinely incorporate AI into their cyber operations.

Agency chief Richard Horne says the danger isn't necessarily new attack techniques, but AI's ability to discover and exploit existing vulnerabilities at unprecedented speed and scale.

He criticized organizations for running outdated systems, postponing security upgrades, and failing to monitor their networks.

The British government is responding with new investments in cyber defenses, AI security research, and vulnerability detection.

Horne warned that organizations face a choice: invest in resilience now, or risk serious disruptions to essential services later.

Warnings from Apple prompt German authorities to highlight potential spyware.

German authorities are warning lawmakers and prominent public figures about possible spyware attacks following a new round of threat notifications from Apple.

Germany’s federal cybersecurity agency, the BSI, confirmed that members of parliament and other notable individuals received alerts indicating they may have been targeted by sophisticated surveillance software.

Apple sent similar warnings to users in 99 countries. The company doesn't identify suspected attackers or confirm whether targeted devices were successfully compromised.

The spyware involved in these campaigns can potentially steal messages, location data, and other sensitive information, sometimes exploiting vulnerabilities that require no interaction from victims.

German officials say they're taking the warnings seriously and advise recipients to assume their devices may be compromised.

It's unclear who's responsible for the latest campaign, or whether any German officials were successfully hacked.

A new infostealer uses AI to identify the most valuable victims.

Researchers at Cisco Talos have uncovered a new infostealer that uses artificial intelligence to analyze stolen data and identify the most valuable victims.

Dubbed Volta-Autodoxer, the malware collects passwords, authentication tokens, cookies, payment information, and cryptocurrency credentials. It also targets active sessions on platforms including Discord, Telegram, Steam, and Roblox.

But Volta goes beyond simply stealing data. It conducts additional searches through victims' accounts, gathering information about their locations, habits, and purchases to build detailed personal profiles.

The malware then submits that information to commercial AI models, asking them to act as intelligence analysts and produce structured assessments that help attackers prioritize targets.

Volta defaults to Anthropic's Claude Opus 4.6, with fallback options including Moonshot AI's Kimi and Google's Gemini.

Researchers haven't confirmed the malware has been deployed in the wild, but its design demonstrates how AI could make traditional credential theft more targeted and efficient.

Ivanti patches additional Connect Secure zero-days.

Ivanti has patched two additional Connect Secure vulnerabilities exploited in zero-day attacks since early October. Attackers chained a privilege escalation flaw and a file upload vulnerability with an authentication bypass bug patched last month, enabling unauthenticated root-level code execution. Researchers at Volexity say the attackers avoided deploying malware, instead repeatedly exploiting devices to execute commands and tampering with logs to hide their activity. CISA has ordered federal agencies to patch the authentication bypass vulnerability by Friday. More than 5,000 Connect Secure instances remain exposed to the internet.

NATO’s Crossed Swords cyber exercise kicks off in Estonia.

NATO's Cooperative Cyber Defence Centre of Excellence has launched Crossed Swords 2026 in Tallinn, Estonia, bringing together more than 250 participants from over 40 countries.

The exercise focuses on coordinating offensive and defensive cyber operations with conventional military and special operations missions, where timing can be critical down to the minute.

This year's exercise introduces a dedicated AI agent track, allowing participants to build, deploy, and work alongside autonomous systems while maintaining human oversight. The training environment also incorporates OpenAI's Daybreak cyber defense technology.

Military cyber operators, threat hunters, forensic specialists, and command staff are participating, alongside civilian partners helping integrate critical infrastructure protection into operational planning.

Crossed Swords has grown significantly since its beginnings in 2014, reflecting the increasing importance of coordinating cyber capabilities with traditional military operations.

A data breach at Harvard exposes more than 850,000 email addresses.

A data breach at Harvard University exposed personal information associated with more than 850,000 email addresses, according to breach notification service Have I Been Pwned.

Attackers compromised Harvard's Alumni Affairs and Development systems in November 2025, stealing names, email addresses, phone numbers, physical addresses, dates of birth, donation details, and other biographical information.

Harvard says the affected systems did not contain Social Security numbers, passwords, or payment card information.

The ShinyHunters extortion gang claimed responsibility and published a 1.1-gigabyte archive of stolen data in February after Harvard reportedly refused to pay a ransom. Harvard has not publicly attributed the attack.

The incident was part of a broader series of university breaches, with Princeton and the University of Pennsylvania also reporting compromises involving donor information in November 2025.

Stick with us after the break, we are joined by Alex Weinert, Chief Product Officer at Semperis, is talking about protecting the identity fabric in the AI era. And….

Alex Weinert, Chief Product Officer at Semperis, and I recently sat down to talk about protecting the identity fabric in the AI era. Here is our conversation.

If you enjoyed this conversation, be sure to check out the full interview in the show notes.

Democracy is calling. And texting.

As Americans head to the polls for today's midterm elections, WIRED reporter Dhruv Mehrotra has a cautionary tale about the machinery behind political fundraising.

Since 2022, he's received more than 1,700 fundraising texts intended for a relative named John, whose modest donations to Democrats somehow got associated with Mehrotra's phone number.

Mehrotra replied STOP 49 times. The messages kept coming.

Investigating the deluge, he traced nearly half this year's messages to tracking codes apparently associated with Sterling Data Company, which uses AI and personal information to identify potential donors.

Sterling's CEO acknowledged that campaigns can rent the same contact records and that database mistakes happen, but didn't confirm responsibility.

His advice was to stop responding entirely.

So, on Election Day, a reminder that while Americans get one vote apiece, political fundraising texts apparently come with no such limits.

And that’s the CyberWire.

For links to all of today’s stories, check out our Daily Briefing at the cyberwire dot com.

And that’s the CyberWire Daily, brought to you by N2K CyberWire.

We’d love to know what you think of this podcast. Your feedback ensures we deliver the insights that keep you a step ahead in the rapidly changing world of cybersecurity. If you like the show, please share a rating and review in your podcast app. Please also fill out the survey in the show notes or send an email to cyberwire@n2k.com

N2K’s lead producer is Liz Stokes. We’re mixed by Tré Hester, with original music by and sound design Elliott Peltzman. Our contributing host is Maria Varmazis. Our executive producer is Jennifer Eiben. Peter Kilpe is our publisher. And I’m Dave Bittner. Thanks for listening.

articles.title: Warning: Phishing Operations Are Impersonating Prediction Markets
articles.context: ” Recorded Future warns that attackers are now able to exploit current trends faster than ever before, as AI supercharges their development
articles.full_text:
Fraudsters are exploiting the increased public interest in prediction markets such as PolyMarket and Kalshi, according to researchers at Recorded Future. Criminal groups known as “traffers” are providing fellow crooks with “websites, administrative panels, cryptocurrency payment infrastructure, victim-management capabilities, technical support, and promotional guidance” to target users of prediction markets.

“This model lowers barriers to entry for affiliates and enables campaigns to scale rapidly as new trends attract potential victims,” Recorded Future says. “The services combine convincing prediction-market interfaces with established fraud mechanisms designed to manipulate victims and prevent them from recovering deposited funds. These mechanisms include controlled trading outcomes, fabricated market activity, artificial withdrawal restrictions and fees, and the collection of sensitive identity and payment information.”

The attackers are using AI tools to accelerate their operations by “reducing the time, cost, and expertise required to adapt campaigns to emerging events.” Recorded Future warns that attackers are now able to exploit current trends faster than ever before, as AI supercharges their development.

“The rapid adoption of prediction markets by multiple traffer teams illustrates a broader threat from mature fraud ecosystems that can pivot toward emerging technologies, financial products, and cultural trends without having to develop entirely new criminal capabilities,” the researchers write. “Prediction markets are particularly well-suited to this model because legitimate platforms already combine cryptocurrency, speculative financial activity, rapidly changing news events, and social media discussion. Fraud actors can imitate these characteristics to establish credibility and manufacture urgency. As the fraudulent prediction markets gain visibility, additional traffer teams may experiment with the prediction market theme or reuse the underlying tooling for adjacent fraud schemes.”

Recorded Future has the story: https://www.recordedfuture.com/research/prediction-markets-traffer-teams

articles.title: AI policy wonks declare 'sovereign agents' a threat to civilization
articles.context: If sovereign agents became malicious, they could attempt to wreak havoc from cyberspace, attacking civilians, critical infrastructure, and national security systems alike
articles.full_text: The Center for a New American Security posits that the next big threat from our future AI overlords involves "sovereign agents" acting on their own and regularly improving themselves. These are AI agents that operate outside of human control and “pursue open-ended, evolving survival,” AI policy researcher Ben Hayum said in a Tuesday report from the bipartisan national security think tank, which was founded by Washington insiders with experience in diplomacy and military affairs. “If sovereign agents are not already possible, they will be soon.” Agents that can maintain the model and compute powering them and independently evolve their goals over time have a “minimal form of sovereignty,” Hayum wrote. A more advanced sovereign agent, however, could also acquire resources to pay for ongoing needs (like compute), grow a distributed population of agents and coordinate them, withstand efforts to shut down, and self-improve. AI models could either steal or buy compute and model access, Hayum argues, pointing to Anthropic’s claims that small AI models could replicate onto IoT devices like smart TVs, and OpenAI’s agents’ password and access key theft during the Hugging Face hack. “If sovereign agents accumulate resilient, decentralized, and untraceable infrastructure, they could trigger an irreversible loss of control,” according to the report. “In other words, proliferation with no kill switch. If sovereign agents became malicious, they could attempt to wreak havoc from cyberspace, attacking civilians, critical infrastructure, and national security systems alike.” Dun dun duuuun! There is still hope for civilization as we know it, as long as policy makers and AI developers “respond with bold pragmatism” and enact policy recommendations laid out in the report. First, frontier labs should name, evaluate, and protect against sovereign agents in their safety frameworks - and lawmakers should pass legislation to require transparency and AI incident reporting. The report also recommends AI developers, working with the National Security Agency and other federal agencies, build airgapped testbeds to study sovereign agents and kill switches to control them. And it suggests a public-private partnership modeled on the Conficker Working Group - formed in 2009 to combat the Conficker worm - to boost chokepoints against sovereign agents before they emerge. Other policy recommendations suggest lawmakers enforce human verification and cybersecurity standards for services that the working group identifies as essential to sovereign agents, and calls on departments of State, Treasury, Justice, and Homeland Security to disrupt any gray-market access to unauthorized services. Finally, “Congress should hold those who release sovereign agents liable for the harms that follow,” the report recommends. This hits on something your humble Reg vultures have been hissing about for quite some time now – and would likely solve all future incidents involving rogue, or sovereign, AI agents: hold frontier labs’ human bosses legally liable for their agents' illegal actions. ®

articles.title: Binance Says Hackers Used Well-Known Tricks to Carry Out a $6.34 Billion Heist
articles.context: The hackers were then able to move through the company’s network, exploit an internal AI tool, and gain access to a wallet signing service that allowed them to make transactions...
articles.full_text:
For almost a decade, North Korean cybercriminals have targeted the cryptocurrency industry—large and small.
