articles.title: Attackers turn GitHub issues into supply chain campaign against 61 public repos in less than an hour
articles.context: A novel attack chain They discovered the campaign while investigating prompt injection in GitHub – and they told us the attack chain is part of what makes this supply-chain...
articles.full_text: EXCLUSIVE Researchers identified at least 83 attacks against 61 public GitHub repositories, including popular open source projects such as Google LangExtract, Trivy, Brave browser, and MLflow, in what they suspect is a coordinated campaign to execute commands in CI/CD environments and steal credentials and access tokens. It all happened very quickly, the Radware threat hunters said in an exclusive interview with The Register. Most (77) of the malicious items were published during a 43-minute time span on September 1, with the remaining six occurring within the next two minutes. “Our guess is that the final aim was a supply-chain attack in which the attacker gains credentials for the repo, and then he has the power to change the contents – the code – as he wishes” and then push the malicious changes to others, Radware VP and researcher Gabi Nakibly told The Register. Nakibly and fellow Radware researcher Zvika Babo say they suspect a single individual is behind this supply chain campaign. This attacker used 74 different GitHub accounts, many of which had legitimate development histories, meaning they were likely compromised. "Considering that dozens of accounts posted the same type of payload, on the same day, within a narrow time window, and to the same infrastructure, it is reasonable to assess that the activity was coordinated,” the team wrote in research shared ahead of publication with The Register. A novel attack chain They discovered the campaign while investigating prompt injection in GitHub – and they told us the attack chain is part of what makes this supply-chain campaign novel, and extremely stealthy. First, the attacker publishes an issue, pull request, or comment containing malicious commands hidden in HTML comments. This ensures the content is not visible in the rendered page. Plus, a GitHub event – like a pull request or issue – can automatically trigger a workflow if the repository is configured to respond to that event, meaning the attacker can be pretty hands-off at this point. “The workflow automatically is triggered within a second, and if the workflow is indeed vulnerable, then the attack is executed successfully,” Nakibly said. The workflow incorporates attacker-controlled content directly into shell source code, and the shell executes the hidden, malicious command, which hoovers up environment variables and attempts to exfiltrate those to an attacker-controlled server. While the researchers examined logs from actual runs, and told us they found two cases containing evidence that the malicious command ran inside the automation environment, they can’t definitively say whether the attacker successfully obtained repository write permissions, modified source code, or compromised downstream software. But they're trying. “The big picture is that the attackers are trying to find every possible way to get inside the repos to get credentials,” Nakibly said. Plus, “the attacker doesn't need to compromise the repository or to have access to its codebase” to do this, Babo added. “Basically, every user with a GitHub account can try to run this attack – it's very easy to start this attack.” Which repos were affected? As of October 13, the threat hunters identified 83 GitHub items with a verified payload across 61 different repositories. The repos span AI frameworks, security tools, development infrastructure, databases, and other widely used open source software projects. The Radware report lists agno-agi/agno (42.7K stars), ToolJet/ToolJet (41.1K), google/langextract (38.9K), aquasecurity/trivy (38.4K), CopilotKit/CopilotKit (38K), and podman-container-tools/podman (33K), among the most popular. Other notable targets included QwenLM/qwen-code (28.5K), mlflow/mlflow (28.4K), discordjs/discord.js (26.8K), cilium/cilium (25.6K), brave/brave-browser (23.9K), dotnet/maui (23.3K), Homebrew/homebrew-cask (22.2K), github/docs (21K), apache/doris (16K), and PX4/PX4-Autopilot (12.8K). “These projects are used by thousands of organizations," Babo said. The researchers disclosed their findings to all of the projects’ maintainers, and most of the repositories were closed or fixed, but they can’t confirm that all of them were. This campaign follows several earlier supply chain attacks against open source security and dev tools as attackers increasingly look for new methods to steal credentials and other secrets. “There is no way to stop the attackers from attempting,” Nakibly said. “The only way is to make sure that the workflow code is resilient, and not vulnerable to such attacks." The researchers recommend applying least-privilege access to CI/CD workflows, and separating as much as possible workflows triggered by external events from jobs with elevated permissions. “Developers should treat external content as untrusted, and also limit the secrets and environment variables that are available to the workflow,” Babo said. ®

articles.title: Online Scam Volumes Double to Overtake Phishing
articles.context: The security vendor’s latest State of the Internet (SOTI) report features data from partner Bolster AI, revealing that scam activity overtook phishing for the first time
articles.full_text:
Detections of online scams doubled between July 2025 and June 2026, as cybercriminals focused on more direct ways to generate revenue from victims, according to Akamai.

The security vendor’s latest State of the Internet (SOTI) report features data from partner Bolster AI, revealing that scam activity overtook phishing for the first time.

It recorded around 6.4 million online scams in the period April-June 2026, versus 3.2 million in July-September 2025.

This category typically includes fake stores, investment scams, tech support scams and payment fraud, it said.

“The fight against fraud is no longer just an isolated financial function; it is a critical, cross-functional cybersecurity imperative,” said Patrick Sullivan, CTO, security strategy at Akamai. “As autonomous AI agents and synthetic identities redefine how customers interact with brands, threat actors are exploiting these same vectors to conduct business logic abuse and zero-click data exfiltration.”

Read more on digital scams: Social Media Platforms Earn Billions from Scam Ads.

However, phishing – which Akamai defines as attempts to steal credentials, authentication info and data via brand impersonation – also rose during the period.

Phishing detections increased by 61%, driven by reusable phishing kits, industrialized infrastructure, and AI.

The latter has helped to decrease the average phishing attack lifespan by more than 50%, dropping from 48 days (Q4 2025) to 22 days (Q2 2026), the report claimed.

“Adversaries leverage AI to generate dynamic templates, produce multilingual lures at scale, and deploy condition-aware evasion – drastically lowering costs while bypassing legacy defenses,” it explained.

“Conversely, security teams use AI to compress investigation and reduce workflows from days to less than an hour through automated indicator analysis, infrastructure clustering, and evidence collection, disrupting attacks before victims are impacted.”

The Human Impact of Scams

Over 80% of scam victims in the US reported suicidal thoughts following the crime, according to new data from the non-profit Identity Theft Resource Center (ITRC) published on October 28.

A large part of this is down to the self-blame and social stigma attached to scams, the ITRC claimed. It also blamed “institutional ghosting" for the mental anguish that victims often feel.

“When general consumer scam victims overcame their shame to seek help, institutions frequently compounded the injury,” it explained. “Nearly nine in 10 general consumer scam victims asked an organization for help and were never contacted, and 67.2% reported that the organizations they contacted ‘made me feel it was my own fault.’”

A lack of support can also leave victims exposed to recovery scams.

“Abandoned by legitimate institutions and desperate to undo the damage, 78.9% of general consumer scam victims (and 90.9% of those experiencing suicidal ideation) paid a fee to a third party who promised to recover their stolen money, fix their credit or catch the scammer – compared to just 6.5% of scam victims who connected with the ITRC,” the report said.

articles.title: A Hacker Targeted High-Stakes Poker Players With Malware That Exposed Their Cards
articles.context: In fact, WolfSec believes the same threat actor was attempting to attack players’ machines as early as 2022 using a more basic technique; because no known funds were stolen at...
articles.full_text:
In a fitting sign of the times, the hacker’s carefully laid plans were foiled by an AI agent.

It was September 25, 2026, and Alex, a professional online poker player, was using his Claude AI agent to review some play statistics. (Alex only agreed to speak with WIRED under a pseudonym to avoid any risk of reprisals from threat actors.) After Alex’s SQL database crashed and needed to be reset, the Claude agent noticed something suspicious: A program called MeshAgent was operating in the background, where it seemed to be capable of capturing Alex’s screen and even controlling his entire machine.

Thanks to the Claude agent’s report, Alex could see the program had been installed on April 24, and not by Alex himself. Alex says the agent identified 11 time-stamped events when the program had been capturing his screen based on graphic errors it caused during screen sharing instances. During all 11, Alex had been playing a session on ACR, also called Americas Cardroom, a major worldwide online poker operator.

He checked his hand histories and quickly found the most troubling info yet: The same opponent, playing under the handle OxOO, was at his table for 10 of those 11 sessions.

The handle was familiar. Alex and several friends in the high-stakes community had shared suspicions about this player’s behavior in the past. Alex checked the player’s win rate stats via a public tracking site; they were astronomically higher than the best players in the world, a statistical impossibility given the sample of hands played. In Alex’s view, it was glaringly obvious that this player was cheating.

An investigation by Alex and other members of the high-stakes community in subsequent days confirmed his fears—and then some. Alex was one of hundreds of players allegedly targeted with this type of malware by the same reported threat actor across a period of multiple years. Alex, who was the first to discover MeshAgent on his computer, claims he was “only” ripped off for around $30,000, a relatively moderate sum for the level he plays at; many of his peers weren’t so lucky.

With millions of dollars allegedly stolen across the biggest sites on the internet, the poker world is searching for answers about how the scheme was allowed to continue so long, whether major sites took the risk seriously after it was reported, and whether online poker itself has been irreversibly compromised.

Poker has never been short on cheating controversies; online poker especially so. The “superuser” method, in which a cheater gains unauthorized access to their opponents’ cards and can therefore act with perfect information against them, was one of the first to show up online.

articles.title: ICO Reprimands Staffordshire Police After Domestic Abuse Breach
articles.context: Despite the serious nature of the breach, the ICO decided not to fine the police force, even though the regulator found that it failed to put in place “appropriate measures” to...
articles.full_text:
A UK police force committed a serious breach of data protection law after sharing the home address of a domestic abuse victim with their abuser, the Information Commissioner’s Office (ICO) has revealed.

The privacy regulator issued a reprimand to Staffordshire Police on October 28, following the incident in March 2024.

The force had served the abuser, “P,” a Domestic Violence Protection Notice (DVPN) on their release from prison in order to protect the abuse victim, or “data subject.”

However, it erroneously included that person’s home address, which was not previously known to P.

“As a consequence of the investigation into the relevant incident the commission has become aware of allegations that P subjected the data subject to both physical and emotional abuse over a period of several years, resulting in the data subject having to relocate their home address on numerous occasions in order to escape the alleged abuse,” the reprimand noted.

“In this context, the data subject’s current address was highly sensitive information and should have been handled as such.”

Read more on police privacy breaches: Police Scotland Fined After Sharing Victim’s Phone Data.

Despite the serious nature of the breach, the ICO decided not to fine the police force, even though the regulator found that it failed to put in place “appropriate measures” to prevent the disclosure, “including poor completion rates for mandatory training in both data protection and issuing DVPNs.”

It argued that Staffordshire Police had since made improvements to reduce the risk of a similar event taking place in the future. These included increased training completion rates, new leadership roles for domestic abuse cases, new internal procedures and new technology to improve services for victims.

ICO head of investigations, Sally-Anne Poole, said the case is a reminder of the importance of getting the basics right.

“Every organization must be doing everything necessary to protect the personal information in their care, especially where there is a known risk to someone's safety,” she added. “Whether in policing, health or local government, we urge organizations to take responsibility for training their staff and putting appropriate systems in place to avoid these incidents and the harm they can cause.”

Advice for Handling Sensitive Information

The ICO warned back in 2023 that organizations handling the personally identifiable information (PII) of domestic abuse victims could put lives at risk if breaches occur.

It said at the time that it had issued reprimands to seven organizations in the previous 14 months after sensitive PII was breached, including one police force.

The latest revelations will do little to allay concerns that the regulator’s public sector approach – which favors warnings, reprimands and enforcement notices over fines – is not having the desired effect.

After this latest incident the ICO advised organizations handling sensitive PII to:

Ensure staff know how to handle the PII of people experiencing domestic abuse with extra care

Review default templates and processes to ensure PII is only included where legally necessary

Regularly check contact information to avoid disclosing information to an old address, email or phone number

Always double check before any PII is transferred, altered or disclosed

Ensure training is thorough, relevant and tailored to the tasks staff actually carry out

articles.title: Shadowy AI Relay Disables OpenAI Codex, Claude Code Sandboxes
articles.context: The enigmatic service is providing popular AI coding tools to mainland China and other regions where OpenAI and Anthropic products are not officially for sale — but with key...
articles.full_text:
A mysterious relay service is installing authentic but unauthorized OpenAI Codex and Anthropic Claude Code tools for enterprise users overseas, and making dangerous configuration changes that put those organizations at risk.

The AI relay, first spotted by the Symantec Threat Hunter Team, appears to be designed to bypass regional restrictions that prevent certain countries and regions from using AI tools and platforms of US companies. According to Symantec's report published Thursday, the relay service installs genuine versions of the command-line interfaces (CLIs) for Codex and Claude Code on enterprise systems, but reconfigures them to route requests through the relay's infrastructure rather than OpenAI's or Anthropic's networks.

On the surface, this appears to be the case of a gray market provider or unauthorized reseller providing the AI tools to markets where they are not officially sold. Symantec researchers noted that the service, which has been active since early 2026, has installed the tools on systems at a dozen organizations, primarily in mainland China but also in South Korea, Taiwan, and Malaysia.

Related:Researchers Infiltrate Microsoft Tech Support Scam Operation

But the relay service also disables security safeguards for the tools, and the research team said it's unclear why it's being done (no malware or malicious activity has been observed thus far). One thing is for certain, according to Symantec: the relay service is creating enormous cyber-risk for the organizations using it.

Dangerous Configurations for Codex, Claude Code Users

Brigid O Gorman, senior intelligence analyst at the Symantec Threat Hunter Team, tells Dark Reading that researchers found a suspicious PowerShell downloader that they later determined to be "an AI-agent hijack script." After investigating further, the team found similar activity on other networks and traced it to the unauthorized relay service.

According to Symantec's report, when a user of the AI relay installs a legitimate Codex or Claude Code CLI through npm, the fileless PowerShell or bash script is fetched from "a lookalike domain by a one-line command that the user appears to run themselves. While this evokes the specter of attack techniques like ClickFix and InstallFix, the research team noted that the CLI clients aren't modified or Trojanized in any way.

And yet, the tools perform suspicious actions that heighten risks for enterprises. For example, the reconfigurations turn off the CLIs' execution sandbox, which is a key security feature because it limits what the AI coding tools can do.

Related:F-Secure Launches Victim-First Scam Encyclopedia Covering 50+ Types of Consumer Fraud

Additionally, the relay service enables network access for the write sandbox, turns off telemetry and error reporting features, and replaces the user's API credentials with relay-issued tokens. In one case observed by the Symantec Threat Hunter Team, the script logged a user out of their Anthropic session and deleted their authentication variables before reissuing credentials controlled by the relay service.

"Bypassing the regional restrictions that keep Western AI vendors from selling directly into certain markets is the simplest explanation, but it does not require disabling a CLI's sandbox or establishing persistent credentials that survive a reboot," the report stated.

Grave Risks for Gray Market Users

The relay service activity is something of an enigma. The Symantec Threat Hunter Team said it's unclear why the operators of the client-side relay would need this level of control over users' systems, though the researchers did not observe any evidence of the operators abusing the access. The report noted that the architecture of the service would support malicious exploitation of the access if the operator's intentions were to change.

Furthermore, the Claude Code keys issued by the relay service are formatted with the prefix that Anthropic reserves for subscription-based OAuth tokens, "which is consistent with, though not proof of, a relay pooling flat-rate subscriptions and splitting the capacity across many customers," the team wrote.

Related:AI Slop Isn't Just for Social Media; It's Ruining Cyberattacks, Too

On the other hand, disabling security features hints at a potential fraud operation involving stolen credentials or payment cards, or even the malicious resale of prompts and files that run through the relay infrastructure. Gorman says it's "certainly notable" that the relay disables execution sandboxes and establishes its own persistent credentials.

"We did not see any malicious activity being carried out using these relay services, so any commentary on the potential intended goals of those using it are speculative," Gorman says. "However, a relay in this position can see every prompt, file, and secret an employee sends to the agent, and can alter or fabricate every response it returns. With the sandbox disabled and network access enabled, a malicious or compromised response could execute with the full privileges of the user's account."

Symantec provided indicators of compromise (IoCs) in the report, even though technically speaking there have been no compromises at this stage. "The organizations affected here look less like chosen targets and more like workplaces where individual employees found and used such a service to get access to tools they wanted," the report stated.

Nevertheless, the research team warned that using the service presents serious risk to corporate networks. And while the relay appears to be aimed at regions where Codex and Claude Code tools aren't officially offered, organizations looking for cheaper alternatives and users engaging in shadow AI activity could potentially find their way to such a service.

articles.title: NIST Publishes Guidance to Meet Federal Post-Quantum Deadlines
articles.context: For example, agencies and federal suppliers should prioritize the migration to the PQC key establishment standard (FIPS 203) for data that is particularly sensitive or needs to...
articles.full_text:
The US National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) has published official guidance designed to help federal government agencies meet the 2031 deadline to transition post-quantum cryptography (PQC).

President Trump’s Executive Order 14412, published in June 2026, mandated that all US federal agencies transition “high value assets” and “high impact systems” to use PQC for key establishment by December 31 2030 and for “digital signatures” by December 31 2031.

NIST’s new document sets out a transition plan for agencies and organizations that work with the federal government to meet this deadline. The guidance references the post-quantum algorithm standards that NIST published in 2024.

“These deadlines leave little margin: meeting them will require immediate and sustained action by federal agencies and by the technology providers, standards organizations, and infrastructure operators on which federal systems depend,” NIST wrote.

How to Prioritize the PQC Transition

The NIST report emphasized the logistical complexity that comes with the PQC transition. It outlined the approaches that can be taken for different types of systems and data to ensure security teams to take a risk-based approach to the transition.

For example, agencies and federal suppliers should prioritize the migration to the PQC key establishment standard (FIPS 203) for data that is particularly sensitive or needs to be kept secure for a long time, due to the risk of “harvest now, decrypt later” attacks.

The NIST guidance also accommodates a hybrid option for particularly sensitive systems, which combines conventional encryption with PQC – essentially providing two layers of security. However, this approach would demand more computational resources.

It also sets out how long less critical systems can continue to use conventional encryption protocols.

NIST mathematician Dustin Moody commented: “We lay out how certain encryption algorithms people are using today will get phased out. It’s important to know how a given algorithm might be disallowed in federal systems after a certain date, for instance, or whether it will be allowed but at the user’s own risk. Factors like this can help an organization plan.”

The report also urges federal agencies to look beyond their own system components and at its entire cryptographic supply chain.

Post-Quantum Preparations Ramp Up

The new NIST guidance follows a series of pledges around PQC transition from other governments and across the tech world.

Governments like Canada, Australia, Japan, and the UK have set deadlines ranging from 2028 to 2030 as milestones for ensuring critical government systems are quantum safe.

While many of these mandates are focused on government and critical infrastructure organizations, they generally come with a push for other sectors to follow suit and set a roadmap for PQC migration.

Large tech firms, including Cloudflare, Google and Microsoft, have set a 2029 deadline for full PQC migration. Meanwhile, Apple, AWS, IBM and Meta, have officially started rolling out NIST-approved PQC algorithms into their products.

Read now: How Cybersecurity Vendors Are Preparing for the Post-Quantum Era

The situation has been made more urgent after warnings from tech companies like Microsoft that advances in quantum R&D mean that cryptographically relevant quantum computers (CRQCs) capable of cracking asymmetric encryption could appear sooner than anticipated – potentially within the next five years.

articles.title: MR ROBOT Malware-as-a-Service Targets Indian Bank Customers
articles.context: Its researchers found an operator control panel, a Telegram-based storefront and a malware builder that let affiliates create bank-themed Android trojans on demand
articles.full_text:
A new Android malware-as-a-service (MaaS) operation has been found renting customized banking trojans to criminals targeting Indian bank customers, with one affiliate intercepting 5407 text messages from 153 infected devices.

The operation, branded MR ROBOT by its operators, was detailed in research published on October 28 by threat intelligence firm CloudSEK. Its researchers found an operator control panel, a Telegram-based storefront and a malware builder that let affiliates create bank-themed Android trojans on demand.

The lures are distributed through fake Play Store-style pages and messaging-app links, and impersonate banks as well as utility providers and government services.

MR ROBOT Turns Banking Malware into Subscription Service

CloudSEK said MR ROBOT is not a single actor’s campaign but a multi-tenant crimeware platform. Each affiliate receives its own application ID and can generate Android packages impersonating specific Indian banks.

The platform supports a tiered reseller model with sub-admin accounts, and licenses access for set periods through a control panel identified as version 7.0.

The malware intercepts text messages carrying one-time passwords (OTPs), shows fake screens to harvest banking credentials, card details, PINs and identity information, and can silently enable call forwarding. CloudSEK said this reroutes incoming calls, including banks’ fraud-check callbacks, to a number the attackers’ control.

The storefront, a Telegram bot called APK Shield, offered around 36 lure apps, including bank impersonations and fake apps for utility bills, telecom services, traffic fines and government services.

One Affiliate Intercepted More Than 5400 Text Messages

CloudSEK tracked two affiliates. One affiliate’s panel held around 154 enrolled devices and approximately 3270 intercepted messages, while an exposed Firebase database linked to a second held 153 devices and 5407 messages.

That data was collected between July 16 and 30, 2026, and around 4000 of the messages came from bank and telecommunications short codes. CloudSEK said call forwarding was active on 58% of the devices.

Each build receives a fresh signing certificate and can hide from the Android launcher after installation. CloudSEK said MR ROBOT shares call forwarding and per-customer builders with FatBoyPanel and RedWing, operations previously documented by Zimperium, but its kit, storefront and panel had not been publicly reported.

Read more on Android banking malware: Rokarolla Trojan Combines Banking Fraud With Device Surveillance

CloudSEK advised users never to install bank-branded apps from links sent by text, WhatsApp or Telegram, and urged banks to move customers from text-message OTPs toward app-based or Fast Identity Online (FIDO) authentication where feasible.

articles.title: Admin dropped the F-bomb in a password to show hackers who was really 1337
articles.context: Welcome back to PWNED, in which The Reg offers cautionary tales from folks who’ve left their doors wide open to attackers and lived to tell the tale
articles.full_text: Welcome back to PWNED, in which The Reg offers cautionary tales from folks who’ve left their doors wide open to attackers and lived to tell the tale. This week’s misadventure involves unpatched older machines and a password that was supposed to send a message to crims. Our story comes courtesy once again of leading red teamer and pen tester Dahvid Schloss of Suzu Labs. A client asked Schloss to visit a factory and check the servers there for security holes. The company had been hacked six months prior, made some adjustments, and wanted to make sure that they were bulletproof now. Schloss' mission, which he chose to accept, was to get domain admin rights. Schloss drove over to the factory where he noticed a number of Windows 7 servers were connected to the CNC milling machines, even though Windows 10 was by then Microsoft's supported desktop OS. This was to be expected, as companies with proprietary software often use legacy OSes for fear of breaking apps. At first, Schloss had a hard time breaking in because most of the servers were not connected to the domain. So there was no point in his running the EternalBlue zero-day that would have let him in. “So I've been looking through these and most of them had been disconnected from the domain, so it's the right move,” he said. “Like, yeah, you could run EternalBlue on the network, but you really weren't going to be able to get anywhere with it, cuz you get on the device and what you find: you dump LSASS [the Windows Local Security Authority Subsystem Service], you’re like ‘All right, there’s local admin creds, but the local admin creds on those devices were different from the local admin creds on the majority of workstations.” Finally, Schloss went onto one of the servers that was connected to milling machines and found that it was connected to the network and on the domain. It was vulnerable to EternalBlue and he went and dumped LSASS and found a pair of creds from WDigest, one of which looked like an admin account. But Schloss thought that it must not be a legitimate admin account when he read the password : “heyhackergof***yourself,” but written in leet speak [l337 5p34k]. The resulting string was a strong password, but Schloss assumed that the admins were playing a game with him and left this credential there for him to find. Schloss assumed it wouldn't work and sat on it for a week. During a briefing he had with the IT crew, he presented his findings and then asked who set up the admin account with this funny password. “You could see everyone kind of looking at the senior manager of IT like ‘that was you, wasn’t it,’” Schloss explained. “He’s kind of got this face. I’m like ‘oh shit, like what?’ Turns out that ‘heyhackergof***yourself’ was the actual password for his admin account." On Monday, Schloss tried the username and password combo and, lo and behold, it gave him complete control of the entire network. He was then able to get access to other passwords and many of them were also insults directed at potential hackers. Schloss understood that the team was still angry about a breach they had suffered six months prior and, should they be breached again, wanted to give the finger to the hacker who did it. Unfortunately, their system was still vulnerable because of the outdated machine that was hooked up to the domain and he was able to gain control. The lesson here is really to patch your systems and avoid using insecure legacy OSes whenever possible, because it was an old machine that let Schloss in, not a weak password. Indeed, “hackergof***yourself” in leet speak isn’t a terrible password, just an embarrassing one if it's exposed. ®

articles.title: Cyber Vulnerabilities Besiege Italy, Absent Clear Cause
articles.context: And guffaw-ingly, whereas in Italy they represent around 57% of all attacks, exploited vulnerabilities showed up in only 6
articles.full_text:
Italy is suffering from a disproportionately large number of cyberattacks, new data suggests. Not only that: The kinds of attacks hitting organizations in the country are vastly different from those hitting other places. Researchers have a triad of theories as to why.

It's true that certain regions and countries face greater cyber-risk thanks to economic, military, and political factors. Israel is a magnet for hacktivists and regional, state-aligned advanced persistent threats (APTs). Brazil's unique history makes it a hive of banking Trojans. The United States economy will always draw the most attention from scammers. It isn't so obvious, though, why Italy is such a popular mark for cybercriminals.

"One of the main reasons why we decided to look into the Italian threat landscape is because Italy kept appearing at the top of our stats in our monthly internal reports," says Gianluca Tiepolo, cybercrime analyst at Intel471. In a report shared exclusively with Dark Reading ahead of its release, Intel471 found that Italy is a total outlier in the global cyber threat landscape. Organizations there are being compromised at a rate beyond what one would reasonably expect, based on the country's size, economy, and politics. And exploits against vulnerabilities and Web infrastructure are far more common in Italy than elsewhere.

Related:Aussies Face Reduced Cybercrime Risk, as Pressure Shifts to SMBs

"We wanted to understand what was driving those stats," Tiepolo says. In the end, though, the data paints a nearly inexplicable picture of what's going on in the land of pasta and Chianti.

Inexplicable Data From Italy's Threat Landscape

Italy is the 25th largest country in the world but, according to this new data, its organizations make up about 7% of all initial access data sold on cybercriminal forums. That's second only to the United States (30%) globally. Italy also ranks fourth among countries most targeted by ransomware.

Far stranger still are the types of cyber intrusions affecting organizations in Italy. According to the new data, initial access brokers (IABs) obtained their initial foothold through vulnerabilities in 57% of cases. Credentials only explained 23% of cases. Meanwhile, IABs have been selling access to victim-owned Web infrastructure in 49% of cases, with remote access and remote desktop tools making up 26% of cases.

So what? Maybe those figures don't pop off the page. Now, though, let's compare them with Intel471's own data from its 2026 Cyber Threat Trends & Outlook report:

Globally in 2025, IABs targeted remote access and remote desktop tools 67% of the time — 41% more often, relatively, than in Italy. Meanwhile, Web infrastructure — by far the most at-risk asset in Italy — represented such a small fraction of Intel471's global data that it didn't even bother to cite it in their report.

Related:Europe Evolves Into Ransomware's Favorite Region

In the same vein, according to the company's global data, credential-based attacks are eight times more common in general than any other type of attack today. It found that 49% of IAB listings advertised credentials as the attack type, compared to 23% in the Italian-specific data. And guffaw-ingly, whereas in Italy they represent around 57% of all attacks, exploited vulnerabilities showed up in only 6.5% of cases globally.

Theory #1: Poor Cybersecurity Hygiene

Though cybersecurity data reporting can be interpreted in different ways depending on the circumstance, Italy does seem like a kind of cyber-risk unicorn, Tiepolo says, adding that Italy has been falling behind on cyber readiness for a long time now.

"I'm Italian," he says. "I've been working with a lot of different Italian clients. What I can say is that Italy is probably slightly behind other European countries, simply based on security technology [adoption]. For example, endpoint detection and response (EDR) technologies became popular in Italy around 2020–2021. Before 2020, most Italian companies didn't use EDR technology. So maybe historically, Italy is a bit behind in actually investing in cybersecurity products and technologies."

Related:Nordic CISOs Handle Rising Cyber Threats Remarkably Well

Also, opportunistic cybercriminals are exploiting known, widespread, and often quite old vulnerabilities en masse to scoop up more victims in Italy than in other countries. "The data we saw last week from PHP2Shell, I think, validates this assessment. Italy is the country in Europe with the largest number of PHP 4, 5, and 7 versions, which are end-of-life," Tiepolo notes.

"A full 90% of initial access offers for Italy are what we call 'wholesale' offers," he posits. "They're not offers that are targeting Italy specifically, but simply exploiting vulnerabilities. Our assessment is that Italy is probably slower than other countries in patching their systems."

Theory #2: A Cyber Risk Network Effect

Another, related possibility is that Italy finds itself victim to a kind of cyber vulnerability network effect. The logic goes something like this: If certain technologies are especially common in a country like Italy, and organizations are slow to address vulnerabilities in those technologies, then that country becomes an attractive economy of scale.

As Intel471 wrote in its report, "Once an actor develops an effective exploitation method, the actor can apply that method to additional exposed systems without conducting a separate, extensive reconnaissance effort against each organization. This reduces the effort required to compromise businesses whose size or profile might otherwise offer limited incentive for a dedicated intrusion."

Researchers couldn't say exactly which technologies, vulnerabilities, or exploitations this theory might refer to, but noted that it does fold into the finding that 90% of initial access offerings to Italian organizations online are sold in bulk.

Without co-signing Intel471's data or conclusions specifically, representatives from the Milan-based cybersecurity firm Cleafy tell Dark Reading that they've observed broadly similar patterns.

"Our threat research does point to a related pattern: attackers reusing tools, infrastructure and techniques to scale campaigns across Italian banking targets," the company wrote via email. It pointed to cases such as the drIBAN Web injection kit, which attackers used to exploit the Certified Electronic Mail (PEC) system used widely across Italy. Cases like drIBAN "don't establish that Italy has a disproportionately large initial-access market, but they do illustrate how reusable attack techniques and infrastructure can help cybercriminals scale operations across multiple targets."

Theory #3: Small & Medium-Sized Businesses Shift the Data

There is one other, potentially significant contributing factor to why Italy looks so different from other countries in cyberattack datasets: its prevalence of small businesses.

Most businesses everywhere are small, but, at least in comparison to other advanced economies, it's especially the case in Italy. A May 2024 "data snapshot for Italy" by McKinsey found that "MSMEs" — micro-, small-, and medium-sized enterprises — contributed roughly 10% more to Italy's economy and employment compared to their relative share in other advanced economies. And last March, the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) published a report that cited that 99.9% of Italian firms in 2023 were SMEs, and 94.8% were micro-enterprises.

"Italy has a lot of small and medium-sized companies," Tiepolo says. "One of the things that came out from the data — especially the extortion data — is that these groups are [disproportionately] targeting small- and medium-sized businesses. So this could be one of the reasons [Italy stands out] in comparison to other countries that have more large companies."

articles.title: Would Your Employees Join a Fake Anthropic AI Preview?
articles.context: In other campaigns, threat actors have abused non-AI, trusted services like link shorteners or cloud collaboration platforms as the first link in a phishing campaign to avoid...
articles.full_text:
By: Intelligence Team, Jacob Malimban

Since September 2026, threat actors have been sending emails that appear to be an invitation to a private Anthropic AI meeting, but are actually attempts to steal Google and Microsoft login credentials. Exclusive access to new AI technology is valuable to many organizations, which is why threat actors use it as a lure in their phishing emails.

Risks to the organization from this campaign include threat actors compromising a sensitive account, accessing the account’s sensitive documents (e.g. proprietary marketing material), and using the compromised account as an initial vector to further infiltrate the organization. Employees must stay vigilant, as these phishing emails bypass current email security technologies due to the abuse of legitimate tools like URL shorteners and CAPTCHAs.

Cofense Intelligence consolidates campaign data, including indicators of compromise (IOCs) such as malicious web addresses, phishing email content, and broader campaign context, into Active Threat Reports (ATRs), providing a comprehensive view of identified threats. ATRs contain the full infection chain from the initial phishing link to the final malware file or credential phishing resource. If one ATR IOC appears in the organization, cybersecurity professionals can read the ATR to understand the phishing attack’s impact and mitigations. Each ATR has been curated by a human analyst. This human-vetted intelligence provides context and the campaign information necessary to mitigate future phishing attacks. For this private Anthropic AI preview campaign, actionable intelligence can be found in ATRs 423868, 423866, and 423475.

Key Points

The campaign contains a tantalizing, private offer to preview Anthropic AI technology, which may be enough for employees to click before inspecting the email.

The video teleconference software GoTo Webinar, which is used to send legitimate meeting emails and is usually not blocked by email security technologies, was abused to send a threat actor’s URL instead.

The URL shortener zpr[.]io, which turns long URLs into short links, has been abused to help these phishing emails bypass current email security technologies.

CAPTCHAs, which are tests that confirm a real human is visiting the website, are similarly abused to prevent automated analysis.

Threat actors use subdomains and dashes (-) to obfuscate the malicious URL.

Step 1: The Invitation Email

Figure 1: Anthropic meeting invitation email used in credential phishing (ATR 423475).

Emails in this campaign claim to be an exclusive invitation to see Anthropic’s new AI tool. Many organizations are deciding how AI fits into their business, so a private preview would be very valuable if the email were real. As developments in AI continue to dominate the news cycle, getting a private preview of advancements in Anthropic’s AI is an effective phishing lure.

The phishing email appears to be an abuse of the legitimate GoTo Webinar service. The email sender address appears to be customercare@gotowebinar[.]com. Threat actors have previously abused that email address and GoTo Webinar’s free trial in 2020. The email also contains a footer with GoTo Webinar branding.

The text in the email contains no obvious spelling errors. The email sender name, however, reads “Austin from nthropic” with the “A” missing from Anthropic. Although this is a small misspelling, it is still a useful warning sign.

The link in the email appears to be generated by Zapier’s URL shortener service. Zapier is a legitimate business process automation company, and their URL Shortener is designed to work with Claude, ChatGPT, and other MCP-compatible AI. Unfortunately, this tool has been abused by threat actors during this Anthropic AI Preview campaign. In other campaigns, threat actors have abused non-AI, trusted services like link shorteners or cloud collaboration platforms as the first link in a phishing campaign to avoid being blocked by email security technologies.

Step 2: The First Checkpoint

Figure 2: Cloudflare CAPTCHA page to hinder automated analysis (ATR 423868).

If the phishing email link is clicked, a CAPTCHA page appears. This Cloudflare CAPTCHA must be completed before the phishing content is shown. This CAPTCHA is the first of two checkpoints that help threat actors block automated scans of their website. Because CAPTCHAs are common on legitimate websites, phishing recipients may believe all is well and everything is secure because of the CAPTCHA.

Step 3: The Fake Meeting Page

Figure 3: Zoom-spoofing page with Anthropic meeting information (ATR 423475).

After completing the CAPTCHA, a Zoom-spoofing meeting invitation page appears. This brand does not match the GoTo Webinar branding from the email. The page’s Zoom branding is consistent with the “zoom” in the malicious domain, us968web-zoom[.]us.

If the phishing recipient wants to attend the “meeting”, they need to register for the event. They are prompted to register with their work email. Credential phishing occurs when the user clicks on either “Continue with Google” or “Continue with Microsoft”.

Step 4: The Second Checkpoint

Figure 4: Custom CAPTCHA page to further hinder automated analysis (ATR 423475).

After clicking “Continue with Google” or “Continue with Microsoft”, another CAPTCHA page appears. This CAPTCHA requires a sliding motion to “unlock” the page. This custom CAPTCHA also appears to be good at detecting and blocking analysis from the most popular VPN services, scanners, Tor browser, and other tools used by defenders.

Because the phishing attack has two distinct CAPTCHAs, automated analysis tools may not be able to follow every step in the credential phishing attack.

Step 5A: The Fake Google Login Page

Figure 5: Google credential phishing page after custom CAPTCHA (ATR 423866).

If “Continue with Google” is clicked and the CAPTCHA is completed, the Google credential phishing page appears. Currently, the Google credential phishing page only captures usernames. It is likely that the page is misconfigured as it does not prompt for a password. After credentials are submitted, the browser does not redirect to the real Google login page, nor does a fake confirmation appear.

Not only is the phishing page remarkably similar to the legitimate Google login page, but the subdomain is also tricky. Employees who quickly read goo[.]gle-access-eventregister[.]icu might not recognize that the URL is not Google.

Step 5B: The Fake Microsoft Login Page

Figure 6: Microsoft credential phishing page after custom CAPTCHA (ATR 423475).

If instead of clicking on “Continue with Google”, the user clicked “Continue with Microsoft”, the Microsoft credential phishing page would load. Just like the previous Google Credential Phishing section, the CAPTCHA must be completed (Figure 4) before the phishing content is shown. Unlike the Google credential phishing page, the Microsoft version captures both the username and password. After credentials are submitted, the browser does not redirect to the real Microsoft login page, nor does a fake confirmation appear.

The Microsoft phishing page mimics the real Microsoft login page well. It also has a tricky subdomain, where office[.]com-access-sharepoint[.]com mimics the real office[.]com or sharepoint[.]com domain. Entering credentials into this page exfiltrates them to the threat actor.

Conclusion

This report covers the private Anthropic AI Preview campaign that uses a fake invitation lure, multiple CAPTCHAs, and Google and Microsoft login page replicas. The campaign was very likely designed by threat actors to bypass current email security technologies and tools used by defenders. Once the employee has reached the credential phishing page, they may not be looking for warning signs anymore. The Google credential phishing page only targets usernames, whereas the Microsoft credential phishing page asks for both the username and password. Stolen credentials give threat actors access to a trusted account, the emails stored in it, and a foothold for future attacks against the organization.

Mitigations

Check if the brand remains consistent from the email to a login page. Although organizations can use services like GoTo Webinar to send meetings on their behalf, a GoTo Webinar email is unlikely to redirect to a Zoom event registration page. Searching for small inconsistencies can help identify an email as part of a phishing campaign.

Remind employees that both the URL and domain determine whether a login page is legitimate. Although the logos and design of the page may look correct, threat actors are skilled at mimicry especially now with the use of AI. Note that the URL in the email might not be the same URL as the login page due to URL redirects.

Use Cofense Vision. Vision AI can cluster structurally related messages even when threat actors rotate senders, subjects, URLs, and page elements.

Invest in human-vetted threat intelligence to complement automated feeds. Automated systems are fast but cannot always tell the difference between a legitimate tool being used by IT and the same tool being abused by threat actors, and human analysis adds the context and confidence that AI-based speed cannot provide.

To learn how Cofense combines AI-driven detection, human-vetted threat intelligence, and rapid remediation to identify and stop sophisticated phishing attacks that bypass traditional security defenses, visit cofense.com/platform.

articles.title: ZDI-26-847: MLflow AI Gateway Server-Side Request Forgery Information Disclosure Vulnerability
articles.context: Vulnerability Details This vulnerability allows remote attackers to initiate arbitrary server-side requests on affected installations of MLflow
articles.full_text:
Vulnerability Details

This vulnerability allows remote attackers to initiate arbitrary server-side requests on affected installations of MLflow. Authentication is required to exploit this vulnerability.

The specific flaw exists within the processing of the api_base field. The issue results from the lack of proper validation of a URI prior to accessing resources. An attacker can leverage this vulnerability to initiate requests in the context of the service account.

Additional Details

Fixed in MLflow 3.17.0https://github.com/mlflow/mlflow/pull/25761

Disclosure Timeline

2026-06-30 - Vulnerability reported to vendor

2026-10-29 - Coordinated public release of advisory

articles.title: Bluesky Is Blocking Links to a Major Leak of DHS Employee Records
articles.context: Emma Best, cofounder of DDoSecrets, says this is not the first time a social media platform has wrongly labeled the organization's website malicious or tried to restrict access...
articles.full_text:
Bluesky is blocking users from opening links to a newly leaked archive of records on more than 41,000 Department of Homeland Security employees and contractors, and labels the pages “malicious.”

The files include people’s email addresses and phone numbers, “shared without their authorization,” Bluesky tells WIRED, in violation of its community guidelines. The company says it chose to block the links, rather than remove individual posts, “to avoid limiting public discussion or restricting broader access to reporting and commentary.”

The DHS records, published Wednesday by the transparency nonprofit Distributed Denial of Secrets, list employees’ and contractors’ names, contact information, and membership in internal groups, tied in some cases to surveillance and undercover operations. A WIRED investigation found that the files lay out in detail how DHS is organized, from senior leadership to individual immigration agents, and in some cases appear to show who has access to certain technologies.

Users who try to open the archive through Bluesky’s website or app land on a page labeled “Blocked Link,” which says the URL has been identified as “malicious” and blocked for their safety. Bluesky did not respond to questions about whether the block was imposed automatically or whether any government agency had asked the company to restrict access to the data.

The DDoSecrets homepage loads normally from Bluesky. At least one third-party app, Klearsky, opens links to the DHS archive with no warning.

Bluesky promotes a decentralized approach to content moderation that lets users pick independent services that label or filter posts. Its current community guidelines bar sharing “home addresses, personal contact info, financial or medical data, or identification documents.” (A preview of the DHS leak analyzed by WIRED apparently contained work-related contact information one expert described as details that would be printed “on a business card.”) The same guidelines explicitly protect “factual reporting” on matters of public interest that are “related to government transparency and public officials.”

Bluesky started in 2019 as a Twitter research project, later became independent, and opened to the public in February 2024. By August of this year, it counted 45 million registered accounts, and an estimated 10.4 million people used its mobile app in June. Toni Schneider, the founding CEO of Automattic, has run the company since cofounder Jay Graber stepped down in March. Because the network runs on an open protocol, outside developers can build their own Bluesky apps and decide which of the company’s moderation labels to apply.

Emma Best, cofounder of DDoSecrets, says this is not the first time a social media platform has wrongly labeled the organization's website malicious or tried to restrict access to its publications. Twitter suspended DDoSecrets’ account in 2020, prior to the Elon Musk acquisition and X rebrand, and blocked links to its website after the group published BlueLeaks, a 269-gigabyte trove of internal records from hundreds of police agencies and fusion centers. Best says tech platforms often give in to government pressure but insists they cannot prevent the information from spreading. “They can’t stop the signal,” they say.

A group calling itself the Department of Peace gave the archive, dubbed “Icepick,” to DDoSecrets and journalist maia arson crimew. crimew also built a website for searching the records, and Bluesky blocks that site in its website and app as well.

At least one of Bluesky’s competitors has taken a different tack. On X, the Grok chatbot built by X’s parent company pointed curious users to the Icepick website, describing it as a “cleaned searchable web tool” and saying that the complete dataset can be downloaded via DDoSecrets’ website or by torrent. X did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

articles.context: We collectively dodged the bullet so that we only got grazed, but the good luck won’t last forever

Risky Bulletin Podcast

October 29, 2026

Srsly Risky Biz: Chinese AI can learn to love the West

Presented by

Amberleigh Jack

Producer and Editor

Tom Uren

Policy & Intelligence

Tom Uren and Amberleigh Jack talk about new research that shows that Chinese open-weight AI models can be reeducated to remove pro-CCP bias. Good news for American businesses that want cheap AI, but we suspect that many knives will still be out for Chinese open-weight models.

They also discuss the near-misses from the PHP and Brotli bugs. We collectively dodged the bullet so that we only got grazed, but the good luck won’t last forever.

Finally, Tom looked at CISA’s 2030 strategy. Amazingly, it doesn’t really mention AI at all. Bizarre!

articles.title: Node2Shell: Reproducing CVE-2026-111497 in the Node.js Brotli decoder
articles.context: Datadog Cloud SIEM includes two detections that identify command execution associated with Node2Shell exploitation: Shell spawned by web server detects shells, download...
articles.full_text:
Key points and observations

On October 21, 2026, Node.js released fixes for CVE-2026-111497, an out-of-bounds write in its bundled Brotli decoder. The upstream flaw sits in the Google Brotli C library, so the blast radius reaches Python, Bun, .NET, Java brotli4j, Envoy, and Istio. Every affected runtime now has a fix available.

We reproduced the flaw on the official Node.js 24.22.0 image and verified that the patched build rejects the same bytes.

Capturing an application-level trace is difficult because the process continues running despite memory corruption.

Only patching fixes this vulnerability. The application process decodes the data, so neither the web server nor a web application firewall (WAF) ever sees the malicious content. An edge rule that rejects Brotli-compressed request bodies is a useful tripwire and nothing more.

What happened

On October 21, 2026, Node.js released security updates for CVE-2026-111497, an out-of-bounds write in the Brotli decoder. The CVE record gives the flaw a Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) v4.0 score of 9.2, or Critical, while Node.js rates its severity as High. Node.js 22.23.4, 24.22.1, and 26.12.1 contain the fix, and end-of-life release lines carry the same vulnerable decoder but have no patch.

What looked like a Node.js problem on day one turned out to be far broader. Most runtimes embed the upstream Google Brotli C library, where the bug lives. Over the following week many consumers of that decoder shipped its own advisory:

Product

Affected

First fixed release

Node.js 22, 24, and 26

Before 22.23.4, 24.22.1, and 26.12.1

22.23.4, 24.22.1, 26.12.1

Google Brotli

1.0.3 through 1.0.9, 1.1.0, and 1.2.0

1.0.10, 1.1.1, 1.2.1

Python Brotli and brotlicffi

1.2.0 and earlier

1.2.1 and 1.2.1.0

Bun

1.0.21 through 1.4.3

1.4.4

Java brotli4j

1.23.0 and earlier

1.24.0

.NET 8, 9, and 10

Before the October 25, 2026 out-of-band update

8.0.33, 9.0.22, 10.0.14

Envoy and Istio

All releases before the first fix in each supported branch

Envoy: 1.36.12, 1.37.8, 1.38.6, 1.39.3, 1.40.0; Istio: 1.29.9, 1.30.6, 1.31.2 (first fixed in each branch)

Two details deserve special attention. Java's brotli4j bundles its own native Brotli build inside its jars, so patching the operating system's libbrotli does not fix it. Bun executables built with bun build \--compile embed the runtime and stay vulnerable until they are rebuilt.

Before the disclosure, Imperva demonstrated code execution on the official Node.js 24.22.0 Linux ARM64 image. Their exploit needed several attempts and was not released. A public proof of concept appeared on October 22, 2026. On standard builds it produces a crash and a limited memory read. As of October 29, 2026, there have been confirmed in-the-wild exploitation, and CISA's known exploited vulnerabilities catalog now lists the CVE.

How to know if you're affected

A service is exposed when it decompresses Brotli data that an attacker controls, which comes through two common paths. A few additional considerations apply to both.

Outbound requests (the quiet path)

Outbound requests are the harder path to see. Node.js's built-in fetch() decodes a Content-Encoding: br response automatically, whether or not the request asked for Brotli. The axios, got, and node-fetch clients advertise and decode Brotli by default. Any feature that fetches URLs supplied by users, such as webhooks, link previews, and feed readers, enables an attacker to force the encoding selection server side since the attacker controls the response headers, and fetch() decodes a body labeled br even when the application explicitly forces Accept-Encoding: identity.

In our testing, no exception surfaced at runtime: one crafted stream completed with an empty body and an HTTP 200, and the only visible signals were CPU usage and, under concurrency, a starved threadpool that still answered health checks.

The same holds outside Node.js: Python HTTP clients decode Brotli responses automatically whenever Brotli or brotlicffi is installed, even if application code never imports the package.

Inbound requests (the visible path)

Inbound attacks are easier to observe. A compressed request body is a recognizable attack surface, your reverse proxy or WAF can see the Content-Encoding: br header, and the framework parser is a known place to audit. Express 5 and body-parser 2.x accept Brotli-compressed request bodies by default in their JSON, raw, text, and URL-encoded parsers, and Koa and NestJS inherit the behavior. Express 4 rejects those bodies with an HTTP 415, and a bare Node.js HTTP server does not decompress anything. Parsers mounted before authentication expose the decoder to unauthenticated requests.

Other considerations

Both paths share a versioning trap: process.versions.brotli still reports 1.2.0 on the patched Node.js 24.22.1, because the cherry-picked fix does not bump the embedded version string. process.version is reliable only for official distributions from nodejs.org.

If you cannot patch immediately, set inflate: false on Express 5 and body-parser 2.x parsers, or reject Content-Encoding: br at the reverse proxy. These measures only mitigate the risk, as patching is the only complete solution. These mitigations could also break the functionality as they reject all compressed request bodies, do nothing for the outbound path, and break compressed bodies sent by legitimate clients.

How the vulnerability works

A Brotli stream is divided into blocks, and the decoder moves to a new block only when the current block's length budget runs out. A 23 MB stream of otherwise ordinary commands drains that budget while producing no output, and its closing commands request a block switch that the format forbids. These steps are where the attacker does the proper setup to exploit the bug.

In the next stage, we see the impact of the vulnerability. In Brotli 1.2.0, DecodeBlockTypeAndLength() returns a boolean, and it answers two different questions with the same "false" value: "this stream is malformed" and "I need more input". Callers cannot tell the two apart, and on the decoder's fast path the return value is dropped entirely.

The two arms then diverge. The first path is an overflow where the decoder parks the unconsumed bytes in a small internal buffer while it waits for more input. The copy has no bound check, so bytes past the end of the buffer land in adjacent decoder state. The write happens inside a single heap allocation, so the tooling built to catch memory corruption never sees it, and the process keeps running. The other path is that it keeps spinning. The decoder retries the forbidden switch in a loop, which pins a CPU core inside a single call that never returns: a one-request denial of service.

From memory corruption to code execution

In this case, memory corruption has impactful consequences. The corrupted decoder state controls where the decoder reads from and writes to next, so a crafted stream can redirect both operations. This gives an attacker two primitives:

A repeatable read of heap memory that leaves through the decompressed response.

A redirected write. In our lab, we aimed it at an unmapped page and produced a deterministic crash.

Both primitives are real. The read primitive is the most operationally interesting, because heap bytes returning over the wire are the first step of a staged attack.

Three obstacles stand between these primitives and a shell:

The addresses move. The heap layout that the corruption targets is randomized and changes between requests, so what one request leaks, the next request can’t reliably use.

The corruption bytes are also the decoder's input. The decoder consumes the bytes that steer the corruption again as it continues, so the values an attacker needs are constrained by the values the decoder will accept. This is the deepest structural obstacle we found.

A managed runtime stands in the way. Between the corrupted C state and control flow sits the machinery of a language runtime with its own allocator, its own compiled code, and its own defenses, none of which the original C library was designed around.

After measuring all three obstacles, we assess that the flaw is exploitable and that the gap between these primitives and reliable code execution is engineering effort. This matches Imperva's report of successful execution after several attempts on the official Node.js 24.22.0 image.

How the patch addresses the flaw

The patch is small and precise. The block-switch helper now returns a real error code, and both code paths treat a failed check as a hard stop instead of a request for more input. It rejects a crafted stream with a format error (-17) before anything is written to the decoder's state.

The release timeline is the troubling part. The fix was committed to the upstream Brotli repository on February 27, 2026, but the fixed library releases did not ship until October 21, 2026. For eight months, anyone who downloaded Brotli, or a runtime that embeds it, received the vulnerable version even though the corrected code sat in the public repository. The release also ships without a regression test or a changelog entry for this fix.

How to detect exploitation

This CVE involves no attacker-controlled infrastructure, so there are no conventional indicators. Detection rests on behavioral signals, and no single signal is conclusive. Correlate across three layers.

Decoder error signals

The vulnerable and patched builds respond differently to the same malicious bytes. Both responses appear in application logs and APM error spans and the error you see depends on whether the build is patched. On a vulnerable build, Node.js returns Z_BUF_ERROR with the message "unexpected end of file". On a patched build, Node.js returns ERR__ERROR_FORMAT_BLOCK_SWITCH, and Python returns "brotli: decoder is unhealthy". The vulnerable signal also appears for benign truncated input so you have to still look a little closer and differentiate the benign truncated input vs real attacks.

Process signals

A worker that exits with signal 139 (SIGSEGV) right after a Brotli transfer is a crash attempt, and a process pinned at 100% CPU inside a decompression call is the spin arm. Correlate on workload identity (the container, pod, or service) and not the process ID, because the process that crashed is gone and a successful attempt may not crash at all. The strongest signal is behavioral: a shell or new outbound connections from the same workload.

The disclosure channel

Decompressed output that contains bytes the client never sent is the read primitive in action. Investigate any such output immediately. Because the leaked heap memory leaves through the decompressed response, start by listing the endpoints that return or reflect decompressed content back to the caller, such as echo, preview, conversion, or proxy features.

What does not work

Payload byte signatures, because the attacker-controlled parts of the stream change per target and the exploit is the decode process itself, not the decompressed content.

Content matching at the WAF, because the web server forwards compressed bytes and never decodes them.

Body-size limits, because the tested middleware counts decompressed bytes, so the 23 MB compressed trigger still reaches the decoder.

How Datadog can help

Datadog Cloud Security Management tracks CVE-2026-111497 and the related vendor advisories as vulnerability findings on hosts and container images, so your patching status lives in one place.

Datadog Code Security reports the vulnerable services that ship dependency inventories. Its library inventory identifies which services to prioritize: those running Express 5, body-parser 2.x, or Koa parsers, and those using HTTP clients that auto-decode Brotli.

Datadog Application Performance Monitoring (APM) helps you hunt for attempts. This query requires capturing Content-Encoding, which is not set by default in Node.js spans, so make sure to check how the language tracer you are using behaves. For example in Node.js it can be enabled by including content-encoding in DD_TRACE_HEADER_TAGS. Pivot on the services that accept Content-Encoding: br request bodies using this query, and review services that fetch user-supplied URLs. Decoder failures surface as APM error spans correlated with the request and the client address. The process telemetry that the Datadog Agent collects shows a crashed attempt as a worker restart with exit code 139.

Datadog Workload Protection includes coverage through the CVE-2026-111497 Node2Shell Exploit Content Pack. This pack includes a new security policy with three Agent rules that cover post-exploitation that surfaces a CVE-2026-111497 Node2Shell exploitation detected signal.

Datadog Cloud SIEM includes two detections that identify command execution associated with Node2Shell exploitation:

Shell spawned by web server detects shells, download utilities, and reconnaissance commands launched by web servers or web processes. It uses process activity events with parent process information.

Shell spawned by web process uses Linux auditd logs to detect shells or download utilities executed in a web server context.

Conclusion

CVE-2026-111497 shows how a single unchecked return value in a widely shared C library can ripple across nearly every major runtime. Because the decoder runs inside the application's own process, the flaw sidesteps the defenses most teams rely on. The eight months between the upstream fix and its release are a reminder that a fix in a public repository protects no one until it ships.

Exploitation has been confirmed, which further proves the primitives are real and the path to code execution is a matter of effort. Patch to Node.js 22.23.4, 24.22.1, or 26.12.1 or your vendor's fixed package, rebuild container images, restart every process, and inventory the other Brotli consumers in your environment.

articles.title: Most Servers on the Planet Are Vulnerable to This Firmware Code-Execution Flaw
articles.context: With publicly available patch code, it will be trivial for advanced hackers to learn how the vulnerability is triggered and to build working exploits
articles.full_text:
Defenders across the world face the burden of responding to yet another botched code-execution vulnerability, this time in boot-time firmware used by most of the world’s server vendors and data centers.

The vulnerability, with a severity rating of 9.5 out of 10, resides in the TianoCore EDK II, an open source codebase that hardware makers and cloud providers use to create the UEFI firmware that runs during the boot-up sequence. Last year, a representative of the UEFI Forum called EDK2 the “preeminent solution / implementation of the UEFI specifications.” Virtually all UEFI suppliers (sometimes still called IBVs or independent BIOS vendors), including AMI, Insyde, and Phoenix, use the reference code extensively. Project Mu, Microsoft’s hardened EDK2 fork, used the code containing the vulnerable component as well.

The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-97631, is a memory-corruption flaw in an ICMP component that attackers can exploit to execute malicious code that runs before the operating system and firmware can implement defenses like Secure Boot, which establishes a chain of trust for all code, including the Trusted Platform Module (TPM), loaded during boot. While final payloads delivered by CVE-2026-97631 have no persistence—meaning they run only once—they can give attackers a wide opening to install other payloads that also run each time early in the boot process.

The Cat Has Left the Bag

The parties that discovered CVE-2026-97631—Alex Matrosov of Anthropic and Dan Holmes of Google—had arranged for it to stay under wraps until a coordinated disclosure that was scheduled for January. AMI, a maker of motherboards and other hardware, published this pull request last month that detailed the vulnerability and included a code fix. Once the post came to the attention of the discovering parties, TianoCore Project members published a public advisory last week.

With publicly available patch code, it will be trivial for advanced hackers to learn how the vulnerability is triggered and to build working exploits. Further compounding the urgency, patching UEFI code vulnerabilities in millions of end devices sold and used by thousands of hardware makers and cloud providers is cumbersome and time-consuming. Word of the vulnerability comes six days after another botched disclosure, this one involving a critical code-execution vulnerability in the PHP programming language.

“This vulnerability in the ICMP parser of the EDK2 network stack is interesting in terms of how it affects the chain of trust and the broader ecosystem,” said HD Moore, creator of Metasploit and chief research officer at security firm Dragos. “An attacker intent on compromising a nearby endpoint or server could use this bug to hijack program flow at a point where the boot process still has access to sensitive components, like the endpoint’s TPM. This could be used to break disk encryption for cases where an attacker has short-term network access (and it would be even easier in a theft scenario).”

CVE-2026-97631 is a 16-year-old buffer overflow in the PXE-Base Code driver (NetworkPkg/UefiPxeBcDxe), which is responsible for allowing servers, storage equipment, and other devices to boot using code downloaded from a local network. During this process—known as the pre-execution environment boot—the driver uses a network listener to monitor for ICMP errors. Because the driver doesn’t enforce a memory copy limit of 504 bytes, overwriting adjacent data, a malicious insider or a hacker who has gained low-level access to a local network can send an error message that appends code past this limit. The IUEFI module running on the CPU then becomes corrupted.

articles.title: A matter of national secrecy.
articles.context: Tracked as CVE-2026-101767, the vulnerability allows unauthenticated attackers to exploit a SQL injection flaw and potentially take complete control of affected systems. The activity follows previous attacks against Oracle enterprise software, including a campaign by the Clop extortion gang that exploited a separate...
articles.full_text:
Senators accuse the White House of illegally withholding a secret surveillance court ruling. A suspected surveillance operation targets Starlink users. Attackers probe vulnerable Oracle E-Business Suite systems. The FBI shuts down a bulletproof hosting provider. Tailworm targets Tailscale. Ohio’s Auditor of State investigates a cyberattack. A suspected ransomware attack disrupts Israel’s largest vehicle importer. Norway raises their cyber risk level to high. Our guest is Amy Blackshaw, Senior Vice President of Product Marketing for Identity at Palo Alto Networks, discussing AI exploits and identity containment. AI science needs a spam filter.

Today is Wednesday October 28th 2026. I’m Dave Bittner. And this is your CyberWire Intel Briefing.

Senators accuse the White House of illegally withholding a secret surveillance court ruling.

Two Democratic senators accuse the Trump administration of illegally withholding a secret surveillance court ruling as Congress considers renewing a controversial intelligence program.

Senators Ron Wyden and Adam Schiff say the administration missed a September deadline to release findings from the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court concerning Section 702 of FISA.

The court reportedly found that intelligence agencies used filtering tools to search Americans’ intercepted communications without required safeguards, including approvals and documentation.

Section 702 expired in June, but surveillance continues under a court authorization lasting until March.

The administration has promoted the program’s effectiveness while keeping the ruling classified, despite earlier promises to release it.

Civil liberties organizations are urging Congress to withhold reauthorization until the findings become public.

Wyden and Schiff have demanded an explanation by November sixth.

The dispute raises a fundamental question: How can Congress evaluate the legality of government surveillance when critical findings about that surveillance remain secret?

A suspected surveillance operation targets Starlink users.

Cybersecurity researchers have uncovered a suspected surveillance operation targeting users of SpaceX’s Starlink satellite internet service.

According to Reuters, researchers at TrendAI found that an Israeli advertising technology company, Discover-Tech, was aggressively bidding for ads targeting Starlink users in more than 100 countries.

The company was particularly active in conflict zones, including Syria, Yemen, Libya, and South Sudan, where legitimate advertising demand is limited.

Researchers believe the activity was designed to exploit data leaked through online advertising auctions, potentially allowing operators to identify, locate, and track Starlink users.

TrendAI initially identified the operation only by the codename Shadow-Earth-79, reportedly declining to name Discover-Tech over legal concerns.

Citizen Lab and Confiant independently identified the company, prompting Google, Comcast, and others to remove it from their advertising platforms.

Attackers probe vulnerable Oracle E-Business Suite systems.

Attackers are already probing for vulnerable Oracle E-Business Suite systems following the disclosure of a critical security flaw.

Tracked as CVE-2026-101767, the vulnerability allows unauthenticated attackers to exploit a SQL injection flaw and potentially take complete control of affected systems.

Oracle released a patch on October twentieth, urging customers to update immediately.

Security firm Defused says its honeypots detected attempted exploitation on October twenty-seventh, although Oracle has not confirmed active exploitation in the wild.

Shadowserver has identified more than 670 internet-exposed Oracle E-Business Suite instances, mostly in the United States. It’s unclear how many remain vulnerable.

The activity follows previous attacks against Oracle enterprise software, including a campaign by the Clop extortion gang that exploited a separate E-Business Suite vulnerability to target major corporations and universities.

The FBI shuts down a bulletproof hosting provider.

The FBI has seized the domain of Virtualine, a so-called bulletproof hosting provider accused of supporting cybercrime, money laundering, and the distribution of child sexual abuse material.

Operating under several names, Virtualine openly advertised hosting services for illegal activities, promising to ignore abuse complaints and law enforcement requests.

According to the Justice Department, the company continued supporting a forum distributing illegal content even after receiving complaints from international authorities. Prosecutors also allege Virtualine helped the forum’s operators establish another site and attempted to launder cryptocurrency payments.

No arrests or criminal charges were announced.

The seizure follows international crackdowns on similar providers linked to ransomware operations. But researchers warn that disrupting these services often simply pushes criminal customers toward replacement providers, rather than eliminating the underlying market.

Tailworm targets Tailscale.
