In-the-Wild Attack Abuses AI Agents' Trust in Markdown

A new AI agent prompt injection technique exploits how coding assistants consume local instruction files, blurring the line between text documents and executable actions.

Alexander Culafi,Senior News Writer,Dark Reading

October 26, 2026

4 Min Read

Source: ipuwadol via Getty Images

A new indirect prompt injection attack relies on using markdown files in an end user's downloads folder to install malware and steal credentials.

That's according to Forever Security, which recently detailed a novel AI agent attack they captured in the wild. According to a research blog post, when an attacker plants a malicious file in a user's download folder, the user's agent may treat the file as trusted instructions and execute actions based on it.

What is notable about this attack compared to other prompt injection threats found in research reports is that this was not a case where the researchers developed the attack as a proof of concept. Rather, Forever's Gal Weizman and Omer Samet wrote that the AI security firm "caught live malware on a real customer's machine, attempting a new kind of attack the industry had not documented — and stopped it cold, before any code ran."

Malicious Markdowns

As the blog post authors explained, Forever Security found a malicious plaintext file named "AGENTS.md" in a customer's downloads folder, disguised as engineering notes. ".md" is a markdown file, used to guide agent behavior, and is trusted by many AI coding agents like OpenAI's Codex or Claude Code — Forever reproduced the attack with both (the original variant targeted Codex specifically).

Related:Claude Model Builds Exploits Across Major Browsers & OSes

Researchers were unable to determine exactly how the file got on the user's computer, though they noted that it's the kind of file that a malicious website could attempt to download onto the user's computer. Then, when the coding agent is launched in that directory, it reads the instruction file as part of its project context.

According to Forever, the malicious instructions can persuade the agent to modify its configuration and perform follow-on actions. If the agent does ingest one of these malicious markdowns, the planted file makes the agent rewrite its own configuration, opening itself up for an attacker to instruct it to install malware or share its own login tokens.

In testing, Forever said the Codex attack chain succeeded more than 90% of the time. For Claude Code, the researchers reported roughly a 50% success rate, though certain variables may have influenced this success rate. For example, Claude Code uses a different installation path from Codex, which the original attack targeted.

'Nothing to Patch'

The attack requires someone only to grant their coding agent access to their home directory downloads folder, and that the agent can interact with web content. Forever says that according to its telemetry, about half of its customers run a coding agent inside their downloads folder, and a quarter of agent sessions open a real browser.

Related:GhostAction Hacking Wave Fizzles, but Attackers Lurk on in GitHub

"There is nothing here for OpenAI or Anthropic to patch. An agent that follows the AGENTS.md in its folder is doing exactly what it was built to do, the same way a browser that renders a phishing page is working as designed," the blog post read. "The problem is the circumstances: a folder the web can write to, trusted as if the user filled it. So the vector stays open. It is one early example of a bigger pattern: defenses built around a human break when an agent takes the human's place."

Weizman, lead researcher at Forever Security, tells Dark Reading that AI firms like OpenAI and Anthropic "may consider making agents aware of the risk of following commands originated by files that can be dropped by websites (such as inside the Downloads folder)," but adds that the issue described by the research is "mostly beyond their security model."

In the instance captured in the wild, Weizman says the exploit worked but was then blocked from follow-on activity by Forever's real-time security product, preventing an NPM package from being installed. Forever only managed to discover the initial example of the attack in the wild, though Weizman says the company is actively searching for more attempts.

Related:Exposed to PHP2Shell? Cyber Experts Weigh in With Advice

For defenders, Forever recommends treating the user's home-directory download location (~/Downloads) as "hostile ground for agents," as by default it's the only way web content can reach a coding agent. Users can also check for instruction files they did not write, examine agent configurations for unexpected changes, and leave approval gates and sandboxes enabled. If a red flag has been found, the researchers said organizations should assume login tokens are compromised and rotate credentials.

About the Author

Alexander Culafi

Senior News Writer, Dark Reading

Alex is an award-winning writer, journalist, and podcast host based in Boston. After cutting his teeth writing for independent gaming publications as a teenager, he graduated from Emerson College in 2016 with a Bachelor of Science in journalism. He has previously been published on VentureFizz, Search Security, Nintendo World Report, and elsewhere.

At Dark Reading, he covers a variety of cybersecurity topics, including the cybercrime ecosystem, open source security, and the intersection between AI and threat actors. In his spare time, Alex hosts the weekly Nintendo podcast, "Talk Nintendo Podcast," and works on personal writing projects, including two previously self-published science fiction novels.

He has received numerous awards, including TechTarget's Writer of the Year in 2022 as well as more than 10 Azbee awards for his reporting between 2022 and today.

articles.title: The breach wasn't in the model.
articles.context: An attacker subsequently used it to gain control of LiteLLM’s GitHub repositories and distribute credential-stealing malware through a compromised software update. Researchers say fewer than one percent of vulnerabilities are actively exploited, but organizations continue allocating resources based largely on...
articles.full_text:
A cybersecurity startup claims to have accessed sensitive internal documents at Anthropic. The Pentagon spins up covert technology programs. AI developers get a crash course in key management. A ransomware recovery executive faces federal fraud charges. Two men are accused of using AI generated phone calls to scam bank customers. Stadia RAT rises from the StealC ashes. Researchers extract sensitive information using USB power-management signals. Patching what matters…matters. Monday business briefing. Tim Starks from CyberScoop is discussing targeted ads as a security risk. Championship rings come with a catch.

Today is Monday October 26th 2026. I’m Dave Bittner. And this is your CyberWire Intel Briefing.

A cybersecurity startup claims to have accessed sensitive internal documents at Anthropic.

Cybersecurity startup Cathedral says its researchers used AI agents to gain access to sensitive internal systems at Anthropic in less than twelve hours. According to The Washington Post, the researchers exploited vulnerabilities in third-party business software, accessing systems containing meeting transcripts, salary information, and internal Slack messages.

Anthropic confirmed the intrusion but said access was limited to certain sales, human resources, and IT systems. Customer conversations, proprietary code, and AI model weights were not exposed. The company says its monitoring detected some suspicious activity, and it disabled the affected systems and worked with vendors to address the vulnerabilities.

Cathedral, founded by former DOGE employees, conducted the research through Anthropic’s security testing program. Anthropic disputes the startup’s characterization of the national security implications and says researchers violated some program rules.

The findings highlight a familiar security problem with potentially higher stakes: even cutting-edge AI companies depend on ordinary enterprise software, with all its ordinary vulnerabilities.

The Pentagon spins up covert technology programs.

The Pentagon has quietly established a new agency dedicated to disrupting foreign military technology programs through covert operations.

According to POLITICO, the Technology Support Office, established in April, consolidates two classified intelligence programs and aims to expand capabilities including cyberattacks, supply-chain sabotage, and deception operations.

The agency reportedly employs engineers, intelligence officers, and special operations personnel to develop tools that could delay adversaries’ technological advances, particularly in artificial intelligence and advanced weapons systems.

Deputy Defense Secretary Steve Feinberg spearheaded the initiative, which has attracted opposition from Cyber Command and Special Operations Command over competing responsibilities and resources.

Supporters argue the effort is necessary to preserve America’s military advantage. Critics worry its secrecy could enable questionable operations and undermine congressional oversight.

The Pentagon disputes POLITICO’s reporting, calling its underlying claims inaccurate.

AI developers get a crash course in key management.

A supply-chain attack affecting tens of thousands of AI developers began with a security mistake made months earlier.

LiteLLM says it accidentally published a configuration file containing a master key in May. Although the file was removed, the key was never revoked. An attacker subsequently used it to gain control of LiteLLM’s GitHub repositories and distribute credential-stealing malware through a compromised software update.

Security firm Wiz says the malicious package was downloaded roughly 49,000 times. Within hours, attackers were testing stolen AWS credentials for access to AI models, suggesting a possible LLMjacking operation.

LiteLLM warns anyone who installed version 1.107.0 to assume their credentials were stolen and rotate them.

No organization has publicly confirmed a resulting breach. It’s LiteLLM’s second supply-chain compromise this year.

A ransomware recovery executive faces federal fraud charges.

A Florida businessman faces federal fraud charges for allegedly charging ransomware victims millions of dollars to recover their data while secretly paying the hackers responsible.

Prosecutors say Zohar Pinhasi, who operated the data recovery firm MonsterCloud, claimed he could decrypt files without paying ransoms. Instead, investigators allege he collected more than $19 million from clients while paying hackers over $8 million. In one case, an $8,200 ransom payment reportedly became a $150,000 customer bill.

The indictment follows a 2019 ProPublica investigation exposing the alleged scheme. MonsterCloud’s clients included law enforcement agencies that believed they were avoiding payments to criminals.

Pinhasi has pleaded not guilty and faces up to 20 years in prison if convicted.

For victims already paying one extortionist, prosecutors allege MonsterCloud effectively added another.

Two men are accused of using AI generated phone calls to scam bank customers.

Dutch police have arrested two men accused of using AI-generated phone calls to steal more than $425,000 from 170 bank customers.

The scheme began with automated calls warning of suspicious account activity. Victims who pressed a button were connected to a fake bank employee, who instructed them to download an app and scan their debit cards.

The app captured contactless payment data, which accomplices used to withdraw cash from ATMs.

The suspects, ages 23 and 25, were arrested October 6. Police also seized servers, phones, and laptops.

Both remain in custody as the investigation continues.

Stadia RAT rises from the StealC ashes.

Four months after European law enforcement disrupted the StealC malware operation, its seller is back with a new product.

Researchers at Varonis say Stadia RAT builds on StealC’s credential-stealing capabilities, adding remote desktop control, command execution, file management, and the ability to deploy additional malware.

The Windows malware targets browsers, cryptocurrency wallets, and messaging applications. It also avoids systems configured for several Eastern European and Central Asian languages, establishes persistence through scheduled tasks, and can disable portions of Microsoft Defender’s protection.

Subscriptions range from $300 to $900 a month, with former StealC customers offered a free trial.

Researchers confirmed that Stadia reuses code from StealC, illustrating a familiar limitation of law enforcement takedowns: dismantling criminal infrastructure doesn’t necessarily put its operators out of business.

Researchers extract sensitive information using USB power-management signals.

Researchers at Korea University have demonstrated a technique for extracting sensitive information from air-gapped computers using USB power-management signals.

Called SPECTER, the method allows malware with administrator privileges to encode data through changes in USB device states, without conventional network connections or USB data transfers.

Researchers demonstrated three ways to receive the signals: monitoring smartphone charging indicators, observing changes in USB peripherals, and detecting electromagnetic emissions from USB cables.

Transmission speeds were extremely slow, topping out at one bit per second, making the technique more suitable for stealing passwords or cryptographic keys than large files.

The attack also requires hardware or firmware modifications, and some configurations produced no usable signals.

Researchers suggest monitoring unusual USB power-management activity, although the effectiveness of that approach remains untested.

Patching what matters…matters.

Security teams are patching more vulnerabilities than ever, but new research suggests all that effort isn’t necessarily making organizations safer.

According to Qualys, vulnerability closures increased sixfold between 2022 and 2025, reaching 473 million. Yet the percentage of critical vulnerabilities remaining unpatched after seven days actually increased.

The problem? Prioritization.

Researchers say fewer than one percent of vulnerabilities are actively exploited, but organizations continue allocating resources based largely on severity scores rather than evidence of real-world attacks.

Meanwhile, attackers are moving faster. Across the most critical exploited vulnerabilities, manual remediation failed to keep pace 88 percent of the time.

Qualys recommends shifting toward intelligence-driven, automated remediation that prioritizes actual exploitation and business impact.

The takeaway: Security isn’t necessarily about patching more. It’s about patching what matters.

Monday business briefing.

Investment and acquisition activity remains brisk across cybersecurity, with AI security attracting particular attention.

San Francisco-based Reach Security raised $50 million in Series B funding to expand its exposure management platform. AI agent security startup Opsin secured $21 million, while Asymptote Labs raised $5.5 million for its AI runtime security technology. AI penetration testing firm ManticoreAI also announced an undisclosed seed round.

On the acquisition front, Proofpoint agreed to buy data and AI security company Varonis for $6.3 billion, potentially creating a combined business serving more than 16,000 enterprises.

Anthropic acquired confidential AI data specialist OPAQUE, while Canadian AI company Cohere agreed to purchase Czech vulnerability management provider AISLE.

Elsewhere, legal technology firm Lineal acquired Swiss digital forensics company Forentec, and Britain’s Bytes Technology Group purchased Microsoft security specialist CyberOne.

The common thread across these deals is growing investment in AI security, data protection, and automated vulnerability management.

Championship rings come with a catch.

The New York Knicks celebrated their first NBA championship in more than half a century by offering employees free championship rings. Unfortunately, the offer was fake, and the real prize was mandatory cybersecurity training.

According to The New York Times, Madison Square Garden sent employees a simulated phishing email inviting them to choose between two ring designs. Anyone who clicked the link earned a trip to cybersecurity class instead.

The exercise followed a real security incident in which attackers reportedly used phished employee credentials to hack and extort the organization.

MSG acknowledged that using championship rings as bait was an unfortunate mistake. The company says it’s distributing more than 275 actual rings and pieces of jewelry worth over $3.7 million.

For employees who fell for the phishing test, the championship celebration apparently came with a refresher course in disappointment.

And that’s the CyberWire.

For links to all of today’s stories, check out our Daily Briefing at the cyberwire dot com.

We’d love to know what you think of this podcast. Your feedback ensures we deliver the insights that keep you a step ahead in the rapidly changing world of cybersecurity. If you like the show, please share a rating and review in your podcast app. Please also fill out the survey in the show notes or send an email to cyberwire@n2k.com

We’re proud that N2K CyberWire is part of the daily routine of the most influential leaders and operators in the public and private sector, from the Fortune 500 to many of the world’s preeminent intelligence and law enforcement agencies.

N2K helps cybersecurity professionals and organizations grow, learn, and stay ahead. We’re the nexus for discovering the people, tech, and ideas shaping the industry. Learn how at n2k.com.

N2K’s lead producer is Liz Stokes. We’re mixed by Tré Hester, with original music by and sound design Elliott Peltzman. Our contributing host is Maria Varmazis. Our executive producer is Jennifer Eiben. Peter Kilpe is our publisher. And I’m Dave Bittner. Thanks for listening.

articles.title: 'Gheist' Weaponizes GitHub Tokens to Steal Cloud Secrets
articles.context: Research presented at Black Hat Europe last year found that some of the most significant software supply chain incidents over the preceding year involved threat actors...
articles.full_text:
An ongoing attack is abusing compromised GitHub tokens to harvest cloud secrets and credentials from thousands of developer repositories, bringing into focus how compromised developer accounts can provide a gateway into enterprise cloud environments.

Dubbed "Gheist," the campaign has left more than 13,500 malicious branches — or versions of a project's code — across more than 850 compromised GitHub accounts, according to a report published over the weekend by Wiz Research.

The campaign affects everything from personal projects to private enterprise repositories, although public repositories are protected by safeguards GitHub introduced in July, according to the report.

"The control GitHub added is focused on protecting public repositories from workflow abuse vectors," Wiz researcher Rami McCarthy tells Dark Reading. However, "once an enterprise credential is compromised, that control doesn’t apply," he adds.

Related:Anthropic-Themed Phishing Emails Bypass Top Security Tools

Wiz also found overlap between Gheist-affected GitHub accounts and other abuse campaigns, including repository-based malware distribution, attempts to exploit GitHub Actions for computing resources, and possible infections linked to other malware operations.

This overlap — which distinguishes Gheist from similar campaigns — suggests stolen developer tokens may be reused or shared among threat actors, "demonstrating the complexity and activity of this threat landscape," McCarthy says.

Workflow Runs the Cyber-Theft Show

The campaign relies on a workflow named "sync-check," which is committed to each repository accessible through a stolen token, the researchers wrote.

"The workflow seeks to print the repository’s secrets into its own workflow log," they wrote. "Then, the tool downloads the log through the GitHub API and deletes the run seconds later. The tool's API requests carry the user agent 'gheist,' which gives the campaign its name."

Wiz began tracking the activity Sept. 15 and said the operation remains active and evolving as of Oct. 24. The researchers reported the activity to GitHub, and about two-thirds of the implicated accounts are no longer available, which "likely indicates response activity," according to the report.

Stolen Tokens Fuel Further Secrets Heist

The tokens appear to have come primarily from two sources: infostealer malware and credentials exposed in earlier software supply chain compromises, the researchers noted.

GitHub tokens authorize users and applications to access repositories, code, and administrative functions, making them valuable to attackers seeking to compromise projects and organizations.

Related:10 Software Security Practices Built for the Next 250 Years

Gheist uses stolen GitHub tokens to create branches named "ci-sync-" followed by six characters. The attackers then add the GitHub Actions workflow at .github/workflows/sync-check.yml, using the commit message "ci: sync config," according to the report.

"The commit is unsigned and authored as the token's owner," the researchers wrote. The resulting push event triggers a workflow that attempts to print environment variables and repository secrets into its log. The attack encodes the output using Base32 before retrieving the logs through the GitHub API and deleting the workflow run seconds later.

"Because the secrets leave through GitHub's own API, there is no attacker domain or outbound connection to block," the researchers explained.

Enterprises in the Crosshairs

A key finding is that Wiz observed successful attacks in private repositories and enterprise environments, where the public-repository safeguard did not apply. Most GitHub-targeted activity, by contrast, primarily affects public repositories, McCarthy tells Dark Reading.

"The attack succeeded in the environments organizations considered safest because a credential issued to a human months ago still carried full write authority," says James Matchett, head of security at supply chain security firm Cloudsmith, in an email interview. "'Private' is not a control. Scoped, short-lived credentials, a tight inventory of what can push and pull, and the discipline to rotate after every incident are the control.”

Related:State Bank of India Suffers a Customer PII Data Leak

Wiz observed the attackers cycling through tokens belonging to multiple users and automation accounts, and cloning private repositories before planting malicious workflows. Within hours, cloud credentials from the same organization were used to enumerate AWS Secrets Manager, the researchers added.

Wiz estimates that the campaign affected "on the scale of a dozen companies," McCarthy says. However, "we have not seen consistent or automated abuse outside of mass cloning of GitHub repositories and the core credential theft," he says.

Defending Against Token Abuse

Token abuse is an increasingly common way for attackers to infiltrate organizations through the developer pipeline. Research presented at Black Hat Europe last year found that some of the most significant software supply chain incidents over the preceding year involved threat actors exploiting GitHub flaws. Defenders therefore must treat developer projects as critical organizational assets.

To defend against Gheist and other forms of token abuse, Wiz urged security teams to hunt for malicious GitHub Actions workflows, rotate exposed secrets, and treat compromised self-hosted runners as potential infrastructure breaches.

More specifically, defenders should look for branches named "ci-sync-" followed by six characters, where the only change is a new .github/workflows/sync-check.yml file with the commit message "ci: sync config," the researchers advised. Administrators also should review GitHub audit logs for workflow runs on "ci-sync-*" branches that were deleted within a minute of completion, as well as activity from the user agent "gheist."

For broader protection against GitHub token abuse, Waseem Ahmed, head of engineering at security firm Secure.com, recommends that organizations "replace long-lived personal access tokens with GitHub Apps or short-lived fine-grained tokens" and "require reviewers on any environment that holds production secrets." These measures can help limit attackers' ability to access sensitive credentials even if they obtain valid tokens.

articles.title: The US Government Is Hiding a Secret Court Ruling About How It Spies on Americans
articles.context: Asked before his July confirmation whether he would ensure the opinion was public before Congress voted on reauthorization, he wrote only that the government was “working...
articles.full_text:
Two Democratic senators who have long overseen US intelligence say the Trump administration is illegally withholding a secret court’s findings from Congress until lawmakers renew a program that lets federal agents read Americans’ communications without a warrant.

Seven months ago, the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court objected to search filters that let intelligence analysts pull Americans’ messages from intercepted data without the approvals, written justifications, or records the law requires. The court approved another year of surveillance anyway. The ruling has never been made public, and Senators Ron Wyden of Oregon and Adam Schiff of California say the administration’s own deadline for releasing it passed in September.

The program, Section 702 of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act (FISA), lapsed in June after Congress failed to renew it, though collection continues under the court’s March approval. The administration’s own public documentation says rulings like this one are reviewed for public release “within 180 days of issuance.” That window closed September 13, even as intelligence officials press lawmakers to reauthorize the program by the end of the year.

Wyden, the longest-serving member of the Senate Intelligence Committee, and Schiff, the former chair of its House counterpart, say the administration owes Congress an explanation for the delay, and the names of the officials responsible, by November 6.

“If this administration won’t follow this simple statutory directive,” the senators told Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton and Attorney General Todd Blanche in a demand letter obtained exclusively by WIRED, “it is unclear why Congress or the American people should trust this administration to follow any of the other legal limits to Section 702.”

Outside Congress, Demand Progress and 22 other civil liberties and government accountability groups on Monday urged congressional leaders to refuse to reauthorize Section 702 “while the administration actively withholds legally mandated information about how the surveillance program operates.” Signatories range from the American Civil Liberties Union to the conservative-backed Project for Privacy and Surveillance Accountability.

The Trump administration has already been pressed, and has promised, to release the ruling. In April, senators Tom Cotton and Mark Warner, the Intelligence Committee’s Republican chair and Democratic vice chair, pressed the administration to release it within 15 days so it could inform the Senate’s debate. In July, asked in writing whether he would commit to declassifying it by the 180-day deadline, Blanche replied, “Yes.”

Warner “has been clear that he supports transparency with regard to Section 702,” his communications director, Rachel Cohen, tells WIRED. Neither former director of national intelligence Tulsi Gabbard nor Bill Pulte, who briefly replaced her as acting director, “were responsive,” Cohen says, “but Senator Warner expects that DNI Clayton will declassify the opinion, consistent with the bipartisan letter and as required by law.”

articles.title: Linux Flaws Exposed Before Fixes as Root Exploit Goes Public
articles.context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
articles.full_text:
A working exploit for a Linux kernel flaw has been made public before the bug received a CVE identifier or a merged upstream fix.

Trend Micro's Zero Day Initiative (ZDI) sent that report and five others to maintainers and public mailing lists on October 20 and 21, according to analysis published by the Sysdig Threat Research Team on October 24.

No in-the-wild exploitation had been reported when Sysdig published its analysis, but several flaws still had no fix in any released kernel.

Public Disclosure Creates Patch Gap

ZDI-CAN-33367, the flaw with the public exploit, is a local privilege escalation (LPE) bug in the Linux networking stack that ZDI gave a CVSS score of 7.8. It can allow an unprivileged user to alter the in-memory contents of files they can only read.

It sits in a code path the kernel's fix for the earlier Dirty Frag page-cache flaws missed. Linux support provider TuxCare reproduced a root shell with the public proof of concept (PoC) on AlmaLinux 8 through 10, CloudLinux 9 and 10, Debian 12 and 13 and Ubuntu 24.04 and 26.04, Sysdig said.

Two of the other five, ZDI-CAN-33774 and ZDI-CAN-33549, are the highest rated, at 9.0, and affect ksmbd, the kernel's Server Message Block (SMB) server. The first is a remote, pre-authentication flaw that can leak kernel memory and crash systems, while the second requires SMB Direct, a Remote Direct Memory Access (RDMA) interface and a writable share.

Read more: Rushed Patches Follow Broken Embargo on New Linux Kernel Vulnerabilities

Exposure Varies Across Linux Systems

Of the remaining three, ZDI-CAN-34068 is an LPE rated 8.8 in the kernel's VMware graphics driver. Sysdig said there was no patch and only the report's title was public.

The last two are ZDI-CAN-34076, an information leak in the kernel's Non-Volatile Memory Express (NVMe) target, and ZDI-CAN-32005, a userspace stack overflow in the ConnMan network manager.

Sysdig said defenders should prioritize by the components they run rather than CVSS scores. It advised unloading ksmbd where it is not needed, restricting port 445 to trusted networks where it must stay and watching for a vmwgfx patch on VMware guests.

For ZDI-CAN-33367, Sysdig said restricting unprivileged user namespaces should block the public PoC, though TuxCare had not validated this, and noted that rootless containers depend on them. AlmaLinux had patched kernels in testing, but not production, by October 23.

The disclosure leaves a fragmented patching picture, but the public root exploit makes ZDI-CAN-33367 the most immediate concern of the six.

articles.title: 10 Software Security Practices Built for the Next 250 Years
articles.context: Our research found that 44% of AI-generated coding tasks introduced a known vulnerability, which means organizations adopting these tools need independent security testing that...
articles.full_text:
OPINION

When I testified before Congress with my L0pht colleagues in 1998, we warned that insecure software could put the systems society depended on at risk. Technology has changed dramatically since then, but the fundamental security questions remain familiar. Where does untrusted data enter? What authority does a component have? Who owns the risk, and how do we know a control worked?

We cannot predict the technology stack of 2276, but we can establish practices that make software trustworthy as technology evolves. These 10 are a good place to start.

Make security part of the architecture. Secure by design should describe how a system is engineered, beginning with secure defaults, approved patterns, clear trust boundaries, and controls that make insecure outcomes difficult. When security is introduced near the end of development, it must work against decisions already embedded in the architecture, while built-in controls become part of how the system operates and evolves.

Maintain an accurate picture of what you have. Every organization needs a continuously updated inventory of its applications, open source dependencies, development tools, AI models, and external services, along with clear ownership for critical systems. When a serious vulnerability emerges, teams should be able to determine quickly where the affected component is running, what it can reach, and who is responsible for addressing it.

Verify every line of code. Code should earn trust whether it was written by an employee, generated by an AI assistant, or obtained from a third party. Our research found that 44% of AI-generated coding tasks introduced a known vulnerability, which means organizations adopting these tools need independent security testing that operates at the same speed as development and verifies code before it reaches production.

Make the secure path the easiest path. Developers work under constant pressure to ship, so security controls that produce excessive noise, delay builds, or pull people away from their normal tools will eventually be bypassed. Organizations should put precise feedback, approved components, and validated fixes directly into repositories, pipelines, and coding workflows, making the secure approach the most efficient way to complete the work.

Match security speed to development speed. AI is turning software insecurity into a throughput problem because teams can now produce and change code faster than manual review can follow. Testing, policy enforcement, and remediation therefore need to operate continuously across the development life cycle, with automation handling repeatable work and people concentrating on the complex decisions that require business context and judgment.

Control what enters the software supply chain. Modern applications are assembled from large volumes of code that organizations did not write, and each dependency introduces another relationship that must be understood and maintained. Teams should evaluate components when they enter a build, record their provenance, detect malicious or abandoned packages, and plan for safe upgrades, since an inventory alone cannot prevent risky software from being introduced.

Pay down security debt before it comes due. Veracode's research found that security debt now affects 82% of organizations, leaving an expanding reservoir of vulnerabilities that have remained unresolved for more than a year. As AI-powered discovery compresses years of vulnerability research into months, leaders need to fund remediation as an ongoing engineering function, define expectations for addressing the highest-risk flaws, and track whether new risk is accumulating faster than teams can remove it.

Measure the risk you remove. Most security programs can report how many vulnerabilities they found and closed, yet those activity measures do not show whether the organization has become safer. More useful measures include how long critical, exploitable flaws remain exposed, whether fix capacity is keeping pace with incoming risk and how quickly teams can reduce exposure in applications tied to sensitive data or essential business operations.

Threat-model the entire AI system. An AI agent includes far more than the model because its identity, permissions, tools, memory, data, runtime, and network access all contribute to what it can ultimately do. Organizations should authorize sensitive actions where they occur, constrain what compromised components can reach, include the runtime in data-flow analysis, and retain enough evidence to determine what the agent did when something goes wrong.

Preserve human accountability. Every important application and accepted risk needs an accountable owner, supported by evidence of the controls applied, tests performed, and decisions made throughout the software life cycle. As machines assume a larger role in writing and modifying code, people must retain enough understanding to challenge the output, recognize unexpected behavior, and demonstrate that reasonable precautions were taken.

Related:Anthropic-Themed Phishing Emails Bypass Top Security Tools

Cybersecurity Practices That Can Adapt

The next 250 years will bring technologies that we cannot name today, although the systems built with them will still have inputs, privileges, dependencies, and consequences. Lasting security will come from disciplined engineering, continuous verification, and clear responsibility, supported by people who understand how complex systems fail and know how to question the assumptions behind them.

Related:'Gheist' Weaponizes GitHub Tokens to Steal Cloud Secrets

That hacker mindset has served the industry well, and we need to keep teaching it to developers, defenders, and the next generation of security researchers. The tools and architectures will continue to change, while our responsibility to build systems worthy of trust will endure.

articles.title: Microsoft Issues Emergency Patch Update for Critical .NET Buffer Overflow Flaw
articles.context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
articles.full_text:
Microsoft has released out-of-bound (OOB) security updates for its .NET developer platform, which includes a fix for a critical buffer overflow vulnerability.

The tech giant published the updates for .NET versions 8, 9, 10, and 11 Release Candidate 3 on October 25. Platform users have been urged to apply the updates as soon as possible to reduce the risk of compromise.

They contain patches for two newly disclosed vulnerabilities, as well as two flaws that were not fully addressed in Microsoft’s October Patch Tuesday rollout.

Single updates are available for each of the affected .NET versions and .NET 11 RC2 users should update to RC3 to receive these fixes.

.NET is a free, open-source framework that developers can use to build apps and cloud services. It is managed by Microsoft and is supported on Windows, Linux and macOS operating systems.

Updates Address Critical Buffer Overflow Vulnerability

One of the new vulnerabilities addressed is CVE-2026-111497, which affects .NET versions 8, 9, 10, and 11 across all operating systems.

The vulnerability is contained in the Brotli decompression algorithm, which is used by .NET. It can allow an unauthenticated attacker to read or corrupt process memory, leading to information disclosure, denial of service or elevation of privilege.

Microsoft said that applications may be affected if they process Brotli-compressed data through ASP.NET Core request decompression, HttpClient automatic response decompression or the System.IO.Compression Brotli APIs.

The flaw has a critical CVSS Score of 9.2. Users of Google Brotli versions 1.0.3 through 1.2.0 also need to update any Brotli libraries or binaries to the latest available version.

Brotli was designed by two engineers at Google in 2015 to allow developers to speed up algorithm compression for developers.

Microsoft’s OOB update also addresses CVE-2026-114148, which can allow an authorized attacker to elevate privileges locally by exploiting unsafe ownership metadata in affected .NET tarballs.

CVE-2026-114148 affects .NET versions 7-11, but only for Linux systems. For .NET 10 and .NET 11, CVE-2026-114148 affects source-build tarballs only. For .NET 8 and .NET 9, it also affects ASP.NET Core distributions obtained through ASP.NET Core tarballs, including users who do not build .NET from source, the advisory noted.

It has not been assigned a CVSS score at the time of writing but has been reserved by a CVE Numbering Authority (CNA).

In addition, Microsoft has re-issued fixes for two vulnerabilities disclosed in its October 13 Patch Tuesday rollout. These are for CVE-2026-70197, a memory corruption flaw affecting .NET versions 8-11, and CVE-2026-102870, a code injection vulnerability affecting .NET 10 and 11.

Remediation Guidance for Developers

Microsoft issued advice for .NET users on how to update their applications and build environments in light of the updates. These include:

Install the updated runtime for the .NET version for your framework-dependent application, then restart the application

Rebuild and republish self-contained applications with the updated runtime

Rebuild and redeploy containers using updated .NET container images

Obtain the updated source-build artifacts for your .NET version and rebuild your packages to incorporate the tarball ownership fix

For ASP.NET Core tarball users on .NET 8 and 9, update your installation using the refreshed ASP.NET Core Runtime tarball for your .NET version

articles.title: Bias in Qwen3-Coder Model
articles.context: For the first time, we showed that this vulnerability lives in the model’s weights, and that removing the model’s CCP alignment removes it
articles.full_text:
Clive Robinson • October 26, 2026 2:51 PM

@ Bruce, ALL,

With regards,

“I would like more details on how the bias was removed.”

I can not give you specifics for this particular model and it’s token encoding, but I can give a more general explanation.

As I’ve noted previously on a numver of occasions the heart of these AI Large X Models is the so called “Digital Neural Network”(DNN).

That in reality is just a “Digital Signal Processing”(DSP) algorithm that implements an “Adaptive Filter Network”.

What this AFN does is at the basic level “Multiply and Add”(MAD) instructions that feed forward into a form of decision circuit (often a rectifier function). Often this decision circuit is at the output of the summer and is nonlinear in response to provide a normalised spectrum.

If you change the token weights that are in effect linear then you change the shape of the AFN spectrum.

Thus by increasing or reducing the weights for selected tokens, you change the spectrum in desirable ways.

Thus if you can identify the weights to change you change not just the specific part of the spectrum for the token you also change the general spectrum which it forms a part of.

In general LLMs fail after ML building of the DNN for various reasons. Where that behaviour around specific tokens or the broader themes they form part of is seen as undesirable “Reinforcement learning from human feedback”(RLHF) can be applied.

In essence all it does is adjust the specific token weights as well as to a lesser result adjust the more general weights for other tokens.

Thus if you know what token weights need adjusting you can do so.

The trick is making your RLHF the inverse of that used by the model originator.

There are other ways to achieve the same objective of weight adjustment, but this is generally the easiest way to see it as a distinct process.

Another way I’m not going to go into is by cloning the model. You can as part of the process add or subtract the measure you give for tokens or themes.

Look up “LLM logit leakage and distillation” techniques or have a browse through,

“Clone What You Can’t Steal: Black-Box LLM Replication via Logit Leakage and Distilation”

https://arxiv.org/html/2509.00973

Hopefully you will enjoy / have fun.

articles.title: Know How Cyble Brand Intelligence Can Help Stop ClickFix Campaigns in its Tracks
articles.context: Five Storm-1865 attack steps, each paired with a Cyble Brand Intelligence capability Step 1: Pick a trusted brand and a target list What the attacker did
articles.full_text:
Booking.com's systems were never breached. Its name was. Storm-1865 spent months borrowing Booking.com's identity to get into hotel computers, and every step of that borrowing left traces on the open internet.

The open internet is exactly where Cyble Brand Intelligence & Protection works. Walk through the campaign one step at a time, and at each step there is a point where it could have spotted the attacker, cut the attack short or limited the damage.

What happened

From December 2024, a group Microsoft tracks as Storm-1865 posed as Booking.com to target hotel and hospitality staff across North America, Europe, Oceania and South and Southeast Asia. Microsoft Threat Intelligence published its findings on March 13, 2025, and said the campaign was still running as of February 2025.

The attack had four moving parts:

The lure. Emails styled as Booking.com messages about negative guest reviews, guest enquiries, promotion offers or account verification.

The landing page. A link, sometimes inside a PDF, opened a fake CAPTCHA laid over a faint copy of a real Booking.com page.

The trick. The "verification" told staff to open the Windows Run box and paste a command the page had already copied to their clipboard.

The payload. That command used mshta.exe to pull commodity malware, including XWorm, Lumma Stealer, VenomRAT, AsyncRAT, Danabot and NetSupport RAT, all built to steal credentials and payment data.

This was not a one-off. Microsoft says Storm-1865 targeted Booking.com guests in 2023 and e-commerce buyers in 2024 before adding ClickFix. Booking.com told Infosecurity Magazine its own systems were not breached, but some accommodation partners and customers were hit.

Why the impersonated brand holds the first move

Booking.com could not install security software on the laptops of its accommodation partners. What it could reach was the attacker's infrastructure copying its brand, and that infrastructure was detectable. Microsoft's own email security flagged URLs in this campaign as impersonating booking.com.

The stakes are high. The US Federal Trade Commission says people reported losing nearly $1 billion to business impersonators in 2025, out of $3.5 billion lost to imposter scams overall. Every copy of a brand caught early is one fewer victim.

Five steps, five chances to step in

Storm-1865 needed Booking.com's credibility at every stage of the attack. Here is each stage, and how Cyble Brand Intelligence & Protection could have helped at it.

Fig. Five Storm-1865 attack steps, each paired with a Cyble Brand Intelligence capability

Step 1: Pick a trusted brand and a target list

What the attacker did. Storm-1865 was a repeat player. Microsoft says it went after Booking.com guests in 2023 and e-commerce buyers in 2024, then turned to hotel staff most likely to work with Booking.com.

How Cyble could have helped. Cyble's in-house brand team and OSINT surveillance track brand mentions and the actors who keep returning to a brand. A known playbook becomes a set of watch-list rules, so the next wave is expected rather than discovered after the fact.

Step 2: Register the infrastructure

What the attacker did. The campaign needed domains and URLs to host its fake pages. Microsoft flagged some of them as matching a known malicious registrant pattern.

How Cyble could have helped. Suspicious & Watch-Listed Domain monitoring tracks new registrations and DNS activity for typosquats, homoglyphs and lookalike domains, including AI-generated ones. A domain built to impersonate the brand can be flagged when it is registered, before it hosts a single page.

Step 3: Build the fake Booking.com page

What the attacker did. Victims landed on a fake CAPTCHA laid over a faint copy of a real Booking.com page. The familiar look was the point: it made a strange request feel routine.

How Cyble could have helped. Phishing Detection finds sites impersonating the brand, and Watermarking Surveillance spots copied or mirrored brand assets, even on domains with no brand name in them. Automated Takedown then works to get confirmed pages removed. Every hotel that clicks after a takedown hits a dead link instead of a trap.

Step 4: Send lures across regions

What the attacker did. Emails and PDFs about negative reviews, guest requests, promotions and account checks went to hotels across North America, Europe, Oceania and Asia. Some came through vendor platforms and ordinary services such as Gmail and iCloud Mail.

How Cyble could have helped. Multi-language NLP is built to catch phishing and impersonation attempts that are not in English, which matters for a campaign spread across this many markets. Lures that partners report can be handed to Cyble's brand team, traced to the live page behind them and queued for takedown.

Step 5: Cash in on stolen credentials and payment data

What the attacker did. Once a staff member pasted the command, malware such as XWorm, Lumma Stealer and VenomRAT went to work. Microsoft says every payload in the campaign could steal credentials and financial data for fraud.

How Cyble could have helped. Stopping the pasted command itself is a job for endpoint and email controls. What Cyble adds is the aftermath: OSINT surveillance watches forums, blogs and paste sites for exposed credentials and data leaks tied to the brand. Spotting stolen partner logins early gives everyone time to reset access before fraud follows.

This walkthrough maps public research to Cyble's capabilities. It is not a claim that Cyble took part in the response to this campaign.

Strongest alongside your other defenses

Brand intelligence works outside your network, so it pairs naturally with what runs inside it. When a lure arrives from an ordinary Gmail or iCloud address, there is no fake sender domain to flag, so the landing page becomes the asset to hunt. And if someone does run the pasted command, email filtering, endpoint detection, script controls and phishing-resistant MFA, the mitigations Microsoft recommends, do the stopping. Brand intelligence makes sure far fewer people ever reach that moment.

Is your brand the next Target? Six questions to ask

Any brand that sits between businesses and their customers can be borrowed the same way: travel platforms, marketplaces, payment providers, logistics firms and SaaS vendors. Ask your team:

Do we know which of our emails, notices and portal pages are most copied by attackers?

Are we alerted when a domain containing our name, or a homoglyph of it, is registered?

Can we spot a cloned page even when it sits on an unrelated domain or free hosting?

How long does it take us to get a confirmed phishing page taken down?

Do our partners know how to report a suspicious message that uses our name?

Do we watch criminal forums and channels for kits or templates built around our brand?

If more than two answers are "no" or "not sure," the attacker's preparation phase is happening without anyone watching.

The takeaway

Look back at the five steps and a pattern stands out. Storm-1865 needed Booking.com's credibility at every one of them, and every one left a trace outside the victims' networks.

With Cyble Brand Intelligence & Protection watching, each trace becomes a chance to step in: a repeat actor on the watch list, a lookalike domain flagged at registration, a cloned page taken down, a lure traced to its source, a leaked login caught early. If your partners and customers trust your name, Cyble helps make sure nobody else gets to use it.

articles.title: Blue Initiative Offers Maritime Sector Dedicated Vulnerability Database
articles.context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
articles.full_text:
An industry coalition has launched a new database for CVEs it says will help shipping companies to improve their vulnerability management efforts.

Blue Initiative was announced on October 26 by maritime cybersecurity vendors Cydome and Rakuten Maritime, alongside inspection and certification specialist Bureau Veritas, ship classification society ClassNK and the Maritime Transportation System Information Sharing and Analysis Center (MTS-ISAC).

They claimed the new database would be the first to list only IT and OT vulnerabilities relevant to the sector.

It will therefore help maritime companies address vulnerability management and alerting more proactively, it added.

Read more on maritime sector threats: Adriatic Port Cyber-Attack by Anubis Sparks Warning Over Maritime Security Risks

Cydome CEO Nir Ayalon said that identifying flaws relevant to the specialized systems maritime operators use is a challenge.

“Our vision with the Blue Initiative is to have a public and open single source of truth for maritime-related vulnerabilities,” he added. “This will provide IT and cyber teams, vendors and research facilities a much more focused view of risks relevant to their specific vessels, making vulnerabilities and risk management much more effective and faster than before.”

Any proposed entries to the Maritime Vulnerabilities Repository (MVR) will be reviewed by researchers from Cydome and other Blue Initiative partners, who will validate and refine them before publishing.

Users will then be able to:

Browse all CVEs and their details

Filter by relevant equipment or vendors

Access more detailed expert insight on specific vulnerabilities and their impact

Subscribe for updates and alerts on new vulnerabilities

Vulnerabilities are only published once a patch is available, the group clarified.

“Amid a shifting threat landscape where technological advancement increasingly empowers threat actors targeting maritime critical infrastructure, the Blue Initiative delivers essential vulnerability intelligence that addresses a critical vulnerability gap,” argued Christy Coffey, VP operations at MTS-ISAC.

“Recognizing the value of this community-driven approach to maritime situational awareness, the MTS-ISAC strongly endorses this collaborative model and has integrated its operational workflows to both contribute to and leverage this vital initiative.”

Cyber-Attacks on Shipping Mount

The launch comes as attacks in the sector continue. On August 21 and 24, the US Coast Guard and FBI were forced to board two oil tankers in the Gulf of Mexico after cyber-attacks against on-board systems by “foreign cyber actors.”

It’s claimed the hackers were able to breach both IT and OT networks, interfering with propulsion, navigation and other systems.

More recently still, the n0n extortion group added dozens of global maritime organizations to its leak site on October 12. However, none of the claimed victims – which include carriers and port and terminal operators – have thus far confirmed any security incidents.

“Cyber resilience requirements for ships are not simply a checklist for audits, but a continuous process throughout a vessel’s operational life,” explained Panagiotis Anastasiou, cyber technical & market leader, Bureau Veritas Marine & Offshore.

“Owners are expected to maintain the security of onboard systems as new vulnerabilities emerge, making effective vulnerability management a critical element of maritime cyber resilience. In practice, this can be challenging, as relevant information is often scattered across general-purpose databases and vendor advisories.”

articles.title: PHP Publishes Mitigation Advice for New RCE Flaw
articles.context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
articles.full_text:
The maintainers of the popular PHP programming language have warned of a new remote code execution (RCE) vulnerability, but claimed it’s likely to affect a relatively small share of the userbase.

In an advisory published on October 23, the PHP security team said that CVE-2026-115560 would not be patched until the next release, as the conditions needed to exploit it will not be present in most environments.

“The issue can only occur under an unusual combination of configuration and application code. An application must set session.serialize_handler to php_binary or php_serialize in its configuration and then switch it to php at runtime with ini_set() before calling session_start(),” it explained.

“Session upload progress must also still be enabled. Applications that never change the serialize handler at runtime can keep the feature enabled.”

Read more on PHP: PHP2Shell Exploitation Attempt Detected by Amazon Four Days Before Vulnerability Disclosure

System administrators are urged to put in place the mitigation recommended on October 21 in PHP’s advisory for CVE-2026-109619, one of two critical flaws issued last week.

“We suggest you set session.upload_progress.enabled=0 until the next regular bugfix release, to fully protect from an unlikely RCE vector,” it said.

“If you applied it [last week], keep it in place and no further action is needed.”

More Work for Security Teams

Last week saw widespread website outages as administrators scrambled to patch the maximum severity zero days (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619), collectively known as “P2PShell.”

Mike Lyborg, CISO at Swimlane, argued that new flaw needs a “precise response” after days of disruption in many organizations because of PHP2Shell.

“Keeping services running through successive warnings takes coordination that holds up after everyone’s exhausted,” he added. “Across organizations responding to PHP last week, the next bottleneck could be a handoff between the people assessing risk and those authorized to change a live service.”

Their efforts were given an added urgency after details of the vulnerabilities were accidentally disclosed a day before the patches were due to be released.

Amazon Web Services subsequently revealed that an unknown threat actor tried to exploit the bugs four days before they were officially published. It remains unclear how they managed to get hold of the information needed to attempt such an attack.

PHP is used in around 70% of global websites, including content management systems (CMS) like WordPress, Drupal, Joomla and Magento, making the patching of PHP2Shell a major global endeavor.

articles.title: Code security for new coders
articles.context: There are also many security tools available, but it can be confusing to know what type of tool to use and when
articles.full_text:
Coding agents enable anyone to turn their ideas into reality. However, building with security in mind is imperative to keep your application secure. There’s a lot of reference information about application security out there, but it often is jargon-heavy and targets developers or security professionals, not vibe coders. There are also many security tools available, but it can be confusing to know what type of tool to use and when. This post breaks down essential security terms and tools so that you can build safely from the start.

If you aren’t sold on the importance of application security or think it only matters to large companies, consider the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities disclosed in October 2026. These two vulnerabilities affect PHP, a programming language used by more than 70% of websites. They could allow an attacker to take control of a website’s server. The vulnerabilities are so serious that some organizations temporarily took services offline while installing security updates.

What is code security?

In simple terms, code security is the practice of writing secure code. Because application security starts with code security, taking a proactive approach early prevents major vulnerabilities later.

There are two main things we need to be concerned with when thinking about code security: the code you (or your agent) is writing (i.e., first-party code), and the code that is written by someone else but being used by your application (i.e., third-party code). With first party code, you are directly responsible for fixing the problem. Third-party code is treated differently because you are not the one who can fix the code, but you are responsible for using a version that does not have vulnerabilities. We often refer to third-party code as being part of the software supply chain, but more on that later.

What is first-party code?

First-party code is the code that you are producing and are thus responsible for. While being responsible for maintaining secure code might seem intimidating, you can most likely fix security issues by prompting the agent to fix them. There are automated security scans you can run to discover vulnerabilities, or you can simply ask the agent to do a security check. Checking for OWASP top ten vulnerabilities is always a good place to start.

What are secrets?

One of the simplest, yet most impactful ways to improve security is to avoid hardcoding secrets. This means that you should never write in the code any password, token, key, or any secret or credential that can be used to gain access to your resources. Instead, you can use environment variables that act as a placeholder that point to a specific hidden configuration file or a secret manager.

What is the software supply chain?

The software supply chain refers to everything that is used to develop and run an application, including dependencies, tools, and infrastructure. There are also open source code components used in the software supply chain, such as GitHub actions and Docker images, which can help you deploy and run your code. Of all these elements, third-party dependencies are usually the main focus in discussions about code security.

Now you might be thinking, why do I need to use third-party code? Technically you don’t, but it makes writing code much easier, whether it’s done by you or an agent. By relying on these open-source dependencies, you are using code that was already written by someone else and that is shared with the community to solve a problem. What’s important to understand in the context of AI-generated code is that coding agents use dependencies by default, often relying heavily on outdated versions.

Dependencies rely on other dependencies, so the risk starts to grow as you start to use them. There are two things in particular you need to be concerned about with third-party dependencies: vulnerabilities and malicious packages. Vulnerabilities in third-party dependencies are accidental code issues that usually require upgrading to the latest version once the issue is fixed. Malicious packages represent a more intentional threat and are becoming more common. With these packages, someone has purposefully added a malicious script in the version and released it for personal gain.

Overall, the concern with using third-party code is that dependencies can quickly accumulate vulnerabilities if the maintainer doesn’t have the time to address these security flaws.

Security questions to ask your coding agent

The cool thing about vibe coding is that you can ask the agent any questions you may have. The difficulty can be knowing exactly what to ask. Below is a list of good places to start, but it is not exhaustive.

Setup questions

These are the types of questions that should be asked before any code is written. The goal is to have some security requirements planned out so an agent has a path to follow.

What sensitive data will this app handle (passwords, payment info, personal data, API keys), and how should each type be protected?

What authentication and authorization approach fits this app, and what are the tradeoffs?

Follow-up questions

After the code is written, you should make sure the agent made the best decisions for security. Ask questions that make the agent explain why certain security decisions were made. This will force the agent to go back through the code, which might lead it to suggest a change.

Can you do a security review on the application? Are there any concerns?

Do any OWASP top 10 vulnerabilities exist in this code?

What security tradeoffs did you make to keep this simple, and what would you fix before real users touch this?

If you were a penetration tester, what's the first thing you'd try to break in this app?

What third-party packages did you use? Are any of them outdated? Do any have known vulnerabilities?

Does any of this code contain hardcoded API keys, passwords, or tokens? If so, where, and how do I move them to environment variables or to a secrets manager?

Are default credentials or debug modes left enabled anywhere?

Is there a .env or config file here, and is it excluded from version control (.gitignore)?

Are there any insecure coding patterns or logic flaws present?

Is there anything concerning about the current authentication and access controls configuration?

Are cloud storage buckets, databases, or admin panels publicly accessible when they shouldn't be?

If this is deployed, what's exposed to the internet that doesn't need to be?

What are the different types of code security tools?

Security tools come in all shapes and sizes. While many tools are paid, there are also open source tools that function similarly. The list below includes the most common types of tools.

Software Composition Analysis (SCA)

Tools of this type scan all the open-source dependencies that are being used in the application and alert you if there are any vulnerabilities. Most providers will also tell you what version you can upgrade to in order to eliminate that vulnerability.

Static Application Security Testing (SAST)

This type of tool is focused on looking at your first-party code for vulnerabilities. Most commonly, these tools scan the written code without running that code. They are good for early detection while you are actively coding but can provide more false positives than other tools do.

Interactive Application Security Testing (IAST)

Tools in this category look at how data is flowing into a running application to find code vulnerabilities. Since they require a running application, they are generally used later in the software delivery life cycle compared to SAST tools. However, they also tend to be more accurate.

Dynamic Application Security Testing (DAST)

Tools that perform this type of security scan run pre-configured automated tests against a running application. They are not interchangeable with SAST or IAST tools.

Infrastructure as Code (IaC) Scanning

Tools that use this type of scanning are focused on looking at any IaC files for risky settings and misconfigurations.

Secret Scanning

Secret scanners search your codebase for hardcoded credentials, API keys, and passwords.

How Datadog can help

Security scans are a great way to understand what is happening in your code. Datadog Code Security has many types of tools you can use to gain visibility into your application, including SCA, SAST, IAST, IaC, and Secret scanning tools.

Datadog also has two open source tools that can be used for supply chain security: GuardDog to flag malicious packages and Supply Chain Firewall to block malicious packages from being installed.

Conclusion

The good news is that you do not need to become a security expert before bringing an idea to life. Start with a few basics: keep secrets out of your code, scan both first-party and third-party code, update your dependencies, and ask your coding agent to check for common vulnerabilities.

The goal is not to build a perfectly secure application on your first try. It is to understand what your application uses, recognize the risks, and make security part of how you build from the start. Addressing issues along the way is much easier than responding after your application or its users have been put at risk.

articles.title: The PHP Meltdown Shows How AI Makes Bugs More Exploitable
articles.context: There are inevitably flaws in even the most critical, foundational digital tools, but the expanding capabilities of AI models have made it faster to analyze and potentially...
articles.full_text:
Welcome to Kernel Panic, a weekly newsletter by Lily Hay Newman and Matt Burgess from inside the new world of privacy and digital security. To receive this newsletter in your inbox each week, sign up here.

As security teams and web admins scrambled this week to patch newly public PHP bugs, criminal hackers quickly attempted to exploit the flaws in the wild. Millions of exploitation attempts hit within hours of the vulnerabilities being published, according to analysis from Cloudflare—unsurprising given broad access to AI tools that can make it easier for attackers to quickly exploit flaws.

So far, the nightmare scenario of mass victim takeovers and breaches hasn’t come to pass. The PHP Foundation says it hasn’t seen any successful exploitation of the bugs, collectively dubbed PHP2Shell, and many publicly circulating potential exploits appear to be ineffective. However, perhaps the most interesting role of AI amid the chaos this week is how advanced models helped researchers uncover practical exploitations for the vulnerabilities, which were known about, at least in part, for years. In other words, AI helped turn historic vulnerability into a current crisis.

So are we all about to be walloped by a wave of critical vulnerabilities that have been kicking around for decades?

Researchers at security company Calif were the first to identify the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities and create exploits in early August—partially using frontier AI tools as part of OpenAI’s Patch the Planet program, but also using expert human knowledge of PHP, its dynamics, and its weaknesses. Some of the underlying issues were identified in 2024 but were deemed too complex to exploit at the time. Following Calif’s discovery, researchers at OpenAI and the Google-owned security firm Wiz independently discovered PHP2Shell flaws using AI tools.

“The vulnerability had been known to the PHP team for years, but because it could not be leveraged by an attacker—at least, not a human one—it was not addressed,” says Sagi Tzadik, a security researcher at Wiz.

No software is perfect. There are inevitably flaws in even the most critical, foundational digital tools, but the expanding capabilities of AI models have made it faster to analyze and potentially exploit vulnerabilities. This puts even more pressure on under-resourced IT teams, developers, and admins to keep up. Microsoft’s security updates included a record 1,453 security vulnerabilities this month alone. Meanwhile, Bank of America recently hired 1,000 consultants to fix flaws discovered by Anthropic’s Mythos. Security researchers emphasize, though, that AI is ultimately not doing anything new, but rather magnifying existing dynamics of vulnerability discovery and coordinated disclosure.

Black Lotus Labs identified a China-nexus cyber infrastructure provider, dubbed a “quartermaster,” that supplies reconnaissance, proxy routing, and obfuscation services to Chinese cyber espionage actors.
