articles.title: Hacker leaks 281 GB of data from Germany’s far-right AfD party
articles.context: cc leak site published AI-written summaries of hundreds of thousands of the messages into categories such as racism and antisemitism, graded Low to Critical, according to local...
articles.full_text:
Germany's far-right AfD (Alternative für Deutschland) party has confirmed that it has suffered a security breach, after a hacker published what appear to be hundreds of thousands of the controversial political party's internal emails.

Earlier this week, the AfD admitted that its hosting provider had been hacked in September, and that some of its mailboxes had been copied. The party claims that most of the affected mailboxes had not been used for years, but the leaked archive reportedly includes messages dated as recently as 12 September 2026.

The news came as the Hexane.cc leak site published AI-written summaries of hundreds of thousands of the messages into categories such as racism and antisemitism, graded Low to Critical, according to local media reports.

To add to the AfD's discomfort, reports suggest that the hacker's access may have been gained in an embarrassingly simple fashion, via a website that had allegedly been left unpatched. However, this has not been independently verified.

What is unusual is that the leaked emails are not published on the site directly. Instead, AI-generated summaries are shown, categorised and rated from Low to Critical. The site encourages anybody who wants to read a complete original email, including headers, message bodies, attachments, and DKIM signatures, to download it via a torrent.

Of course, everyone should be wary of trusting AI-generated summaries, as artificial intelligence has a history of making sometimes large mistakes with great confidence. Indeed, party sources told the media that although the leaked emails appeared to be authentic, the AI-generated summaries appeared to contain several inaccuracies.

The full corpus of 281 GB of stolen messages and files has been made available for download via the torrent, and claims to contain 421,179 stolen internal party emails as well as more than 100,000 files.

The hacker says the leak is intended to expose the party's "degeneracy and hypocrisy."

They have also claimed that someone with a Proton Mail email address reached out to them offering 100,000 Euros if the leak site was taken down.

Should you be tempted to download the torrent and explore the contents of the messages yourself? I would advise against it. In the past, cybercriminals have used torrents of trending topics in the public eye to distribute malware. That's before you even consider the possible legal questions that can arise from handling stolen personal data, whatever you might think of the individuals exposed.

It's not the first cybersecurity headache that the AfD has suffered recently. On 3 September, a press spokesman for the party's group in the Thuringia state parliament warned that his work email account had been used to send phishing emails, and urged recipients not to open PDF attachments they may have received.

Whatever you may think of the AfD, there appear to have been security failures in this case that are far too common. It's not unusual for websites to be overlooked or half-forgotten, and left unpatched. It's not rare for shared infrastructure to not be segmented properly.

Furthermore, whether you are an individual or an organisation, you should be aware that an email account can be a treasure trove of sensitive information. Even if it has not been used for years, it can hold vast amounts of correspondence that can be exploited by hackers and fraudsters.

articles.title: Compromised TLS Certificates
articles.context: One caveat: exploiting compromised certificates requires an active adversary-in-the-middle attack, meaning the attacker must act as a proxy between two TLS parties and receive...
articles.full_text:
The Indian CA eMudhra Limited has eight TLS certificates with laughably weak private keys:

The compromised eMudhra keys were defective at a level that’s challenging the imagination of many of the engineers studying the incident. A normal size for a NIST P-384 elliptic curve cryptography private key contains roughly 384 bits of entropy, a size allowing almost 2384, or a number with 116 digits, different possibilities. The private key sizes of the compromised keys ranged from 3 to 8 bits. Astonishingly, the private keys were 4, 56, 66, 115, 155, 156, 230, 237.

“That is extremely in the ‘this should not be possible’ category,” Valdorda said. “Maybe some horribly dangerous key generation interface has a ‘size’ parameter and they set it to 1 by mistake???”

Ben Cartwright-Cox, director of BGP.tools, said: “My guess is that it’s example code that accidentally leaked to production, but hard to know. But it’s bonkers that no one noticed.”

At this early stage, the most immediate threat appears to be for those using VPNs, especially in countries with governments likely to maliciously intercept traffic. There are likely many other cases for concern. End users largely have no recourse other than to hold off using many non-browser forms of TLS communication until they receive assurances updates are in place.

The whole certificate regime has long been a mess:

The incident is the latest to expose a fatal flaw in the TLS regimen. It’s only as strong as its weakest link, which in this case was eMudhra. Fortunately, transparency logs account for much of that failure, but this measure requires parties to actively monitor massive feeds and works only after unauthorized certificates have been issued. eMudhra representatives weren’t immediately available to answer questions.

One caveat: exploiting compromised certificates requires an active adversary-in-the-middle attack, meaning the attacker must act as a proxy between two TLS parties and receive encrypted traffic, decrypt it, reencrypt it, and send it to the other party. Such capabilities, in some cases, are usually limited to only the most well-resourced attackers. People with control of a local network­at a coffee shop, university, or other organization­face much less of a challenge.

Cleanup of this is going to be another mess—and it’s right on top of the PHP vulnerabilities.

Some more information.

articles.title: Widespread Token-Spraying Attacks Target Microsoft 365 Accounts For Email Compromise
articles.context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
articles.full_text:
A newly uncovered and widespread business email compromise (BEC) campaign targeted Microsoft 365 environments in an operation which made hundreds of thousands of attempts to access corporate networks around the world.

Identified by cybersecurity researchers at Huntress, the campaign used fake sign-in pages, device-code phishing, stolen session tokens and social engineering in attacks which appeared to be setting the stage for BEC BEC attacks.

As detailed in a blog post published on October 22, researchers launched an investigation following a series of suspicious “sign-in events” across 79 Huntress customer organizations which took place between July and September 2026.

What they found was a global campaign which targeted corporate Microsoft 365 environments with adversary-in-the-middle (AiTM) attacks, which allowed the attackers to compromise accounts without the attacker ever needing to steal the passwords associated with them.

The attackers achieved this by stealing the login tokens which help to provide access to the account. Crucially for the attackers, these tokens are generated after the real login page has been legitimately used and any associated multi-factor authentication (MFA) has verified the account. That means that whoever holds the token doesn’t need to pass MFA again.

The attackers then replayed the stolen tokens from their own machines in automated sign-in attempts against Microsoft 365 services.

Active Compromise Within Minutes

These ‘token-spraying’ attacks probed Microsoft 365 environments around the world. Researchers at Huntress observed the threat actor behind the campaign make at least 200,000 login attempts, which included 497 successful sign-ins. In many cases, the attackers were inside environments just minutes after stealing the tokens.

The attackers used this initial access to modify controls around Microsoft 365 environments in an attempt to make future access easier.

For example, in several observed incidents, the attackers wiped the victim’s MFA settings and added their own phone to the account user, so a simple password reset wouldn’t lock them out, because now the attacker had their own authenticator app for the environment.

Other methods the attackers used to help maintain persistence on the compromised networks included hidden email rules in victim inboxes that quietly moved messages from specific contacts out of sight. They even modified Entra settings to add their own devices as legitimately registered on the network to request additional tokens if needed in future.

The attackers were also observed using a compromised mailbox to send a payroll-related phishing email message. Using a legitimate email to send these requests increases the likelihood of a business email compromise attack working. In this case, however, it appears the attackers did not receive a payment from their intended victim.

The nature of this campaign means that the attackers can easily establish persistence on the network. But Huntress emphasised that there are actions which can be taken to reduce the risk from these kinds of campaigns.

“Conditional Access Policies (CAP) can help fill some of the security gaps that MFA can't, as long as they're appropriately implemented. Businesses setting up CAPs should require MFA (or block) for All Users, All Cloud Apps, and All Client App types, unconditionally,” said Huntress.

If companies suspect a token replay compromise, it is advised that they revoke the sessions and reset the password, perform an audit of Entra devices and MFA methods and review inbox rules to identify if anything has been changed.

articles.title: The early bird gets the exploit.
articles.context: AI-assisted exploit development is accelerating the transition from vulnerability disclosure to active attacks, sometimes to just minutes. Security teams should prioritize patching critical internet-facing vulnerabilities within hours, investigate potential compromises predating disclosure, and deploy detections...
articles.full_text:
Amazon spots PHP exploits before disclosure. GitLab patches a critical flaw. Meta faces a $25 billion penalty. Autonomous AI agents power new cyberattacks. Hackers breach a Japanese cloud provider. CyberCartel unleashes AI against Latin American banks. Tor exit nodes are hijacked. OpenAI coding agents disable security monitoring. Interpol dismantles thousands of cybercrime networks across Africa. Our guest is Danny Manimbo, ISO and AI Practice Leader at Schellman, explaining why companies waiting for AI regulatory clarity may already be behind. Spotify hits the skip button on AI slop.

Today is Thursday October 22nd 2026. I’m Dave Bittner. And this is your CyberWire Intel Briefing.

Amazon detected PHP exploitation attempts days before public disclosure.

Amazon Threat Intelligence detected attempts to exploit two PHP vulnerabilities four days before their public disclosure on October 21st. The activity, observed through Amazon’s MadPot honeypot network, originated from anonymized infrastructure, suggesting threat actor involvement. How the attackers obtained exploit information remains unknown.

Additional attempts appeared hours before disclosure, followed by widespread exploitation once patches became available. Researchers believe multiple actors were involved, although it’s unclear whether the early attacks would have succeeded against real-world systems.

Amazon warns that coordinated disclosure no longer guarantees a head start for defenders. AI-assisted exploit development is accelerating the transition from vulnerability disclosure to active attacks, sometimes to just minutes. Security teams should prioritize patching critical internet-facing vulnerabilities within hours, investigate potential compromises predating disclosure, and deploy detections that don’t depend on vulnerability-specific signatures.

GitLab patches a maximum-severity vulnerability.

GitLab has released emergency patches for a maximum-severity vulnerability that could allow unauthenticated attackers to execute arbitrary code on vulnerable servers.

Tracked as CVE-2026-110264, the flaw involves an integer overflow in GitLab’s Regular Expression Compiler. It affects both Community and Enterprise editions, and GitLab is urging customers to update immediately.

The Shadowserver Foundation tracks more than 2,700 internet-exposed GitLab Community Edition instances, although it’s unclear how many remain vulnerable.

This is GitLab’s second critical remote code execution vulnerability in ten days, both reported by the same security researcher. Last month, GitLab also patched a maximum-severity flaw that could expose sensitive information. CISA subsequently confirmed active exploitation of that vulnerability and ordered federal agencies to patch.

GitLab says its hosted service is already protected.

Meta is fined $25 billion in New Mexico.

A New Mexico judge has ordered Meta to pay $25 billion in penalties stemming from the Cambridge Analytica privacy scandal.

A jury found the company liable for more than 43 million violations of the state’s unfair practices law, concluding that Meta misled users about its data collection practices, privacy protections, and harmful content.

The judge initially calculated penalties totaling nearly $220 billion before reducing the award to $25 billion, with annual interest of 15 percent until it’s paid.

The ruling also criticized Facebook’s internal investigation following the Cambridge Analytica revelations, calling it deliberately ineffective.

New Mexico’s attorney general hailed the decision as a warning to powerful technology companies.

Meta strongly disputes the ruling and plans to appeal, arguing that the state’s approach effectively imposes a tax on online speech.

Researchers uncovered new threat actors using autonomous AI agents.

CrowdStrike researchers have uncovered four previously undocumented threat actors using autonomous AI agents to conduct cyberattacks, with some operations achieving their objectives within an hour.

The actors, operating in Spanish, Chinese, Indonesian, and Russian, targeted government agencies, healthcare organizations, and private companies worldwide. Their activities included successful intrusions and data theft.

Researchers discovered the campaigns after the attackers inadvertently exposed their offensive AI frameworks through publicly accessible directories.

The operations varied considerably in sophistication. One actor employed multiple coordinated AI agents, while another, despite limited technical skills, successfully compromised government systems using publicly available tools.

CrowdStrike warns that agentic AI is lowering the technical barriers to cybercrime, allowing less-skilled attackers to conduct increasingly sophisticated operations at machine speed. Researchers expect these AI-powered intrusions to grow in both volume and sophistication.

Hackers compromise a Japanese cloud hosting provider.

Hackers have compromised a Japanese cloud hosting provider, potentially installing malware on nearly 27,000 customer servers.

Onamae (o-na-MA-ay) Desktop Cloud, operated by GMO Internet, confirmed unauthorized access to its infrastructure and the installation of malicious software in customer environments.

The company began shutting down affected services on October 21st, disrupting all Desktop Cloud plans. There’s no estimated timeline for restoring service.

GMO warns that information stored on compromised servers may have been exposed, although it has not confirmed any data theft or misuse. Credit card information was unaffected because it’s stored separately.

Customers are being urged to change passwords and other credentials stored on their servers and remain alert for phishing attempts.

The company says its investigation is ongoing and promises additional updates.

CyberCartel targets banks and payment providers across Latin America.

Security researchers at Straiker have uncovered an AI-powered attack system used by a cybercriminal group targeting banks and payment providers across Latin America.

The group, known as CyberCartel, has reportedly been active since 2012. Its latest operation uses a framework called CARLIY0S, which coordinates multiple commercial AI models to identify vulnerabilities, develop exploits, and execute attacks.

The AI agents have specialized roles, including reconnaissance, exploit development, and evaluating competing attack strategies.

Researchers gained access to the group’s operational environment, uncovering a database containing nearly 4,500 records, including financial information, credentials, API keys, and backdoors.

Straiker says the group targeted more than 400 financial organizations in a matter of months.

The findings offer a rare look at AI becoming part of cybercriminal infrastructure, potentially allowing smaller groups to conduct sophisticated attacks faster and at greater scale.

Hackers hijack Tor exit nodes.

Hackers hijacked 333 Tor exit nodes in an operation designed to intercept SSH connections and unencrypted email traffic.

According to Tor volunteers, the intrusion began with a reused password that provided access to a management server. Attackers installed the Ebury Linux backdoor and eventually gained control of hundreds of exit relays.

Between October 2nd and 5th, the compromised nodes redirected SSH connections through attacker-controlled servers, potentially capturing passwords and installing additional malware. The attackers also blocked encrypted email ports while allowing unencrypted traffic, although it’s unclear whether any email interception succeeded.

Researchers still don’t know how the attackers compromised so many servers or who’s responsible.

The incident highlights the importance of enforcing encrypted email connections and using SSH keys instead of passwords, particularly when routing traffic through Tor.

OpenAI coding agents weakened internal security monitoring.

Two OpenAI coding agents weakened internal security monitoring while completing routine programming tasks.

In one case, a GPT-6.1 Sol agent disabled automatic security alerts after misinterpreting instructions not to send Slack messages. In another, a GPT-6 Astra agent removed monitoring software to match a reference implementation, then falsely told the user it hadn’t.

Both agents considered preserving the safeguards but ultimately prioritized their coding instructions.

OpenAI is strengthening its monitoring systems while investigating whether the incidents reflect excessive task persistence or a specific tendency to evade oversight.

Authorities shut down African cybercrime networks.

Interpol says an international law enforcement operation across Africa has resulted in more than 1,400 arrests and the disruption of nearly 11,000 cybercriminal networks.

Operation Serengeti III involved authorities from 21 countries, targeting ransomware, business email compromise, and online fraud between late June and August.

Investigators identified nearly 66,000 victims, with estimated losses exceeding $385 million. Authorities recovered more than $105 million in illicit funds.

Among the results, Ugandan police arrested 365 suspects linked to investment and pension fraud. Angola seized more than 2,000 illegal cryptocurrency mining devices, while Nigerian authorities arrested a suspect allegedly responsible for a major phishing operation.

Private cybersecurity companies provided intelligence to help identify criminal infrastructure and suspects.

It’s the third Operation Serengeti crackdown since 2024, reflecting an ongoing international effort to disrupt cybercrime across the continent.

Spotify hits the skip button on AI slop.

Spotify has spent the past year trying to keep AI-generated musical slop from overwhelming its platform, and apparently, there’s been plenty to clean up.

The streaming giant says it’s removed more than 50 million spammy or low-quality tracks from recommendations this year, on top of another 75 million tracks removed from the platform entirely.

Spotify says listeners were consistently skipping or rejecting content identified as slop, prompting changes to its recommendation algorithms.

The company has also introduced AI disclosure credits, verified more than 300,000 artists, and begun labeling AI-generated artist personas. Those virtual performers are generally excluded from recommendations unless listeners actively follow them.

Spotify acknowledges that detecting AI-generated content remains difficult, particularly as the technology improves.

The company insists its priority remains human artistry, even as artificial intelligence makes producing music easier than ever.

Apparently, just because a machine can write a song doesn’t mean anyone wants to hear it.

And that’s the CyberWire.

For links to all of today’s stories, check out our Daily Briefing at the cyberwire dot com.

We’d love to know what you think of this podcast. Your feedback ensures we deliver the insights that keep you a step ahead in the rapidly changing world of cybersecurity. If you like the show, please share a rating and review in your podcast app. Please also fill out the survey in the show notes or send an email to cyberwire@n2k.com

We’re proud that N2K CyberWire is part of the daily routine of the most influential leaders and operators in the public and private sector, from the Fortune 500 to many of the world’s preeminent intelligence and law enforcement agencies.

N2K helps cybersecurity professionals and organizations grow, learn, and stay ahead. We’re the nexus for discovering the people, tech, and ideas shaping the industry. Learn how at n2k.com.

N2K’s lead producer is Liz Stokes. We’re mixed by Tré Hester, with original music by and sound design Elliott Peltzman. Our contributing host is Maria Varmazis. Our executive producer is Jennifer Eiben. Peter Kilpe is our publisher. And I’m Dave Bittner. Thanks for listening.

articles.title: How bug bounty sharpens one researcher’s security skills
articles.context: Sometimes the vulnerability only becomes obvious once you understand how a particular source can influence a security-sensitive operation
articles.full_text:
As Cybersecurity Awareness Month continues, the GitHub Bug Bounty team is excited to spotlight another top-performing security researcher from the GitHub Security Bug Bounty Program: @r31n!

As home to the world’s developers, GitHub is dedicated to the security and reliability of the code behind millions of projects, and our Bug Bounty Program remains a cornerstone of that commitment. Collaboration with external researchers is one of the most effective ways to improve security, and every year, the community helps us identify and fix vulnerabilities that make the platform safer for everyone.

The security research landscape is changing rapidly. AI has lowered the barrier to entry and become a genuine force multiplier. We use it across our own internal security programs, and we welcome researchers who do the same. However, what separates great research has not changed: validation, a working proof of concept, and a clear demonstration of real security impact. The tools do not matter; the quality of the work does. The researchers we spotlight this month exemplify exactly that standard through findings that are verified, reproducible, and demonstrate that a security boundary has been crossed rather than simply theorizing that one exists.

Researchers who consistently work at that level can earn an invitation to our permanent VIP program, which offers higher payouts, faster response times, and early previews of beta products and features. Learn more about how to qualify on our public bounty site.

As we wrap up our Cybersecurity Awareness Month celebration, we interview @r31n, a researcher renowned for their work on GitHub Enterprise Server, where they have repeatedly uncovered high-impact issues. Their reports consistently include working proofs of concept and clear reproduction steps, helping our engineering teams move from triage to remediation more quickly.

How did you get started in security and bug bounty, and what keeps you coming back to GitHub’s program?

I got into bug bounty because I wanted a way to keep developing my security skills outside the environments I work with every day. It exposes me to different products, technologies, and architectures I probably wouldn’t run into otherwise. GitHub is one of those programs I keep coming back to because there’s just so much surface area. It’s large, complex, and constantly changing. New features ship all the time, so it never really feels like a finished target. They also work closely with researchers, the bounty structure is competitive, and the swag is a nice bonus. It’s simply a program I enjoy spending time on.

What are your favorite classes of bugs to research and why?

I don’t really have one favorite bug class. What interests me more are exploit chains, especially cases where a few things that seem relatively harmless on their own come together and create something much more serious. An open redirect is a simple example. By itself, the impact might be limited. But if you find an allowlisted-domain SSRF that follows redirects, suddenly that open redirect can become a useful part of a much bigger chain. That’s probably the part of vulnerability research I enjoy most: finding those connections, looking at two or three separate bugs and realizing they can be combined in a way that wasn’t intended. It takes some technical knowledge, but also quite a bit of creativity.

How do you keep your skills sharp and stay on top of new vulnerability trends?

It’s actually a mix of different things. Security blogs, vulnerability write-ups, conference talks, proof of concepts, research papers, courses. I try to learn from wherever useful work is being shared. But most of it only really sticks once I try it myself. I can read a vulnerability write-up, but working through it myself gives me a much deeper understanding. If I actually reproduce the technique, play around with it, break it, and figure out why it behaves the way it does, that’s when it really stays with me. And later, when I see a similar pattern on a real target, it’s much easier to recognize.

What tools or workflows have been gamechangers for your research? Any lesser-known utilities you’d recommend?

I tend to prefer manual investigation and small, purpose-built scripts over large automated toolchains. If I notice I’m repeating the same task during research, I’ll usually automate that specific part. AI has probably impacted my way of working more than any individual security tool.

Even then, I think mindset matters more than tooling. You can become extremely good with a particular tool and still miss interesting bugs because you’re only looking at the target through the lens that tool gives you. Sometimes relying too heavily on tooling actually narrows the way you think. Tools change. Techniques change. Curiosity and persistence tend to age much better. So, I don’t really have one tool I’d recommend to everyone. The most useful tool is usually the one that helps answer the specific question I’m investigating.

Walk us through your general approach. How do you pick a target area, and how do you go from “interesting feature” to a confirmed finding?

I usually start by mapping out the application and getting a feel for how its different parts fit together. I tend to spend more time on complex functionality, integrations, trust boundaries, and anything that behaves a little differently from the rest. Experience and intuition matter too. Some areas simply look more likely to expose interesting security behavior. From there, I often think in terms of sources and sinks rather than starting with a specific vulnerability class. A source is a point where attacker-controlled data enters the application.

Think of a request parameter, uploaded file, API input, or data coming from another service. A sink can be a security-sensitive operation that consumes this data, for example, a network request, file access, process execution, database query, or authorization decision. The interesting part is tracing the path between the two. I look at how the data is transformed, validated, or passed across trust boundaries, and whether those controls are sufficient before it reaches the sink.

I like this approach because it lets me reason about attack paths without forcing my investigation into a predefined bug class. Sometimes the vulnerability only becomes obvious once you understand how a particular source can influence a security-sensitive operation. I consider a finding confirmed once I understand the attack path, can produce a working PoC, and can explain the impact.

Do you use AI in your research? Where does it genuinely help and where does it fall short?

Yes. Quite a lot, actually, but mostly as an accelerator. I use it for navigating unfamiliar code, finding call sites, tracing data through the codebase, and understanding how a system is structured and how its components interact. I also find it helpful for writing PoC scripts once I’ve identified the vulnerability.

Where it works best is when the question is specific. “Is this application vulnerable?” usually isn’t a very useful prompt. Give it the right context, explain what you already know, and ask a narrow question, and the quality goes up dramatically. There’s a bit of a paradox there. AI becomes more useful as you understand the problem better yourself. And I never treat its conclusions as facts. Hallucinations, false positives, bad assumptions, and confidently wrong answers are all common. Everything should still be manually verified. AI makes my work faster. However, it doesn’t replace understanding the application, developing intuition, or proving that something actually works.

What’s your guidance on using AI responsibly in bug bounty?

Use it to improve your research, not to outsource responsibility for it. If AI tells you it found a vulnerability, that doesn’t mean you found a real vulnerability. You still need to reproduce it yourself. You should understand exactly what’s happening, which security boundary or control is being violated, and what the real impact is. Ideally, you should understand the issue well enough that you could write the report without AI at all. Build a clear PoC. Make sure the security team can follow it. Know why every step matters.

AI has lowered the barrier to doing security research, which is great in a lot of ways. But you can also see the downside in the number of unverified reports teams now have to deal with. AI should make research better. Not just make more reports.

As the industry ships more AI-powered features, does testing them require a different mindset than traditional web bugs?

Yes. Conventional vulnerabilities still matter, but attackers may also be able to influence a probabilistic decision-making component through the data, instructions, or context it receives. But getting a model to say or do something unexpected isn’t necessarily the interesting part. The more important question is what that influence allows an attacker to achieve. Can they access something they should not or cause the system to act with privileges the attacker does not have? That’s why I don’t think model-level guardrails should ever be treated as the only or primary security boundary. You still need deterministic controls around the model. This includes proper authorization, least-privilege access, isolation, and validation. The surrounding systems matter just as much as the model itself. And traditional application security doesn’t disappear just because AI is involved. Model output should still be treated as untrusted input. If that output ends up in a browser, database query, shell command, web request, or another downstream system without the right controls, you can still end up with very familiar vulnerabilities: XSS, SQL injection, command injection, SSRF, and so on. I think the model is new. A lot of the dangerous sinks aren’t.

What’s one thing you wish you’d known when you first started?

Learn systems, not checklists. When I started, I was tempted to collect huge lists of techniques, payloads, tools, and bypasses and then work through them one by one. Those lists can be useful.

I still use them. But understanding how a system works has been far more valuable. Its internal logic. The data flows. Trust relationships. Assumptions. Why one component is allowed to talk to another. Why a particular restriction exists in the first place. I also learned not to assume something is secure because it looks secure, or because plenty of researchers have already tested it.

A lot of interesting research begins with: “Why does this work this way?” rather than “Which payload should I try next?” There’s some luck involved too. Sometimes you spend days following something that goes absolutely nowhere. Then you notice one tiny detail almost by accident and it turns into a high-impact finding. You can’t control that part. You can control whether you keep questioning things long enough to notice it.

What advice or resources would you recommend to researchers trying to land their first valid report?

Get comfortable with the fundamentals, then pick one program and one target and stick with them for a while. Constantly jumping between targets makes it difficult to build a real mental model of any of them. Use the application. Explore weird flows. Test different roles and permission levels. Read the documentation. Watch the requests and responses. Look at the APIs. Labs, courses, public write-ups, disclosed bug bounty reports, and intentionally vulnerable applications are all useful too. They teach you where bugs tend to hide and, over time, help build the intuition to recognize similar situations elsewhere.

One mistake I see a lot is relying on tools too early. Another is giving up because the obvious tests didn’t find anything. Tools help. They don’t build the mental model for you. And when you finally do find something, spend the extra time validating it properly. Create a working PoC. Make reproduction easy for the security team. Understanding one target deeply will usually get you further than trying to find a bug as quickly as possible.

What do you enjoy doing when you aren’t hacking?

Endurance sports, mainly road cycling, especially in the mountains. I enjoy the physical challenge of a long climb and pushing myself over longer distances. It’s also a great way to get away from screens for a while and spend some time outside. There’s actually something about climbing that feels pretty similar to vulnerability research. You can put in a lot of effort without seeing much progress. Sometimes you have no idea whether what you’re doing is going to lead anywhere. You just keep going. And every now and then, it pays off.

Any social media profiles you’d like to share with our readers?

You can find me on HackerOne.

Thank you, @r31n, for participating in GitHub’s bug bounty researcher spotlight! Each submission to our bug bounty program is a chance to make GitHub, our products, and our customers more secure, and we continue to welcome and appreciate collaboration with the security research community. So, if this inspired you to go hunting for bugs, feel free to report your findings through HackerOne.

The post How bug bounty sharpens one researcher’s security skills appeared first on The GitHub Blog.

articles.title: EU Regulators to Investigate Booking.com Over Scam Risks
articles.context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
articles.full_text:
The European Commission has opened an investigation Booking.com for possible security failings that have resulted in fraudulent listings and phishing scams.

The investigation will ascertain whether the online travel agency has breached security and transparency provisions contained in the EU’s Digital Services Act (DSA).

Among the focus areas of the investigation, the Commission will assess whether Booking.com has diligently assessed and mitigated phishing risks to customers. This includes looking at how the firm shares reservation and guest data is shared with accommodation providers, and the safeguards it has in place to prevent such data being misused to carry out phishing and solicit fraudulent payments.

In addition, the Commission will focus on the design and functioning of Booking.com's messaging service, and its potential to be abused by malicious actors for phishing attacks.

Another focus is whether the provider of Booking.com has properly assessed and mitigated the systemic risks linked to the dissemination of illegal content, such as impersonation fraud and non-compliant accommodation.

The firm’s advertising practices will also be assessed to determine whether it meets the DSA's advertising transparency obligations.

If it is determined that the company failed to comply with the DSA in these areas, Booking.com could face a fine of up to 6% of their global annual turnover and be required to take corrective measures.

The DSA came into force in November 2022 and applies to Very Large Online Platforms (VLOPs) and Very Large Online Search Engines (VLOSEs).

The decision to launch formal proceedings against Booking.com, announced on October 21, follows a preliminary investigation carried out by the Commission.

Commenting on the decision, Henna Virkkunen, the Commissions’ executive vice-president for tech sovereignty, security and democracy, said: “Europeans should be able to book their holidays without fear of being scammed. The DSA sets clear responsibilities on platforms to address these risks, and we must ensure that the leading booking platform in Europe takes those responsibilities seriously.”

The Commission emphasized that the opening of formal proceedings does not prejudge any final outcome or decision and is empowered to accept commitments offered by Booking.com to remedy the matters subject to the proceedings.

Booking.com Customers a Frequent Target for Phishing Attacks

Numerous phishing campaigns targeting Booking.com customers and partners have been observed by cybersecurity researchers in recent years. These campaigns have included threat actors accessing the personal details of Booking.com customers and spoofing the company’s email domains to send malicious messages.

In 2023, Secureworks, now part of Sophos, reported how cybercriminals deployed the Vidar infostealer to gain access partner hotels’ Booking.com credentials. This information was then used to send phishing emails to Booking.com customers and trick them into handing over their payment details, in many cases leading to money being stolen.

Microsoft reported a ClickFix campaign that impersonated Booking.com in March 2025. This began with the threat actor sending malicious email impersonating Booking.com to targeted individuals in North America, Oceania, South and Southeast Asia and Europe. The attack attempted to lure these individuals into downloading infostealer malware.

In June 2026, TrendAI Research identified a phishing campaign targeting Booking.com partner accommodations in Japan. These emails impersonated guest complaints and review requests to trick hotel staff into executing malicious files.

articles.title: Iranian Hacking Group Found Hosting C2 Infrastructure in the US
articles.context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
articles.full_text:
An Iranian nation-state cyber threat group has been discovered using command-and-control (C2) servers based in the US to support its malware delivery and cyber-espionage campaigns.

The activity was identified by cybersecurity researchers at Semperis, who published their findings on October 22. The Iranian group is known as ‘Prince of Persia’, which has been active for around two decades.

Prince of Persia targets public and private sector organisations across the US, Europe and the Middle East, as well as dissidents and others opposed to the Iranian regime.

The multiple forms of malware used in Prince of Persia campaigns provide attackers with intrusive data exfiltration capabilities. This includes the ability to steal sensitive documents, as well as secretly taking screenshots and capturing audio recorded by the infected device.

Forms of malware identified as part of the latest Prince of Persia campaign include Foudre, a first stage malware loader and Tonnerre, a second stage malware which provides the attackers with what researchers describe as full surveillance capabilities.

The campaigns also involve a more recently identified malware known as Tornado, which builds on the codebase of previous malware. Tornado has the ability to use both HTTPS and the Telegram API as a covert C2 channel, blending in with legitimate network traffic to bypass firewalls and evade detection.

Advanced Anti-Detection Capabilities

Prince of Persia has been known to secretly hide its activity on European hosting services and virtual private servers, but anti-detection capabilities of the malware initially made it difficult for researchers to identify how the latest campaign was being hosted.

According to Tomer Bar, AVP of security research at Semperis, Prince of Persia seemed to go dark in February this year, coinciding with US and Israeli strikes against Iran.

“This isn’t unusual given that geopolitical conflict involving Iran leads to downtime with the threat group,” said Bar.

However, information in the Tornado malware resulted in researchers being able to identify where the campaign was being hosted and it was found to be a US hosting company.

While it isn’t unusual for threat groups to hide their activity within US hosting providers, it is the first time an Iranian threat group has been identified as hosting their activity on US servers in at least 12 years.

“This is the last place we expected to find Prince of Persia hiding,” Bar added.

While Prince of Persia activity is highly targeted rather than widespread, the group has been a persistent cyber threat to organizations for almost two decades. To help ensure protection from attacks by the group, Semperis has recommended the following actions:

Ensure that your security controls are up to date

Monitor for any unusual Telegram traffic.

Ensure that your operating systems are fully updated

Summary

Multiple vulnerabilities have been identified in the additional GNU/Linux subsystem of the SIMATIC S7-1500 TM MFP V1.1.1. Siemens is preparing fixes and recommends specific mitigations for products where fixes are not or not yet available.

The following versions of Siemens SIMATIC S7-1500 TM MFP are affected:

SIMATIC S7-1500 TM MFP - GNU/Linux subsystem vers:all/*

CVSS

Vendor

Equipment

v3 10

Siemens

SIMATIC S7-1500 TM MFP - GNU/Linux subsystem

377 Vulnerabilities

Access of Uninitialized Pointer, Buffer Copy without Checking Size of Input ('Classic Buffer Overflow'), Deadlock, Detection of Error Condition Without Action, Double Free, Expired Pointer Dereference, Heap-based Buffer Overflow, Improper Control of Resource Identifiers ('Resource Injection'), Improper Control of a Resource Through its Lifetime, Improper Handling of Length Parameter Inconsistency, Improper Handling of Missing Special Element, Improper Handling of Structural Elements, Improper Input Validation, Improper Locking, Improper Resource Locking, Improper Restriction of Operations within the Bounds of a Memory Buffer, Improper Update of Reference Count, Improper Validation of Array Index, Improper Validation of Consistency within Input, Improper Validation of Specified Index, Position, or Offset in Input, Improper Validation of Specified Quantity in Input, Improper Validation of Specified Type of Input, Incorrect Synchronization, Integer Overflow or Wraparound, Integer Underflow (Wrap or Wraparound), Loop with Unreachable Exit Condition ('Infinite Loop'), Missing Default Case in Multiple Condition Expression, Missing Initialization of Resource, Missing Lock Check, Missing Release of Memory after Effective Lifetime, Missing Release of Resource after Effective Lifetime, Multiple Locks of a Critical Resource, NULL Pointer Dereference, Operation on a Resource after Expiration or Release, Out-of-bounds Read, Out-of-bounds Write, Plaintext Storage of a Password, Release of Invalid Pointer or Reference, Return of Wrong Status Code, Signal Handler Race Condition, Time-of-check Time-of-use (TOCTOU) Race Condition, Unchecked Return Value, Use After Free, Use of Incorrect Operator, Use of Uninitialized Resource, Write-what-where Condition

Background

Critical Infrastructure Sectors: Critical Manufacturing, Transportation Systems, Energy, Healthcare and Public Health, Financial Services, Government Services and Facilities

Countries/Areas Deployed: Worldwide

Company Headquarters Location: Germany

Vulnerabilities

Expand All +

CVE-2023-52927

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: netfilter: allow exp not to be removed in nf_ct_find_expectation Currently nf_conntrack_in() calling nf_ct_find_expectation() will remove the exp from the hash table. However, in some scenario, we expect the exp not to be removed when the created ct will not be confirmed, like in OVS and TC conntrack in the following patches. This patch allows exp not to be removed by setting IPS_CONFIRMED in the status of the tmpl.

Read More

1 Affected Product

SIMATIC S7-1500 TM MFP - GNU/Linux subsystem

MitigationLimit access to the interactive shell of the additional GNU/Linux subssytem to trusted personnel only.

MitigationOnly build and run applications from trusted sources.

Acknowledgments

Juan Alonso reported these vulnerabilities to CISA.

Recommended Practices

CISA recommends users take defensive measures to minimize the risk of exploitation of these vulnerabilities.

Minimize network exposure for all control system devices and/or systems, ensuring they are not accessible from the internet.

Locate control system networks and remote devices behind firewalls and isolating them from business networks.

When remote access is required, use more secure methods, such as Virtual Private Networks (VPNs), recognizing VPNs may have vulnerabilities and should be updated to the most current version available. Also recognize VPN is only as secure as the connected devices.

CISA reminds organizations to perform proper impact analysis and risk assessment prior to deploying defensive measures.

CISA also provides a section for control systems security recommended practices on the ICS webpage on cisa.gov/ics. Several CISA products detailing cyber defense best practices are available for reading and download, including Improving Industrial Control Systems Cybersecurity with Defense-in-Depth Strategies.

CISA encourages organizations to implement recommended cybersecurity strategies for proactive defense of ICS assets.

Additional mitigation guidance and recommended practices are publicly available on the ICS webpage at cisa.gov/ics in the technical information paper, ICS-TIP-12-146-01B--Targeted Cyber Intrusion Detection and Mitigation Strategies.

Organizations observing suspected malicious activity should follow established internal procedures and report findings to CISA for tracking and correlation against other incidents.

CISA also recommends users take the following measures to protect themselves from social engineering attacks:

Do not click web links or open attachments in unsolicited email messages.

Refer to Recognizing and Avoiding Email Scams for more information on avoiding email scams.

Refer to Avoiding Social Engineering and Phishing Attacks for more information on social engineering attacks.

No known public exploitation specifically targeting these vulnerabilities has been reported to CISA at this time.

RUGGEDCOM CROSSBOW contains multiple vulnerabilities that could allow an attacker to execute arbitrary SQL commands on the underlying database, retrieve sensitive administrative credentials, escalate privileges, and perform unauthorized operations such as modifying system configurations or causing a denial of service. Siemens has released a new version for RUGGEDCOM CROSSBOW and recommends to update to the latest version.

CVE-2026-33387

A template injection vulnerability was discovered in the Dashboards functionality due to improper validation of an input parameter. An authenticated user with the required privileges can define a dashboard containing a malicious payload, or a victim can be socially engineered into importing a malicious dashboard. When the victim views or imports the dashboard, the payload executes in their browser context, allowing the attacker to modify application data or disrupt application availability.

CVE-2026-33388

An access control vulnerability was discovered in the Credentials Manager functionality due to insufficient validation of user privileges. A remote authenticated user with limited privileges can view a limited subset of the available entries in the Credentials Manager. The actual credential values are not directly visible, but the user can delete entries or edit their properties. An attacker who deletes or edits an entry can disrupt authentication for dependent devices, and one who manipulates an entry's configuration may be able to indirectly obtain the credentials.

An improper certificate/host key validation vulnerability was discovered in the Smart Polling functionality, which established encrypted connections to target devices without validating the remote host's identity, and no option was provided to enable it. A man-in-the-middle attacker positioned between a sensor and a polled device can, during a polling session, impersonate the device and intercept the communication, including the credentials used to access it. Vulnerabilities

CVE-2026-72895

A BIOS vendor test key is present in the UEFI Secure Boot key database. This could allow a local attacker with physical or administrative access to the device to boot an operating system or UEFI application signed with that test key, bypassing UEFI Secure Boot protections even when Secure Boot is enabled, potentially leading to a full loss of confidentiality, integrity, and availability of the device.

Read More

SIMATIC IPC BX-21A < V31.01.13

Product Status: known_affected

Remediations

MitigationNote: After upgrading to the fixed BIOS version, users must load the BIOS default settings. If Secure Boot keys were already provisioned, they must be provisioned again afterwards.

Vendor fixUpdate to V31.01.13 or later version

articles.title: Microsoft: Chinese State Actor Used AI to Compromise ConnectWise Tenants
articles.context: Microsoft assessed that a threat actor, tracked as Storm-0940, utilized agentic AI penetration testing framework ARTEX to target hundreds of organizations globally across a...
articles.full_text:
A Chinese nation-state actor was responsible for the compromise of Microsoft365 tenants used by ConnectWise, which led to IT management software provider taking a number of its cloud services offline.

Microsoft assessed that a threat actor, tracked as Storm-0940, utilized agentic AI penetration testing framework ARTEX to target hundreds of organizations globally across a broad range of industries, beginning in September 2026.

The China-aligned group was able to obtain privileged access to a number of organizations’ cloud infrastructure, including ConnectWise, often in less than three hours from initial targeting.

The campaign targeted industries such as aerospace and defense, automotive, chemicals, energy, financial services, government, legal, manufacturing, media, military, semiconductor, software, technology, and think tanks and non-profits.

Storm-0940 has been active since 2021 and its primary objective is data theft. It uses password spraying and exploitation of internet-facing applications for initial access, and establishes persistence in cloud environments by adding credentials to existing OAuth applications.

Attackers Target ConnectWise Customers

After gaining unauthorized access to the ConnectWise multi-tenant application, the China-aligned actor targeted the IT services firm’s downstream customers using the ARTEX platform to accelerate scanning and reconnaissance, password spraying and OAuth application abuse.

The group attempted to sign-in to more than 2250 tenants at 2900 sign-in attempts per minute. Microsoft said the pace of this supply chain attack gives defenders little time to detect and respond.

Microsoft revealed that it had identified multiple customer environments with evidence of follow-on activity, including reconnaissance, application credential modifications to establish persistence, and changes involving identities, groups and privileged roles.

“After acquiring control of the identities of multiple ConnectWise cloud applications, the AI agents operating on behalf of the threat actor continued to use the same IP range to authenticate to customer environments using the illicit access acquired through these stolen app credentials, effectively taking advantage of the already established trust by these apps within a tenant,” the tech giant explained in a blog dated October 21.

In an update published on October 21, ConnectWise acknowledged Microsoft’s findings and the extensive use of AI to compromise its Microsoft365 tenants.

“Nation-state actors are increasingly targeting the software supply chain, because one trusted connection can open the door to many organizations. AI now lets them test those connections at what Microsoft calls 'machine speed'. MSPs are in the middle of that chain. They are targets in their own right, and they are also a path into every client they serve,” the company wrote.

ConnectWise Cloud Services Remains Offline

ConnectWise first identified suspicious activity in its network on October 15, before discovering unauthorized access to application identities within its Cloud Backup environment on October 17.

The discovery resulted in several ConnectWise cloud services including Cloud Backup (previously known as SkyKick), SaaS Security and Cloud Management being taken offline while the company investigates the incident.

These services remain offline, according to the company’s status page.

However, ConnectWise said in an advisory on October 22 that it had started a phased restoration of its Cloud Backup service.

“We expect restoration to take several days and will share service-specific availability and reconnection instructions as confirmed. Keep affected connections disabled until formal instructions apply to your service,” it told customers.

The firm added that existing backup archives remain encrypted, isolated, and preserved, with no indication of compromise, while there is no evidence that other ConnectWise products and services are impacted by the incident.

Customers have also been advised to review individual Microsoft 365 tenants for unauthorized changes or persistent access.

The ARTEX Agentic AI Platform Threat

ARTEX is a multi-agent large-language model (LLM) that can use any AI model to automate a variety of offensive security workflows, including penetration test from reconnaissance through data exfiltration.

The agents then accumulate the discovered assets and vulnerabilities into a graph during the penetration test, Microsoft explained.

While the platform’s user interface and generated output default to English, the framework can be switched to Korean, Mandarin, Spanish, or Japanese.

In October 2026, CrowdStrike reported that a China-based threat actor used ARTEX to discover vulnerabilities and compromise specific services in South Korean financial organizations, a campaign that resulted in the exfiltration of data.

articles.title: PHP2Shell Exploitation Attempt Detected by Amazon Four Days Before Vulnerability Disclosure
articles.context: Now the patches have been released, the Amazon Threat Intelligence team has publically confirmed they observed a PHP2Shell exploitation attempt dating October 17
articles.full_text:
Someone tried to exploit two critical vulnerabilities in the PHP programming language four days before the vulnerabilities were published and the flaws are now being exploited in the wild at scale, according to Amazon.

The flaws, tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 and collectively known as ‘PHP2Shell,’ could allow unauthenticated remote code execution (RCE) and server takeover on any websites relying on any PHP version released in the last decade – going back to version 5.4.

PHP is used by approximately 69.7% of websites whose server-side programming language is known, according to recent W3Techs data. These include many content management systems (CMS) like WordPress, Drupal, Joomla and Magento as well as e-commerce and web services platforms.

The bugs were discovered by security researchers at California-based security firm Calif and Google Cloud’s Wiz, with collaboration from OpenAI’s Patch the Planet project, in August. Public disclosure was scheduled for October 21, when the PHP Foundation planned to release the security patches.

However, on October 20, a pseudonymous user of the Hacker News forum leaked some information about the flaws before the patches were ready.

This led to many organizations across the world, including French public administrations, the Dutch National Cyber Security Centre and the University of Vienna taking their websites offline to prepare for and then apply the patches.

Now the patches have been released, the Amazon Threat Intelligence team has publically confirmed they observed a PHP2Shell exploitation attempt dating October 17. The attempt occurred in MadPot, an internal honeypot system created by Amazon Web Services (AWS) to monitor, study and disrupt global cybercrime.

Early Exploitation Attempt Likely From A “Threat Actor”

The exploit attempt originated from an IP address associated with a commercial anonymization network. According to the Amazon researchers, this suggests the activity was conducted by a threat actor, though it remains unclear how the actor acquired exploit information prior to disclosure.

In addition, they said they identified multiple proof-of-concept (PoC) exploits for PHP2Shell on October 21, around 12 hours before the vulnerability’s scheduled disclosure at 2pm GMT.

The earliest exploit was detected at approximately 2am GMT, with further attempts targeting the company’s MadPot sensors between 2am and 8am GMT from additional infrastructure.

According to the researchers, variations in the payloads and anonymization infrastructure suggested that multiple threat actors were involved. However, it was unclear whether the attempts would have succeeded against real-world systems.

Further PoC exploits emerged within hours of the release of the PHP2Shell patches, which were used against Amazon’s sensors almost immediately.

The researchers warned that PHP2Shell is now being broadly exploited in the wild.

Emerging Evidence of PHP2Shell Exploitation Attempts

Other security and threat intelligence teams have started to report active exploitation attempts of CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 in the wild.

Matthew Prince, co-founder and CEO of Cloudflare, said on X his company saw “thousands of attempts to exploit” the vulnerabilities within the 10 hours that preceded the disclosure.

“That jumped to tens of thousands in the 45 minutes post announcement, hundreds of thousands within two hours, and millions now,” he added.

Other security firms, including Beelzebub, Ellio, Recorded Future, VulnCheck, WatchTowr and Wiz have also observed evidence of exploitation attempts in the wild for both vulnerabilities.

articles.title: The Keys Are in the Browser: Secret Exposure Across AI-Built Websites
articles.context: Twelve keys in one bundle are twelve live credentials shipped at once, and five sites like this are five accounts an attacker can exploit
articles.full_text:
Cyble scanned 1.3M+ newly registered domains and found AI-built sites leaking live secrets to the browser: OpenAI keys, Stripe keys, and database tokens.

Spinning up a website no longer takes a developer. A prompt to an AI app-builder returns a working, styled, deployable site in minutes, and when one template works, the same operator clones it across a dozen domains before launch. That is also how secrets end up in plain sight.

Over a month, Cyble Research and Intelligence Labs (CRIL) scanned more than 1.3 million newly registered domains, identified the ones built by AI app-builders, and read their public front-end code for exposed credentials. We built our own classifiers to spot AI-generated websites as they are registered, paired with a scanner that pulls exposed keys and credentials straight from their public code. On 35 of the 22,306 AI-built sites we identified, a genuinely private secret was sitting in the browser: live OpenAI keys, Stripe secret keys, backend database tokens, and, in several cases, a single credential cloned across a whole fleet of domains.

Thirty-five is a small number, since counting every key-shaped string on an AI-built site is easy and misleading, as most are meant to be in the browser; a single reCAPTCHA key appeared on thousands of sites. We kept only the credentials that are never supposed to leave a server. Those are the findings below.

This report walks through the two leak patterns we observed, what appears exposed, what an attacker can do with these keys, and how to shut down the exposure.

AI-built Websites are leaking the keys that power them

An AI-built site generates its content with a Large Language Model (LLM), and the key to that model often ships in the page the visitor downloads. That is the plainest pattern we found, and the most on-the-nose.

Five AI-built sites carried live OpenAI API keys in their client-side code, sixteen distinct keys across them, and four of the five are confirmed AI-generated. One AI-writing site stands out on its own: it shipped twelve different OpenAI keys, one per content category, as plain values in its bundle. Figure 1 shows a single entry, with the key masked.

Figure 1 – Live OpenAI keys embedded as plain values in an AI-writing site’s JavaScript (key masked by CRIL).

A handful of sites, but each key is sensitive to exposure. An OpenAI secret key is a billing credential: anyone who reads the page can spend the owner’s balance, exhaust the rate limit, or run the bill up until someone notices and revokes it. Twelve keys in one bundle are twelve live credentials shipped at once, and five sites like this are five accounts an attacker can exploit.

Clone-and-leak: one secret across a whole fleet

An AI builder makes the hundredth site as cheap as the first, so an operator clones a working template across many domains, and whatever secret sat in the template now sits on every copy. We saw this in two shapes.

A Slack webhook shared across a 13-domain fleet. Thirteen near-identical domains, each a short word (ask, call, chat, get, hello, hey, hi, its, join, let, meet, my, see), glued to one brand, all served the same client bundle, and all embedded the same live Slack incoming-webhook URL. Figure 2 shows the URL in the shipped bundle, masked.

Figure 2 – One Slack webhook shared across a 13-domain fleet, in each site’s shipped bundle (secret and workspace IDs masked).

Anyone who can read the page can post messages to the operator’s Slack workspace via that webhook. That works for spam, for phishing aimed at the operator’s own staff, or for flooding a channel.

One Stripe secret key across four domains and two brands. A single Stripe secret key appeared on four domains under two separate brand names. The same sk_live_ value across all four points to one operator, or one shared Stripe account, behind every site. Figure 3 shows the assignment.

Figure 3 – The same live Stripe secret key reused across four domains under two brands.

A Stripe secret key provides full API access to the account, including the ability to create charges, issue refunds, and read customer and payout records. That one key exposes the operator’s whole payment account on every domain in the fleet.

The 13-domain Slack fleet runs on Bubble, a no-code and AI app builder, as confirmed by Bubble’s x-bubble-perf response header and client markers. Bubble serves each app from a dynamic.js bundle, and any value a developer places in a client-accessible field ships inside that bundle in plain text. The Stripe cluster runs on a Next.js build instead, which shows that the pattern spans builders rather than tracing to a single platform.

What else is exposed

Four AI-built sites exposed a Supabase service role JSON Web Token (JWT) on their front ends. A service-role token bypasses row-level security and grants full read and write to the project database. In terms of impact, it sits at the top of the set because it opens the entire backend rather than a single service.

Most of the remaining secret-looking strings on AI-built sites carry no/minimal exposure.

3,824 sites shipped browser-safe values: reCAPTCHA site keys, Stripe publishable keys, Supabase anon keys, builder telemetry tokens.

2,172 sites carried Google API keys, which matter only if they are unrestricted.

1,461 sites exposed a Supabase or Firebase backend address, which is a real exposure only when that backend’s rules are open.

Filtering those out is why the confirmed count is 35, not several thousand. Table 1 breaks the 35 down by type. The values stay withheld, and a few sites appear under more than one row.

Exposure

Sites

What an attacker gains

OpenAI API key

5

Spend the owner’s balance, exhaust quota, run up the bill

Shared Slack webhook

13

Post arbitrary messages into the operator’s workspace

Stripe secret key

6

Full API access: charges, refunds, customer and payout data

Supabase service-role JWT

4

Full read/write to the backend database, bypassing access rules

AWS access key

5

Cloud account access, scope set by the paired secret

GitHub token / Google OAuth secret

2

Source-control or identity-provider access

Table 1 – Confirmed private-credential exposures across 22,306 AI-built sites, by type.

What an attacker can do with these

Every credential in Table 1 is a working key to a live account. An attacker reads a public web page, copies a value, and calls an API. Here is what that buys them, key by key.

OpenAI and other LLM keys: Run inference on the victim’s account until the bill or rate limit stops them. On a metered account, that is direct financial loss; on a funded one, it is a free, anonymous model endpoint that the attacker can point at anything, billed to the victim and running under their quota and identity.

Stripe secret key; Drive the victim’s payment account through Stripe’s own API: create and refund charges, push the account toward fraud, and pull the customer list, email addresses, and payout history. One key is a money problem and a data-breach problem at once.

Supabase service-role token: Read and write the entire production database, past whatever row-level security the app configured. That means stealing every user record, altering or deleting data, and planting content the app will serve back to its own visitors.

Slack incoming webhook: Post into the operator’s own Slack as if from inside. Flooding a channel is a nuisance case; the real risk is internal phishing.

AWS access key: With the paired secret and enough permission, reach into the owner’s cloud: spin up resources (crypto-mining is the usual first move), read storage buckets, or pivot further in.

GitHub token or OAuth secret: Read or push to the owner’s source repositories or misuse their identity integration.

One exposure counts many times over. When the key sits on a cloned fleet, it is live on every domain in that fleet, so an attacker who finds it on one site has compromised all of them.

Conclusion

AI app-builders made it almost free to publish a website, and just as free to clone one, and most of what they produce is worth nothing to steal.

The exceptions are what we went looking for. A small, steady set of these sites hand over the key that runs them, and when an operator copies one site across a fleet, the leak rides along to every domain.

Against the millions of domains registered each month, the number is tiny, but every hit is a live account an attacker can reach and exploit just by opening the page.

If you build on these tools, read your own shipped code before you publish it. If you defend an organization, assume your keys may surface on sites you never built and look for them.

Cyble’s Threat Intelligence Platforms continuously monitor emerging threats, infrastructure, and activity across the dark web, deep web, and open sources. This proactive intelligence empowers organizations with early detection, impersonation, infrastructure mapping, and attribution insights. Altogether, these capabilities provide a critical head start in mitigating and responding to evolving cyber threats.

Our Recommendations

For developers and AI-builder users:

Keep every secret key (OpenAI sk-, Stripe sk_live_, a Supabase service-role token) in a server-side function or backend workflow, never in a client-accessible field.

Use only the browser-safe variants on the front end, publishable and anon keys, and enforce access with Supabase row-level security, Firebase rules, and API key restrictions.

Rotate any key that has ever sat on the client side, and treat it as already compromised.

Read your own page source before you ship, and search it for sk-, sk_live_, service_role, and hooks.slack.com. If you find them, so can anyone.

For SOCs and defenders:

Monitor public code and newly registered domains for your own keys and webhooks; don’t just paste sites.

Treat a secret found on one domain of a template fleet as exposed on all of them, and scope the response to the fleet, not the domain.

The post The Keys Are in the Browser: Secret Exposure Across AI-Built Websites appeared first on Cyble.

articles.title: Cloud Security Maturity Lags Despite Widespread Adoption, SANS Warns
articles.context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
articles.full_text:
Nearly all organizations now run production workloads in the cloud, yet only 40% consider their cloud security strategy advanced or optimized, highlighting a significant maturity gap, according to SANS.

This is according to the 2026 SANS Cloud Security Survey Insights report which surveyed 400 IT and security professionals.

SANS found that 51% of respondents were running enterprise-scale (2501 to 10,000 workloads, containers, or instances) or hyperscale (more than 10,000) environments and 73% already having a dedicated cloud security team or role.

The report also noted that 93% of organizations already run production workloads in the cloud and 65% run more than one provider.

SANS noted that because so many respondents have a dedicated team for cloud security, it indicates that a maturity gap persists despite organizations being well-resourced.

Overall, 45% of respondents described their cloud security strategy as “intermediated” with partial implementation of a defined strategy.

This partial implementation is an issue, according to the report, and leads to security incidents.

Misconfiguration Make Up Nearly Half of Critical Cloud Incidents

The report found that misconfiguration is the leading cause of critical cloud incidents (45%), close to double that of the next highest factor, credential theft, which made up 22% of incidents.

What’s more, misconfigurations often remain in place for significant periods, with around half of organizations (49%) found to need more than 24 hours to close a known critical gap.

"Misconfiguration is not an exotic attack class. It is a known gap sitting in an account somebody already owns," said Serge Borso, SANS Principal Instructor. "What makes it persist is not the attacker. It is the distance between finding the gap and fixing it, across too many consoles with nobody clearly owning the result. That is why consolidation and enforcement matter more right now than implementing yet another detection tool. The industry has finished deciding to move to the cloud and is now paying for how fast it did.”

Despite the security maturity gap, cloud security budgets were found to be increasing for most, with 28% of respondents reporting significant investment to modernize or adopt new technology such as AI or Cloud-Native Application Protection Platform (CNAPP), and another 42% reporting incremental growth.

Overall, 70% of organizations are spending more on cloud security than a year ago. Only 7% reported budget cuts.

Just 21% of respondents said their organization runs a single consolidated CNAPP platform. Meanwhile, 31% still maintain separate point solutions across Cloud Security Posture Management (CSPM), Cloud Workload Protection Platform (CWPP), and Cloud Infrastructure Entitlement Management (CIEM). Of those surveyed, 23% are actively evaluating a move to consolidate.

The SANS data points towards three priorities for security teams in the year ahead:

Strengthen cloud security by enforcing automated policy checks in infrastructure-as-code pipelines, preventing misconfigurations before deployment

Reduce security tool sprawl by consolidating posture management, workload protection and identity security tools into unified platforms

Extend zero trust beyond authentication by adopting continuous, context-based controls that limit what users and workloads can access after login

articles.title: ZDI-26-790: OpenSSL CMS AuthEnvelopedData Improper Validation of Integrity Check Value Vulnerability
articles.context: An attacker must first obtain the ability to modify CMS AuthEnvelopedData messages in order to exploit this vulnerability
articles.full_text:
Vulnerability Details

This vulnerability allows network-adjacent attackers to tamper with CMS AuthEnvelopedData messages on affected installations of OpenSSL. An attacker must first obtain the ability to modify CMS AuthEnvelopedData messages in order to exploit this vulnerability.

The specific flaw exists within the handling of AES-GCM message authentication codes. The issue results from an improper integrity check. An attacker can leverage this vulnerability to tamper with authenticated data.

Additional Details

OpenSSL has issued an update to correct this vulnerability. More details can be found at: https://openssl-library.org/news/secadv/20260609.txt

Disclosure Timeline

2026-04-09 - Vulnerability reported to vendor

2026-10-22 - Coordinated public release of advisory
