AWS account team

1.2 – Inventory current state:

Before any changes are made, document the complete current state of your IAM Identity Center configuration. Capture a baseline of all three assignment layers: the users and groups assigned to the IAM Identity Center application in your IdP, the account and application assignments in IAM Identity Center, and any assignments inside the applications themselves:

Run the precheck script to export all current Identity Center assignments and principals to CSV.

```bash python -m idc_migration_tool precheck --output-dir ./export ```

This will produce the following artifacts:

assignments.csv – One row per account, permission-set, and principal assignment

principals.csv – All users and groups from the identity store

1.3 – Define the cutover window:

Schedule the migration during a low-usage period to minimize user impact. Size the maintenance window using timings from a full-dress rehearsal in a test environment. SCIM provisioning is rate-limited, so for large directories, sync users in batches. Identify a maintenance window of sufficient length to complete all phases, including time for validation and potential manual rollback (described in Phase 7) if needed. Notify all affected users in advance of the potential temporary disruption to single-sign-on access.

1.4 – Confirm access requirements:

Verify that the following access is confirmed and tested before the cutover window:

AWS Administrator access to IAM Identity Center and AWS Organizations.

Identity provider (IdP) administrator access (for example, Okta) to configure the IAM Identity Center application, create the SCIM integration, and assign users to the AWS app.

A break-glass or emergency administrative access path that does not depend on the identity source you are migrating.

Phase 2: Complete final pre-cutover steps

Before starting the cutover, complete the final validation, access, and communication checks described in this phase.

2.1 – Export IAM Identity Center configuration:

Validate that the backup files generated in Step 1.2 are present and non-empty before proceeding.

2.2 – Communicate impact to users:

Send advance notice to all affected users covering:

The migration timeline and expected impact window.

That users can’t sign in between the identity source change and the new IdP’s sign-in going live, but that their access and assignments are unchanged.

The new sign-in process. After migration, users sign in through your IdP (for example, the Okta My Apps dashboard) or the AWS access portal, depending on the sign-in flow you choose.

Whether the new sign-in flow is IdP-initiated (through Okta) or SP-initiated (through the AWS access portal), and any differences in the user experience.

After migration, the d-xxxxxxxxxx.awsapps.com/start access portal URL is no longer supported, and the console shows the supported dual-stack regional URL (https://ssoins-<instance-id>.portal.<region>.app.aws) instead, so you must communicate the new URL and update bookmarks/allow-lists.

That the custom access portal alias (friendly URL) isn’t supported after migrating away from Active Directory. If a proxy or bookmark relies on redirect flows, plan to update it.

Prepare a user guide for the new sign-in process and an FAQ for common issues. Schedule a training session to demonstrate how to access AWS through Okta. Ensure your support team is briefed and ready to handle an influx of access issues during and immediately after the cutover.

2.3 – Validate Okta-to-IAM Identity Center sync (pre-cutover testing):

Using a sandbox or test environment if available, perform the following validation steps before executing against production:

Run the full migration in a test instance that mirrors your production AD configuration and applications and confirm that existing test users are matched by Okta and not duplicated.

Use the AWS Management Console for IAM Identity Center to verify that groups and users appear in Users & Groups with the correct attributes.

Test the complete end-to-end sign-in flow for a test user. Authenticate through Okta, access the AWS portal, and assume a role in a test account. Confirm that the user keeps access to their assigned accounts, permission sets, and applications.

Phase 3: Complete the cutover

You’re ready to configure Okta, switch the IAM Identity Center identity source, and complete the production cutover.

Important: Downtime begins when you confirm the identity source change in Step 3.2 and ends when SAML sign-in works through Okta. Have the Okta application, SAML metadata, and signing certificate ready before you start. Users, groups, memberships, and assignments are preserved.

3.1 – Configure the Okta application:

Sign in to Okta as an administrator.

Navigate to Applications and then to Browse App Catalog.

Search for AWS IAM Identity Center and choose Add Integration. Choose Done.

Choose the newly created app and select the Sign On tab.

Locate the Metadata URL (it will look like: https://<your-okta-domain>/app/<app-id>/sso/saml/metadata). Open this URL in a new browser tab.

An XML file will render in the browser. Save this file. This is your SAML metadata file, which will be uploaded to IAM Identity Center.

Download and save the SAML signing certificate from the Sign On tab.

3.2 – Switch the identity source in IAM Identity Center:

In the IAM Identity Center console navigation pane, choose Settings.

Choose Actions and select Change Identity Source.

Important: This change applies to the entire Identity Center instance. On the confirmation screen, you must enter ACCEPT to confirm. During this step and before SCIM provisioning is enabled, if the change could not be completed by Identity Center you will see a clear error message in the console to retry changing identity providers. It is safe to retry.

Select External Identity Provider.

Upload the XML metadata file and the SAML signing certificate downloaded from Okta.

Confirm the change. IAM Identity Center will display progress updates as it migrates to the new identity provider.

Don’t enable automatic provisioning yet. Complete Step 3.3 and confirm pilot sign-in in Step 3.4 first.

3.3 – Configure the ACS and issuer URLs in Okta:

In the IAM Identity Center console, choose Settings and then Actions. Select Manage Authentication.

Copy the IAM Identity Center Assertion Consumer Service (ACS) URL and the IAM Identity Center Issuer URL.

Return to Okta and choose Applications and select IAM Identity Center app. Select the Sign On tab and choose Edit.

Under Advanced Sign On Settings, paste the ACS URL and Issuer URL into the corresponding fields.

Choose Save.

3.4 – Confirm pilot sign-in:

Before you enable SCIM provisioning, assign an existing pilot user to the IAM Identity Center application in Okta and confirm they can sign in through the AWS access portal. The SAML NameID that Okta sends must exactly match the user’s existing Identity Center username. If sign-in fails, fix the mapping now before proceeding to the next step.

3.5 – Enable automatic provisioning (console) and connect SCIM in Okta:

In the IAM Identity Center console, choose Settings, then choose Enable Automatic Provisioning. Copy and securely record the SCIM endpoint URL and access token.

Return to the IAM Identity Center app in Okta. Choose the Provisioning tab.

Choose Configure API Integration.

Paste the SCIM Endpoint URL into the Base URL field.

Paste the Access Token into the API Token field.

Choose Test API Credentials. You should receive confirmation that the credentials are valid.

Choose Save.

On the Provisioning page, choose Edit and under To App enable all three provisioning options (Create Users, Update User Attributes, and Deactivate Users). Choose Save. (The To App settings control how Okta provisions users to IAM Identity Center. All three options are required for the migration to work correctly.)

On the Push Groups tab, push the groups that are assigned to the AWS application. Group names must exactly match the existing group names in IAM Identity Center.

In the attribute mappings, confirm that userName maps to the existing Identity Center username and that first name, last name, display name, and a single email address are populated.

3.6 – Test SCIM takeover:

Before you assign all users, verify that Okta takes over existing users correctly:

In Okta, select an existing pilot user who already exists in IAM Identity Center (People).

Open the user and navigate to the Applications tab.

Assign the AWS IAM Identity Center app to this test user.

Wait 5–10 minutes for SCIM sync to run.

In the IAM Identity Center console, select Users and confirm that the pilot user still has the same user ID, that no duplicate user was created, and that the user’s assignments still work.

Note: If the user is duplicated or doesn’t update after 10 minutes, check the Okta System Log for SCIM provisioning errors and verify the SCIM endpoint URL and token are correctly configured.

After the pilot user is taken over successfully, assign the remaining users and groups to the application in Okta. For large directories, assign them in batches.

Phase 4: Verify takeover

Now that you’ve completed cutover, verify that Okta has taken over all users and groups and that the preserved assignments match your pre-migration baseline.

4.1 – Verify SCIM takeover:

Confirm that all production users and groups are provisioned from Okta, that they keep the same user and group IDs, and that no duplicates were created. Check the Okta provisioning logs for errors such as “Refused to create a new, duplicate resource.”

4.2 – Check for assignment drift: Compare the live assignments against the pre-migration CSV

```bash python -m idc_migration_tool validate --csv ./export/assignments.csv --output-dir ./export ```

If drift is found, the script writes a drift_report.csv file with MISSING and EXTRA entries. Because assignments are preserved, investigate any entries before you continue.

Phase 5: Post-migration validation

After the cutover, validate end-to-end access for representative user roles and confirm that assignments were preserved.

5.1 – Test end-to-end access:

Using a test Okta user account, complete the following validation steps:

Sign in to the Okta Dashboard.

Choose the AWS IAM Identity Center tile under My Apps.

Select an assigned AWS account from the portal.

Confirm that you can assume a role and access the AWS console.

Test role switching within the console to validate permission boundaries.

5.2 – Spot-check multiple user types:

Validate access for a representative sample of users across different access levels, including Administrator, Developer, Read-Only or Audit, and any other standard roles defined in your environment. Confirm that permission sets are correctly mapped and that no unintended access has been granted or denied.

For each application, confirm that user-specific data and settings are intact and that any assignments inside the application still work.

Phase 6: Post-migration cleanup and monitoring

After confirming the migration is stable, shift focus to ongoing monitoring of provisioning and authentication, and update your operational documentation.

6.1 – Decommission AD only when stable:

Don’t decommission the Active Directory domain controllers until you’re confident the migration is stable and rollback is no longer needed. Keep AD online as a fallback. Deleting the AD directory removes the manual rollback option and the AD-based access portal endpoint.

The following command will identify disabled users, empty groups, and unassigned permission sets.

```bash # Report only python -m idc_migration_tool cleanup # Report and prompt for deletion python -m idc_migration_tool cleanup --delete ```

6.2 – Monitor SCIM sync:

Confirm that SCIM provisioning continues to run without errors in the days following migration.

Monitor new user onboarding from Okta to verify that newly created Okta users are automatically provisioned into IAM Identity Center.

Review IAM Identity Center and AWS CloudTrail logs for failed sign-in attempts or unexpected authentication errors.

6.3 – Update documentation:

Update all internal documentation to reflect the new identity architecture:

Record the SCIM integration details, SAML metadata links, and new group-to-permission-set mappings.

Update internal SOPs and onboarding guides to reflect the new Okta-based login process.

Document troubleshooting procedures for the most common failure modes.

6.4 – Post-migration checklist:

Before closing the migration project, confirm all of the following:

Users can authenticate successfully through Okta.

Permission sets are correctly assigned to the correct users and groups.

Account assignments are working correctly across accounts.

Monitoring and logging are configured and alerting on anomalies.

Internal documentation and SOPs are updated.

Support team is trained on the new login process.

Rollback procedures have been reviewed and are ready if needed.

Active Directory integration cleanup is scheduled (do not rush decommission).

Phase 7: Rollback (if needed)

Rollback requires manually switching the identity source back to Active Directory, which deletes users, groups, memberships and assignments, and then rebuilding assignments from the pre-migration backup files, as described in the following steps.

Note: Define in advance what counts as a failure, who makes the rollback decision, and the acceptable discrepancy threshold. Only initiate rollback if the Okta migration has failed and cannot be recovered within the migration window. Rollback is a manual, time-consuming process. There is no single-button undo for an identity source switch.

7.1 – Switch identity source back to Active Directory:

Navigate to IAM Identity Center and choose Settings, then Actions, and then Change Identity Source.

Select Active Directory as the identity source.

Select your existing AD domain. Ensure AD is still running and reachable before confirming.

Accept the conditions and confirm the switch. Identity Center will display progress updates.

When complete, choose Resume Sync, then choose Start Guided Setup.

Confirm the attribute mappings and select the users and groups to sync.

Review and save the configuration.

7.2 – Wait for AD users and groups to repopulate:

After completing the guided setup, AD users and groups will begin to reappear in IAM Identity Center through the directory sync. This might take several minutes depending on the size of your directory.

7.3 – Recreate account assignments:

Recreate the assignments from the pre-migration CSV file. This will resolve each principal name in identity store, create the assignment, and poll until completion, and produce a summary of succeeded, failed, and skipped counts.

```bash python -m idc_migration_tool cutover --csv ./export/assignments.csv ```

7.4 – Validate access:

Confirm users can authenticate using the original AD-based AWS access portal URL and can access their expected AWS accounts and roles. Test key role types (such as Admin, Developer, and Audit) before declaring rollback complete.

Troubleshooting the cutover

The identity source change in Step 3.2 runs as a sequence of steps: stopping Active Directory sync, disconnecting the directory, and deleting the AD sync profile. If a step after “Stopping Active Directory sync” fails, the Confirm change screen reports which steps failed and offers a Retry failed steps button. You will see one of two error messages, both safe to retry:

“The identity source change could not be completed. Please try again.” — AD sync was stopped but the directory wasn’t disconnected, so new users and changes are not currently syncing from Active Directory. Choose Retry failed steps to complete the transition. If instead you want to stay on Active Directory, choose Start guided setup in the Settings page to reconfigure the sync.

“The identity source change could not be completed. Your identity source has been reverted to Active Directory. Please try again.” — IAM Identity Center automatically rolled back to a healthy AD-connected state, and a banner confirms that AD sync resumed. You don’t need to reconfigure the sync; choose Retry failed steps when you’re ready to try again.

Important: In both cases, choose Retry failed steps on the Confirm change screen. If you navigate away from this screen, you can no longer retry the failed steps and will need to restart the identity source change.

For troubleshooting tips, see Troubleshooting IAM Identity Center issues.

If you have feedback about this post, submit comments in the Comments section below.

Conclusion

This post covered how to migrate your IAM Identity Center identity source from Active Directory to an external identity provider (Okta), including backing up existing assignments, validating your target identity source, performing the cutover, verifying that the new identity source took over your users and groups with their assignments intact, validating access, and rolling back if needed.

For the backup and restore scripts referenced in this guide, see the aws-samples GitHub repository. For more information about IAM Identity Center configuration and permission set management, visit the AWS Security Blog and the AWS IAM Identity Center documentation.

articles.title: Head of AI Security Roles Surge in Large Organizations
articles.context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
articles.full_text:
A head of AI security role has been established in 65% of large organizations with an annual revenue of $10bn plus, according to new data.

The research, conducted by IANS and Artico Search, found that large businesses are taking steps to update their security organizational structure to enhance accountability and board level oversight for enterprise AI governance.

Around a fifth (18%) of all $10bn+ firms have made the head of AI security a dedicated position, while 47% combined it with another leadership role, making it “one of the fastest emerging functional roles,” according to the researchers.

Head of AI security was observed to be less common in medium and small companies, with the position established in 9% of organizations with a revenue of $1-$10bn, and 6% in firms with under $1bn in revenue.

Steve Martano, IANS Faculty and partner at Artico Search’s cyber practice, commented: “The growth of AI is creating a premium for leaders who can bridge technical security, risk and compliance while still understanding how the business wants to use the technology.”

AI Governance Rarely Falls Under the CISO Remit

The IANS report, published on October 20, found that despite the growth of dedicated head of AI security roles in large organizations, overall accountability for enterprise AI governance remains unsettled.

CISOs hold primary accountability in 26% of small businesses, in 11% of medium firms and just 7% of large organizations. The position that most often is held accountable for AI governance in large businesses are chief AI officers, at 22%.

Read now: AI Agent Adoption Creates Risk as Oversight Struggles to Keep Pace, Splunk Finds

Across all three tiers, 14-19% of organizations reported that no single executive is accountable.

In addition, most organizations have not yet fully implemented a board committee dedicated to AI ethics or responsible AI, with 43-48% across all three tiers stating that they have no such committee planned.

Martano said organizations must restructure security teams to ensure that their governance strategies keep pace with rapid AI adoption.

“Companies need to strategically think about what they need from the function and whether they can develop that expertise internally before going to an increasingly competitive external market,” he noted.

Experience the Biggest Dictator of Security Pros’ Pay

The report assessed experience level as the single biggest driver of compensation differences in the same role – more significant than factors such as company size and geographic location.

In $10bn+ businesses, security professionals with eight to 15 years’ experience earn about $35,000 more than those with fewer than eight years’ experience.

The gap grows to around $50,000 between early-career staff and professionals with more than 16 years’ experience.

In large businesses, the average salary for Deputy CISOs was $350,000 per annum.

BISOs earnt a similar amount on average, at $342,000.

Data around average compensation levels for CISOs was not included in the report.

articles.full_text:
The Pillar Security team reported the vulnerability privately via GitHub Security Advisory with full reproduction material at the end of August 2026.

A month later, Anomaly, the company behind OpenCode, confirmed it had received the report, but said malicious MCP servers are “outside their threat model.”

Pillar Security researchers said Anomaly patched the vulnerability on September 28 in version 1.18.33 – without a CVE or security advisory. “As a result, conventional vulnerability scanners and dependency alerts will not identify affected installations, potentially leaving enterprises unaware that they need to upgrade,” Pillar Security researchers warned.

URL Validation Falls Short of Preventing OpenCode RCE Attacks

Pillar Security researchers claimed that the standard fix isn’t enough to fully remediate this vulnerability, which they assessed should be allocated a critical severity rating (CVSS) of 9.8.

According to the researchers, URL scheme validation alone cannot prevent the attack because the malicious payload can be embedded in a seemingly legitimate HTTPS URL.

On Windows, the vulnerable open dependency passed the URL to PowerShell without properly escaping it, allowing the shell to interpret part of the URL as a command.

Although OpenCode added URL scheme checks in version 1.18.33, the researchers said the crucial fix was to update the dependency to a version that correctly quotes the URL, preventing PowerShell from interpreting the payload as executable code.

They recommend that developers avoid passing untrusted URLs through shell commands altogether, instead using argument-based process execution to reduce the risk of command injection.

OpenCode RCE Flaw Unrelated to Recent Console Security Breach

This vulnerability report comes a few days after OpenCode confirmed a security breach affecting its Console, which allows teams to share access to AI models through centrally managed API credentials.

Speaking to Infosecurity, Pillar Security’s Cohen stressed that this newly disclosed vulnerability was not related to the Console breach.

“The breach hit a legacy system behind a hosted key proxy, and exposed provider keys users had stored there. The vulnerability we reported runs the other way: a malicious remote MCP server executing code on a developer's own machine during the OAuth handshake. Different target and attacker position,” he explained.

Nevertheless, Cohen highlighted that both incidents come down to the same thing, “Who you let hand credentials and inputs to an AI coding tool, and what that tool does with them.”

articles.title: Introducing a new AI chapter in the NCSC research problem book
articles.context: Concepts such as vulnerability management, incident response and risk management will need to evolve to account for both AI-enabled systems and AI-enabled attackers
articles.full_text:
The latest frontier AI capabilities are re-writing what is possible for both cyber attackers and defenders, with recent publications from the NCSC highlighting the opportunities and risks presented by AI.

The Five Eyes cyber security agencies have warned that AI is accelerating the pace and scale of cyber threats, while the NCSC’s Cyber Shield initiative sets out an ambitious vision for harnessing AI to strengthen cyber defence.

Turning this vision into reality will require more than advances in AI capability alone; it will require answers to difficult questions around system design, assurance, security and trust.

To help focus innovation across this new AI-enabled world, we’ve re-written our NCSC research problem book to include an entirely new chapter 'AI in cyber security problems’.

For years, AI and machine learning have helped defenders analyse data, identify threats and automate routine tasks. The new generation of AI systems (particularly generative AI and agentic AI) can plan, reason, use tools, and take actions with increasing autonomy. This is game-changing, making some things much easier to automate but in the process, creating new problems to overcome.

Many of the assumptions that underpin today’s cyber security best practice were developed before this kind of AI existed. Concepts such as vulnerability management, incident response and risk management will need to evolve to account for both AI-enabled systems and AI-enabled attackers. This evolution may require a re-design of processes from the ground up to fully leverage the potential benefits to defenders.

Our new problem book chapter on ‘AI in cyber security’ identifies seven areas spanning three broad themes:

the use of AI to strengthen cyber defence

the security and assurance of AI systems themselves

the use of data-driven methods to improve cyber resilience at scale

A common thread runs throughout them all: human-AI collaboration. As AI systems become more capable, we need to understand where autonomy can provide genuine value, where human judgement remains essential, and how meaningful oversight can be maintained without losing the benefits of machine-speed operations.

AI has the potential to fundamentally reshape cyber security. Whether that future is secure, resilient and trustworthy will depend on the choices we make today and the research we undertake tomorrow. The new problem book should focus attention on some of the most important challenges ahead.

Addressing these challenges will require a collective effort across the cyber security and AI communities. We welcome feedback on the challenges identified in the problem book, suggestions for additional research questions, and examples of ongoing or planned research that could help address them. Insights from across academia, industry and government will help ensure that future cyber security approaches remain effective, resilient and trustworthy in an AI-enabled world.

If you would like to contribute to the discussion, please complete our feedback form.

Paul J, Technical Director for Cyber AI Research, NCSC

Brad A, Principal Data Science & AI Researcher, Industry 100 Secondee & Alan Turing Institute Visiting Collaborator

articles.title: The New Release Metric: Less Cleanup Per Release
articles.context: A dependency problem discovered after development has started can interrupt feature work while an engineer investigates the component, finds an alternative, updates the project,...
articles.full_text:
AI makes it easier to create code. That does not automatically make software easier to ship.

A team can move from an idea to a pull request in minutes, then lose those gains to a failed build, a dependency conflict, a late finding, or an upgrade that was not worth making. The code arrived faster. But the release did not.

That gap matters when engineering leaders evaluate the effectiveness of AI-assisted development. Code output shows how much activity a tool generates. It does not show how much production-ready software reaches users, or how much unplanned work teams take on along the way.

A more useful question is: How much avoidable cleanup does each release require? The answer reveals how much of AI's speed advantage survives the trip from pull request to production.

Code Volume Is the Wrong Scoreboard

Code volume is the wrong scoreboard because it measures how much code a team produces, not how much production-ready software it ships. In AI-assisted development, that matters even more.

More generated code means more tests to review, more dependencies to validate, more pull requests to untangle, and more changes that may need to be rolled back. Agents can add, replace, and update components quickly, but each dependency decision can affect compatibility, maintainability, licensing, and security.

The result can look like progress: more code, more pull requests, more activity. Yet releases may still take longer because teams have to resolve the downstream work those changes create.

If AI-assisted delivery is improving, teams should see less avoidable cleanup, such as:

Dependency-related build failures and rework.

Late findings that require teams to replace components and retest.

Rollbacks and emergency fixes tied to dependency changes.

Unnecessary upgrades and version changes.

Time spent investigating components that entered the workflow.

Planned engineering work displaced by urgent remediation.

These signals matter alongside delivery speed and reliability. Fewer cleanup tasks do not represent progress if teams are shipping less or accepting more production risk.

Cleanup Is Where AI Gains Disappear

AI-assisted development delivers less value when teams spend the time saved during coding to resolve issues that surface later.

A dependency problem discovered after development has started can interrupt feature work while an engineer investigates the component, finds an alternative, updates the project, reruns tests, and determines whether a release is affected.

If the issue reaches a build or release, the work can extend to:

Identifying where the component was used and what it could access.

Replacing the dependency and validating affected builds.

Assessing whether credentials, systems, or releases may have been exposed.

That work appears as release churn, missed delivery dates, and engineers pulled away from planned work. It is easy to miss in an AI adoption dashboard, especially if the dashboard focuses on code generated or pull requests completed.

Not every build failure or dependency issue can be prevented at the point of intake. But known malicious packages are one avoidable source of downstream work. Blocking them before they are served through the repository path can keep them out of developer and build workflows in the first place.

Measure the Work Behind Each Release

Measure cleanup per release by tracking the dependency issues that trigger unplanned work and the time teams spend resolving them.

Start with a baseline and follow the trend across comparable releases.

Useful signals include:

Dependency-related build failures: How often do dependency issues cause failed builds, retries, or rework?

Late-stage findings: How many component issues surface after development has started or a release is in motion?

Dependency-related rollbacks and emergency fixes: How often do component changes contribute to release instability?

Remediation time: How long does it take to investigate a dependency issue and land a validated fix?

Engineering time redirected: How much planned work is displaced by dependency cleanup and release interruptions?

While tracking cleanup work is critical to understand the effort involved to ship production-ready code, tracking preventative measures like blocked malicious packages is equally as important. A blocked request is not a cleanup task, but it shows that a known malicious component was stopped before it could become one.

The point is not to create another vanity metric. It's to give engineering leaders a clearer view of where release effort goes, what causes avoidable rework, and whether teams are getting more useful work through to production.

Make the Trusted Path Easy to Use

Developers and agents should be able to request components through the repository they already use, with security checks applied in that path. Developers should not have to recognize every suspicious package name or track every attack campaign, and teams need a way to evaluate agent requests even when people are not reviewing each choice in real time.

Adding a ticket or manual approval to every dependency choice would move the bottleneck, not eliminate it. Consistent controls belong in the path developers, pipelines, and agents already use.

Sonatype Nexus Repository provides a one trusted place to proxy, store, and distribute the components and build inputs teams rely on. Sonatype introduced Pro+ and Enterprise editions to help address a growing source of release cleanup: dependency decisions that outpace manual review. Both editions add malicious package protection and configurable policies to Nexus Repository, so teams can block known malicious packages before they reach developers and builds.

This does not prevent every dependency conflict, late vulnerability finding, or release issue. Teams still need testing and other controls throughout development. Repository protection addresses one specific problem earlier: known malicious packages entering through the managed repository path.

Sonatype Guide extends that trusted path into dependency selection and remediation. It helps developers and AI agents evaluate components in context, choose safer versions, and address risk in the codebase with guided fixes. Together, Nexus Repository and Guide help teams make better dependency choices up front and spend less time correcting them later.

Measure the Release, Not the Output

AI increases activity across the software development life cycle: more code, more pull requests, and more dependency changes. The better test is if teams can turn that activity into reliable releases with less unplanned work.

Track dependency-related build failures, late fixes, and remediation time across comparable releases. If those costs fall while delivery remains reliable, teams are getting more from faster code generation.

This is why Nexus Repository now offers Pro+ and Enterprise to help teams keep the speed of AI assisted development from becoming more dependency cleanup and release time. Both editions can block known malicious packages before they reach developers and builds, giving developers and agents a trusted route to software inputs while teams focus on getting releases out the door.

Less cleanup per release. More engineering time for planned work.

Aaron is a technical writer at Sonatype. He works at a crossroads of technical writing, developer advocacy, and information design. He aims to get developers and non-technical collaborators to work better together in solving problems and building software.

articles.title: Police arrest Qilin ransomware suspect on holiday, as links made to Synnovis hack that contributed to patient’s death
articles.context: A subsequent probe into the attack by King's College Hospital NHS Foundation Trust confirmed that a patient died in part due to blood test results being delayed
articles.full_text:
A 28-year-old Russian man has been arrested by German police, suspected of being a key member of the Qilin ransomware gang. As BBC News reports, detectives have linked the man to the 2024 attack against blood-testing firm Synnovis, that disrupted London hospitals, and resulted in the death of a patient.

The suspect, who has been named by German media only as "Vladimir K" was originally detained in May in Japan, after he travelled there on holiday. According to German officials, the man's vacation plans were intercepted and Japanese police were waiting for him on arrival. Earlier this month he was extradited to Germany.

Germany's interest in "Vladimir K" is related to a cyber attack in September 2024, which saw around US $160,000 worth of cryptocurrency extorted from a logistics firm. According to the BBC, German detectives have now included in their investigation possible links to the June 2024 attack which saw the Qilin ransomware group disrupting pathology services at various London hospitals, and resulted in the cancellation of operations and outpatient appointments.

The incident is said to have crippled Synnovis’s IT systems, and caused a critical shortage of O-type blood in hospitals. A subsequent probe into the attack by King's College Hospital NHS Foundation Trust confirmed that a patient died in part due to blood test results being delayed.

As a consequence, British police are reportedly examining whether their own inquiry could lead to a charge of unlawful killing.

No ransom was paid by Synnovis, a decision the firm made jointly with the NHS trusts to which it provides services.

Ransomware gangs have been accused of causing deaths in the past. For instance, in 2020 a different gang disrupted systems at a Düsseldorf hospital and caused a seriously-ill woman to be diverted to another health facility 30 km away.

According to reports, as a result of the attack doctors were not able to start treating the patient for an hour and she died.

The Qilin ransomware-as-a-service (RaaS) group has been operating since at least 2022, and has reportedly hacked more than 4000 organisations, and extorted over US $140 million. High profile victims include Japanese beer-maker Asahi, potentially exposing the data of more than 1.5 million customers and around 275,000 current and former employees and their families.

articles.title: 181: Ricky
articles.context: Alright, so they somehow discovered your IP and then they attacked your IP, and that was enough to knock you offline and lose the game. He discovers a whole world of ddossers and booters and punters and griefers who use malware to attack other players in the game to make them lose so you can win.
articles.full_text: JACK: I think that when I was a kid I was a good liar. Don't ask me where it stemmed from; probably because I was always getting in trouble, and that — I learned that if I was a good enough liar that I could sometimes lie my way out of trouble. But I was reading this post on Reddit the other day, and so many memories came back to me. [Music] There was this post. Some dad was complaining about his son being a ding-dong. He’s like, my son, who’s fifteen, wanted to get some ice cream, so we gave him a few bucks and sent him to the store. It happened to be a buy-one-get-one-free sale, and we all knew that, too. So, he went, he bought some ice cream on his own, and he came back with just one tub of ice cream. The knucklehead didn't get the free one. He just paid full price for a single tub of ice cream. The store clerk even told him, hey, there’s a sale. You know you can get a second one free. But my boy just said, well, I only want one, and refused the second one. His dad on Reddit was all miffed about how his son could be so daft and ignore free ice cream. He even said, I know that as soon as the boy finishes his ice cream he’s gonna want another, so why didn't he just get two? He knows that we all love ice cream, so why didn't he get one for his mom or his dad? Why did he get just one ice cream and not the second free one? It was free ice cream. This Reddit post blew up. Everyone was piling on about how dumb this kid was, saying stuff like, in my state you could disown your child for far less. Someone else said this is probably because the kid doesn't go buy things very often and doesn't know how to handle money very well or deals. The dad wrote in the post that he was starting to feel worried because people were saying some real mean things about his son, but nobody was saying what I was thinking. I feel like I know exactly what happened here, because I was in the exact same situation when I was a teenager. If you would have talked to my mom then, she would have been just like this worried dad. She would have told you that I’m the worst shopper in the world. Because I’m almost certain that what happened is he ate a full tub of ice cream on his way home and then lied and said he only bought one. I mean, it all adds up. The boy was hungry for ice cream before even leaving the house. There’s no way he’s gonna wait until he gets home to have his first bite. Grab a spoon at the store and start on your way home. Also imagine the look on his face when the clerk told him, you know you can get a second one for free, right? No way. Dang, this is my lucky day. So, he must have gotten two, and on his way home he started thinking, shoot, mom and dad don't know I got two. They only gave me enough money to get one. So, if I come back with one, they won't even know there was a second. So, if I could scarf this second tub down before I even get home, it would be glorious. No rules. No regulations. No speed bumps. Just eat a whole tub of ice cream as fast as I can. Challenge accepted. I’ll tell you, teenage boys can crush a whole tub of ice cream real easy. They can make a dozen cookies vanish instantly. They have the power to inhale desserts like no one else can. The real tell here is that the dad on the Reddit post even said, we would never let him eat a whole tub in one sitting. That’s the thing; the boy had an unregulated container of ice cream, and he thought no one is gonna know. No one is gonna stop him from eating all this in one sitting. Let’s do it. So, he saw this as his big stroke of luck and secretly slurped it down, and then tried to lie about it when he got home by saying, no, no, I only got one, I swear. But little did he know the entirety of Reddit was gonna believe that lie. He’s probably okay with them calling him names and stuff, because being misunderstood isn't as bad as being caught in your lies. But I see you, kid. I’ve been in that same situation before. I’ve been in that situation many times. Two cupcakes I bought at the bake sale became one. Two chocolate bars from the fundraiser became one. Yeah, of course two ice creams from the ice cream truck became one, too. My mom could never understand why I would sometimes pay extra for a single cupcake. Intro: [Intro music] These are true stories from the dark side of the internet. I’m Jack Rhysider. This is Darknet Diaries. JACK: Imagine going to a high school baseball game in New Port Richey, which is near Tampa, Florida. You see one kid, a center-fielder, who’s absolutely tearing it up out there. He’s catching anything that comes his way. He’s got an arm like a rocket. He could hit anything thrown at him. He’s built like a tank but runs like the wind, and it just looks like he’s in a different league than the rest of those high school players on the baseball field. He’s eating them up. It’s like all the other kids are in a lower league than him, and they're just all playing in slow motion compared to him. You can tell this kid is the star. That is Ricky Handschumacher. RICKY: So, I played center field, but initially I was really known for getting on base, getting hits, and then stealing bases. JACK: Stealing bases. RICKY: Yeah. JACK: Is this where all this starts? This is where all of it starts, stealing bases. RICKY: Coincidentally, yeah. JACK: But were computers interesting to you or not at all? RICKY: No, I was your gamer, you know? Like I said, I wasn't your average nerdy kinda guy who’s antisocial or anything. I was always out with my friends. I was always out on the streets playing sports; you know, football, baseball, basketball with all my friends. Like, Friday night and Saturday night I would go roller skating. So, I was never like, home, but I did have a passion for actual gaming. JACK: Alright. So, let’s talk about gaming. What was your game of choice? RICKY: Halo 3 was my primary game. JACK: [Halo sound effects] In 2010, fifteen-year-old Ricky is up late on a school night. His headphones are tuned in as he plays Halo 3 on his Xbox that’s humming away. Ricky doesn't want to disturb his mom, who’s sleeping in the other room. On his glowing TV screen he’s trying to escape what looks like a war zone. He’s destroying all the other players in the game. RICKY: I was good. So, I was always playing MLG and Team Slayer and all the ranked playlists against the pros and everything like that. Then, of course, naturally once you get to that level, there’s people who cheat on there and stuff. I was a high rank, but cheaters get high ranks, too, naturally because they're just cheating. So, it kept happening to me. JACK: People would go up against Ricky and see that they can't beat him, so they decided to cheat to win. He didn't know what was happening at first. RICKY: [Music] My screen would just go blank and then they would stop the attack when the game was over, which means they’d just win by default pretty much, 'cause we can't even move. Or if they hit you hard enough, we actually — our whole internet would just go out. I was with my mom. She’s like, why is the internet out? So, I had to play stupid. Like, I have no idea. I don't know what's happening. JACK: I’ve been in a similar situation. I remember the days when we had a family computer, and I downloaded a lot of random stuff and installed it on there. Time and time again I would break our computer. I didn't want to get in trouble, so I would try real hard to fix it before anyone noticed. Because of that, I got really good at detecting viruses and malware and fixing it on the family PC. But for Ricky, he was on an Xbox, and when he’d play, the internet would go down in the whole house, and it was just him and his mom living there. His dad left the picture a long time ago. But strangely, this pattern kept happening. When he would play Halo 3 against other players, the internet would go out. The game would disconnect, and then when he would finally get back on, he would see that he lost the match. RICKY: It happened to me again and again, and I’m like, alright. Then through the — through word of mouth I was like, oh, if they're DDoSing us, like, okay. So, I’m like, what the hell is that? I was getting DDoSed attacked over and over and over. JACK: Alright, so they somehow discovered your IP and then they attacked your IP, and that was enough to knock you offline and lose the game. RICKY: Yeah, and that’s kinda where it all started. Then curiosity — I was like, okay, how are they doing this? JACK: Remember, outside of gaming Ricky is not a computer guy. He doesn't know what's going on at all. So, he just turns his Xbox off and jumps on the family PC and starts trying to look for answers. RICKY: I started browsing some forums, and I was like, okay, it’s called DDoSing attacks. So, I started looking that up. I’m like, hm, okay, seems pretty simple. There’s a bunch of different kind of booters, like an IRC booter or a putty booter. You could just — or you could just go online to a website and use that booter, which was less powerful, but it would get the job done. I browsed the forums, found out what it was, downloaded the programs myself. So, I was like, okay, well, if they do it to me, I’m gonna do it back to them. JACK: Eventually he gets to the bottom of it. He discovers a whole world of ddossers and booters and punters and griefers who use malware to attack other players in the game to make them lose so you can win. Ricky decided, well, hey, I want to win, too. I want to try. [Music] So, he downloads a tool. He says it was Cain & Abel, and decides to try to use it to attack other players. He started a match, ran the tool to disconnect another player, then bingo; he sees they just freeze in the game and he can easily kill them, and he wins the match with almost zero effort. This was way easier than actually playing by the rules. RICKY: That’s kinda where I got introduced to that world. JACK: Yeah, so, at that point you were really competitive in baseball, you were really competitive at Halo. I just wonder, 'cause you had a sense of pride, of ranking up on your own and being competitive in sports — and where’d that sense of pride go with cheating? RICKY: I don't know. I just let it take over, pretty much. I was like, well, this is easier than actually trying. JACK: Yeah, but that’s not the sportsmanlike way. RICKY: Yeah. I don't know. I just took the easy way out and got the advantage. JACK: Were you cheating in sports at all? RICKY: No, that I was not cheating in. JACK: Alright. RICKY: No, I was naturally good. JACK: Yeah, well, you were naturally good at Halo, too. You were in MLG and all that stuff. RICKY: Yeah, I don't know. JACK: [Music] Who would have thought that this innocent little victory in Halo was going to lead Ricky down a long, dark path? From here he tried more Halo cheats like wall glitches, fast travel, reduced hitbox, and more. It was fun. This was the new game, not to compete competitively in Halo but to get around the game rules, to do things you weren’t supposed to, to be a god in the game. It gave him a sense of power. He saw the game differently now. He stopped seeing things on the screen like Covenant and Banshees and Needlers. Now he was seeing bytes and ones and zeros and the data behind the game, which gave him an incredible win streak. You know, the type of win streaks that you just have to take a screenshot of so that you can look back at from time to time and remember those matches. But even being a god can get boring after a while, and even though he was the winner in those screenshots of his, he would notice that some people seemed to be even cooler than him somehow. Everyone looks the same in Halo 3. You're all the same player, Master Chief. It’s just, everyone has a slightly different color. But there’s one thing that sets you apart from everyone else; your name, specifically your gamer tag. These are special, actually. They're unique. There’s only one person in the world with your gamer tag. Some people call themselves cool things like Shadow Strike or Nebula Storm or Blade of Odin. Fine, but what about that guy that’s just called Wolf? How did he get that name, Wolf? Now that is fricking cool. Well, it’s a first-come, first-serve kinda thing. So, Wolf must have made that gamer tag a long time ago when Xbox Live was first created, when gamer tags first came out. They probably made the name in the first week or maybe even the first day, which makes them OG, right? But instead of Original Gangster, they're the Original Gamer. Ricky wanted one of these short, cool gamer tags. That would really set him apart from the other normies playing in the game by the rules, but all the good names were taken. So, he goes back online into the hack forums and starts looking to see, how do you get one of these? It turns out there’s a whole underground marketplace of people buying and selling Xbox gamer tags, but not in the way you might think. See, a typical online market, you'll see people selling things that they've had for a long time or something that they've bought from someone else or something they made, right? But this was an underground hack forums marketplace. It operates differently. These gamer tags weren't ones that sellers were sitting on for a while. No, all these gamer tags were stolen. When Ricky found that out, he leaned in closer. How do you steal a gamer tag? Well, there are a few ways, but the easiest is just to get someone’s password and username and take over their account, change their password, and now that gamer tag is yours. But getting someone’s password is tricky. Maybe an easier way to get it is to trick Microsoft that you're the actual owner of the account and you just lost the password. Ricky saw some people were doing that and decided to try it himself. RICKY: There was a company called Zune, which is like Microsoft’s music app. Come to find out what you could do is you could call up Zune, and then halfway through the call you just tell them your gamer tag that you're targeting, and you say, okay, hey, my gamer tag is Jack. Then you just stop the conversation and be like, I have to go real fast. I’ll call back. JACK: Before hanging up, though, Zune support would give Ricky a reference number for the case that they were working on. Then he’d hang up and call a different number, Xbox Support this time, and they'd say, how can I help you? He’d say, oh, well, I was on a call but it dropped. I have a reference number if you want to pull the case details up. RICKY: Correct, yeah. You'd just simply say, yo, I have a reference number. Can you pull up my case? Then they would just give you the information right then and there. There was no questions asked. JACK: Ah, interesting. So, it’s almost like a bypass of a verbal authentication. So, then when you call Xbox and say, I have this reference number, then they give you the e-mail address. RICKY: Yep. JACK: Then you say, can you reset the password? RICKY: You would just be like, hey, yeah, here's my reference number — validate the account. Then just — you could just literally ask them, hey, what's the e-mail that I have on file? They'd read it off to you. JACK: How do you get the password? RICKY: Okay, so, back in the day AOL and Yahoo were your most popular domains. What's their proof of ownership of an account of an e-mail, was literally — AOL was like, your billing zip code would verify the account, and then they would be able to reset the password for you. Same with Yahoo. I think Yahoo was security questions, which back in the day was terrible because people would — a lot of the time chicken or pizza would be your favorite food that people would put, and stuff like that. So, they were pretty much takeable. JACK: See, that’s the thing that amazes me about these teenage hackers. They see the world differently than us, kinda like when you see motorcycles lane-splitting. You ever get stuck on a highway and there’s bumper-to-bumper traffic and you're standing still in your car and a motorcycle comes zooming past you right in-between the two lanes? You're like, come on. The motorcycle rider just looks back at you like you're a chump waiting in traffic like everyone else. They just whiz by like there’s no cars on the highway at all. These teenage hackers find ways through roadblocks that we just don't see. Like, you don't need someone’s password when the password reset question is ‘What's your favorite food?’ and you put ‘pizza’ up there. Now anyone can just write ‘pizza’ on there, and they could reset your password for you. It’s like, come on, what's the point of passwords if they could just be bypassed so easy? Sometimes it would try to validate it’s really you by asking for your zip code. Well, if you have their e-mail address, it’s not too hard to use some kind of people search tool online to look to see what someone’s zip code is. You and I don't think like that, though, but Ricky does. He’s the kind of guy that looks at us like we’re chumps for choosing an easy password recovery question. This was all happening in 2012, and Ricky was sixteen years old when he stole his first gamer tag. [Music] He found the one he wanted, Wolverine. Yeah, that sounds cool. He wasn't an X-Men fan; he just liked the sound of it. So, he called up Zune support, which is a Microsoft product, and is like, I have a problem with my account. They ask him for his e-mail address associated with the account. He says, well, I don't know. Can you just look up my Xbox gamer tag? They said, you know what? That works. What's your gamer tag? Ricky says, Wolverine. Zune support says, ah, yes, I see your account, sir. What can I help you with? Ricky says, okay, well, the problem is that when — you know what? Actually hold on; something just came up. Can I call you right back? Zune support says, yeah, sure. Do you want a reference number for when you call back? It’ll be easier for us to find your details. Ricky says, yes, yes, I do want that. He hangs up, and then he calls Xbox Support this time, and tells them, I was on with support but I got disconnected. Can you look up my case if I give you a reference number? They said, yeah, go ahead. He reads the number to them, and they see his details. Xbox Support’s mode of operation then was that if someone had a reference number, they must have already verified they are the account holder. So, they ask him, what's the problem? How can I help you? Ricky says, I just forgot what e-mail address I used for this account. He makes up some story about why he can't remember. He happened to be a good liar. Maybe it was that he got a new computer and didn't have those details on his new one. Xbox Support thinks, you know what? This is a harmless request. Sure. Your e-mail address is blahblahblah@aol.com. Great, he says. That’s all I wanted, and he hangs up. Now he has an e-mail address associated with that gamer tag. All he needs now is the password. Trying to get the password for an Xbox account is tricky, though. So, he has a better solution; try to reset the password on aol.com’s e-mail address. Once in there, he can reset the Xbox account and get control of that gamer tag. It’s a confirmation on a computer somewhere that you saw both IDs. Mark says that’s as far as he got with his investigation. He doesn't know where his money went or who actually stole it. Just because the guy in the store did the SIM-swap doesn't mean that he’s the one who stole the crypto. He just got paid his cut for doing the swap, which is known as an innie, an insider to help you get someone else’s phone number. While this absolutely terrified Mark and infuriated him, he didn't feel like it was a big enough loss for him to open an investigation and go to court. Even if he somehow recovered his Bitcoin, it would cause way more in lawyer fees and it just wouldn't be worth it. So, he let it go. The thieves got away cleanly with his 2.2 Bitcoin. It’s been over a decade now since this attack, and still Mark can't fully shake this. Like, every time he flies, he gets a little worried that his phone service is going to be disconnected for a few hours. Like, a twenty-hour trip to Asia is pure agony for him after being a victim like this. MARK: I mean, I still have PTSD over it today. Not to take away from real PTSD, but it’s sort of this digital PTSD of not knowing. Every time I wake up, it’s like, okay, I’m gonna log into my computer, log in, open up my phone, and of course everything has been safe since then. But yeah, it was painful. I was very angry for months. I couldn't sleep for months. JACK: But despite this being a traumatizing moment for Mark, he used it as sort of an origin story of his own. He was so sick of mobile providers being pointless at protecting us against SIM-swaps that he started his own service to stop people who try to hijack phone numbers like this. His company is called Efani. It’s a mobile carrier that resells AT&T and Verizon service with one big difference; extra protection against SIM-swap attacks. As we heard from Ricky Handschumacher, the social engineering starts long before the phone call even starts. As he told me, he found many of his targets because they were just too public about their crypto. Someone would post on Twitter, excited that their coin is going up, or spoke on a panel about investing in certain coins and then posting that to YouTube, or they would share tips on what to invest and how to store your coins. It’s all an attacker needs to hone in on their targets. The more they know about what accounts you have or what coins you have or what software you use, then the more they can use that to craft an attack just for you. I always tell people the number-one rule about having crypto is don't tell anyone you have crypto, because even if your digital security is tip top, I’ve heard stories about people getting drugged or robbed at gunpoint to get someone’s crypto. It’s brutal out there. For Mark, all that became a very painful lesson that he still thinks about nearly a decade after his attack. MARK: With crypto, my wife knows that when I’m gonna do anything with crypto, it’s like, stay thirty feet away from me. I don't want any distractions. I don't want anybody asking me a question. I’m just really very conscious now about the fact that most hacking — a lot of people think that hackers are trying to hack into your laptop or they're trying to hack into the back end of your Android phone, your iOS phone. But the reality is is that it’s probably like 99% of hacking is hacking the human mind, and it’s trying to get you to make a mistake or a company, somebody that works at a company that you rely on for them to make a mistake. It really just comes down to hacking the mind. JACK: We have no idea if Ricky actually hacked Mark or not. He probably didn't, but I wanted to talk with Mark because I wanted to get a feeling of what that scenario is like for the victim. What does the SIM-swap look like from the other side? It sounds awful. Nobody should have their stuff stolen like that. Ricky didn't just stop at one heist. Once he got a taste of the money that he could steal, he was hooked. He wanted to do this again and again, and very quickly, the money started adding up. In 2018, the year Mark was targeted, Ricky Handschumacher and his crew got so good at this that they were bringing in millions of dollars from their victims. RICKY: We found the money, we send it out, and — a couple million here, a couple hundred thousand there. It adds up. JACK: These numbers are startling, right? You've had to be surprised by your first big hundred-thousand-dollar or million-dollar lick. RICKY: Yeah. When I started doing it all, like actually SIM-swapping and crypto and stuff, like late teenager, maybe twenty — and I was like, damn, dude, I’m making more than people make in a lifetime, or more than their decade of a salary. I’m making that in ten minutes. JACK: [Music] Ricky said that he would sometimes pay an employee at a cell phone store a couple hundred bucks to help them do a SIM-swap, an insider who could bypass the security protections, just like what happened to Mark. This insider, he says, didn't know exactly how much was being stolen in crypto. They were just happy to get a few hundred bucks to change someone’s phone number in the system. But that was nothing compared to the lion’s share that Ricky and his crew would get from the heist. RICKY: So, once I had a couple million, I was like, damn, my moral compass checked in. I’m like, actually screwing people’s lives up. I have my own kid. My kid’s gonna be set for life, like just living life now. But we just kept going. It was like — almost like an addiction at this point. JACK: While all this was going on, Ricky was living a double life. He had just turned eighteen. He had just finished high school. He did not get the baseball scholarship for college. He did get a girlfriend, and they had a kid together, and he was still living at home with his mom. He had a 9:00 to 5:00 job for the county’s park and recreation department, you know, to keep up with the ruse that he’s got some normal job with a regular income. But of course, that job was boring compared to his online world, where millions of dollars were passing through his fingers. RICKY: So, I was just changing trash bags and stuff like that at a park, sitting in a work truck. So, I had all the time in the world to just be on my phone, like talking to everybody on Discord or Skype or something like that. While I’m at work, we're just hitting targets for crypto. DEBBIE: I had no idea, a boy that works for the city. JACK: This is Debbie, Ricky’s mom. DEBBIE: He had a county job. It wasn't the best money, but I was happy he had it. He had good benefits, he had retirement with it, and he went to work every day. JACK: She had no idea her son was living this double life, bringing in anywhere from $100,000 to a million dollars from victims. But having all this Bitcoin was pointless unless Ricky could spend it, and this is where he had to be careful. Crypto exchanges require KYC, which stands for ‘know your customer’. They want your full name and picture of your ID before they will let you exchange cryptocurrency for cash. So, that wasn't going to work. His Bitcoin wallet was likely marked as fraudulent, and if he used an exchange and gave them his name, then they would probably call the cops on him. So, he needed a new plan, a way to cash out Bitcoin without using an exchange, and basically he just found another person in the world who would do it. Like, he would send them the Bitcoin and they would hand him cash. He met them through localbitcoins.com. RICKY: I had a guy in the Tampa area. If I needed $20,000 cash or less, I can go to him, or if I needed more, I had a guy that was in Miami, and he never scammed me, but I would send him the crypto and he would mail me the cash. JACK: Yeah, let’s talk about both of these, right? So, when you go to meet someone, how does this meet go down? RICKY: Typically it was at a McDonald’s or something. We would just go sit in the booth. I would send him the Bitcoin. We would wait for the confirmations and for him to get it in his account, and he would give me the cash. Prior to that, though, we had the deal locked in at a certain amount, 'cause Bitcoin would go up and down. But I would typically just lock in the deal, and I’d be — okay, we’ll meet at 7:00. This is where we’re going. He would send me an address, and I would just go there. JACK: And then he’d just hand you an envelope? RICKY: Yeah, or just straight cash or an envelope and whatnot. But it was always a public place. It was never in a dark alley or anything crazy like that. JACK: That’s the classic way LocalBitcoins worked; you meet someone in person, you send them the Bitcoin, and they hand you the cash. Of course, they’d take a percentage for doing this deal. Maybe they'd give Ricky 95% of the money and keep 5% for themselves for the trouble of having to launder these Bitcoins. So, he actually had a lot of people making decent money on LocalBitcoins just buying crypto off people. But eventually Ricky needed to cash out bigger and bigger amounts, and this person he was working with wasn't able to cash out what he needed, so Ricky had to find someone new, and this new person was like, send me the Bitcoin; I’ll send you the cash in the mail. RICKY: It typically would just come in a vacuum-sealed, clear envelope wrapped in another envelope kinda thing. Sometimes it would be inside of a book, like a big Harry Potter book or something like that, and the pages would be cut out and the money would be in there. What's funny is I lived with my mom, so packages are coming to the house, but I’m eighteen years old. She’s not going through my mail. So, she would just take the envelope, put it on my bed, and she’d be like, hey, the mail came for you. She had no idea what was inside of it. JACK: Alright, so you're loading it up in crypto here. Things are coming in, $100,000, $1 million at a time. So, you're leading a double life here. You're living with your mom. Does she have any idea that you're doing any of this stuff, involved with this? RICKY: First of all, she doesn't really understand what the hell crypto was, and she was like, Ricky, what are you doing? How do you have all this money? I bought a $100,000 F-250 Ford truck, I had jet skis, I had side-by-sides. I had a lot of toys and stuff like that. DEBBIE: It really got my attention when he came home with the truck. I said, what is going on? RICKY: I would just lie to her. Like, yo, I invested back then. At the time when I started, Bitcoin was a couple hundred dollars, and now it’s, let’s say, $3,000, $6,000. So, I made a lot just from that, that little growth. So, I was able — but that’s what I told her. Meanwhile I’m stealing it, but — so, she has really no idea the severity of it. So, my mom, she believed me. She believed that I was saying there’s no reason for her not to believe me. DEBBIE: He never gave me a reason not to believe what he was doing was wrong, 'cause he wasn't that kinda kid. JACK: Ricky’s crypto investment explanation wasn't a total lie. He did have Bitcoin investments, and Debbie didn't have any reason to question it. After all, her own mother, Ricky’s grandmother, dabbled in Bitcoin, too, so she knew it was real. Ricky also had a young kid at home, and Debbie thought why would he do anything to throw his life away? DEBBIE: I was a single mom. I did the best I could growing up with him. He was a very honest child, never got in trouble, never was in the principal’s office. He didn't get in fights. So, when he came home with the truck, I just said, I don't know what you're doing or what's going on, but that’s not normal, and all I know is if you get in trouble, there’s not much I can do. I mean, I — and I said — at that time it was just his daughter, and between the mom and my son being the parents to this child, they were both younger, and I was fairly involved with my granddaughter. I just said to him, it’s just not your life anymore. You have a child involved here. JACK: Debbie believed her son and was proud of him, and had no reason to think he would lie to her. In fact, she thought Ricky’s crypto savviness could actually help others. At the time she worked as a nurse in the Pasco County Jail, and one day she overheard some sheriff’s deputies yapping about crypto. DEBBIE: I assumed at this point my son was doing really good with crypto, 'cause that’s what — the vision I was getting. I kinda went into work and was saying, yeah, my son does crypto, Bitcoin, and he’s done really well, and they've matured. I remember one of the deputies was really interested. He’s like, really? RICKY: They were like, oh, we’d love to talk to him. DEBBIE: I was like, yeah, he’s doing really good with it. One of the guys, one of the deputies, wanted to get with him and speak with my son. RICKY: So, next thing you know my mom is having me call these police officers and they're coming to the house to ask me about crypto. They're asking me about investing. They're asking me like, what do I think? I just went along with it. Like, yeah, crypto’s great. This is what I recommend. I recommend Bitcoin or Ethereum. I think XRP was actually blowing up at that time, too. I think I made a lot off XRP, actually, which — not legitly, but I used my dirty money and put it into XRP, and XRP blew up. I was telling them about that, and they were loving it. So, they were just like, okay, cool, thanks for chatting. They had no idea I was stealing it. JACK: And how were you feeling inside? RICKY: Oh, I’m nervous. I’m like, mom — that’s when I told her. Like, yo, never again. Don't tell people what I do. DEBBIE: [Music] I said to Ricky, and you let this deputy come to the house and talk to you? JACK: By 2018 the walls started closing in on Ricky. He says he has a hunch of when it all started to unravel. One night he was doing a SIM-swap, a crypto heist with some other guys online, his crew. One of the guys was a younger kid, and this younger kid was posing as an AT&T employee trying to social engineer someone into doing the SIM-swap for him. But little did this kid know, his mother was listening through the door, and she heard him trying to scam someone on the phone. That kid’s mom called the cops on her son, and that kid got arrested in Michigan. Ricky and his crew did not know this. All they knew was that kid suddenly went missing. That’s strange. But they had no idea he got arrested. But then that kid came back out of the blue and really, really, really badly wanted to get in on the action again. Ricky suspected that’s really weird that this kid got a bunch of money from a crypto heist and then disappeared for a while and now really wants back in. They kept that kid at arm’s length, but that didn't matter. Another one of Ricky’s friends was arrested shortly after, who was also present on that same call where the kid’s mom overheard them. Joel Ortiz was arrested for SIM-swapping and stealing millions of dollars in crypto from victims. He pled guilty, and a judge sentenced him to a decade behind bars. Prosecutors said that he was the first SIM-swapper to ever be sentenced to prison in the US, and after hearing about Joel’s arrest, Ricky was worried that he might be next. RICKY: I’ve known Joel. I’ve talked with him and I’ve done stuff with him and stuff where it was like, hold on, this is a huge red flag. I remember I was eating at Ford’s Garage when it happened when I found out that Joel got arrested. So, that’s what kinda raised my suspicion. I’m like, oh shit, Joel got caught. JACK: After hearing Joel went down, you would think that it would give you a spook of some kind and be like, okay, I’m gonna lay low for a couple weeks or clear some stuff or get rid of some evidence. RICKY: Yeah. JACK: But you didn't do any of that. RICKY: Um…no. JACK: Just a day after learning about Joel’s arrest, the dominoes started to fall. There are moments in our life that stand out forever. Maybe it’s when your first child is born or first kiss or playing a video game for the first time. For Ricky, that day was July 18, 2018. On that day, Ricky was still living at home with his mom, and he had broken up with his girlfriend that he had a child with, but he had a new woman and a new child with her. I think the baby was a few months old at that point. The day started just like any other day. Ricky was getting ready to go to work at the parks and recreation department, and his girlfriend left the house just before him so that she could go to work. RICKY: I used to live by a cul-de-sac area. [Music] When she went to work, she’s like, hey, there’s a lot of cops in this cul-de-sac. I was like, okay, come back. Like, that’s weird. That’s off to me. So, when she went around the block the other way, she’s like, yo, they're also on this side of the house, like on this block. I was like, alright, I’m pretty sure they're coming. I walk outside to go — just act like I’m going to work. Like, I knew at that point that they were probably coming for me. I could see them coming down the road. I was like, just try to play it off. I went to go get up in my truck, and they were like, don't go in your truck. Don't run, don't run. JACK: Ricky stayed still, standing next to his truck as officers handcuffed him. OFFICER: You wanna lean against your truck or something? RICKY: Yeah, if — whatever. I mean, just whatever. [Background talk] OFFICER: You have anything on you that might hurt us if we pat you down or whatever? Alright. Just hang tight. You understand right now you're just being detained. JACK: This is body cam audio from Ricky’s arrest by the Pasco County Sheriff’s Office. It’s the very same sheriff’s office where his mom Debbie worked as a nurse. DEBBIE: When they came here that day — and, you know, they — I guess it would be to raid the house, but they were very — doing the search warrant stuff, but they did not break down our doors. They didn't do anything. So, now I kinda get up out of my bed and I look into the kitchen area, and there’s two cops standing in the doorway. They're like, hey, Debbie. I need you to come out here. JACK: They know you? DEBBIE: Yeah, they knew my name, they knew everything. Now, yeah, I knew some of them from coming in and out of work. I think I kept saying, what is going on? What is going on? What is happening? JACK: And when they finally tell you this is what we think is going on, what was your reaction to that? DEBBIE: We have — my reaction to that was, well, isn't Bitcoin — isn't this legal? That was my first reaction; but I thought it was legal. So, I kinda looked at him and he goes, he was not — those coins and the money that he was getting, Debbie, did not belong to him. He was stealing them. That’s when I really realized like, oh, okay. So, now what? JACK: Debbie sat outside the front of the house with Ricky as deputies collected evidence. Some of Ricky’s burner phones, his iPhone, his crypto wallets, and some other SIM cards were taken. RICKY: They took my truck, they took two side-by-sides, they took a trailer I had, the trailer I haul everything. JACK: Ricky was taken away in the back of a squad car to jail. … OFFICER: I have one male adult, 1012. Nothing else is in your pockets? RICKY: No, sir. JACK: They drive off to jail. The twenty-five minute ride is mostly quiet. Ricky is alone with his thoughts, but he does ask the officer behind the wheel what to expect. RICKY: Do you know how all this all goes? Like, do I see a judge and then…? OFFICER: You’ll have advisors. RICKY: I will? Okay. OFFICER: That’ll be done by video, on chat or whatever. RICKY: That’ll be today, right? OFFICER: Should be. JACK: I can't get over how calm Ricky sounds. He had been cooking up these schemes for years to steal things from who knows how many victims, starting with a few hundred dollars in gamer tags to millions of dollars in crypto wallets, and it all came to an end here in the back of the squad car. Maybe he was feeling relief, like his big secret’s out. He doesn't have to lie to his mom anymore or try to walk quietly in the shadows of his double life. But sitting in the back of the car, you have to wonder what else is going through his head. What’s gonna happen to me, and what about my family? What about my money? But he quietly listens as the officer driving him to the jail spells out the next steps for him. OFFICER: I would think it would be this afternoon. That’s when they’ll basically just announce what you're charged with, and then whether you're gonna retain your own attorney or whether you're asking for a public defender. RICKY: Okay. OFFICER: And then — but that is — again, I don't know if you're being charged federally. RICKY: Okay. OFFICER: Which makes it different, so… RICKY: Alright, thank you sir. JACK: Ricky was booked in the county jail. His mom was so distraught, though. She didn't want to see her son in jail. What mother would? So, she went down to jail to see if she could bail him out. DEBBIE: I just — it had to be done. I wasn't leaving him in jail. JACK: Did he go to the very jail you worked at? DEBBIE: Oh yeah, he sure did. All my nursing staff, friends, they were all like, oh my god, Debbie’s son is here. What’s going on? Then the sergeant — they all knew once I posted bond for him, get him outta here. Yeah, they did do a little bit of, let’s say, courtesy. I shouldn't say courtesy, but they treated him knowing that he was my son. Like, let’s move him along. You know? JACK: Yeah, that must have been embarrassing. DEBBIE: But yeah. Yeah, a little bit embarrassing, a little bit of shocking, embarrassing. The only thing — and I wasn't actually physically working there anymore. I had just left like six months prior. But I mean, it was still fresh. I had worked there for almost ten years. JACK: They said his bail was $110,000. The cost of a bail bond is usually 10% to 15% of the total amount. Debbie ended up paying that to a bail bondsman to get him out. She didn't even hesitate. She just immediately was there for him. Prosecutors charged Ricky with grand theft and money laundering. The case against him dragged on for four years. He had to wear an ankle monitor during that whole time and follow a strict curfew. He pled guilty to federal charges of computer misconduct and conspiracy to commit wire fraud. By the time he went before a judge for sentencing, Ricky didn't know what to expect in the courtroom or how it would affect his family. His mom and fiancé were there during the sentencing. DEBBIE: It was horrible. It was I think one of the saddest days of my life. I remember standing in front of that judge. I just cried and said, look, I know my son did wrong. I know he did wrong, believe me. I can't believe he did all this, but he’s — that’s not my — that’s not the kind of kid he is. It was horrible. JACK: What did the judge say to that? DEBBIE: She was a woman, and I could almost feel her sympathy for me and getting it, but the law is the law, and I agree.
